# Mohnish Pabrai on YouTube: Ideas by Year and Topic

Source: the 125 videos on the Mohnish Pabrai YouTube channel. Transcripts came from the published PDFs on chaiwithpabrai.com, matched to each video by talk date and venue. 113 talks yielded 2384 dated ideas. 12 short clips and early presentations have no published transcript and are listed at the end.

### Cloning & learning from great investors (8)

- **Since hardly anyone followed Buffett's approach and hardly anyone had his returns, he concluded the two facts were linked and decided to replicate the approach himself.** In 1994, at age 30 with $1 million from selling part of his business, he set a 30-year game: compound at 26% (his license plate reads COMPOUND 26), doubling every three years, 2^10 = roughly 1,000x, turning $1 million into $1 billion. Even failing by 90-97% would still be fine. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2013-07-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PpBPzNoltbs)
- **Something in the human genome makes cloning attractive to maybe 1-2% of people at most, which is why nobody replicated the Buffett partnership model for 30 years.** Buffett's 1956-1969 partnership was the most successful hedge fund ever and was described in books selling millions of copies, yet he found no fund anywhere that had replicated it when he opened his in 1999. He wants his gravestone to read 'He was a cloner'. _[Buffett Partnership]_ — [2013-07-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PpBPzNoltbs)
- **Mechanically buying what Buffett buys after it is public, at the month's worst price, and selling when he sells, beat the S&P 500 by 11.5% a year from 1975 to 2005.** The study by professors at the University of Nevada and Ohio State implies about 21.5% a year versus roughly 10% for the S&P, with no business-school degree required, and yet nobody has set up a fund to do it. Almost everything Pabrai Funds owns was copied from some other great investor, filtered to what he can understand and finds undervalued, limiting him to two or three decisions a year. _[Warren Buffett, IBM]_ — [2013-07-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PpBPzNoltbs)
- **His fee structure, copied from Buffett, has zero management fees, the first 6% to investors, one-fourth of returns above that to him, with a high-water mark; if the industry adopted it the industry would disappear.** If the fund is up 10% he gets 1%; if up 5% or down he gets nothing. The fund's legal setup cost $8,000 after he handed a lawyer the book chapter describing the Buffett partnership and said 'copy this'. _[Buffett Partnership, Pabrai Investment Funds]_ — [2013-07-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PpBPzNoltbs)
- **Dakshana is a scaled clone of Anand Kumar's Super 30 in Bihar, which took 30 ultra-poor, super-smart kids a year and got 80-100% of them into the IITs for free.** Anand refused Dakshana's funding and had no interest in scaling, but strongly endorsed Pabrai copying the model on his own and offered to help. _[Anand Kumar, Super 30, Dakshana Foundation]_ — [2013-11-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QeLk7UTKxoU)
- **Be a shameless cloner: use 13F filings of about 20 great investors to cut the universe of 50,000 stocks down to a few dozen.** Buffett, Ted Weschler, Todd Combs, Seth Klarman, Longleaf and David Einhorn are his 'analysts at zero pay' who report four days a year (Feb 14, May 14, Aug 14, Nov 14). Only one stock in his portfolio is not a cloned position. _[Berkshire Hathaway, Longleaf Partners, Seth Klarman, Third Avenue, David Einhorn, Ted Weschler, Todd Combs]_ — [2013-11-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ot6pzc9ZwfU)
- **Free or near-free tools like Value Investors Club, SumZero, GuruFocus, Corner of Berkshire and Fairfax, the Manual of Ideas and EDGAR replace an analyst team.** Value Investors Club, set up by Joel Greenblatt and John Petry, curates amateur write-ups by paying $5,000 a week for the best idea; the Manual of Ideas costs about $900 a year and digests 13Fs; EDGAR Online is $10 a month. _[Value Investors Club, Joel Greenblatt, Manual of Ideas, GuruFocus, SumZero]_ — [2013-11-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ot6pzc9ZwfU)
- **Mechanically buying what Buffett bought after it was public beat the S&P by more than 11 percentage points a year over 30 years.** Two professors (Ohio State and University of Nevada) assumed the worst broker and worst prices on the last day of the month; result was roughly 20-21% a year vs 10% for the S&P. Beating indices by 3 points puts a manager in the top 0.5%, yet no student has started a 'Berkshire Clone Fund'. _[Berkshire Hathaway, Warren Buffett]_ — [2013-11-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ot6pzc9ZwfU)

### Circle of competence & checklists (10)

- **Stick within your circle of competence, act only on extreme distortions, and you need only two or three buys and two or three sells a year; you don't need to be right all the time.** He quotes John Templeton that no investor is right more than two out of three times. If you understand a business you know what it is worth; buy when the world values it far below that, sell when far above, and otherwise do nothing. _[John Templeton]_ — [2013-07-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PpBPzNoltbs)
- **Three post-2009 changes: a healthy appreciation for holding cash, a pre-investment checklist built from other great investors' mistakes, and regular conversations with one other fund manager on Munger's advice.** The checklist asks whether past mistakes would have been obvious at the time of investment; since 2009 the error rate has been almost zero with hardly any loss of capital. Until 2008 he never discussed investments with anyone; now he talks to one exceptional manager and they disagree often but it still helps. _[Charlie Munger]_ — [2013-07-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PpBPzNoltbs)
- **Munger's Peoria portfolio: owning pieces of the local McDonald's franchise, best office building, Ford dealership and similar basic assets at reasonable prices and never selling would make an investor with a tiny circle of competence extremely wealthy.** Outsiders would call it undiversified and all in one geography, but simplicity is powerful and you do not need esoteric things to do well; the same would apply in Aurangabad, Maharashtra. _[Charlie Munger, McDonald's, Ford]_ — [2013-07-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PpBPzNoltbs)
- **A one-person investment shop beats a large team because circles of competence differ and analysts create a bias for action.** Buffett, Munger and Guy Spier all operate alone; with a 10-person team you get only Cliff Notes of secondary research and end up saying no to most ideas. Pabrai had zero new ideas in the past 17 months, which a team would not have tolerated. _[Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger, Guy Spier]_ — [2013-11-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ot6pzc9ZwfU)
- **It is not the size of your circle of competence but knowing its boundaries that determines results.** John Arrillaga became a billionaire investing only in real estate within a couple of miles of Stanford; Munger's Peoria example of owning stakes in the Ford dealership, McDonald's franchise, best apartment and office building would compound spectacularly. _[John Arrillaga, Charlie Munger]_ — [2013-11-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ot6pzc9ZwfU)
- **Saying no to Apple in 2007 and Amazon in 2003 was correct even though each was a 10X or 100X, because they were outside his circle of competence.** A venture capitalist investor laid out the iPhone/app store thesis eerily accurately; Pabrai still passed because he does not do tech or rapid change. This illustrates why an analyst bringing good ideas would rightly be frustrated. _[Apple, Amazon]_ — [2013-11-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ot6pzc9ZwfU)
- **The research process is designed to get to a 'no' as quickly as possible, in escalating stages from two minutes to a few weeks.** First filter is circle of competence, second is valuation (needs to be at least 50% off intrinsic value), then 15 minutes, a few hours with filings, a few days of drill down, and finally the checklist, which mostly surfaces things he did not know. — [2013-11-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ot6pzc9ZwfU)
- **Expanding your circle of competence happens naturally through curiosity and reading; it is better to be an inch wide and a mile deep.** If you are an inch wide and 200 feet deep, put energy into going deeper before going wider. — [2013-11-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ot6pzc9ZwfU)
- **Leverage is the largest source of investment failures, so the checklist has about 25 questions on it; ideally look for large cash flows with virtually no leverage.** Whether debt is recourse or non-recourse, plant-level or corporate, and cash-flow coverage of interest all matter; being a good credit analyst is a huge advantage. — [2013-11-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ot6pzc9ZwfU)
- **The 90-odd-question checklist was built by reverse-engineering real permanent losses of respected investors, not by blue-sky thinking.** Questions cluster into leverage, moats, management/ownership and miscellaneous (unions, environment). Sources include Berkshire's Dexter Shoes, NetJets and Berkshire Mills, and Longleaf's loss on pre-bankruptcy GM where labor and capital intensity were the obvious failure points. _[Dexter Shoes, NetJets, Longleaf Partners, General Motors]_ — [2013-11-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ot6pzc9ZwfU)

### Valuation & margin of safety (5)

- **He does not invest unless there is a prospect of doubling or tripling in two to three years, and the hurdle rises as cash falls, so the last 5-10% of assets requires at least 5x.** This escalating hurdle ensures the last dollars go out only during the most distressed times and effectively forces a cash cushion; he was sitting on more than 20% cash for most of 2012 and about 10% in mid-2013. — [2013-07-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PpBPzNoltbs)
- **Look at a stock as if buying the whole company: if you would not put 70% of your family's assets into it and hold it unsellable for five to ten years, do not buy a single share.** He is not interested in the 200-rupee share price but in the INR 5,000 crore market cap; asking whether a family with INR 8,000-9,000 crores would happily own the whole company for 10 years saves a lot of trouble. _[Infosys]_ — [2013-07-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PpBPzNoltbs)
- **The absolute lowest bar is buying at half of intrinsic value; paying $13 for something worth $18-19 is an automatic pass.** If he pays $13 he wants to be convinced it will be worth at least the mid-twenties within a couple of years. Valuation is the most common reason for exclusion after circle of competence. — [2013-11-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ot6pzc9ZwfU)
- **Focus on the downside: if you spend enough time on what can go wrong, the upside takes care of itself.** He cites Buffett's rule number one, don't lose money, and notes distressed bonds at 30-50 cents on the dollar can be a safer proxy for equity when the business is only temporarily distressed. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2013-11-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ot6pzc9ZwfU)
- **A zero-growth business with utility-like stable cash flows is worth 10-14 times cash flow, and one growing 5-10% a year is worth at least 15 times.** Buying a stable no-growth business at five or six times cash flow gives good odds of a double. High variability of cash flows produces wider gyrations from intrinsic value and hence opportunity. — [2013-11-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ot6pzc9ZwfU)

### Portfolio concentration & selling (4)

- **You cannot beat the index by trying to beat the index; make few bets, big bets, infrequent bets, only when the odds are heavily in your favor.** You can be wrong a lot and still be fine; even with several investments going to zero in the 21-month drawdown the record looks fine. Focusing on cannibals (companies buying back stock), spinoffs and cloning makes things much easier. — [2013-07-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PpBPzNoltbs)
- **Write a six-or-seven-sentence thesis before buying, review metrics every three to six months, and treat a stock as a sale candidate at 90% of intrinsic value.** He knows the selling conditions before he buys; he may also swap a 75-80 cent dollar for a 40-cent dollar when he has no cash, and prefers holding at least a year for long-term gains in US funds. — [2013-11-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ot6pzc9ZwfU)
- **After losing about 67% in 2008 while fully invested, he adopted a tiered cash-cushion rule so the fund can play offense in dislocations.** First 75% of the fund can go into 2-3X ideas, next 10% needs 3X, next 5% needs 4X, last 10% needs 5X or better; a permanent 10-20% cash cushion is fine because dislocations are nearly certain. Anything bought in Q4 2008 or Q1 2009 is a 4-5X since. _[Pabrai Investment Funds]_ — [2013-11-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ot6pzc9ZwfU)
- **Position sizes come in three thresholds: 2%, 5% and 10% of assets, replacing the pre-2008 practice of 10% bets.** 2% is for asymmetric but hairy bets like Freddie and Fannie preferreds bought at 7-9% of par, or the 2008 commodity basket where every 2% position was a multi-bagger; 5% is a normal opportunity and 10% for high conviction. Four or five industries is enough diversification. _[Freddie Mac, Fannie Mae]_ — [2013-11-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ot6pzc9ZwfU)

### Compounding & long-term holding (2)

- **Compounding is the eighth wonder of the world: the chess-board rice story ends at 2^64 minus 1 grains, worth about $300 trillion, the entire net worth of the planet.** US total net worth was about $70 trillion at the time. When he discovered Buffett in 1994, Buffett had compounded at 31% a year for 44 years (1950-1993), doubling every 2.6 years, so he was already on the 18th square of the board. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2013-07-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PpBPzNoltbs)
- **His record by mid-2013: 43.4% a year from 1995-1999 personally, 37.2% gross (29.4% net) for Pabrai Funds 1999-2007, then -47.1% annualized over 21 months, then about 32.8% for 4.25 years, leaving 25.8% over 18.5 years versus the 26% goal.** The $1 million became $5.1 million by 1999. Pabrai Investment Funds launched July 1, 1999 with $1 million from eight friends plus $100,000 of his own. Unlike tennis, in investing you get better as you get older because all knowledge accumulates. _[Pabrai Investment Funds]_ — [2013-07-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PpBPzNoltbs)

### Moats & business quality (3)

- **Great businesses are often pure clones: Microsoft, Walmart and Burger King built enormous value by copying rather than innovating.** Most of Microsoft's revenue comes from cloned products (Windows, Word from WordPerfect, Excel from Lotus, SQL Server from Oracle). Walmart copied Kmart and Sears for its first 20 years and Sam Walton would be worth about $150 billion today. Burger King has two people picking sites who simply follow McDonald's studies. India does not need Walmart to come in; an entrepreneur just needs to replicate the model. _[Microsoft, Walmart, Kmart, Sears, Burger King, McDonald's]_ — [2013-07-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PpBPzNoltbs)
- **Cloning does not conflict with moats; Buffett himself has made dozens of non-moat investments, and you can do extremely well in a shallow-moat business if you pay next to nothing for it.** Example: Buffett bought the debt of Finova Capital, a bankrupt subprime lender, to participate in the restructuring, and did many arbitrage deals in the 1950s and 60s. Given his current size he now goes mostly moat-based. The ideal is a great moat at a great or fair price, but there are many ways to skin the investing cat. _[Finova Capital, Warren Buffett]_ — [2013-07-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PpBPzNoltbs)
- **Commodity businesses can have moats as durable as Coca-Cola or Geico if they are first-quartile low-cost producers.** A zinc mine producing at 40-50 cents a pound makes money in any economy while high-cost mines are mothballed. In late 2008 he bought first-quartile producers like Teck Cominco at $4-5 (down from $50 in four months) and it went back to $40-50. _[Teck Cominco, Coca-Cola, Geico]_ — [2013-11-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ot6pzc9ZwfU)

### Markets, cycles & macro (2)

- **Stock markets are auction-driven with faceless buyers and sellers, so they systematically produce 50-100% price swings within a year while the underlying business barely changes.** GM ranged from $18 to over $36 in 52 weeks and Infosys from about 2,200 to 2,800 rupees, whereas a used car or a private-company sale moves 5-10% because an intelligent buyer faces an intelligent seller. Without the stock market Buffett could not have achieved his record. Obscure companies (a jute producer in Calcutta) swing even more, and the entire shareholder base turns over every six months to two years. _[General Motors, Infosys, Facebook, Tata Motors]_ — [2013-07-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PpBPzNoltbs)
- **For the most part ignore macro; micro trumps macro because 90% of a business's eventual results come from what happens inside it.** Fed tapering, the European crisis and exchange rates are irrelevant to the cash flow of the 24-hour drive-thru McDonald's near his home in Irvine. If that McDonald's produced $400,000 a year and sold for $5 million (12x cash flow), the questions are how long the cash flow lasts and what could reduce it. _[McDonald's]_ — [2013-07-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PpBPzNoltbs)

### Stock case studies (2)

- **General Motors became a position only after both Berkshire and David Einhorn showed it as a top holding, prompting a multi-week drill down.** He initially rejected GM (high capex, unions, consumer tastes) when it appeared in Berkshire's Q1 2012 13F, then read a dozen books including Rattner's Overhaul and Sloan's My Years at GM; the position is up 100-120% and he bought cheaper than Weschler did. _[General Motors, Berkshire Hathaway, David Einhorn, Steve Rattner]_ — [2013-11-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ot6pzc9ZwfU)
- **Horsehead Holdings (ticker ZINC) is a free option: cash flow of $130-170 million on a $700 million market cap even at low zinc prices, with $25 million more per 10-cent rise in zinc.** Zinc is at 85 cents a pound versus a historic 50 cents to $2 range; the thesis does not depend on zinc rising, but a move to $1.30-2.00 would be a large upside. The position is about five years old. _[Horsehead Holdings]_ — [2013-11-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ot6pzc9ZwfU)

### Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US (1)

- **He does not invest in India because his armchair, never-meet-management style would get his head handed to him there; Indian investing requires being local and handicapping management like private equity or venture capital.** In the US he can say the probability of losing money to fraud is near zero (no case in 18 years, losses were from his own stupidity) because businesses and managements have long histories; in India he could not. If investing in India he would want a structure allowing public, private and real estate and would focus on businesses that could 10x or 20x in five to ten years. He recommends tracking Chetan Parikh and Amitabh Singhi. _[Chetan Parikh, Amitabh Singhi]_ — [2013-07-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PpBPzNoltbs)

### Psychology & temperament (3)

- **Envy and ego are the most destructive human traits; eliminate them and you are far along the path of doing well.** He uses Rajat Gupta's downfall as a Shakespearean lesson: off-the-chart success undone by envy of someone richer but less capable. Ego is 'a false sense of self; we came from ashes and dust'. He returns to it later citing Munger on the Ten Commandments and covetousness. _[Rajat Gupta]_ — [2013-07-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PpBPzNoltbs)
- **Patience is the number one skill for beating the market; there is never a need for rapid response and two or three ideas a year is enough.** GM became cheaper while he researched it for three to four weeks, so he bought at lower prices than Berkshire originally paid. _[General Motors]_ — [2013-11-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ot6pzc9ZwfU)
- **Shorting is a stupid bet: maximum upside is a double, maximum downside is bankruptcy, and it chains you to a quote machine.** Buffett and Munger say they were almost always wrong on timing of short candidates; ridiculous prices like Twitter's can get more ridiculous, and every CEO goes to work to add value against you. _[Twitter, Bill Ackman]_ — [2013-11-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ot6pzc9ZwfU)

### Buffett & Munger lessons (1)

- **Buffett spends nearly all his time on how he could lose money, not how much he could make, just as he walked with bent knees as a child to avoid falling.** From Alice Schroeder's biography 'The Snowball'; the downside focus is what Pabrai says he has developed a much greater appreciation for since 2007-2009. _[Warren Buffett, Alice Schroeder]_ — [2013-07-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PpBPzNoltbs)

### Mistakes & lessons learned (3)

- **2008-09 went wrong because of hubris after eight years without a down year, missing the housing bubble entirely, and owning businesses dependent on a functioning financial system while fully invested with no cash.** Delta Financial went from a $65 million position to zero and another position lost almost $40 million. Redemptions forced him to sell solid businesses at pennies on the dollar, compounding the damage. We learn nothing from success; every stumble in his life has led to growth. _[Delta Financial]_ — [2013-07-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PpBPzNoltbs)
- **Investors can have a healthy error rate and still do very well; Templeton says being right two out of three times hits the ball out of the park.** When analyzing mistakes, ask whether the failure point was obvious front and center before the investment, not something obscure. _[John Templeton]_ — [2013-11-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ot6pzc9ZwfU)
- **His original, non-cloned Japanese net-net basket returned only about 2.5% and reinforced that his own ideas 'all suck royally'.** Per Graham, net-nets are not the ideal buy when whole markets are cheap; the Japanese market rallied from multi-decade lows but the net-nets did not, whereas a basket of Japanese blue chips would have done fantastically. Baskets are anomalies; he prefers picking the best business in an industry. _[Ben Graham]_ — [2013-11-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ot6pzc9ZwfU)

### Career, entrepreneurship & life (10)

- **The secret to becoming wealthy: a week has 168 hours, a job takes 40-50, so use the remaining 30-40 hours for a single-minded pursuit of a second business while someone else pays the paycheck.** At 24 he worked on his business 7:00-8:30 am, 6 pm to midnight and all weekend, taking vacation days for client meetings and deliberately doing just enough not to be fired. It took 10 months to land the first client and two more weeks for the second; his bosses offered a higher salary if the business failed. If a venture fails, start another; something will hit. That business became TransTech, later left to start Pabrai Funds. _[TransTech]_ — [2013-07-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PpBPzNoltbs)
- **When you start a business you do not need all the answers or money, only passion, drive and a few answers, while keeping the risk small.** Dakshana did not know how to find scholars, so he hired a 64-year-old IIT Madras grad consultant at 5,000 rupees a day (500 an hour) to research; after three people mentioned JNV schools the model was found. Three lakh rupees of research at risk was no problem. Sam Walton likewise kept learning as he went. _[Dakshana, Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalaya, Sam Walton]_ — [2013-07-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PpBPzNoltbs)
- **Humans are driven by peers, so Indians need to know the stories of Indian entrepreneurs like Vinod Khosla, Bharat Desai, Prem Watsa and every Patel motel owner, not just Gates, Jobs and Walton, because their path creates the path for us.** He credits TiE with lighting that path 'with a million floodlights' by bringing these stories to the community. _[Vinod Khosla, Sabeer Bhatia, Desh Deshpande, Kanwal Rekhi, Bharat Desai, Prem Watsa, TiE]_ — [2013-11-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QeLk7UTKxoU)
- **Venture-backed startups are less than 0.1% of the million-plus new US businesses each year, an anomaly that can safely be ignored; you do not need money or VCs to get a business off the ground.** Most of the successful entrepreneurs he named never wrote a formal business plan or chased venture capitalists. — [2013-11-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QeLk7UTKxoU)
- **The secret is to keep your full-time job and use the other 40-50 hours in a 168-hour week to build your startup as a second job, so there is no pressure and the rent stays current.** In 1990 at age 25 with no money he worked one or two hours before work and until midnight after, plus weekends, eating a Subway sandwich every night; after 10 months he had two clients and resigned. The fatal mistake is to quit, live off savings and chase VCs. _[TransTech]_ — [2013-11-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QeLk7UTKxoU)
- **His two venture capitalists were Visa and MasterCard, which backed him with $70,000, took no board seats, gave no advice and took no equity.** A year after quitting he replaced the credit cards with a low-cost bank line of credit, and four years later the company was recognized as an Inc 500 fastest-growing business. His old boss offered him his job back at higher pay if the business failed. _[Visa, MasterCard]_ — [2013-11-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QeLk7UTKxoU)
- **The Dakshana journey has added a dimension to his life he clings to, and he is gradually giving up baggage about creature comforts like one-star hotels, mosquitoes and dirty toilets in rural India.** On his first 2007 trip to Bihar, then the 'kidnapping capital of India', he took two armed guards. The discomforts still bother him but less than six years earlier; the journey is the destination. _[Dakshana Foundation]_ — [2013-11-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QeLk7UTKxoU)
- **If you are procrastinating on a startup, get going, and along the way help a few less fortunate humans; you can't change the world but you can change it for one, ten or a few thousand people.** He closes with Robert Frost's road less travelled and recommends the book 'The Billionaire's Apprentice' as one of the best he read that year. _[The Billionaire's Apprentice]_ — [2013-11-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QeLk7UTKxoU)
- **Students should start an auditable track record now with a real-money brokerage account traded like a $100 million portfolio, then raise money from friends, family and fools.** After three to seven years the data will show whether you are meaningfully better than most investors; if you outperform by 3-5%, investors will swim to you in shark-infested waters. — [2013-11-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ot6pzc9ZwfU)
- **The human brain is optimized to specialize between ages 13 and 19, and his teenage years helping his serially-bankrupt entrepreneur father were his most important training.** Buffett bought his first stock at 11 and Gates logged 15,000 programming hours by 19-20; Germany's tracking of kids into vocational work at 12-13 explains its manufacturing strength. US schools should let clearly directed teens specialize. _[Warren Buffett, Bill Gates]_ — [2013-11-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ot6pzc9ZwfU)

### Philanthropy & Dakshana (8)

- **Dakshana itself is a clone of Anand Kumar's Super 30 model, adopted with his blessing.** He says he is 'too stupid' to have invented a model as good as Dakshana's; he asked Anand Kumar if he minded it being cloned and Kumar offered to help. _[Dakshana, Super 30, Anand Kumar]_ — [2013-07-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PpBPzNoltbs)
- **Philanthropy is the same as investing: figure out which endeavor delivers the highest social return and put everything into it rather than sprinkling money across causes.** His father said 'we come to this world naked and leave it naked', so surplus assets should be recycled to society, per Buffett's influence. Education for poverty alleviation has a huge multiplier, and Dakshana's partnership with the Government of India (JNV schools) means the government does the heavy lifting and Dakshana's ROI is off the charts. _[Dakshana, Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalaya]_ — [2013-07-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PpBPzNoltbs)
- **Dakshana produces single-generation transformations: a tailor's son from Gachibowli scored India rank 63 in the 2010 IIT entrance exam out of half a million takers.** Ashok Kumar was selected in 10th grade at a JNV, coached for two years, studied computer science at IIT Bombay and interned at Microsoft; the family home had only two chairs when Pabrai visited. _[Dakshana, IIT Bombay, Microsoft]_ — [2013-07-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PpBPzNoltbs)
- **Passing on a large inheritance is a burden, not a gift, so the only logical thing to do with wealth beyond what you can consume is to efficiently recycle it back to society.** Cites Buffett: give kids enough to do anything they want but not enough to do nothing. His children had zero interest in the money, and because he compounds money for a living the numbers would only grow. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2013-11-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QeLk7UTKxoU)
- **Most charities are all heart and no head, run by people who have never met a payroll; non-profits should be run by businessmen with great hearts and narrowed to one or two causes with the highest social return on invested capital.** Reading many charity annual reports he found not one discussed failures or lessons learned; they were marketing machines focused on maximizing dollars, doing good work inefficiently. There is no difference between running a for-profit and a non-profit. — [2013-11-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QeLk7UTKxoU)
- **When net worth crossed $50 million in 2007, he and Harina committed 2% of net worth every year, at least $1 million, to the Dakshana Foundation to test these ideas in the real world.** The focus chosen was education toward the alleviation of poverty: teach fishing rather than give fish, then decide what kind of fishermen to create. _[Dakshana Foundation]_ — [2013-11-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QeLk7UTKxoU)
- **From a standing start in 2007, Dakshana sent 457 impoverished kids to the IITs out of 1,033 taken on, a 44% acceptance rate against the IITs' typical 2%.** Most parents were illiterate manual laborers or marginal farmers. Dakshana took 434 new scholars in 2013, hoped for 1,000 the next year, and had a stretch goal of sending 2,020 kids to the IITs in 2020, which would make one in seven IIT students the child of a poor farmer or laborer. _[Dakshana Foundation]_ — [2013-11-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QeLk7UTKxoU)
- **Dakshana deliberately rejects hires with non-profit or education-sector experience because they carry stupid ideas that take a long time to deprogram; a blank slate works better.** None of his senior management had ever worked at a non-profit or in education. _[Dakshana Foundation]_ — [2013-11-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QeLk7UTKxoU)

### Cloning & learning from great investors (8)

- **Tom Peters was right: you can lay out all your trade secrets to competitors and they will not change their behavior, which is why cloning is so powerful and so rare.** Peters' story of the self-serve gas station owner who gave random free full-service and took business from a rival who never adapted; Pabrai tested it by explaining everything to employees leaving TransTech to compete with him, and not one followed any of it. _[Tom Peters, TransTech]_ — [2014-02-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fkF9Npxfmn8)
- **Cloning is an exercise in humility, admitting everyone else is smarter than you, and my entire livelihood is based on it: Pabrai Funds was cloned from the Buffett Partnerships.** From 1969 when Buffett closed his partnership to 1999 nobody had cloned the most successful hedge fund model in history, so he did and his family's net worth is significantly higher for it; he is now buying an insurance company because that is the Berkshire Hathaway model. _[Buffett Partnership, Pabrai Investment Funds, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2014-02-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fkF9Npxfmn8)
- **Cloners are not doomed to trail: Microsoft, Walmart and Pepsi are clone businesses, and when you clone you add your own nuance, which becomes the advantage.** Word cloned WordPerfect, Excel cloned Lotus, Bing clones Google, and Microsoft needs 5-7 versions to get it right yet built a great business; Sam Walton copied Sears for 20 years with no new ideas except small towns and extreme cost discipline (four to a hotel room, coach only). Pabrai Funds cloned Buffett but is different when you drill down. _[Microsoft, Walmart, Sam Walton, Sears, Kmart, Pepsi, Coca-Cola]_ — [2014-02-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fkF9Npxfmn8)
- **Match investing approach to ability: an 80 IQ should dollar-cost-average into the S&P 500, a 90 IQ into Berkshire Hathaway, and a 100 IQ can simply copy Buffett's disclosed trades.** A 30-year study (1976-2006) by professors at Ohio State and Nevada found that buying Buffett's picks at the month-end high after public disclosure and selling at the month-end low when he sold returned 21.5% annualized, beating the S&P by 11.5 points a year, with 15 minutes of work a month. Beating the index by 3 points makes you one in 200. _[Warren Buffett, Berkshire Hathaway, S&P 500, IBM]_ — [2014-02-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fkF9Npxfmn8)
- **Always bowl with bumpers: almost my entire portfolio is stock picks cloned from other great investors, and I have no original ideas.** What matters is the score, not whether you used bumpers; he looks at what a smart investor did, checks whether he understands it, buys the same thing and gets paid for it. He notes a new cloning ETF had just launched. _[Pabrai Investment Funds]_ — [2014-02-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fkF9Npxfmn8)
- **Cloning the Buffett partnership structure (no management fee, performance fee only, annual reporting, no holdings disclosure) is itself a competitive advantage because almost nobody else does it.** He started Pabrai Funds in 1999, 30 years after Buffett closed his partnership, and found no one had replicated the structure; 15 years later the share of funds using it is still a rounding error, less than 1%. _[Pabrai Investment Funds, Buffett partnerships]_ — [2014-10-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i6fWxvsW6Nk)
- **Cloning 13Fs is like bowling with bumpers: focus on the top three to five positions of great investors, because those ideas have already passed through a good filter.** Looking only at the top five positions of Einhorn, Ackman, Icahn, Buffett and Klarman gives a pond of under 100 stocks a year, and the 30th position of a manager is not going to help you much. _[David Einhorn, Bill Ackman, Carl Icahn, Warren Buffett, Seth Klarman, Dataroma]_ — [2014-10-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i6fWxvsW6Nk)
- **Pabrai Investment Funds is a straight clone of the Buffett Partnership model, which no large hedge fund had copied in the 30 years after Buffett closed it in 1969.** No management fees, long-term focus, long-term investors, and few, big, infrequent bets; humans have a peculiar aversion to copying, which is a significant advantage for those who do. _[Buffett Partnership, Pabrai Investment Funds]_ — [2014-12-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JSHVXBBb9bI)

### Circle of competence & checklists (2)

- **When looking at a stock, look for a reason to say no as fast as possible: first is it in the circle of competence, second is it super cheap, then spend 30 minutes hunting for a showstopper before going deeper.** There are 25-50,000 stocks worldwide and a serious look takes weeks, so you could cover at most 50 a year; you need shortcuts that eliminate most of the universe quickly. — [2014-10-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i6fWxvsW6Nk)
- **If you are questioning whether something is in your circle of competence, it is not; operate dead center of the circle, not near the edges.** John Arrillaga only buys real estate within two miles of Stanford and can answer the competence question in three seconds; Pabrai will not invest unless he can nail the thesis in three sentences. The circle grows by osmosis over a lifetime, especially each time you lose money, so focus on staying inside it rather than expanding it. _[John Arrillaga]_ — [2014-10-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i6fWxvsW6Nk)

### Valuation & margin of safety (4)

- **The target is close to a 100% probability of at least 2x in two years with near-zero chance of anything else; the probability of a permanent loss of capital should be under 1%.** He dismisses his own book's probability framing as 'stupid': losing 0-30% should be under 1% probability, losing more than 30% should approach zero, returns between 1x and 2x under 10%, and above 2x the rest. _[The Dhandho Investor]_ — [2014-10-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i6fWxvsW6Nk)
- **In private deals with intelligent sellers you should expect to pay a full price, but small growing private businesses can still return 5-10x in five to seven years, unlike sub-$50 million public 'zombie' companies burdened by public-company overhead.** Low interest rates depress insurance company valuations, making it a good time to hunt; Dhandho can add value by improving the investment portfolio of an insurer that sits entirely in fixed income. _[Dhandho Holdings]_ — [2014-10-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i6fWxvsW6Nk)
- **For a cheap, growing business you do not need to agonize over the exit multiple; if earnings compound as expected, any reasonable multiple gives a great result.** Using a student's Jammu and Kashmir Bank at 6x earnings and near 1x book: a well-run Indian bank should grow at about 2x GDP, roughly 15% a year, so $100 million of earnings becomes $200 million in five years and a 10x, 15x or 20x multiple gives $2-4 billion versus a $600 million market cap; the real risk is only the loan book. _[Jammu and Kashmir Bank, HDFC Bank, ICICI Bank]_ — [2014-10-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i6fWxvsW6Nk)
- **Because value investors buy after screening for cheapness, they naturally catch stocks at the low end of their swing range, which alone can deliver 50-60% gains even when the thesis was wrong.** He has seen this in his own portfolio: investments where he was wrong in hindsight still made decent gains simply from buying at a low point and the natural ebb and flow of the stock. — [2014-12-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JSHVXBBb9bI)

### Portfolio concentration & selling (2)

- **Berkshire is a reasonable holding near Buffett's buyback floor of 1.2x book, but with small capital you ought to find things that do better than Berkshire, Fairfax or Leucadia.** Allan Mecham of Arlington held over 50% in Berkshire and levered it against the buyback floor, but Pabrai notes Buffett would not defend the floor in a 2009-type scenario, recalling Rick Guerin; Fairfax targets 15% long-term returns and Leucadia must be re-handicapped now that the founders are gone. _[Berkshire Hathaway, Fairfax Financial, Leucadia, Allan Mecham, Arlington Value]_ — [2014-10-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i6fWxvsW6Nk)
- **Selling is harder than buying; write a simple paragraph on intrinsic value before buying, look to sell at about 90% of intrinsic value, and update the estimate every three to six months.** Approach every stock as if buying the entire business: with Apple at a $700 billion market cap, ask whether a family with $1.5 trillion would buy the whole company at that price. _[Apple, Benjamin Graham]_ — [2014-12-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JSHVXBBb9bI)

### Compounding & long-term holding (3)

- **The number one skill in investing is extreme patience; the Fidelity accounts that performed best were those whose owners had forgotten they existed.** Real business change happens over years, not days or weeks; he admits only one stock in his portfolio is more than three years old and that his portfolio would do incredibly well if he simply went away for 10 years. _[Fidelity]_ — [2014-10-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i6fWxvsW6Nk)
- **Cost basis is irrelevant; hold a blue chip only on a view of the future, by asking how and when its market cap doubles or triples from here.** Hero MotoCorp returned 45-50x (maybe 100x with dividends) over 20 years, but with a 60,000 crore market cap the question is how it gets to 120,000 or 200,000 crores; India's lack of capital gains tax makes holding compounders a beautiful place to be. _[Hero MotoCorp, Hero Honda, ITC]_ — [2014-12-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JSHVXBBb9bI)
- **It is very hard to make up lost years: sitting in cash for years waiting for a perfect 20-year moat destroys the annualized return even if the eventual investment compounds at 20%.** One lakh sitting idle from 2014 to 2020, then quadrupling by 2027, is only about 11% a year over 13 years; think in terms of opportunity cost and the best available option today. — [2014-12-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JSHVXBBb9bI)

### Moats & business quality (4)

- **In any market three or four players control 80%, so if your plan is to take 2-10% of a market you have not segmented it properly; don't start unless you have a clear plan to win 50-60% share.** Inverting Davidow's law, as Munger advises, the '$10 billion market, I just need 10%' pitch is a fatal flaw; either the segmentation is wrong or the offering isn't compelling. _[William Davidow, Charlie Munger]_ — [2014-02-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fkF9Npxfmn8)
- **A business whose primary objective is making money is myopic and unsustainable; core principles that are good for the ecosystem produce profit as a byproduct.** Costco caps gross margin at 15% on any product; raising it to 20-25% would boost near-term profit but violate member trust and hurt the long run. Businesses that ignore employee and client wellbeing do not do well long term. _[Costco]_ — [2014-06-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DzOEp7GRwAU)
- **Recurring revenue is a concept you cannot give enough weight to; a bank keeps its customers for decades while a retailer must win each purchase anew.** Banking relationships stay forever whereas retail stickiness, once in decline as at Sears, is almost impossible to reverse; Amazon is an example of a retailer with real stickiness. _[Jammu and Kashmir Bank, Amazon, Sears]_ — [2014-10-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i6fWxvsW6Nk)
- **Moats are elusive and can evaporate, so it is very hard to be confident any business, even Unilever, P&G or Hero Honda, will hold its moat for 20 years.** Walmart and Costco have significantly eroded P&G's pricing power in the US; waiting 10 years to buy a 20-year moat requires being right for 30 years. _[Procter & Gamble, Unilever, Walmart, Costco, Hero Honda, Nestle]_ — [2014-12-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JSHVXBBb9bI)

### Management & capital allocation (2)

- **A great operator can make a fully priced business not fully priced; the 3G team can squeeze blood out of a rock.** If you understand what 3G did at Burger King and AB InBev and is likely to do at Kraft and Tim Hortons, you can assume they will extract more margin than historical levels even with a stagnant top line. _[3G Capital, Burger King, AB InBev, Kraft, Tim Hortons]_ — [2014-10-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i6fWxvsW6Nk)
- **Replicating Berkshire inside an insurer requires two very rare skills: identifying a talented investment manager, and then leaving that person completely alone.** Buffett disagreed with about 90% of Lou Simpson's monthly trade reports but never once called him about it; most insurance boards could not recognize a Lou Simpson standing in front of them, and going to a team yields an institutional average at best. _[Lou Simpson, Berkshire Hathaway, Warren Buffett, GEICO]_ — [2014-12-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JSHVXBBb9bI)

### Markets, cycles & macro (3)

- **Negotiated markets between intelligent buyers and sellers of productive assets, like Iowa farmland, produce smooth, rational prices; stock markets are auction-driven and therefore swing wildly, which is the value investor's opportunity.** Iowa farmland went from about $5,000/acre in 2010 to $8,700 in 2013 with rents at 3-6.5% of value and barely moving year to year, whereas randomly picked stocks (Park Electrochemical, Premier Gold Mines, a Singapore nano-cap) showed 68% to 5x swings in 52-week ranges. _[Park Electrochemical, Premier Gold Mines, Communication Design International]_ — [2014-10-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i6fWxvsW6Nk)
- **A whole-market selloff marks down businesses whose value did not change at all, which a private seller would never accept.** Service Corp, the funeral-services company, fell 2% on a day the Dow dropped 300 points and fell sharply in 2008-09 even though human mortality did not change; a private funeral home seller would tell a buyer demanding a 2% cut to take a hike. _[Service Corp International]_ — [2014-10-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i6fWxvsW6Nk)
- **Stock markets are auction-driven, not negotiated transactions between intelligent buyers and sellers like Iowa farmland, so prices swing 50-100% a year on emotion and that volatility is the value investor's edge.** Iowa farmland sold for about $2,100 an acre in 1980 and was still there 25 years later, under $9,000 in 2013 (versus a million dollars an acre in Gurgaon), with rents of $200-250 an acre; random BSE stocks he pulled up showed 60-100% 52-week ranges. _[Iowa farmland, IFCI]_ — [2014-12-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JSHVXBBb9bI)

### Stock case studies (1)

- **'Unknown upside without downside' is a powerful mental model because markets are very bad at pricing uncertainty.** His fund's first investment in 1999 was Silicon Valley Bank, a conservatively run bank at a small premium to book that held an undisclosed basket of warrants in dot-com startups; the stock doubled quickly and he exited. Earlier, in 1995, he made 100x on CMGI bought at a small premium to cash, though in hindsight he should have sold at 5x. _[Silicon Valley Bank, CMGI, Pets.com]_ — [2014-10-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i6fWxvsW6Nk)

### Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US (3)

- **Ignore currencies and do not hedge; if the business thesis works out, currency moves should not matter much, and closer to home you understand more.** Hedging is expensive and he has no view on currencies; going global carries risks locals would spot, but no-brainers abroad are still worth pursuing. In late 2014 he found little to buy in the US and his current idea was outside the US. — [2014-10-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i6fWxvsW6Nk)
- **In India, the best investments are not quantitatively cheap stocks but relatively small businesses with long runways, high returns on capital and good management that could be worth 10-30x in five to ten years.** Investing in India is more like private equity: you must do far more work understanding management and ownership; buying and selling is fine as long as it is done in the mindset of owning the whole business. — [2014-12-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JSHVXBBb9bI)
- **Indian markets are mostly outside his circle of competence because he is not on the ground, but Modi's arrival created a chance for the government to get out of the way and produce GDP and profit tailwinds.** After 67 years of socialist or half-capitalist leaders, he made a few bets with muted downside, mostly in banking, since banks grow at a multiple of GDP. _[Narendra Modi, Indian banks]_ — [2014-12-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JSHVXBBb9bI)

### Psychology & temperament (8)

- **Don't try to sell something you wouldn't buy yourself, and never put lipstick on a pig, because customers' subconscious sees through lies.** From Munger's rule and David Hawkins' Power vs. Force: a lie is detected subconsciously even if not consciously, which is why P&G will never market a claim that isn't true and a genuine improvement, and why 40,000 people flock to Omaha for Buffett's truthful 'attractor field'. _[Procter & Gamble, David Hawkins, Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger]_ — [2014-02-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fkF9Npxfmn8)
- **Cialdini's reciprocation bias is uncalibrated, so a $50 Cross pen mailed with every Pabrai Funds package creates goodwill and obligation that can be repaid with a million-dollar wire.** Like the Moonies' airport flower but with a 100% acceptance rate; fewer than 1 in 200 return the pen, and even non-investors feel good about him. Humans evolved to store meat in neighbors' bellies and remember favors without calibrating their size. _[Robert Cialdini, Pabrai Investment Funds]_ — [2014-02-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fkF9Npxfmn8)
- **Always choose truth over diplomacy even when it causes near-term pain, because trust compounds and small lies erode it.** Drawing on David Hawkins' 'Power vs. Force', he told investors candidly in 2008 that the fund's 67% drop was partly his own mistakes, not just the crisis, and redemptions were benign because investors trusted him; Buffett likewise starts annual reports with mistakes and tells managers 'give me the bad news first'. _[David Hawkins, Warren Buffett]_ — [2014-10-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i6fWxvsW6Nk)
- **Design your environment to discourage activity: no Bloomberg, no team, trades after hours, no discussion of current positions with investors, and many non-investing pursuits.** Discussing positions publicly creates commitment and consistency bias that makes it hard to sell when wrong; he plays bridge 4-5 hours a week, racquetball and biking, and only acts when an idea is a total no-brainer. _[Guy Spier]_ — [2014-10-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i6fWxvsW6Nk)
- **The best investment is a company that is very cheap, has good growth prospects and generates high returns on capital, and the temperament required is to do nothing daily and act only when no spreadsheet is required.** Jammu and Kashmir Bank is cheap because it is 53% state-owned in a militarized region hit by Srinagar floods, yet India issues almost no new bank licenses and Modi wants to bank the unbanked half of the country; he tells the student not to sell before October 8, 2024. _[Jammu and Kashmir Bank]_ — [2014-10-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i6fWxvsW6Nk)
- **The two-year rule: he is an unwilling seller of a stock at a loss until at least two years have passed since purchase, unless intrinsic value is clearly below the price.** Most things he buys proceed to decline immediately after purchase; the rule is a circuit breaker against taking instruction from the market and shakes out market-driven psychology. — [2014-12-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JSHVXBBb9bI)
- **Having a trusted sounding board with no vested interest is a huge advantage, and he no longer moves on any idea without at least one such conversation.** Munger says he always had someone to talk to and that even Einstein needed one; when Guy Spier said he added nothing, Charlie replied that articulating an idea to another person exposes flaws, and it would not work with a monkey because Mohnish would know it is a monkey. _[Guy Spier, Charlie Munger, Daily Journal]_ — [2014-12-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JSHVXBBb9bI)
- **He will not discuss current holdings until they are sold, because publicly stating a view makes it harder to change your mind when the evidence turns.** Asked about J&K Bank and South Indian Bank, he declined, citing Buffett and Munger's practice and saying he would rather look stupid later than commit publicly. _[J&K Bank, South Indian Bank]_ — [2014-12-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JSHVXBBb9bI)

### Buffett & Munger lessons (6)

- **Live by an inner scorecard, not an outer one: do what you believe is right regardless of whether the world agrees.** At his 2008 charity lunch, which he treated as gurudakshana to thank Buffett for all the cloning, Buffett's first point was the inner scorecard: would you rather be the best lover in the world but known as the worst, or the reverse? Buffett doesn't care what the world thinks, as his unconventional personal arrangements showed. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2014-02-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fkF9Npxfmn8)
- **Owning Berkshire Hathaway is a great, simple choice with no taxes until you sell; I hold one share now but have held significant amounts when it was cheaper.** He keeps one share to stay eligible for the annual meeting and buys more when it gets cheap. _[Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2014-02-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fkF9Npxfmn8)
- **His philanthropy came from overdosing on Buffett, not from his parents, and business people have a huge amount to add to philanthropy.** Most people do not realize they are on a treadmill and their choices narrow by 70 or 80; the paybacks from taking the leap are much better than making more money. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2014-06-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DzOEp7GRwAU)
- **Buffett's inner scorecard means marching to your own drummer and not caring what the world thinks, which is essential because value investments are usually cheap for a reason many people believe and require contrarian conviction.** At their lunch Buffett asked whether you would rather be the world's best lover but known as the worst, or the worst but known as the best; Pabrai exit-interviewed everyone afterwards and counted about 54 topics covered over three hours. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2014-10-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i6fWxvsW6Nk)
- **Rick Guerin's story shows that leverage and being in a hurry can wipe out even a brilliant investor; if you are slightly above average and spend less than you earn you cannot help but get wealthy over a lifetime.** Guerin was levered into the 1973-74 crash, got margin calls and had to sell his Berkshire shares to Buffett at about $40; Buffett said 'Charlie and I always knew we were going to get very rich, but we weren't in a hurry. Rick was in a hurry.' _[Rick Guerin, Berkshire Hathaway, Blue Chip Stamps]_ — [2014-10-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i6fWxvsW6Nk)
- **Value investing's biggest personal impact was leading him to Buffett and Munger as people, whose non-investing values, including the fallacy of large inheritances, shaped his life and made Dakshana possible.** Both men do not care about the money they make beyond keeping score; emulating their non-investing qualities can only improve your life, and his kids are not interested in large inheritances either. _[Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger, Dakshana Foundation]_ — [2014-12-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JSHVXBBb9bI)

### Mistakes & lessons learned (1)

- **Stay away from businesses in secular decline; owning them has attributes similar to shorting, and Buffett knows of zero successful retailer turnarounds.** He lost money on Sears and learned that Eddie Lampert is a first-rate investor but a third-rate retailer; the people who shop at Sears are dying and no one born today will shop there, whereas Buffett's batting average is near perfect on banks and media but horrible on retailers. _[Sears, Eddie Lampert, Nebraska Furniture Mart, Warren Buffett]_ — [2014-10-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i6fWxvsW6Nk)

### Career, entrepreneurship & life (16)

- **Entrepreneurship is what makes the wheel turn; Munger says Costco has done more good for the world than the Rockefeller Foundation.** Jobs, growth and social good all start with an entrepreneur dreaming an impossible dream, which is why he respects TiE's mission. _[Costco, Charlie Munger, Rockefeller Foundation]_ — [2014-02-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fkF9Npxfmn8)
- **Marketing is an exact science with laws like physics; ignore them and, like gravity, they will still bite you.** He learned this in the mid-1980s from William Davidow's Marketing High Technology (Davidow ran R&D then marketing at Intel) and the Miller-Heiman books Strategic Selling, Conceptual Selling and Successful Large Account Management; 90-95% of entrepreneurs don't know the rules and predictably hit a brick wall. _[William Davidow, Intel, Miller-Heiman]_ — [2014-02-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fkF9Npxfmn8)
- **The stronger the marketing, the weaker the sales engine can be; do the marketing homework and even a leper can make sales.** He considers himself a poor salesman and a strong marketer; skimping on marketing means spending 50x the time banging your head on the sales end. He raised ~$150 million in about six weeks for an insurance company purchase without leaving Irvine and it oversubscribed. — [2014-02-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fkF9Npxfmn8)
- **Your initial idea is probably 10-70% right, so in the early days pay close attention to customer feedback; what works is usually a tangent, not what you came up with.** InstallShield's founder Viresh pitched seven tools at a trade show and the eighth afterthought bullet, a software installer that didn't yet exist, was the one lead that became the company. Pabrai noticed 50% of his new fund's investors were Indians (2% of the US population), a signal a good marketer would hone the next message around. _[InstallShield]_ — [2014-02-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fkF9Npxfmn8)
- **Most Inc. 500 entrepreneurs started as arbitrage players with non-enduring advantages, staying a few months ahead of competitors until they found something scalable.** Amar Bhide's The Origin and Evolution of New Businesses documents this; the CompuLink founder made non-standard cable lengths on consignment for Florida computer stores, earned supernormal profits for months until branded makers caught up, kept hopping ahead, and eventually built an 1,800-person cable installation services business. _[Amar Bhide, CompuLink, Inc. 500]_ — [2014-02-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fkF9Npxfmn8)
- **Make your startup look larger: I carried a 'Vice President Marketing' card at TransTech rather than 'President and CEO' when pitching Fortune 500 clients, and Bhide found half of successful founders did the same.** Founders independently added 'international' or 'global' to company names; reading the book's list of what worked lets a new entrepreneur incorporate proven tactics. _[TransTech, Amar Bhide]_ — [2014-02-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fkF9Npxfmn8)
- **Build competitive advantage one tiny cloned best practice at a time; small things like a law firm's elegant mailing label or a $400 Caliper personality test before every hire add up to something meaningful.** He never hires even interns without the Caliper test, including a 15,000-rupee-a-month Dakshana alum where the test is 50% of the wage, because bad hires are among the most expensive things that can happen to a company; the CEOs he tells rarely adopt it because the cloning gene is missing. _[Caliper, Dakshana]_ — [2014-02-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fkF9Npxfmn8)
- **Build a brand for infrequent big-ticket relationships the way Multani Jewelers did with a one-rupee Diwali card every year for 20 years; I clone it with physical family-photo greeting cards.** Humans love looking at other humans (Facebook users look most at their own pictures), so a family picture card beats a Christmas tree card; as everyone moves online, his use of the US Postal Service keeps rising because physical cards now stand out more. _[Multani Jewelers, Facebook]_ — [2014-02-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fkF9Npxfmn8)
- **Live sales meetings are incredibly expensive in time and money; build a back end strong enough that you can do things the Amazon way with no phone number.** A local meeting blows half a day and an out-of-town one costs $1,000-plus and a day or two; during his $150 million raise he visited only one investor, in Irvine, and did the rest by phone. If the marketing message isn't buttoned down the live meeting won't be fruitful anyway. _[Amazon]_ — [2014-02-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fkF9Npxfmn8)
- **Talking to another human is the least efficient way to pick up data; reading is the densest way to educate yourself and catch market signals.** Spend maximum time with customers in the early days, but afterwards be a voracious reader rather than a voracious meeter of people, because meetings are mostly banter with little essence. — [2014-02-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fkF9Npxfmn8)
- **There are 100 ways to succeed: Steve Jobs waited for perfection and Bill Gates shipped half-baked, and both worked; my bias is to ship something you love and would use yourself.** Advice to a founder with a patented whitening gel: it's a gut call, call the next iteration version 2.0 after a year, but if you have reservations keep it in the lab longer. _[Steve Jobs, Bill Gates]_ — [2014-02-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fkF9Npxfmn8)
- **Munger says Costco has done more good for the world than the Rockefeller Foundation, so entrepreneurship is probably the best way to help society, but keep the capitalist and philanthropic lives separate.** Costco's mission is to serve members, not philanthropy; the capitalist Mohnish drives the engine that funds the philanthropic Mohnish, and philanthropy only matters because we do not live forever. _[Costco, Charlie Munger, Rockefeller Foundation]_ — [2014-06-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DzOEp7GRwAU)
- **Dhandho Holdings clones the Berkshire/Fairfax/Markel model of buying insurance companies, leaving the operators alone and taking over the investment side, because almost none of the 3,000 US P&C insurers do this.** He raised about $150 million in Q1 2014, agreed to acquire a private insurer, and intends a permanent-capital, never-sell vehicle; the US P&C industry takes in about $550 billion of premiums a year but good underwriters almost never have investment skill, so finding and freeing a 'Lou Simpson' is the rare edge. _[Dhandho Holdings, Berkshire Hathaway, Fairfax Financial, Markel, GEICO, Lou Simpson]_ — [2014-10-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i6fWxvsW6Nk)
- **The world misprices the talent of stay-at-home moms; Pabrai Funds runs entirely on part-time staff at under $100,000 a year of payroll on $700 million of assets.** His part-time staff handle everything including SEC compliance; he also says running his earlier IT services company taught him more about operating businesses than running a fund does. _[Pabrai Investment Funds, TransTech]_ — [2014-10-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i6fWxvsW6Nk)
- **The long-term strategic plan for Pabrai Funds is simply to avoid stupid decisions and make as few decisions as possible.** If he were not managing the fund he would return the capital; he does not consider it work and reads about 100-150 pages a day versus Buffett's reported 500. _[Pabrai Investment Funds]_ — [2014-10-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i6fWxvsW6Nk)
- **Dhandho Holdings was set up to own and control insurance companies because hundreds of well-run US P&C insurers are clueless on the investing side, a void the 50-year-old Berkshire model should have filled.** Raised about $150 million in Q1 2014 and just received regulatory approval to buy Stone Trust Insurance in Louisiana, about $70 million a year of mostly workers' comp premiums, adding capital and taking over float management while leaving underwriting alone; about 3,000 US P&C insurers collect $550 billion a year. _[Dhandho Holdings, Stone Trust Insurance, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2014-12-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JSHVXBBb9bI)

### Philanthropy & Dakshana (14)

- **There are only two choices for an estate, your gene pool or society, and large inheritances are a burden that distorts children's lives.** He quotes Buffett's line about giving kids enough to do anything but not enough to do nothing, and says a couple of million each is fine but $20 million does them no favors. He recycles all his assets to society out of enlightened self-interest, not altruism. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2014-06-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DzOEp7GRwAU)
- **Most charities are all heart and no head, run as marketing machines that never report failures or lessons learned.** Their leaders have never met payroll or had 99% of their net worth in a business near bankruptcy; he believes there is no difference between running a for-profit and a non-profit, and non-profits should narrow to one or two well-defined causes. — [2014-06-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DzOEp7GRwAU)
- **Dakshana was set up in 2007 when net worth crossed $50 million, giving 2% of net worth a year to allow real-world experimentation with his ideas.** That gave at least $1 million a year; he wanted to teach fishing rather than give fish, and found the model in Anand Kumar's Super 30 in Bihar, which he cloned with Kumar's blessing after Kumar declined funding and scaling. _[Dakshana Foundation, Super 30, Anand Kumar]_ — [2014-06-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DzOEp7GRwAU)
- **From 2007 to 2014 Dakshana sent 458 impoverished students to the IITs out of 1,033 scholars, a 44% success rate versus a 2% national acceptance rate.** Most scholars come from rural India with illiterate farmer or laborer parents; 250 scholars took the 2014 exam with at least 70% expected to be accepted, and the stretch goal is 2,020 IIT admits in 2020, which would make one in seven IITians a Dakshana scholar. _[Dakshana Foundation]_ — [2014-06-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DzOEp7GRwAU)
- **Giving money away effectively is much harder than making it, so start young while you have the energy rather than in your 60s or 70s.** He planned to reach zero assets by 80, assumed he might spin his wheels for 10-15 years, started at 42, and got traction within weeks; Dakshana's constraint is not money but the pace of government and other entities. _[Dakshana Foundation]_ — [2014-06-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DzOEp7GRwAU)
- **Dakshana's secret sauce is the government's Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalaya system, which pre-selects the top 2% of rural kids through a language-independent IQ test.** Rajiv Gandhi created 600 residential JNV schools, one per district, taking 80 kids each from 2 million test-takers across 20 languages; Dakshana's under-5-crore layer works only because 3,000 crores on JNVs sits below it and 3,000-4,000 crores on IITs above it, with an MOU delivering a government spreadsheet to Irvine after 10th standard. _[Dakshana Foundation, Jawahar Navodaya Vidyalaya, Rajiv Gandhi]_ — [2014-06-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DzOEp7GRwAU)
- **Perpetual foundations that give away the legal minimum 5% sprinkled over hundreds of programs, never comparing social ROI, exist mainly to keep their managers employed.** The MacArthur Foundation spreads 5.2% over at least 300 programs with no comparison; with five programs you should pick the best four, then three. Henry Ford would be flabbergasted by the Ford Foundation, and professional managers without founder conviction produce today's results. _[MacArthur Foundation, Ford Foundation, Rockefeller Foundation]_ — [2014-06-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DzOEp7GRwAU)
- **Do most giving while alive and set sunsets, as Gates and Buffett have mandated, because future entrepreneurs will find problems today's donors cannot conceive.** Bill and Melinda Gates required the foundation to reach zero 50 years after their deaths and Buffett required his gift to be spent within 10 years of his death, both because they saw the abuse; a law limiting foundations to five or ten causes would help. _[Bill Gates, Gates Foundation, Warren Buffett]_ — [2014-06-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DzOEp7GRwAU)
- **Capitalism has a feedback loop that philanthropy lacks, so he inverted the problem and funds only areas with a measurable feedback loop.** An entrepreneur's idea is mostly wrong at first and market signals force zigzags until it works, while a foundation earning over 5% can sprinkle forever. Dakshana's loop is the annual IIT and NIT acceptance percentage, a number controlled by the IITs that the management team analyzes and adjusts to. _[Dakshana Foundation]_ — [2014-06-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DzOEp7GRwAU)
- **Nonprofits should swing for the fences: focus on one or two causes and concentrate endowment assets, even 90%+ in one stock, as Munger advises.** Dakshana cloned the Bihar 'Super 30' IIT coaching model and follows Buffett/Munger principles; because he and his wife give 2% of net worth each year, a total loss in one year would not terminate the foundation. _[Dakshana Foundation, Super 30, Ford Foundation, Rockefeller Foundation]_ — [2014-10-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=i6fWxvsW6Nk)
- **Philanthropy should be the opposite of investing: extreme concentration on one or two narrowly defined problems and a willingness to go high risk and completely fail.** Munger sees no problem with a foundation holding 90% in one stock; Dakshana's assets are usually in no more than three or four stocks and have often been close to 90% in a single position, because the goal is moonshots, not preservation. _[Dakshana Foundation, Charlie Munger, Ford Foundation, Rockefeller Foundation]_ — [2014-12-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JSHVXBBb9bI)
- **The 2%-of-net-worth-per-year giving model treated the first decade of Dakshana spending as tuition money that could vaporize without concern.** When their net worth passed $50 million he and his wife committed 2% a year (at least $1 million), cloned from Buffett's 5%-a-year gift to the Gates Foundation; he expected 10-15 years of failure but got traction in about 12 weeks. _[Dakshana Foundation, Gates Foundation, Warren Buffett]_ — [2014-12-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JSHVXBBb9bI)
- **Dakshana's model is high leverage: about 1-1.25 lakh spent per scholar gets 60-70% into IIT and forces the government to spend 25-35 lakhs educating a poor kid it would otherwise have ignored.** A tailor's son from a Hyderabad slum earning under Rs 4,000 a month ranked 63 out of 500,000, went to IIT Bombay computer science, was hired by Google at about $100,000 a year and moved his parents into their own house within three months; the whole thing cost $2,000. _[Dakshana Foundation, IIT, Google, Super 30, Anand Kumar]_ — [2014-12-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JSHVXBBb9bI)
- **Dakshana got traction in 12 weeks by hiring one honest retired IIT Madras graduate on 800 rupees an hour, letting him roam, and following the leads to the JNV school system and an MOU with the government.** 550 Jawaharlal Navodaya Vidyalayas admit the top 2% of 2 million fifth-graders via a corruption-free test, but the nearest coaching centre could be 400 km away; by September 2007 Dakshana had 320 scholars in eight regional schools, the first batch got 22% into IIT, and the only rule is that next year must be better than this year. _[Dakshana Foundation, Jawaharlal Navodaya Vidyalaya, Bansal Classes, Kota]_ — [2014-12-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JSHVXBBb9bI)

## 2015

2 talks, 50 ideas.

**Talks**

- 2015-12-03 · [Boston College, Carroll School of Management Presentation, December 3, 2015](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7F2IGzES7Uc) · 25 ideas
- 2015-12-22 · [Mohnish Pabrai's Presentation and Q&A at MDI, Gurgaon on December 22, 2015](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OFkApI6zZtY) · 25 ideas


### Cloning & learning from great investors (2)

- **Cloning is the starting point, but every borrowed idea must pass independent filters: circle of competence, understanding the business, what it is worth, the risks and the checklist.** He calls himself the shameless cloner with 'no internal ideas', borrowing freely from Einhorn and others, then discussing with Guy Spier; independence of thought and strong conviction remain the most basic requirements for a decent investor. First rule of cloning: look at where concentrated investors have put the most money, ideally their largest position. _[David Einhorn, Guy Spier, Valeant, Horsehead Holdings]_ — [2015-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7F2IGzES7Uc)
- **Investing knowledge is cumulative, so an investor's best days can be ahead of him as long as he keeps pumping content into his brain and learning from others' mistakes.** Read Forbes, Fortune, Businessweek, the Economist, the NYT, WSJ, FT and books by great authors; learning from other people's mistakes is cheaper than your own. He never owned Valeant but read the biography of ITT's Harold Geneen after Munger's comparison to understand it. _[Valeant, ITT, Harold Geneen]_ — [2015-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7F2IGzES7Uc)

### Circle of competence & checklists (6)

- **The idea funnel is designed to reject: is it in my circle of competence (usually no), and is the price below half of what it is worth (usually no); only the small sliver that survives gets deep reading.** 'We are not looking for a reason to invest in; we are looking for a reason not to invest.' Survivors go to Guy Spier for independent reading, then the checklist, then position sizing. _[Guy Spier]_ — [2015-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7F2IGzES7Uc)
- **The size of the circle of competence does not matter; knowing its boundaries does, and a tiny circle can make a fortune.** Munger's friend John Arrillaga built a $2-3 billion fortune only on real estate within a mile or two of Stanford; Munger's Peoria example: buy the Ford dealership, McDonald's franchise, best apartment building and best office building at the right price and sit for 60-80 years. _[John Arrillaga, Charlie Munger]_ — [2015-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7F2IGzES7Uc)
- **He avoids industries with rapid change and looks for no-brainers that can be explained in three or four sentences.** He understands lowest-quartile-cost commodity producers well and is still learning the power of brands and intangibles; he made a small investment in Google as an exception. Don't force the circle to expand, it expands by osmosis through reading. _[Google]_ — [2015-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7F2IGzES7Uc)
- **You can become extremely wealthy without ever predicting when a bubble will pop — 99% of things belong in the 'too hard' box.** Buffett's desk has a box labeled 'too hard'; before investing Pabrai asks 'is this a no-brainer?', and since no-brainers are hard enough, there is no reason to go to areas slightly off from a no-brainer or to short Tesla. _[Warren Buffett, Tesla]_ — [2015-12-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OFkApI6zZtY)
- **What matters in a circle of competence is not its size but knowing its boundaries.** Munger's friend John Arrillaga became a billionaire investing only in real estate within two miles of Stanford; Munger says owning the best apartment building, office building, McDonald's franchise and Ford dealership in a small town is enough to sit on your ass for life. _[John Arrillaga, Charlie Munger]_ — [2015-12-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OFkApI6zZtY)
- **It's better to be an inch wide and a mile deep than a mile wide and an inch deep.** Keep the very long term in focus, don't try heroics like finding the next Amazon or Google, follow Buffett's two rules, and you don't need to know a lot about many things. — [2015-12-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OFkApI6zZtY)

### Valuation & margin of safety (4)

- **Use Munger's inversion to test valuations: a 15% return on Amazon implies a $5 trillion market cap in 20 years, which the law of large numbers makes implausible.** Amazon at ~$320-330 billion would need to double every five years; the entire US stock market is ~$20 trillion and global wealth ~$100 trillion growing 1-2% a year, so one company becoming 10-20% of the US economy is not credible. 'Count me a sceptic.' _[Amazon, Charlie Munger]_ — [2015-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7F2IGzES7Uc)
- **Risk and uncertainty are different things, and markets punishing uncertainty creates low-risk, high-uncertainty opportunities.** WL Ross Holdings (WLRH), a $500 million SPAC with ~$10 per share of cash bought below $9.97, has huge uncertainty about what Wilbur Ross will buy but almost no risk since fees are refunded and cash returns if no deal is done; the WLRHU units add a half-share option kicker. _[WL Ross Holdings, Wilbur Ross]_ — [2015-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7F2IGzES7Uc)
- **The Nifty Fifty of 1972 shows that even truly great, enduring businesses can be terrible investments at 70-100 times earnings.** McDonald's traded near 90x, Disney 80x, Coke 70-100x in 1971-72 while everything else traded at 'who cares'; the market crashed in slow motion in 1973-74 losing 40-50% and the Nifty Fifty were taken out back one by one even though McDonald's went on to widen its moat for 45 years. _[Nifty Fifty, McDonald's, Disney, Coca-Cola]_ — [2015-12-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OFkApI6zZtY)
- **Use a 10% discount rate regardless of the rate environment and don't spend much time on macro.** Keeping the hurdle at 10% is probably why he can't find anything to buy in 2015; better to understand businesses across a wide range of outcomes, though Buffett's view that rates stay low for a long time may give stocks a tailwind. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2015-12-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OFkApI6zZtY)

### Portfolio concentration & selling (2)

- **Position sizing runs at 2%, 5% and 10% of assets with a 10% maximum, and winners are never trimmed because he would rather water the flowers and cut the weeds.** He started with a 10x10 portfolio, then after the financial crisis moved to baskets (e.g. a commodities basket) and tiers: 2% for asymmetric bets like Fannie/Freddie preferreds, 5% for good conviction, 10% for the most serious ideas. The first 75% of the portfolio goes into likely doubles, the next 10% into triples, 10% into 4x and 5% into 5x ideas; at the depths of a crisis one should be fully invested. _[Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac]_ — [2015-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7F2IGzES7Uc)
- **Pabrai Investment Funds never put 35% in anything — positions max out at 10% at cost and are allowed to grow.** He has never sold down a position purely because it grew large; the key is the long runway, as the Amex example shows. _[Pabrai Investment Funds, American Express]_ — [2015-12-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OFkApI6zZtY)

### Compounding & long-term holding (1)

- **$5,000 saved at 18 and compounded at 15% for 60 years becomes $20 million — the long runway and no heroics is all you need.** He put his daughter's $4,800 summer earnings into a Roth IRA and showed that 15% doubles every five years, 4,000x over 60 years; starting at 38 instead of 18 cuts the result to a quarter. Berkshire doubles roughly every seven years — the key in life is how many doubles you get. _[Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2015-12-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OFkApI6zZtY)

### Moats & business quality (5)

- **Other things being equal you are better off buying businesses with huge runways that will appreciate, even paying up for them, rather than merely cheap assets.** Tom Gayner's example: $50 in the S&P at the 1972 Nifty 50 peak became $2,800, but $3 in just three of the Nifty 50 (with 47 going to zero) is worth more than that; buying Amex the day before the salad-oil crisis and holding converges over time to Buffett's return from buying 40% lower. The 1999 Mohnish was a cheapskate; the 2015 Mohnish prefers a good business at a fair price. _[Tom Gayner, Markel, American Express, Walmart]_ — [2015-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7F2IGzES7Uc)
