- **Evaluating moats is one of the hardest things in investing because capitalism's creative destruction means almost all moats eventually get destroyed.** Kodak had a monopoly on film and Xerox owned its market in 1972, yet both were destroyed; the goal is enduring moats at great prices where the rest of humanity does not see the moat. Guy Spier considers Nestle bulletproof. Rapidly changing industries are the enemy of the investor: of the 1972 Nifty 50 tech names only IBM survived, and he would not bet Netflix or GoPro exist in 2068. _[Kodak, Xerox, Nestle, Guy Spier, IBM, Netflix, GoPro]_ — [2015-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7F2IGzES7Uc)
- **Netflix is a pipe whose long-term economics are unclear because content owners have the clout to capture the $10 a month.** Contrast with Micron, an oligopoly D-RAM supplier (three in the world, number two after Samsung) earning close to $4 billion while Netflix earns $240 million yet has a $50 billion market cap; the cable-versus-content battle in the US shows content providers win, per David Einhorn's letter. _[Netflix, Micron, Samsung, David Einhorn]_ — [2015-12-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OFkApI6zZtY)
- **Long-term compounding machines matter more than entry price, so focus on durable assets rather than cheap ones.** Tom Gayner's example: buying American Express at $100 the day before the salad oil crisis versus Buffett's $60 makes almost no difference on an annualized basis today; that is why Munger pays up for Costco. Buffett admits he wasn't smart enough to hang on to Disney bought in the sixties. _[Tom Gayner, American Express, Costco, Disney, Walmart, Charlie Munger]_ — [2015-12-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OFkApI6zZtY)
- **Capitalism is hell-bent on destroying moats, so enduring moats are very rare and identifying them is the hard part.** If you do find a great long-duration moat you can put 10% into it and do other things with the other 90%; Pabrai does not target a market cap and historically has not invested in very large companies, ending up there only recently because that is where opportunity was. _[Pabrai Investment Funds]_ — [2015-12-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OFkApI6zZtY)

### Management & capital allocation (1)

- **There is no point meeting management: the average CEO is a great salesman and you will only be impressed; judge managers by their long track record of what they said versus what they delivered.** He never reaches out to management and tells those who contact him not to waste their time; he now puts far more weight on ultra-high-quality management than in 1999 and his portfolio is much richer in it. Wilbur Ross at WLRH is a high-quality manager available at no premium. _[WL Ross Holdings, Wilbur Ross]_ — [2015-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7F2IGzES7Uc)

### Markets, cycles & macro (9)

- **Bubbles are far more common than people think and recur wherever humans oscillate between fear and greed.** He cites Ron Insana's book Trend Watching, which lists bubbles happening somewhere in the world almost all the time; as long as humans are involved in markets there will be bubbles. _[Ron Insana]_ — [2015-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7F2IGzES7Uc)
- **Investors can be completely right about a transformational trend and still lose their entire investment.** 1921 auto investors were right about population growth, industrialization and auto sales (1.5-2.5 million then vs 18 million forecast in 2015) yet nearly all lost everything as hundreds of car makers died; 1959-62 'tronics' investors were right about Moore's Law and 1999 dotcom investors were right about the internet, with the same result. _[Stanley Steamer, Lafayette, Powertron Ultrasonics, boo.com, Kozmo]_ — [2015-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7F2IGzES7Uc)
- **Mega bubbles recur roughly every 38-40 years because the investors who lived through the last one must exit the scene before the next can take hold.** The motors, tronics and dotcom bubbles were each ~38-40 years apart and the 1972 Nifty 50 and today's are 43 years apart; he expects the next big one around 2036-2042, with investors again saying 'this time it's different'. — [2015-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7F2IGzES7Uc)
- **The 1972 Nifty 50 'buy great businesses at any price and hold forever' idea ended with 80-90% drops in blue chips during the 1973-74 crash.** McDonald's traded at 86x earnings, Disney at 82x and Polaroid at 91x in 1972; the slow-motion 1973-74 crash (over 60% end to end) was worse than 1929 and the Nifty 50 were 'taken out back and shot one by one'. _[McDonald's, Disney, Polaroid, Coca-Cola, Kodak, Xerox]_ — [2015-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7F2IGzES7Uc)
- **In 2015 there is a new Nifty 50 concentrated in a sliver of tech stocks, and the best advice is to stay away from the high flyers.** Amazon at 576x+ earnings, Netflix north of 200x, Tesla and SolarCity unprofitable, Uber at $50 billion; 141 unicorns worth a combined $500 billion, most of which he does not expect to deliver for investors. Money is being funneled from fixed income and old-economy stocks into these names. Netflix is a great business but over 99% of its content is other people's and must be paid for; he quotes Einhorn expecting Micron to be worth more than Netflix. _[Amazon, Netflix, Tesla, SolarCity, Uber, Twitter, Facebook, GoPro, Groupon, Square, Micron, David Einhorn]_ — [2015-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7F2IGzES7Uc)
- **Investors can be completely right about a transformative macro trend and still lose their entire investment.** In the 1922 motors bubble there were hundreds of car companies and nearly all 1921 investors lost everything even though auto growth was real; the same happened with the 1959 'tronics' bubble (Astron, Vulcatron, Powertron Ultrasonics) and the 1999 dot-com bubble (Boo.com, WebVan). _[Motors bubble 1922, Tronics bubble 1959, Dot-com bubble, Boo.com, WebVan]_ — [2015-12-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OFkApI6zZtY)
- **Big bubbles recur roughly every 38-40 years because the generation that lived through the last one has to leave the scene.** A 30-year-old in 2000 would be 70 by 2040, so nobody at the table remembers the movie; when Buffett raised the motors bubble during the dot-com era, a magazine cover asked 'What's wrong, Warren?'. Smaller bubbles, however, are building almost all the time. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2015-12-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OFkApI6zZtY)
- **In 2015 the US market shows a Nifty Fifty-like polarization with world-class companies at ridiculous valuations.** Amazon at 600x earnings, Netflix at 240x, Facebook at 95x; about 80 US companies trade above 100x P/E, the only time close to the 120 seen in the dot-com era, and the top 10 Nasdaq names are ~30% of $7 trillion of value. _[Amazon, Netflix, Facebook, SolarCity, Uber, Flipkart]_ — [2015-12-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OFkApI6zZtY)
- **The 2015 bubble is in both public and private markets, and it may pop one company at a time.** GoPro was valued at $9 billion for a camera in a waterproof case before being taken down; Twitter lost $48 billion of value; 141 unicorns hold a combined $500 billion valuation, and VCs with participating preferences are nearly guaranteed their money back, which lets them bid valuations up. _[GoPro, Twitter, LivingSocial, Uber]_ — [2015-12-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OFkApI6zZtY)

### Stock case studies (5)

- **Tesla is a capital-intensive manufacturer priced like a capital-light tech business, while GM is ignored despite being far larger and ahead on electric cars.** Tesla: ~$30 billion market cap, $4 billion revenue run rate, losing $400 million a year, under 50,000 cars; scaling to 200,000 cars would take tens of billions of capex, and even at 8% margins (best car companies make ~7%) the PE would exceed 100. GM makes 9-10 million cars, is number one in the US and China, generates $10 billion heading to $12-13 billion in cash flow, buys back stock with NOLs shielding income, and has the $30,000, 200-mile Chevy Bolt coming two years before an equivalent Tesla. _[Tesla, General Motors]_ — [2015-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7F2IGzES7Uc)
- **Silicon Valley Bank in July 1999 was a way to get the upside of the dotcom bubble without the downside.** His first Pabrai Funds investment: a solid, profitable bank valued with zero credit for hundreds of undisclosed warrants in venture-backed companies; as the bank monetized the warrants and disclosed them the stock re-rated and he made 3-4x in about a year. _[Silicon Valley Bank]_ — [2015-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7F2IGzES7Uc)
- **Fiat Chrysler was a no-brainer: a company with over $100 billion of revenue at a market cap under $5 billion, and the Ferrari spinoff alone is now worth $10 billion.** Bought about three and a half years earlier and still held; Ferrari sells 7,000 cars vs. Fiat's ~5 million, yet the spun-out sliver is worth 2x what the market priced the whole business at. He would have said autos were too ugly to invest in before 2012, so staying flexible matters. _[Fiat Chrysler, Ferrari]_ — [2015-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7F2IGzES7Uc)
- **Mark Cuban's smartest move was hedging 100% of the Yahoo stock he received for broadcast.com.** Yahoo paid $5.7 billion in stock for broadcast.com; Cuban insisted on hedging the entire position, which is why his net worth survived the crash while other deals like IAC buying Ask.com for $1.9 billion were value destroyed. _[Yahoo, broadcast.com, Mark Cuban, IAC, Ask.com]_ — [2015-12-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OFkApI6zZtY)
- **GM is far cheaper than Tesla and has no technological disadvantage, but GM is not sexy and Tesla is.** Tesla has $4 billion revenue and loses $400 million a year, so even at BMW-like 8% margins you would pay 100x; GM has $150 billion revenue, cash flows heading to $10-14 billion, a captive finance arm earning $1-2 billion and a China business earning $2 billion, and is launching a 200-mile $30,000 electric car two years ahead of Tesla. _[General Motors, Tesla, BMW]_ — [2015-12-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OFkApI6zZtY)

### Psychology & temperament (5)

- **Judge yourself on Munger's inner scorecard, not the market's outer scorecard, during multi-year periods of underperformance.** Pabrai Funds lagged its benchmarks over the prior five years (like Sequoia Fund in its first five years) and was down close to 70% in 2008 vs. ~37-38% for the market; his motto: if wealth is lost nothing is lost, if health is lost something is lost, if character is lost everything is lost. Pabrai Funds, started in 1999 with none of the high flyers, was up 70% in its first year through the dotcom burst. _[Sequoia Fund, Pabrai Investment Funds, Charlie Munger]_ — [2015-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7F2IGzES7Uc)
- **The single greatest skill an investor can bring is extreme patience.** 'If you are a guy or girl who loves to watch paint dry, you will be a great investor.' Buffett and Munger spend much time reducing mistakes and holding great moats untouched for decades. — [2015-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7F2IGzES7Uc)
- **When a cab driver gives you stock tips, you are at the top.** In January 2000 a Pakistani cab driver in Chicago asked Pabrai what he thought of Cisco and said he had put money into Cisco and Yahoo — the modern equivalent of the 1929 shoeshine boy. _[Cisco, Yahoo]_ — [2015-12-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OFkApI6zZtY)
- **You don't need exposure to every sector — when a sector goes crazy, just avoid it and be willing to look stupid in the short term.** Pabrai Investment Funds launched in July 1999 in the frenzy of the internet bubble and was up 70% the first year by sidestepping dot-coms and buying cheap non-dotcom stocks; the day Nasdaq peaked in 2000 Berkshire hit a multi-year low. _[Pabrai Investment Funds, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2015-12-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OFkApI6zZtY)
- **Inactivity and patience are the core of everything in investing.** Inactivity is a great skill; spend your time talking to students rather than trading. — [2015-12-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OFkApI6zZtY)

### Buffett & Munger lessons (1)

- **Munger told him a good investment operation needs to focus on just three things: cannibals, cloners and spinoffs.** Cannibals are companies aggressively buying back stock, like all of Berkshire's permanent holdings (American Express, Coca-Cola, IBM, Wells Fargo); back tests for a planned Dhandho Holdings ETF showed incredible outperformance from cannibals; Greenblatt's book covers spinoffs. _[American Express, Coca-Cola, IBM, Wells Fargo, Dhandho Holdings, Joel Greenblatt]_ — [2015-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7F2IGzES7Uc)

### Mistakes & lessons learned (2)

- **Liquidation value can be an illusion when a business employs many people, which is the lesson of his Sears mistake.** At a June 2009 lunch Charlie Munger shook his head at Sears in Pabrai's portfolio, recalling how he and Buffett barely got out of Diversified Retailing's Baltimore department stores; monetizing Sears real estate meant firing 100,000+ employees, and Amazon is eroding the value of mall real estate anyway. He sold and redeployed into other depressed stocks. _[Sears, Charlie Munger, Eddie Lampert, Diversified Retailing]_ — [2015-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7F2IGzES7Uc)
- **Putting the Kelly formula in his book was a mistake; it does not apply to one-off investment bets.** Kelly works for 5,000 repeated coin tosses at 51/49 odds, not for the one-off bets investors make; he would remove it from any new edition of The Dhandho Investor. — [2015-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7F2IGzES7Uc)

### Career, entrepreneurship & life (2)

- **Go to work for people you like, admire and trust, and don't defer life; be like the fisherman, not the banker.** Buffett's advice says nothing about comp or blue-chip status, only people; deferring is like 'saving sex for old age'. Life is finite, we leave naked, and once basics are covered you should not work anywhere that is not high quality all the way; hit the reset button if so. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2015-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7F2IGzES7Uc)
- **The small investor has a huge advantage over institutions because a one-lakh bet can be meaningful and the opportunity universe is far wider.** Pabrai and Srini can't dish out capital at that rate and need businesses of a certain size; the downside for a small investor is too many things to look at, so you must hone in. — [2015-12-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OFkApI6zZtY)

### Philanthropy & Dakshana (5)

- **Dakshana is a cloned model — Pabrai copied Anand Kumar's Super 30 after reading a 2006 Business Week article.** Super 30 converted high-potential rural brains into global talent at about $700 a student; Anand declined donations but agreed to let Pabrai steal and scale the model, and seven Dakshana alumni now teach in the program. _[Dakshana Foundation, Super 30, Anand Kumar]_ — [2015-12-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OFkApI6zZtY)
- **With limited resources, put them where the return to society is highest — a high-IQ brain given the same resources produces a dramatically different outcome.** In a population of a billion the number of top 1-2% brains being wasted approaches infinity; 888 Dakshana scholars have been admitted to IIT out of 1,715, a 52% hit rate versus ~2% overall. _[Dakshana Foundation]_ — [2015-12-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OFkApI6zZtY)
- **Large inheritances are a disservice to your children; recycle excess wealth back to society.** Quotes Buffett: it is fine to put Jesse Owens's son on the 10-meter line but not the 15-meter line; his father said you take nothing with you, so assets beyond what you consume should go to society rather than the gene pool. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2015-12-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OFkApI6zZtY)
- **In charity, swing for the fences — sixers are the only way to move the needle.** Pabrai was comfortable with Dakshana's outcome being zero and expected to hit his head against a brick wall for 10 years; he didn't care about the reputational impact and was willing to make bold bets. _[Dakshana Foundation]_ — [2015-12-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OFkApI6zZtY)
- **Dakshana follows the UCLA/Harvard endowment model: don't lecture scholars about giving back, just tap the future millionaires on the shoulder in 10-15 years.** The original idea of asking scholars to give 10% of lifetime earnings was dropped; alumni give back anyway, e.g. 20 Kharagpur alumni receive new Dakshana admits at the train station and mentoring networks exist at every IIT and NIT. _[Dakshana Foundation, UCLA]_ — [2015-12-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=OFkApI6zZtY)

## 2016

4 talks, 84 ideas.

**Talks**

- 2016-05-24 · [Mohnish Pabrai Lecture at Univ. of California, Irvine (UCI), May 24, 2016](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfxOvdiac94) · 25 ideas
- 2016-09-26 · [Mohnish Pabrai's Lecture to Univ. of Puerto Rico MBA Class – Sept. 26, 2016](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FO5V7jcBNMM) · 9 ideas
- 2016-10-14 · [Mohnish Pabrai Lecture at Peking University (Guanghua School of Mgmt) - Oct 14, 2016](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jo1XgDJCkh4) · 25 ideas
- 2016-11-03 · [Mohnish Pabrai Lecture at Boston College (Carroll School of Mgmt) - Nov 3, 2016](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IOoaNYQHaYY) · 25 ideas


### Cloning & learning from great investors (6)

- **Reading a company's entire history of annual reports gives an information and synthesis edge that most investors are unwilling to earn.** Buffett and Munger read every Coke annual report from 1919 to the late 1980s and learned that unit case volume had never fallen in a single year, through the Depression, WWII, Korea and 1970s stagflation. Pabrai himself sent Munger a Dropbox of every GM annual report since 1911 (24,000 pages) and began reading them himself, calling it fascinating. _[Coca-Cola, General Motors, American Express, Charlie Munger]_ — [2016-05-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfxOvdiac94)
- **When cloning, look at the highest-conviction ideas of concentrated investors; it is not too late weeks after their purchase if you can reverse-engineer the logic and it still looks cheap.** A 50-stock portfolio with nothing above 3% reveals no conviction, whereas a 15-stock portfolio where the top three are half the pie does. By mid-1989 it was public that Buffett was buying Coke at only about 10% above his cost, and two years later it had doubled. _[Coca-Cola, Warren Buffett]_ — [2016-05-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfxOvdiac94)
- **Guy Spier's mental model of looking around the world for replicas of a proven great business (Coke bottlers, Moody's) is a superior way to find undervalued compounders, but it only pays if you hold.** In 2001 Spier bought CRISIL, India's number-one credit rating agency in which S&P owned 10%, made about 4x and sold; it went up 130 times after he sold, which alone would exceed his entire $160 million fund today. Moody's economics: pay an analyst $100,000, collect $4 million in fees. _[Guy Spier, CRISIL, Moody's, S&P, Coca-Cola]_ — [2016-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jo1XgDJCkh4)
- **The simplest way to find bargains is to be a shameless cloner: ask Li Lu what he owns, or reverse engineer 13F filings of smart investors, and you need no analysts.** Li Lu is 'a hundred times smarter than me' and a better analyst than anyone he could hire, and he doesn't need to be paid. _[Li Lu]_ — [2016-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jo1XgDJCkh4)
- **Guy Spier's model: identify a great US business (Coke bottlers, Moody's) and then hunt for its analogues in other countries where the market may not have priced the same economics.** Applying this, Spier bought CRISIL in India in 2001-02 and added in 2004-05, then sold after 2-3x. The 2001 purchase is now up 200x and the 2005 purchase 43x; untouched, it alone would be ~$150-160M, roughly 50% of his ~$160M fund. S&P/McGraw Hill paid $8.5M for 10% of CRISIL in 1998 at an $85M market cap; CRISIL is now ~$25B and S&P owns ~75%. Even at CRISIL's nosebleed P/E today, Pabrai says it would probably be a mistake to sell, since Indian debt instruments in 10-50 years will dwarf today's. _[Guy Spier, CRISIL, Moody's, S&P, McGraw Hill, Coca-Cola bottlers]_ — [2016-11-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IOoaNYQHaYY)
- **International cloning is possible even without 13Fs, via Indian broker disclosures of 1%+ holders and Bloomberg shareholder data for Korea and China.** India requires brokers to disclose anyone owning over 1% of a public company; he subscribes to Alpha Ideas which compiles this quarterly. He has found Korean and Chinese investments owned by investors he admires this way. _[Alpha Ideas]_ — [2016-11-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IOoaNYQHaYY)

### Circle of competence & checklists (5)

- **Follow the Munger grocery-store approach: keep a list of businesses you love and wait for them to go on sale, rather than Graham's approach of buying whatever is most discounted.** After feeling sheepish at Columbia for not having such a list, he built one of admired businesses covering 80-90% of likely candidates and plans a weekly check on prices. He missed buying on February 8, 2016 when indices tanked because he was in India and not paying attention. _[Ben Graham, Charlie Munger]_ — [2016-05-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfxOvdiac94)
- **Do not allocate top-down across categories; investing is opportunistic bargain hunting and ideas arrive unpredictably, sometimes none in a year and sometimes five in a week.** During December 2008 to February 2009 so many ideas came at him that he had one or two days to process each, versus the usual weeks or months. He has never done top-down. — [2016-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jo1XgDJCkh4)
- **He never meets management, visits plants or seeks superior information; the edge comes from superior analytics on commonly known information plus patience that most market participants lack.** After six weeks studying the auto industry, which he had hated all his life for its capex, unions and consumer taste, he found many of his assumptions wrong using only public data synthesized from many sources. Investors trying to go from 10 to 12 to 15 in weeks would out-compound Buffett if it worked, and it doesn't. _[Guy Spier, Moody's]_ — [2016-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jo1XgDJCkh4)
- **You do not need an opinion on everything; put hard questions like the trajectory of oil demand in the 'too hard' pile and bet only on high-probability events.** He is confident tire volumes will be 20-40% higher in 2025 than 2016 but cannot say whether crude consumption will rise or fall. Buffett keeps a physical 'too hard' box on his desk; on a visit Pabrai found it empty and Buffett filled it with papers for a photo. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2016-11-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IOoaNYQHaYY)
- **To ask whether something is in your circle of competence is to answer it: if you are wondering, it is not.** He attributes this to Charlie Munger and adds that in investing you want absolute no-brainers; any doubt means you should not go there. _[Charlie Munger]_ — [2016-11-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IOoaNYQHaYY)

### Valuation & margin of safety (7)

- **For most investments, if you can't do the math in your head it should be an automatic pass; great investments come from overlapping mental models, not spreadsheets.** No DCF or spreadsheet was ever built for the Coke investment in almost 30 years; Buffett and Munger used dozens of models whose interplay produces Munger's Lollapalooza effect where one plus one becomes eleven. _[Coca-Cola, Charlie Munger, Warren Buffett]_ — [2016-05-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfxOvdiac94)
- **Coke reaching 2 trillion by 2034 from 190 billion in 2016 requires about 14.5% a year, which Pabrai doubts on fundamentals, though a cyclical 30-40 multiple could get it there.** Munger's 1996 speech needed only 7.5% a year from a 125 billion market cap. Coke sat at a 40 multiple in 1999, so a crazy multiple at the right time might deliver the number. _[Coca-Cola]_ — [2016-05-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfxOvdiac94)
- **Don't focus on being fully invested; hold cash comfortably until something intelligent shows up, and don't buy unless it is at least 50% off.** Comfort with uninvested funds is part of patience. The area he wants to improve is finding non-obvious 50-cent dollars: See's was a 25-cent dollar and Coke in the late 1980s was a great bet, but neither was obvious. _[See's Candies, Coca-Cola]_ — [2016-05-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfxOvdiac94)
- **His core mental model is to buy companies at half or less of what they will be worth in two or three years, because a 50-cent dollar revalued in three years compounds at 26%.** Finding things half off in an auction-driven market is not that hard, and if the revaluation happens in two years the return is 35-36%. Markets are a weighing machine in the long term. — [2016-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jo1XgDJCkh4)
- **Category three, the one that has shown up most in his portfolio, is when the market confuses risk with uncertainty: low risk plus high uncertainty usually produces high reward because markets hate and misprice uncertainty.** IPSCO in 2005 had a $2.5 billion market cap, $900 million of excess cash and two years of contracted earnings of $650 million a year, so 90% of the market cap would come back in cash in two years. He put 10% in at $45 and sold at the $157 buyout in 2007, nearly 4x in 2.5 years. _[IPSCO]_ — [2016-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jo1XgDJCkh4)
- **Category 3, the one that shows up most in his portfolio, is where the market confuses risk with uncertainty: low risk of permanent loss but high uncertainty about outcomes gets punished with a very low price.** IPSCO in 2005 had a $2.5B market cap, $900M cash and ~$650M/yr of visible earnings for two years ($2.2B total) with no visibility beyond; he held it from ~$40 until a Swedish buyout at ~$160 in early 2007. Markets 'don't have much respect for companies with volatile earnings.' _[IPSCO]_ — [2016-11-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IOoaNYQHaYY)
- **Category 5 is 'upside without downside': a solid business at a modest price that carries a free, undisclosed moonshot option.** In 1999 Silicon Valley Bank traded at a modest premium to book while holding undisclosed warrants from its venture-backed borrowers. He bought at $10-12, captured ~2.5x in about 2.5 years, and the stock went 4x. CMGI in his personal portfolio (10% of $1M, bought near book, sold for 100x) was similar. _[Silicon Valley Bank, CMGI]_ — [2016-11-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IOoaNYQHaYY)

### Portfolio concentration & selling (3)

- **The key is to make very few, very infrequent bets, and when seven moons line up, bet big.** Pabrai used to run a 10-stock, 10%-per-position model; during the financial crisis he found baskets of cheap businesses useful, and now sizes at 2%, 5% or 10% depending on discount to value and probability of loss. Fewer bets with deeper knowledge is better, and he suggests a concentrated real-estate investor with deep knowledge may have it more right than he does. — [2016-05-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfxOvdiac94)
- **The classic buy-at-50-cents, sell-at-90-cents value approach is flawed because it forces you out of the rare multi-baggers that drive most long-term wealth.** For over two decades he bought at 50 cents on the dollar and sold at 90 cents, expecting convergence in 2-3 years (a 30%+ or low-to-mid 20s return). Looking back, he found many cases where he made a 2x-4x, sold, and the stock then went up 10x. _[Blue Dart, Satyam, Kotak Mahindra Bank]_ — [2016-11-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IOoaNYQHaYY)
- **He now owns one category-1 'can be run by idiots' business for the first time and has decided never to sell it; even at 10x he would not sell.** He believes its moat will exist 100 and possibly 300 years from now; he will leave it alone and play his 'Mickey Mouse games' with shipping companies separately. If it reached 50x in his lifetime he still would not sell at 10x. — [2016-11-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IOoaNYQHaYY)

### Compounding & long-term holding (9)

- **For most people the path to wealth is simple: spend less than you earn, put it in an S&P index, never borrow against it or spend it, and start early.** He told his 18-year-old daughter that $5,000 in a Roth IRA compounding at 10% for 50 years becomes about 650,000-700,000 via rule of 72 (seven doublings); even 7% doubles every 10 years, and the S&P has done about 9% a year. Non-professional investors should index rather than try to pick managers. — [2016-05-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfxOvdiac94)
- **Buying a 50-cent dollar and selling at 90 works, but an even better model is buying and holding long-runway businesses even at 20 times earnings.** At the 2008 lunch Buffett named GEICO his favorite Berkshire company because of its runway, having gone from 2% to nearly 10% market share and planning to pass State Farm on his 100th birthday. Pabrai admits the lesson to sometimes pay up has not been seared in because he is a bargain hunter. _[GEICO, State Farm, Coca-Cola]_ — [2016-05-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfxOvdiac94)
- **Fluency in compounding math in your head, using the rule of 72 and 2^10 = 1,024, is a huge life advantage.** At 7% money doubles every 10 years, so $24 for Manhattan in 1626 becomes roughly $12 trillion by 2016, far more than Manhattan's land is worth given total US wealth of about $80 trillion; Buffett used this example in a late-1950s partnership letter. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2016-09-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FO5V7jcBNMM)
- **Almost anyone can retire wealthy: an 18-year-old minimum-wage worker saving $1,500 a year at 7% ends up with over $1 million at 68.** The first $1,500 alone becomes $48,000 after five doubles; a middle-class librarian who left a college $4 million simply followed this plan. Starting at 18 versus 28 makes a huge difference, and never raid a 401k or IRA for vacations. — [2016-09-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FO5V7jcBNMM)
- **The two levers of compounding are the length of the runway and the rate, and it is all about the number of doubles.** He put his daughter's $5,000 internship pay into one stock in her IRA at 18; at 15% (doubling every five years) it becomes $5 million at 68. Buffett's one wish is to live as long as possible so he can keep compounding; he started at 11 and told his wife at 24 they would be wealthy beyond their dreams. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2016-09-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FO5V7jcBNMM)
- **Compounding at 26% doubles money every three years, turning $1 million into $1 billion in 30 years, which is the key to Buffett's success and the game he set out to play in 1995.** 26% for 30 years is 2^10 = 1024x. From 1995 to 2014 his own record was roughly 26% a year, though he was down about a third over the previous two years as of 2016. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2016-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jo1XgDJCkh4)
- **You only truly learn a business after you own it, which is when you can recognize which holdings are real multibaggers that should not be touched.** Pre-purchase analysis tells you something, but ownership teaches more; he can name three or four current holdings that could be huge home runs and is willing to let them play out because even one 10x is worth it. — [2016-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jo1XgDJCkh4)
- **Accidentally holding 100 shares of Blue Dart for 21 years turned about $100 into $11,000, showing what buy-and-hold could have done with his whole India basket.** In 1994-95 he put $30,000 of a $1 million portfolio into four Indian stocks. Satyam went from ~45 rupees to ~7,000 (100x, $15k to $1.5M, sold near the 2000 peak); had he held, Blue Dart would have been a 60x ($7,700 to $465,000) and Kotak a 50x ($1,500 to $75,000); Skypack lost half. _[Blue Dart, Satyam, Kotak Mahindra Bank, Skypack Courier]_ — [2016-11-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IOoaNYQHaYY)
- **Long holding periods are doubly valuable because deferred capital gains taxes act as a free loan from the government for the whole period.** Holding for 10-30 years and paying tax once is like investing in a retirement account. In California his marginal state rate is north of 12% on top of ~20-22% federal long-term gains, so deferral matters even more. — [2016-11-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IOoaNYQHaYY)

### Moats & business quality (11)

- **Coke was See's on steroids because it traveled globally, had no aftertaste limiting consumption, and needed no retail space or rent.** See's could never expand beyond California despite repeated attempts, while Coke is sold everywhere except Cuba and North Korea. Unlike fudge, a person can drink five Cokes a day for life without monotony. Compare See's 65% return on invested capital with Coke's even better economics. _[Coca-Cola, See's Candies, McDonald's]_ — [2016-05-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfxOvdiac94)
- **The runway matters more than past growth: humans need 64 ounces of water a day, prefer flavored water, and Coke could plausibly capture half the flavored half, giving decades of volume growth.** Buffett and Munger looked at unit volume, number of humans, GDP growth and per-capita consumption (Mexico is highest in the world, other countries at 1/100th of that). A 1938 Fortune article said the ride was over, yet $40 invested in Coke in 1938 became 25,000 by 1993. _[Coca-Cola]_ — [2016-05-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfxOvdiac94)
- **Coke's concentrate/syrup model is extraordinarily capital-light because the bottlers and restaurants bear the CapEx while Coke controls syrup pricing.** Of a 25 cent can, Coke gets 6-7 cents at almost no cost, spends about 10% on advertising and keeps 25-30% pretax. In the mid-1980s bottlers spent 1.3 billion a year on CapEx versus Coke's 160 million (about 12%); Coke had 17,000 employees versus half a million at bottlers. The fountain model is even better since restaurants pay 15 cents and charge 2 dollars. Microsoft's model of giving Dell one copy of Windows was even better than syrup. _[Coca-Cola, Microsoft, Dell, McDonald's, Burger King]_ — [2016-05-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfxOvdiac94)
- **Private-label colas can never get traction against Coke because global scale leaves them no room to undercut and because the mouth is a personal space where people won't take the low bid.** Coke makes about 2 cents and the bottler a couple of cents on a 25 cent can, so a competitor with identical costs pricing at 21 cents makes nothing. Virgin Cola and Sam's Choice never worked; humans are creatures of habit and won't switch what goes in their mouths. _[Coca-Cola, Virgin Cola, Sam's Choice, Wrigley]_ — [2016-05-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfxOvdiac94)
- **Brand spending compounds across decades and is subsidized by others; Buffett said even 100 billion could not take away Coke's market leadership.** Coke has always spent under 10% of revenue on branding; the cans, red trucks, painted restaurants in rural India and China, and FIFA/Olympics/Disney sponsorships are largely paid by bottlers and exploit Munger's association tendency. What Coke spends in 2016 still has residual effect 50 years out, and red and yellow are primary colors humans are drawn to. _[Coca-Cola, McDonald's, Wells Fargo]_ — [2016-05-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfxOvdiac94)
- **Insurance is a good business because of float but has commodity attributes, and owning one taught him he would much rather own See's Candies.** Dhandho bought a Louisiana workers' comp insurer with about 60 million in premiums in five states. Buyers treat insurance like a tax and take the cheapest bid, so the economics are nothing like Coke's. _[Dhandho Holdings, See's Candies]_ — [2016-05-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfxOvdiac94)
- **Category one of 10-100 baggers is businesses with huge tailwinds, deep moats, long runways, high ROE, no debt, that an idiot can run; buy them, forget the PE ratio and hold forever.** Examples are See's Candies, Coca-Cola (poorly managed for decades of its 100-year history), Moody's, Visa, MasterCard, American Express and Maotai in China. He has never had one of these in his portfolio; if he gets one he will never sell. _[See's Candies, Coca-Cola, Moody's, Visa, MasterCard, American Express, Maotai]_ — [2016-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jo1XgDJCkh4)
- **Category two is the same tailwind/moat/high-ROE businesses that cannot be run by idiots but do have great management, such as Amazon, Costco, Geico, Kotak, Blue Dart, Restaurant Brands and Domino's.** These franchises have phenomenal economics but need solid management on top to keep them; they produced the massive runs he saw with Blue Dart and Kotak in India. _[Amazon, Costco, Geico, Kotak Mahindra Bank, Blue Dart, Satyam Computers, Restaurant Brands, Yum Brands, Domino's Pizza, McDonald's]_ — [2016-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jo1XgDJCkh4)
- **Category 1 multi-baggers are businesses with such wide, deep moats that idiots can run them; they rarely get cheap enough for a cheapskate to buy.** Examples: Coca-Cola, See's Candies, Moody's, Visa, MasterCard, American Express, beer and tobacco companies (human vices). Coke grew nonstop for 125 years despite decades of poor managers. He admits he almost never owns these because he shops the bargain bin. _[Coca-Cola, See's Candies, Moody's, Visa, MasterCard, American Express]_ — [2016-11-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IOoaNYQHaYY)
- **If the 2008 financial crisis could not destroy Moody's moat, nothing will; a moat that survives its worst-case seismic event is the ultimate one to own.** Moody's charges 10-30x its cost to rate debt; an analyst paid $200k brings in ~$5M revenue; there are 50,000+ rated debt instruments vs ~5,000 stocks. Despite selling 'poison ratings' in 2008, fines and regulatory attack, the stock went from a $60 2007 high to nearly double. He regrets navel-gazing instead of buying in 2008-10 and says next time he will call his broker. _[Moody's, S&P]_ — [2016-11-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IOoaNYQHaYY)
- **Category 2 multi-baggers are great franchises that need competent, non-idiot managers; they are more common than category 1 but their moats are less robust.** Examples: Amazon, Costco, Geico, Kotak Mahindra Bank, Blue Dart, Satyam, Restaurant Brands International, Yum Brands, Domino's, Marriott (which owns under 1% of the hotels carrying its brands yet gets a cut of every night's stay). He owned three of these (Kotak, Blue Dart, Satyam) and was not smart enough to keep two of them. _[Amazon, Costco, Geico, Kotak Mahindra Bank, Blue Dart, Satyam, Restaurant Brands International, Yum Brands, Domino's Pizza, Marriott International]_ — [2016-11-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IOoaNYQHaYY)

### Management & capital allocation (2)

- **Great business models tend to attract dumb managers who look good anyway, so the arrival of real capital allocators at a great business is the trigger to buy.** Coke had bought shrimp farms in Thailand and other unrelated businesses. From 1981 Roberto Goizueta (marketing plus finance) and Don Keough (operator) dumped everything non-beverage including Paramount Pictures and aggressively bought back stock; Goizueta owned 2.5% of Coke. Buffett watched seven years of this before buying in 1988. Great business plus great manager is the holy grail. _[Coca-Cola, Roberto Goizueta, Donald Keough, Paramount Pictures]_ — [2016-05-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfxOvdiac94)
- **Strategic investors have domain knowledge but usually lack a value-investing sense of price, because great CEOs must be optimistic builders while value investors are skeptics; follow strategic acquirers into other markets only if they are proven capital allocators.** Most CEOs cannot tell when their own stock is undervalued for buybacks. Buffett, John Malone and Sam Zell are good at buying companies, whereas Japanese buyers grossly overpaid for US trophy real estate in the 1980s by anchoring on their own bubble. He admits his own skepticism about what could go wrong is why he sold winners too early. _[Warren Buffett, John Malone, Sam Zell, Starwood]_ — [2016-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jo1XgDJCkh4)

### Markets, cycles & macro (2)

- **Shipping and office real estate go through perpetual boom-bust cycles because owners extrapolate current rates to infinity, order at the top, and scrap at the bottom, so capacity shrinks exactly when rates are about to go exponential.** Around 2002 Frontline owned 70 of the world's 400 VLCCs, all on daily charters ranging from $5,000 to $300,000 a day, losing money below $12-13,000 and earning supernormal profits above $30-40,000. He bought at about $6 when rates were $5-10,000 a day, sold at $9, and it would have been 30-35x had he held; ship owners will never learn because human nature does not change. _[Frontline, John Fredriksen, The Shipping Man]_ — [2016-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jo1XgDJCkh4)
- **Shipping's boom-bust cycle is structural: ship owners project present rates to infinity, order ships at peak rates, and the 3-4 year build lag means new supply arrives together and crushes rates, which triggers scrapping and sets up the next boom.** VLCC spot rates range from $5-6k/day (loss-making) to $300k+/day; above $30k the company makes a lot of money. Old rust-buckets get scrapped for 10-20% of original cost when rates collapse, and after Exxon Valdez (1992 double-hull mandate) single hulls were scrapped even faster. Same dynamic as class-A office buildings. _[Frontline, Exxon Valdez]_ — [2016-11-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IOoaNYQHaYY)

### Stock case studies (9)

- **Berkshire's Coke purchase was a massive concentrated bet at a non-cheap price: 1.3 billion, about one fourth of Berkshire's book value, with the last shares bought at 25 times trailing earnings.** Bought between 1988 and 1990, the position has not been touched for nearly 30 years and Pabrai expects it won't be even after Buffett and Munger are gone. Market cap at purchase was roughly 15-20 billion versus about 190 billion in 2016. _[Coca-Cola, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2016-05-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfxOvdiac94)
- **Fiat Chrysler in 2016 is an IPSCO-like bet: at $6 and change with management guiding to roughly $5 of earnings in 2018, it is priced at 1.2 times one year's earnings, so he will hold to 2018 and see.** The company has $130 billion in car sales and Jeep sales in China expected to rise about five times in three years. At 5-7x earnings the stock would be 5-7x his money. _[Fiat Chrysler, Jeep]_ — [2016-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jo1XgDJCkh4)
- **Teck Cominco in 2008 was a classic low-risk/high-uncertainty situation: a 90% drop in seven weeks over a bridge loan on world-class low-cost mines that banks would rather extend than seize.** The stock went from $50 to $4; he bought at $4-5 and sold at $30, a 7x in a few months, after China came in as an investor; it later went to $50. _[Teck Cominco]_ — [2016-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jo1XgDJCkh4)
- **Category four is bankruptcies, reorganizations, public and busted LBOs and special situations, where following a grave dancer like Sam Zell generally goes well.** Zell and Martin Whitman bought Mission Insurance's $630 million of NOLs for about $30 million around 1998-99, then a barge company that also went bankrupt, then a waste-to-energy company with $2 billion of assets and debt for $30 million (Danielson Holding). Pabrai bought at $9 after it rose from $1, doubled in 13 months and sold; from $1 it became a 40x. _[Sam Zell, Martin Whitman, Mission Insurance, Danielson Holding, Pritzkers]_ — [2016-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jo1XgDJCkh4)
- **Category five is 'upside without downside', or playing a bubble by buying a cheap sound business that owns a free option on the mania.** In the late 1990s Silicon Valley Bank traded slightly above book value while holding undisclosed warrants from every dotcom borrower; he made 2.5x in 2.5 years and would have made 5x with one more year. CMGI, an internet incubator bought just above book, went 100x and turned $100,000 into $10 million; he sold 20-30% off the top. _[Silicon Valley Bank, CMGI, Amazon, Yahoo, pets.com]_ — [2016-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jo1XgDJCkh4)
- **Fiat Chrysler is a current IPSCO-like 'set it and forget it' bet: a sub-$10B market cap against management's guidance of $5.50+ EPS and net-cash balance sheet in 2018.** Stock under $7 vs guided 2018 EPS of $5.50 implies ~1.3x P/E; management guides 2018 EBIT over 9B euros while the street models ~3B. The 2014-2018 plan has been delivered 'in spades' for three years; Jeep output rose from ~250k in 2009 to ~1.4M in 2016 with China targeted at 500k by 2018. He admits a 'man crush' on CEO Sergio Marchionne clouds his view and stresses it is not a stock tip. Of Value Line's 1,700 companies usually only one or two trade below a P/E of two. _[Fiat Chrysler, Sergio Marchionne, Jeep, IPSCO]_ — [2016-11-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IOoaNYQHaYY)
- **Blue-chip cyclicals with bridge-loan overhangs can collapse 90% in weeks because their natural 'widows and orphans' shareholder base flees; banks would rather extend and pretend than liquidate.** Teck Cominco fell from $45 to $4 in 10-12 weeks in 2008 after a debt-funded metallurgical coal acquisition. He bought under $5 as a 2% bet in a basket of commodity plays (no losers), a Chinese strategic investor bought a stake two months later, and he sold at ~$35 for a 7x in a year before it hit $55. He missed the repeat opportunity when it fell below $5 again in early 2016. _[Teck Cominco, Teck Resources]_ — [2016-11-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IOoaNYQHaYY)
- **Category 4 is bankruptcies, reorganizations, public LBOs and special situations, where tax-code masters like Sam Zell create unusual dynamics.** Zell bought bankrupt Mission Insurance's $650M of NOLs for $30M, renamed it Danielson Holdings (Marty Whitman chairman), married it to a barge company that then went bankrupt ('bankruptcy to the power of bankruptcy'), then bought a waste-to-energy business that became Covanta. Pabrai bought at ~$9 via two rights offerings and sold in 18 months for ~90%; holding would have been a 4x. He names Buffett, Jay Pritzker, Zell and Leucadia as tax-code experts. _[Sam Zell, Covanta, Danielson Holdings, Mission Insurance, Marty Whitman, Leucadia, Jay Pritzker]_ — [2016-11-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IOoaNYQHaYY)
- **Captive finance arms of manufacturers like John Deere, Ford and GM are remarkably stable, earning more nearly every year even through 2008-10, and deserve at least 15x earnings.** John Deere's finance arm has made money every year since 1992 in a nearly straight line while equipment earnings swung. GM Financial earns ~$1B, guided to $2B in a few years (worth ~$30B) and GM's China JV produces ~$2B a year like clockwork; together ~$4B is worth at least $60B, yet GM trades under $50B with $20B cash, ignoring trucks, Cadillac and parts. That is why he owns GM. He adds that the market is there to serve you, not instruct you: value is its own catalyst and he has never done catalyst investing. _[GM, GM Financial, GMAC, John Deere, Ford Credit]_ — [2016-11-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IOoaNYQHaYY)

### Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US (1)

- **India honored its promise to let foreign capital exit tax-free: $15,000 in Satyam came back as $1.5 million with no questions asked.** Skeptical of exchange controls in 1995, he allocated only $30,000 across four Indian stocks and had to fly to Mumbai to open accounts and receive physical certificates. He sold Satyam within 5% of its all-time high at over 100x earnings and the money was wired out flawlessly. _[Satyam Computers]_ — [2016-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jo1XgDJCkh4)

### Psychology & temperament (9)

- **Buffett and Munger succeeded because of three traits: extreme patience, extreme decisiveness when opportunity appears, and no concern about being different from the crowd.** Pabrai channels Peter Kaufman's framing: patience must be bliss not agony (you should be happy watching paint dry), decisiveness means betting big rather than a 2% position when a rare opportunity appears, and being different is the hardest for humans. He believes these traits are largely inborn and you can't convert a high-speed trader into this model. _[Peter Kaufman, Charlie Munger, Warren Buffett]_ — [2016-05-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfxOvdiac94)
- **Ignore a security's past performance and avoid anchoring; focus only on the future.** Pabrai admits he is guilty of anchoring on past performance. Buffett and Munger put a quarter of their capital into Coke a hundred years after it was formed without being tainted by how much it had already grown. _[Coca-Cola]_ — [2016-05-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfxOvdiac94)
- **Study businesses for the sake of understanding how the world works, not to decide whether to invest, because commitment bias pushes you to act after spending time.** Reading without a transaction in mind builds wisdom rather than smartness; Munger had insights on Valeant without reading its reports that hedge funds with armies of analysts lacked. Set your life up with large chunks of reading time. _[Valeant, Charlie Munger]_ — [2016-05-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfxOvdiac94)
- **People subconsciously detect lies, so eliminate even small white lies; when choosing between truth and diplomacy, choose truth.** From David Hawkins' 'Power vs. Force', read about 20 years earlier: you feel weak around a used car salesman and strong around the Dalai Lama or Buffett and Munger; telling his wife candidly that a dress could be better cost some dates but made the relationship stronger. _[David Hawkins]_ — [2016-09-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FO5V7jcBNMM)
- **Humans do not care what the truth is; they care that you tell the truth, and they forgive even egregious failures when you own them.** In 2008 his funds lost two-thirds of their value; instead of blaming the crisis he detailed his own mistakes to the 450-500 investor families and received only about two phone calls and a couple of emails, mostly supportive. _[Pabrai Investment Funds]_ — [2016-09-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FO5V7jcBNMM)
- **Every stock he buys goes down first, what Bruce Berkowitz calls 'premature accumulation', so he is used to it and does not sell on the initial drop.** Tesoro fell from $7.50 to $1.33 within three months of purchase and Frontline fell from $6 to $4 within weeks; in both cases he sat tight and the stocks recovered many-fold. _[Bruce Berkowitz, Tesoro Petroleum, Frontline]_ — [2016-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jo1XgDJCkh4)
- **The number one skill an investor needs is extreme patience: you make money by waiting, not by buying or selling, and the business is best suited to gentlemen and gentlewomen of leisure.** Blue Dart did nothing for six years, he sold it, and it had its run in the next 15 years. Munger says you don't make money when you buy or sell but by waiting; every trade tends to hurt the investor. _[Charlie Munger, Blue Dart]_ — [2016-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jo1XgDJCkh4)
- **Everything about the market is designed to make you active, so set up tricks like never submitting orders while the market is open.** He sends orders to his broker after midnight for next-day execution when nothing is moving, and rarely trades during market hours. Brokers make nothing if you buy one company and keep it forever. — [2016-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jo1XgDJCkh4)
- **Suffering comes from our reaction to events, not the events themselves, so down-and-out periods should be treated as temporary conditions like collapsed shipping rates.** His parents went through multiple bankruptcies in his childhood yet his mother never got depressed; his father paid a Hindu astrologer he knew was a fraud because 'he is my rope' out of the well. He cites 'if wealth is lost nothing is lost, if health is lost something is lost, if character is lost everything is lost.' — [2016-11-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IOoaNYQHaYY)

### Buffett & Munger lessons (7)

- **See's Candies was the education in brands and pricing power that made the Coke investment possible; without See's they would never have bought Coke.** Bought in 1972 for 25 million (Buffett would have walked at 30 million) when it earned 2 million on 8 million book; by 1984 it earned 13 million on 20 million book with only about 2% annual unit growth. Buffett's only input was setting the price list every January 1st, raising prices far above inflation with no loss of sales. Munger says they were 'barely smart enough' to buy it and could have paid 100 million. _[See's Candies, Coca-Cola, Chuck Huggins]_ — [2016-05-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfxOvdiac94)
- **Munger's Glotz inversion: build a 2 trillion dollar company from 2 million by 2034 via naming, cold beverages, association and social proof, fountains plus bottles, aura of secrecy, and by not losing the brand name, not creating envy, and not changing the flavor.** The math: 7 billion humans, 64 ounces a day, half flavored, half of that to Coke at about 4 cents a serving yields roughly 117 billion in profit and a 2 trillion market cap. Coke in fact violated the inversion rules: it lost the 'Cola' half of its name, signed fixed-price syrup contracts with bottlers around 1900, drew territories by a day's horse ride, and the New Coke fiasco responded to John Sculley's Pepsi Challenge. _[Coca-Cola, Pepsi, John Sculley, Charlie Munger]_ — [2016-05-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfxOvdiac94)
- **Be aware of and leverage Munger's latticework of mental models, because our brains have evolutionary distortions of reality.** He recommends Munger's 'Psychology of Human Misjudgment' speech and picks three of the roughly 30 models that had a significant positive impact on his life. _[Charlie Munger]_ — [2016-09-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FO5V7jcBNMM)
- **The Munger approach of waiting for businesses you love to drop in price is superior to Graham's approach of buying whatever is most discounted, so make a list of remarkable assets and the prices at which they become exciting.** Graham goes into the supermarket and buys the most heavily discounted item; Munger keeps going back until the thing he loves goes on sale. The Munger way requires more patience and self-knowledge, then you wait for the world to come to you. _[Ben Graham, Charlie Munger]_ — [2016-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jo1XgDJCkh4)
- **Run the Buffett-Munger model with no staff and no analysts: do not delegate investment research, because a hired analyst's ideas would be rejected 95% of the time and you would eventually buy things you don't believe in to be nice.** The only way to add people is to give them their own pools of capital with full autonomy, as Buffett did with Ted Weschler and Todd Combs at $9 billion each. He has about 400 investor families, takes no calls or meetings before they invest, and is 'open for business' two days a year at annual meetings. The first violation he looks for in any investment operation is team size above one. _[Warren Buffett, Ted Weschler, Todd Combs]_ — [2016-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jo1XgDJCkh4)
- **Each investor gets a limited quota of truly great businesses in a lifetime; the key is to recognize when one is in your portfolio and not be in a hurry to act.** He credits Charlie Munger with this observation. The best action when you own such a business is 'to take an afternoon nap, not put a sell order in.' _[Charlie Munger]_ — [2016-11-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IOoaNYQHaYY)
- **Munger's grocery-store approach (find what you love, wait for it to go on sale) beats Graham's (buy whatever is most discounted), though Pabrai admits he can never bring himself to pay full price for a great business.** He praises Tom Russo and Tom Gayner for playing only in categories 1 and 2, with the mild critique that Russo shows less price discipline. Buffett called not selling Coke at 40x earnings in 1999-2000 a mistake in hindsight, but Berkshire will likely hold Coke for decades more, which may be wise. _[Charlie Munger, Ben Graham, Tom Russo, Tom Gayner, Warren Buffett, Coca-Cola]_ — [2016-11-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IOoaNYQHaYY)

### Mistakes & lessons learned (6)

- **His biggest mistake by dollars was Delta Financial in 2008, which went bankrupt and cost about 60 million, roughly 10% of assets; mistakes are blessings if studied.** Earlier, his dot-com venture Digital Disruptors in 1999-2000 lost him about 2 million personally and outside investors 3 million, but those lessons helped Pabrai Funds sidestep trouble in its early years. John Templeton said you'll be wrong one third of the time; even Buffett and Munger have many mistakes such as Gen Re but were right on the large ones. _[Delta Financial, Digital Disruptors, Gen Re, John Templeton]_ — [2016-05-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfxOvdiac94)
- **He was smart enough to buy hundred baggers but not smart enough to hold them; four of his 14 stocks from 1995 eventually rose more than 50 times and he sold almost all of them early.** Blue Dart (bought for $7,700) became a 60x he sold after six years of doing nothing; Kotak Mahindra went up 50x after he sold; Satyam went from 45 to 7,000 rupees (130-140x) and CMGI went 100x, both cashed out in the dotcom bubble. Blue Dart he only held 21 years by accident because one certificate was flagged as fake. _[Blue Dart, Kotak Mahindra, Satyam Computers, SkyPack, CMGI]_ — [2016-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jo1XgDJCkh4)
- **He missed most of Tesoro's 200x run because he sold at a double after a 10x from the bottom, even though he already knew from the conference calls that CEO Bruce Smith was an exceptional manager.** No new US refinery has been built in 30 years due to NIMBY, and state-specific fuel standards make refining less of a commodity business. He bought 10% of assets at $7.50, watched it fall to $1.33 (taking the portfolio down 8%), and sold at $15; from purchase it eventually rose about 40x. _[Tesoro Petroleum, Bruce Smith]_ — [2016-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jo1XgDJCkh4)
- **Cyclical businesses run by gifted managers can become 30-200 baggers from the trough, so 'take the double and leave' in a cyclical can be a costly mistake.** He bought Tesoro in mid-2002 at $7.50 (down from $30; $480M market cap vs >$1B estimated value), watched it fall to $1.33 ($85M market cap), held, and sold at $15 for a 100% gain. Tesoro's market cap is now $10B plus a $6B Tesoro Logistics spin-off and dividends exceeding the original market cap; 200x from the bottom tick and 30x+ from his price. He under-appreciated CEO Bruce Smith. He also notes US refining is not a pure commodity: no new refinery in 30 years (NIMBY) and state-specific blends make each refinery unique. _[Tesoro, Tesoro Logistics, Bruce Smith]_ — [2016-11-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IOoaNYQHaYY)
- **Selling Frontline at 90% of liquidation value was a mistake born of a juvenile understanding of human nature's swings; with 'Frontline 2.0' he will ride past liquidation value.** Bought Frontline in 2002 at ~$6 against ~$9 liquidation value with debt at the ship level (lenders could only repossess ships). Had he held, $56 in dividends plus the Ship Finance spin-off ($24 in dividends, $14 stock) would have made ~$130, nearly 25x. He has found an unnamed shipping company trading at half liquidation value that he is now researching. This time, once it doubles he may take the principal off and let the rest ride with a taper, since a cyclical is not a Coke and will crash and burn someday. _[Frontline, Ship Finance]_ — [2016-11-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IOoaNYQHaYY)
- **Passing on Apple in 2007 despite an eloquent pitch about the app store and changing human habits was a costly blind spot caused by refusing anything above a single-digit P/E.** A VC friend and fund investor explained the iPhone ecosystem and 'habit economy' in 2007. In 2016 Apple trades at under 12-13x earnings ex-cash with unit sales dropping but earnings rising because over a billion devices carry apps; he still finds a shipping company at half liquidation value more tangible than Apple at 12x, which 'may be a mistake but is the way I'm wired.' _[Apple, Blackberry, Nokia, Uber]_ — [2016-11-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IOoaNYQHaYY)

### Career, entrepreneurship & life (6)

- **If you are not fired up on Monday morning, don't go to work and hit the reset button; every reset has led to higher highs.** He ran TransTech from 1990 to 1999, lost interest after discovering Buffett in 1994, and his YPO forum helped him hire a CEO and write a job application to Buffett (rejected in a week). He sold TransTech a month after the CEO joined and offered a 40-year non-compete. He also copied the Buffett partnership zero-fee, 6% hurdle structure, which nobody had replicated in 30 years, and told his first eight investors their mission was to bring in friends, family and fools. _[TransTech, Pabrai Investment Funds, Buffett Partnerships]_ — [2016-05-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfxOvdiac94)
- **Trust, not contracts, runs the world, and the payoff to trustworthiness is exponential: lying 1 in 1,000 times versus 1 in 100 makes an exponential difference in life outcomes.** Trust takes 5, 10 or 20 years to establish and has been a compounding tailwind for him; he cites Trump's 'Teflon' ratings as evidence that people reward candor over PR-packaged talk. — [2016-09-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FO5V7jcBNMM)
- **Do not quit your job to start a business; build it in the 'second 40 hours' of the 168-hour week and resign only once revenue and cash flow show traction.** At 24 he worked on TransTech on evenings and weekends, deliberately performing just above firing level, and resigned after 11 months in 1991 once he had clients; his boss and his boss's boss became Pabrai Funds investors in 2001. _[TransTech, Pabrai Investment Funds]_ — [2016-09-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FO5V7jcBNMM)
- **You can attempt the second-40-hours startup five times and fail five times at no real risk, because today's tech and app businesses need what is between your ears, not capital.** He tried two or three ideas before TransTech that never got traction, losing only $3-4,000 each; work with people you like, admire and trust, as Buffett says. _[TransTech]_ — [2016-09-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=FO5V7jcBNMM)
- **The rules for loving this business are no staff, no trading during office hours, and not even going to work when the market is open; keep the calendar empty as Buffett advised.** He wakes at 9 or 9:30 with no alarm, has 30 books on his desk and no meetings; the key to life is to find CRISIL, the Moody's of India, and go to sleep for 20 years. Young managers should spend less than they earn, compound the difference to independence and become their own boss. _[Warren Buffett, CRISIL]_ — [2016-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Jo1XgDJCkh4)
- **Pick investing as a calling only if you would do it for a schoolteacher's pay; your external life must align with your internal wiring or you will not go far.** In 1999, via YPO, industrial psychologists did a 360 analysis and gave him a 20-page 'owner's manual' at age 34 for $2,000, concluding that running his 170-person IT company was far from his wiring while Pabrai Funds fit perfectly. One psychologist became an early fund investor because he had 'cracked your brain open.' He recommends Jiro Dreams of Sushi and Life is Beautiful. _[YPO, Pabrai Investment Funds, Jiro Dreams of Sushi]_ — [2016-11-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IOoaNYQHaYY)

### Philanthropy & Dakshana (1)

- **Large inheritances are a burden on kids, so he started giving 2% of assets a year in his early forties to have years to make mistakes and learn.** Dakshana was set up in 2007 when net worth crossed 50 million; it prepares very poor, gifted Indian kids for the IIT entrance exam, forcing government subsidies once they get in. They bought a 110-acre campus near Pune for 10 million (8 million paid off) and half the funding now comes from outside donors. _[Dakshana Foundation]_ — [2016-05-24](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jfxOvdiac94)

## 2017

3 talks, 75 ideas.

**Talks**

- 2017-06-07 · [Mohnish Pabrai Lecture at Univ. of California, Irvine (UCI), June 7, 2017](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bLjoL5zhBxA) · 25 ideas
- 2017-11-30 · [Mohnish Pabrai Lecture at Boston College (Carroll School of Mgmt) - Nov 30, 2017](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_1aGen3q2_g) · 25 ideas
- 2017-12-22 · [Mohnish Pabrai Lecture at Peking University (Guanghua School of Mgmt) - Dec 22, 2017](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=z74NaYRyMJo) · 25 ideas


### Cloning & learning from great investors (4)

- **Mindlessly cloning the Buffett Partnership's fee structure - zero management fee, 6% hurdle, 25% above it - created a moat competitors cannot cross.** Started in 1999 with $1 million from eight friends using rules copied from Lowenstein's biography; at $840 million a 1-and-20 shop would collect $8.4 million 'just for breathing'. A manager earning 10% with 2-and-20 fees leaves 6.4%, so 36% of returns vanish in friction, which is why most active managers trail the S&P. _[Pabrai Investment Funds, Buffett Partnership, Warren Buffett]_ — [2017-11-30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_1aGen3q2_g)
- **A team in an investment operation is an oxymoron: you cannot delegate any part of the investment process, so he runs $840 million with no analysts and no full-time employees.** Total payroll for part-time admins is under $150-200k a year. If he had 10 high-IQ analysts presenting three great-looking ideas a week, he is almost sure results would be worse. _[Pabrai Investment Funds]_ — [2017-11-30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_1aGen3q2_g)
- **The best source of ideas in recent years has been unsolicited emails from 'Joe Public', not analysts.** His 9x Indian stock came from an elegant analysis emailed by Parry Pasricha, whom he has never met, producing about $170 million in gains so far. He reads printed emails for 15 minutes a day at 11am; Value Investors Club and SumZero are other sources. _[Rain Industries, Parry Pasricha, Value Investors Club, SumZero]_ — [2017-11-30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_1aGen3q2_g)
- **Be a relentlessly curious student: meet companies to learn, not to invest, and go to sleep a little wiser each day as Munger says.** On his India trip he planned to meet six companies including a housing finance firm with a long list of questions, purely to understand things better when he leaves; once enough data is taken in, occasionally things fit and you can act. _[Charlie Munger]_ — [2017-12-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=z74NaYRyMJo)

### Circle of competence & checklists (8)

- **Filter every stock tip by two numbers: unless the gap between current price and claimed value is at least 5x, preferably 10x, throw it away.** Two years earlier an unknown sender's 10-page write-up showed a 10x delta; after two hours of checking every number he put $20M of Pabrai Funds into the Hyderabad-based company, now worth north of $50M and possibly $100-200M, having never met management. — [2017-06-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bLjoL5zhBxA)
- **Skip the Fortune 500 entirely and go fishing where the fish are: hated sectors, unloved countries, distressed situations.** GE is followed by two dozen analysts and no report will show a 5x or 10x gap, so he dismisses the thousand largest US businesses in two seconds; Buffett's too-hard box holds 98% of what he sees; Qatar's tanking market is a better hunting ground than GE. _[GE, Qatar]_ — [2017-06-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bLjoL5zhBxA)
- **Stay within a narrow circle of competence: specialization is a huge advantage and the narrower and more intense, the better.** Munger's friend John Arrillaga became a billionaire investing only in real estate within a few blocks of Stanford, buying when pessimistic, selling when euphoric, never levered; Pabrai says China largely falls in his too-hard pile (one China and one Hong Kong holding). _[John Arrillaga]_ — [2017-06-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bLjoL5zhBxA)
- **Only invest in businesses you can explain to a five-year-old in two minutes; take a pass on anything like Amazon whose cash flows to 2045 nobody can estimate.** The market prices Amazon to the penny, yet the odds it has precisely figured out cash flows from 2018 to 2045 are as close to zero as imaginable; even Bezos doesn't know them. _[Amazon, Jeff Bezos]_ — [2017-11-30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_1aGen3q2_g)
- **Be extremely unreasonable in equity markets - never compromise on your criteria, because you always have the option of sitting in cash and only acting when all the ducks line up.** He cites Eli Broad's book The Art of Being Unreasonable; with fear and greed cycling across tens of thousands of listed businesses, something will show up if you keep reading. _[Eli Broad]_ — [2017-11-30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_1aGen3q2_g)
- **China is outside his circle of competence, so despite 400% on Maotai he holds only one Chinese stock and will not chase more without help.** Managing about $870 million, he says if he focused on China he would 'get his head handed to him' because he cannot judge culture, nuances or honesty; there is only one Maotai in the world, and he asks students to send Chinese ideas to mp@pabraifunds.com. _[Kweichow Moutai, Pabrai Investment Funds]_ — [2017-12-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=z74NaYRyMJo)
- **Buffett's 'too hard' box, where 98-99% of ideas go, is the model: wait for rare anomalies within your circle of competence and act only then.** He saw the too-hard box on Buffett's desk during an office tour with Guy Spier. His example is a US steel company at $45 with $15 cash per share, no debt, and contracted earnings of $15 a share for two years; the stock rose to 75, then 90, and he sold at 150 when a buyer emerged. _[Warren Buffett, Guy Spier]_ — [2017-12-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=z74NaYRyMJo)
- **John Arrillaga became a billionaire investing only in real estate within one mile of Stanford, proving a tiny circle of competence and specialization beat breadth.** Arrillaga never used much debt, bought when things went down and sold when everyone got euphoric; a Minnesota-only fund similarly beat the market. Having a lot of things to look at is not an advantage; become really good at a few things and wait. _[John Arrillaga, Charlie Munger]_ — [2017-12-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=z74NaYRyMJo)

### Valuation & margin of safety (4)

- **There is always a bull market somewhere: with ~100,000 listed stocks globally, several hundred are always trading far below intrinsic value.** Markets are almost but not fully efficient, and there is a huge gap between those two statements; Buffett says he'd be a bum on the street with a tin cup if markets were efficient. — [2017-06-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bLjoL5zhBxA)
- **Risk and uncertainty are different things, and the best setups combine very low risk with very high uncertainty.** Low-uncertainty businesses like a funeral home in Peoria are priced like bonds; in 2001-02 Frontline, with ~40% of the global VLCC fleet on spot rates, fell to $3 when rates collapsed to $10-12K/day versus ~$11 of distressed liquidation value, and he doubled his money in six months. _[Frontline]_ — [2017-06-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bLjoL5zhBxA)
- **Buy what is hated and unloved, and judge by the long term rather than one or two quarters.** He bought an Indian company with a market cap under $100 million earning $50 million a year that the market hated, and bought Maotai when its price fell during the anti-corruption crackdown because government consumption would normalize over time. _[Kweichow Moutai]_ — [2017-12-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=z74NaYRyMJo)
- **He never buys anything unless he believes it is worth at least double its price.** If he buys at 20 RMB it must be worth at least 40; he tells students not to send ideas where 80 RMB is worth 110, only ones where 80 is worth 200 or 300, because everything he buys goes down first and a high compounding rate needs big discounts. — [2017-12-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=z74NaYRyMJo)

### Portfolio concentration & selling (6)

- **Few bets, big bets, infrequent bets is one of the core tenets of value investing.** From the late sixties to late eighties Buffett, Munger and Guerin made only about five meaningful decisions (control of Blue Chip, See's, Wesco, Buffalo News, Freddie Mac), roughly one every four or five years; the 60% of Blue Chip bought for about $24 million is today worth about $60 billion. _[Blue Chip Stamps, See's Candies, Wesco Financial, Buffalo News, Freddie Mac, Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger, Rick Guerin]_ — [2017-06-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bLjoL5zhBxA)
- **Keep a few percent of net worth in cash so you can act in size when a rare no-brainer shows up.** Rick Guerin says keep $10 million in checking in case something shows up; Pabrai rephrases it as keeping one, two or five percent of net worth waiting to be deployed when extreme odds appear. _[Rick Guerin]_ — [2017-06-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bLjoL5zhBxA)
- **For mere mortals, about 10 stocks in a few different industries is plenty; 50 stocks will not help you.** Munger's example is owning fractions of the McDonald's franchise, Ford dealership and best office and apartment buildings in one small town; the right number depends on conviction and moat durability, since almost all moats erode over time. _[Charlie Munger, McDonald's, Ford]_ — [2017-06-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bLjoL5zhBxA)
- **Don't cut the flowers and water the weeds: he will not trim a winner just because it has become 35-40% of a fund.** PIF3 (about $240 million) has roughly $90 million in one Indian company that went about 9x from under $11 million invested 30 months earlier, plus about $45 million in Fiat; two stocks are $135 million. He expected 5-10x in five years in 2015 and is approaching 10x in 2.5 years. A 20% drop 'bounces off'; only at 60% would he even think about it. You really learn a business only after you own it; his understanding has gone up 3-4x since purchase, revealing better management and a wider moat than he thought. _[Rain Industries, Fiat Chrysler, PIF3]_ — [2017-11-30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_1aGen3q2_g)
- **After 2008 he moved from a 10x10 portfolio to three position sizes of 2%, 5% or 10%, using 2% baskets when a whole sector is cheap and he cannot pick the best name.** In the crisis the entire commodity sector collapsed, so he put 2% into a number of commodity companies and had no losers. He still prefers 10% positions because too many stocks means you know each less; Maotai started at 3-4% because of culture concerns and has grown to about 10% of the fund. _[Kweichow Moutai]_ — [2017-12-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=z74NaYRyMJo)
- **Knowing is not enough; conviction is shown by what percent of your net worth you put in, and position sizing is the hardest question after the decision to invest.** A Goldman banker who did the Tencent IPO never bought a share. Guy Spier put only 0.2% of his $160 million fund into Maotai when Pabrai pitched it, while Li Lu (Yong Pingan) would have put 25%. Pabrai's own Maotai checklist: liquor company with a thousand-year brand, no competition, limited supply, and a fifth of the world's population rising. _[Kweichow Moutai, Tencent, Guy Spier]_ — [2017-12-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=z74NaYRyMJo)

### Compounding & long-term holding (8)

- **Finding just one five-bagger every ten years turns a few thousand dollars into tens of millions over a lifetime.** $5,000 at 20 compounding 5x per decade becomes 25K at 30, 125K at 40, 625K at 50, 3M at 60, 15M at 70 and 75M at 80; with 20,000 working hours per decade you should be able to find one. — [2017-06-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bLjoL5zhBxA)
- **Avoid leverage; the most controllable element of compounding is the length of the runway, so spend less than you earn and start very early.** His daughter's $5,000 IRA at 18 compounding 15% (doubling every five years, 2^10 = 1024) becomes $5 million tax-deferred at 68; never cash out a 401k, never carry credit card debt, and even an index fund doubling every ten years yields 32x over 50 years. — [2017-06-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=bLjoL5zhBxA)
- **Compounding has three variables - starting capital, rate of compounding and length of runway - and you must become fluent in doing this math in your head.** Rule of 72: 7% doubles in 10 years, 10% in 7 years; ten doubles is 2^10 = 1024, roughly 1,000x. Buffett still does all his compounding math in his head with no computer in his office. $24 for Manhattan in 1626 compounding at 7% would be about $13 trillion by 2016 - the Native Americans just had an incompetent investment officer. _[Warren Buffett, Buffett Partnership]_ — [2017-11-30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_1aGen3q2_g)
- **Because compounding is geometric, the vast majority of wealth arrives late - so maximize your runway and compound until one day before dying.** Buffett's net worth was under $30 million at 40 and about $300-400 million at 50; 99 and two-thirds percent of it came after age 50. Buffett's only wish is that people say 'man, he was old' when they look at his corpse, and he checked life-expectancy tables from age 16. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2017-11-30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_1aGen3q2_g)
- **His 'COMLB 26' license plate is a mantra: compound $1 million at 26% (doubling every 3 years) for 30 years and it becomes $1 billion.** After selling his IT company in 1994 at age 30 he had about $1 million; from 1995-2000 he compounded north of 70% a year (10x in five years), and Pabrai Funds did about 36% gross from 1999-2007 before losing two-thirds in the financial crisis and recovering from 2009. _[Pabrai Investment Funds, Warren Buffett]_ — [2017-11-30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_1aGen3q2_g)
- **The Rule of 72 and the $24 Manhattan story show that a modest 7% return over long enough periods becomes astronomical.** If the Native Americans had compounded the $24 from 1626 at 7%, doubling every 10 years and adding three zeros per century, they would have about $13 trillion today, versus roughly $100 trillion total US wealth, so they would have come out ahead. He calls the Rule of 72 'elastic math' and says you must train yourself to think geometrically rather than arithmetically. — [2017-12-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=z74NaYRyMJo)
- **Compounding has three variables (starting capital, rate of return, length of runway), and the rate is the only one you truly control, so maximize it and protect your runway by not spending.** He tells 25-year-old students they have a 65-year runway to age 90, and that a Tesla bought today costs 120 million dollars at 15% over 50 years, so skip the Tesla and even the Starbucks; Buffett declines wine at parties and picks up pennies because every penny is the start of another billion. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2017-12-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=z74NaYRyMJo)
