### Cloning & learning from great investors (7)

- **Cloning is an enormously powerful mental model, and because humans are genetically bad at cloning, a shameless cloner gets a huge advantage in life.** In 1999 he photocopied pages of Roger Lowenstein's Buffett biography and told his lawyer to create that partnership structure. Dakshana and the Pabrai Funds fee structure are both clones he could never have invented. Young managers he advises to use zero fees and no team all nod and none of them do it. _[Warren Buffett, Roger Lowenstein, Dakshana Foundation]_ — [2019-02-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_0XPurSI9cQ)
- **The Buffett-partnership 0/6/25 fee structure (no management fee, 6% hurdle, 25% of the excess) is both fairer to investors and a competitive advantage that almost no competitor will copy.** On a 10% return the manager takes 1% versus 3.6% under 2-and-20; compounding at 9% versus 6.4% over 30 years produces an 80-90% difference in ending wealth. After one fund fell 70% in the financial crisis, he collected no fee from 2007 until 2017 and never considered resetting or renegotiating, which he calls unethical. Managing $500 million and returning 20% yields a fee of about $17 million with only half a million of expenses. _[Warren Buffett, Pabrai Investment Funds]_ — [2019-02-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_0XPurSI9cQ)
- **Cloning is one of the most important models: when you see someone doing something smart, just incorporate it.** He could not have come up with the empty calendar or investor-communication ideas himself; he copied them from Warren and Charlie. _[Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger]_ — [2019-05-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kax8XnBU1ik)
- **He needs no analysts because he only needs two or three stocks a year; his source is open source, with ideas emailed by strangers.** Buffett and Munger have zero analysts. Of 50,000 stocks, at least 3,000 are severely underpriced and he needs to understand only three or four. Rain came from a stranger in Vancouver whom he later took to dim sum; he also watches what Li Lu does. _[Li Lu, Rain Industries]_ — [2019-05-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kax8XnBU1ik)
- **The 10 Commandments of Investment Management: no management fees, no investing team, accept being wrong a third of the time, look for hidden P/E-of-1 stocks, never use Excel, always have a rope out of the deepest well, be singularly focused like Arjuna, never short, never use leverage, and be a shameless cloner.** He calls cloning the most important commandment: 'Don't be ashamed to copy the best. After all, it is the road to success.' On shorting he notes that what Tesla shorts forgot was the time scale, not the outcome. _[Tesla]_ — [2019-05-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N0TwWxGxYs0)
- **Never pay for research, third parties or expert networks; do all your own work because that is what Buffett does and anything else is a 'Buffett violation'.** Due diligence has ranged from three hours to three months; he hated the auto industry so much he spent three months trying to find reasons not to buy Fiat Chrysler in 2012 before capitulating, and it is up 8x since. The industry pattern of teams, management fees and diversification 'operates stupidly'. _[Fiat Chrysler, Warren Buffett]_ — [2019-05-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N0TwWxGxYs0)
- **Cloning is a starting point for research, not a buy signal; buying off Dataroma five minutes later deserves to get your head handed to you.** The top two or three high-conviction ideas of great investors have already passed a significant filter, making them a great hunting ground, but many who cloned Buffett on IBM lost money; use it as a basis to form your own intrinsic value view. _[IBM, Warren Buffett, Dataroma]_ — [2019-05-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N0TwWxGxYs0)

### Circle of competence & checklists (6)

- **Even the best analysts are wrong a third of the time, so keep the humility that at least 4 out of 10 decisions will be mistakes and focus on being right on the big ones.** John Templeton said the best analyst is wrong one-third of the time; of the roughly 80 businesses Berkshire bought in 50 years, a third to 40% didn't work out, especially retailers and furniture and jewelry stores after Borsheims and Nebraska Furniture Mart, while Buffett's record in banks and levered institutions is nearly unblemished except Irish banks. Everyone has areas of competence and areas where they are not good. _[John Templeton, Warren Buffett, Berkshire Hathaway, Borsheims, Nebraska Furniture Mart]_ — [2019-02-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_0XPurSI9cQ)
- **The size of your circle of competence does not matter; staying inside it does, and any doubt about understanding a business means stay away.** John Arrillaga became a Forbes 400 billionaire investing only in real estate within a mile of the Stanford campus. You don't need to know a lot of things to do well in investing. _[John Arrillaga, Charlie Munger]_ — [2019-02-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_0XPurSI9cQ)
- **You only truly learn a business after you own it, not when you analyze it.** He bought Rain in 2015 planning to make 5x and sell, but after owning it for three years and meeting the reclusive CEO in Hyderabad, he now wants to hold Rain and Sunteck for 10-15 years as an owner. _[Rain Industries, Sunteck Realty]_ — [2019-05-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kax8XnBU1ik)
- **The model is not to find investments but to find the flimsiest reason to say no as quickly as possible; circle of competence and a 60-second valuation glance kill most ideas.** A pharma company is rejected on the name alone; if it is not near a P/E of 1 it is gone. Ideas that survive get 5 minutes, then 15. A tip that says a stock at 10 is worth 13 is dismissed even granting the thesis, because he wants stocks worth 60 trading at 10. Finding two or three ideas a year is enough. — [2019-05-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N0TwWxGxYs0)
- **A tiny circle of competence is enough to get extremely wealthy; you can trade IQ points for patience and stick-to-your-circle genes.** Munger's friend John Arrillaga became a billionaire developing real estate only within five miles of Stanford, buying when vacancies were high and selling at low cap rates, passing on 99.999% of great investments. Envy of the idiot neighbor making money is detrimental to financial health. _[John Arrillaga, Charlie Munger]_ — [2019-11-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kdGltV0eomU)
- **Don't consciously try to expand your circle of competence; study businesses like HBS case studies and act only when seven moons line up and it is a no-brainer.** He never reads anything on US healthcare, pharma or biotech because the sector is driven by non-market, corrupt forces; you can ignore 80-90% of the economy and still do well, but it is worth understanding Amazon and Google because so much flows through them. _[Amazon, Google]_ — [2019-11-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kdGltV0eomU)

### Valuation & margin of safety (10)

- **It is not enough to buy great businesses; price matters, because a great business bought at 45 times earnings that de-rates to 15 times delivers terrible returns.** Coca-Cola bought in 2000 at about 45x earnings returned roughly 2% a year through 2019 even though the business did well. Microsoft was earning about $10 billion on a $600 billion market cap in 2000, fell to under $200 billion, and produced almost no return until 2013-14; he told early Microsoft employees who became his investors to sell, and none did. _[Coca-Cola, Microsoft]_ — [2019-02-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_0XPurSI9cQ)
- **Markets have an irrational expectation of smoothness and confuse risk with uncertainty, so businesses with low risk but high uncertainty get extreme valuations that an investor can exploit.** Buffett bought the Washington Post at an $80 million market cap that fell to $60 million when private buyers would have paid $400 million; sellers agreed on the value but wouldn't tolerate near-term uncertainty. IPSCO around 2004 traded at $45 with no debt, $15 in cash and $15 a share of contracted after-tax earnings in each of the next two years; it went to $65, then near $90, and a Swedish firm bid $160 for it. _[Washington Post, Warren Buffett, IPSCO]_ — [2019-02-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_0XPurSI9cQ)
- **It is not about the great business, it is about the great investment; a mediocre company can be a great investment and vice versa.** If investing were just about identifying the best-quality businesses it would be a simple game because everyone can see which businesses are great and prices them accordingly. _[Guy Spier, MasterCard, Sunteck Realty]_ — [2019-05-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kax8XnBU1ik)
- **The starting price you pay matters: Coca-Cola at 40x earnings in 2000 returned under 3% a year through 2018 even though it stayed a great business.** Berkshire's Coke went up 12-14x from 1988 to 2000, then the multiple compressed from over 40 to 17. Buffett later acknowledged not selling around 2001-2002 was probably a mistake, though he prefers to be a collector of great businesses and Berkshire's cash math differs. _[Coca-Cola, Berkshire Hathaway, Warren Buffett]_ — [2019-05-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kax8XnBU1ik)
- **Investors should value businesses on the actual operating record, not the stock chart.** Rain's chart was flat from 1991 to 2015, but the record showed bold acquisitions, bankers willing to lend $1B to an Indian company, cyclical trough earnings that were still positive, and consistently well-executed capital projects. _[Rain Industries, Warren Buffett]_ — [2019-05-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kax8XnBU1ik)
- **Don't fixate on discount rates or DCFs; look for obvious no-brainers that hit you over the head with a two-by-four.** Fiat Chrysler had a $5B market cap in 2012 and he thought it could earn $5B a year in five or six years; that was the entire DCF. Munger says he has never seen Buffett run a discounted cash flow. _[Fiat Chrysler, Charlie Munger, Warren Buffett]_ — [2019-05-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N0TwWxGxYs0)
- **IPSCO was third-grade math: $15/share cash plus $30/share of contracted cash flow over two years exceeded a stock price in the forties, so all the plants and know-how came free.** Around 2003-04 the tubular steel maker had no debt, confirmed backlog with locked margins, and even though earnings could go to zero or negative after two years the risk-reward was very favorable. _[IPSCO]_ — [2019-11-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kdGltV0eomU)
- **Heads I win, tails I don't lose much: downside protection is fundamental to every investment, per Buffett's rule number one.** With GrafTech the floor is covered and the upside is hard to gauge; with Fiat Chrysler in 2012 you got all of Chrysler (Jeep, RAM) for free plus a hidden advantage in the 2009 UAW contract signed in 20 minutes under Auto Task Force pressure, which made Detroit one of the cheapest places on the planet to build a car. _[GrafTech, Fiat Chrysler, IPSCO, Warren Buffett]_ — [2019-11-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kdGltV0eomU)
- **Ideas that go from 13 to 18 are not worth my time; I want at least a 3-5x, ideally 5x in five years, though 5x in ten years is fine.** He reviews portfolio companies at least quarterly since real change takes years, and triages incoming writeups in escalating steps of 10 minutes, then 30 minutes, then two hours; a natural gas pitch promising 80x was passed because it was a directional bet on prices. — [2019-11-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kdGltV0eomU)
- **Look at owner earnings after capex; high capex is not a deal killer, and even the capex-heavy auto business gave a 4x in seven years on Fiat excluding Ferrari.** The best businesses like MasterCard, Amazon and Google need no capex, and a Singapore friend refuses any capex business and does fine, but memory players have high capex alongside high owner earnings. _[Fiat Chrysler, Ferrari, Micron, MasterCard, Amazon, Google]_ — [2019-11-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kdGltV0eomU)

### Portfolio concentration & selling (3)

- **Exits are far harder than entrances and his own record on exits is terrible, usually leaving a lot of money on the table; a rough rule is to consider selling near 90% of intrinsic value.** Growing pies beat discounted pies even when bought at a smaller discount, because intrinsic value rises over time and stays above the stock price, letting you hold for a long time. — [2019-05-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N0TwWxGxYs0)
- **In a crisis when ideas arrive like a fire hydrant, a basket of 2% bets makes sense; in normal times go to the 10% maximum once a great opportunity is found.** In 2008-09 his portfolio was down ~70%; he sold Fairfax Financial (which had equity puts and CDS) and businesses at 3x earnings to buy other things at 3x earnings, and made many 2% commodity bets. No stock bought in 2009 lost money and many were 5x-plus. _[Fairfax Financial]_ — [2019-05-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N0TwWxGxYs0)
- **Guy Spier is light years ahead of me at holding: his untouched 2012 Fiat Chrysler bet plus gifted Ferrari shares turned $10 million into roughly $70 million, while I sold Ferrari at $50-120 thinking it was fully priced.** Guy bought 2 million shares at ~$5 (a 5% bet of a ~$200 million fund) and received 200,000 Ferrari shares now worth ~$165 each (~$33 million); Pabrai bought ~12 million shares as a 10% bet, made ~$100 million on Ferrari, but would have had ~$220 million had he held. Ferrari has never spent a dollar on advertising in 70-plus years. _[Fiat Chrysler, Ferrari, Guy Spier, Aquamarine Fund]_ — [2019-11-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kdGltV0eomU)

### Compounding & long-term holding (3)

- **His earlier framework of buying at a 50-60% discount and selling in three years has the flaw that you must keep finding new ideas and pay a lot of tax; buying great businesses with long runways cheaply is better.** He admits that in 25 years he has not paid as much attention to great businesses as he should have, though unlike Guy Spier he will never go into preservation mode and wants to 'hit it out of the park'. _[Guy Spier]_ — [2019-05-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kax8XnBU1ik)
- **Ideally what we want is long-term compounders with huge runways and a flywheel that is hard to penetrate, like Costco possibly dwarfing its US footprint with China.** Costco's first China store got mobbed; it is only in a handful of countries today, so the model has decades of possible rollout, though outcomes remain uncertain. _[Costco, Amazon, Jim Sinegal]_ — [2019-11-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kdGltV0eomU)
- **My aspiration is to buy Moutai at a PE of one and still hold it at a PE of 100 when earnings have grown 20-30x; I am trying again with Micron, which I think is a misunderstood compounder.** He says God keeps giving him compounders (Moutai, Ferrari) that he is too dumb to keep, and this time he will try to hold even at four or five times the current value, though holding is very hard for him. _[Micron, Kweichow Moutai, Ferrari]_ — [2019-11-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kdGltV0eomU)

### Moats & business quality (5)

- **Moutai has the ultimate moat and is very hard to disrupt, whereas MasterCard's 2% take rate could be disrupted the way Chinese payment systems already bypass it.** Moutai has a thousand-year history, is embedded in people's heads, holds large inventory and keeps raising prices with China's rise; he owns Moutai but notes it is fully priced because everyone knows the story. _[Kweichow Moutai, MasterCard]_ — [2019-05-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kax8XnBU1ik)
- **Motherson Sumi has an incredible, unusual moat: automakers like BMW call it to rescue failing suppliers and pay it to take them over.** Chaand Sehgal never solicits acquisitions; BMW writes a ~$100M cheque plus a supply contract, he replaces the plant head with an under-35 insider, never relocates plants, and the plant is profitable within a year. Stock went from 9 cents at 1994 IPO to 146, about 30% annualized; of about 200 Indian CEOs he met, none is better, yet he does not own it at 27x trailing PE. _[Motherson Sumi, Chaand Sehgal, BMW, Fiat Chrysler, Magneti Marelli]_ — [2019-05-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kax8XnBU1ik)
- **The most exciting investments are hidden moats: great businesses no one else sees yet, bought before the 30 analysts arrive.** MasterCard, Motherson Sumi and Moutai are followed by 30 analysts so there is no mispricing; Rain is unfollowed and may be viewed like Motherson in 5-10 years, at which point it could trade at 30x earnings. _[Rain Industries, MasterCard, Motherson Sumi, Kweichow Moutai]_ — [2019-05-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kax8XnBU1ik)
- **The needle coke tightness could run well beyond five years because no non-China plant has been built in ~40 years, a new one takes ~7 years and several hundred million dollars, and EV batteries compete for the same coke.** Only four needle coke producers exist outside China (two US, two Japan); the know-how to build plants is nearly gone and no non-China player has announced capacity, so the seven-year clock keeps rolling forward. _[GrafTech]_ — [2019-11-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kdGltV0eomU)
- **Almost every company in existence today will eventually be a zero; creative destruction means almost no business survives 30-50 years, let alone 100.** The Good to Great companies mostly faltered; GE is about the only hundred-year compounder and look where it is; GEICO was on its knees in the 1970s. He can bet Moutai survives 50 years but is unsure about Costco or MasterCard, which is another reason to own more than one stock. _[GE, GEICO, Kweichow Moutai, Costco, MasterCard, Jim Collins]_ — [2019-11-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kdGltV0eomU)

### Management & capital allocation (7)

- **Rain's CEO did brilliant public LBOs, borrowing $1.5 billion of non-recourse high-yield debt to buy businesses 5-10x his size with nothing down.** In 2008 Rain bought a $1B US business at 11-12% interest, later a $700M European business with the debt placed on the first one, then refinanced to 5.5%. Recent capex of $140M generates $100M pretax a year, and reinvesting at such rates could make Rain a $400-500M-a-year earner. _[Rain Industries, Jagan Reddy]_ — [2019-05-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kax8XnBU1ik)
- **In small owner-run companies like Sunteck and Rain the key-person risk is real: if something happens to the operator, he would have to exit.** For MasterCard it does not matter who runs it; for Rain and Sunteck the bet is that the operator is phenomenal, so he must watch that risk. _[Rain Industries, Sunteck Realty, MasterCard]_ — [2019-05-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kax8XnBU1ik)
- **Assess whether a wealthy promoter still has the drive to grow: he asked Sunteck's 68% owner whether he aspires to turn $1 billion into $10 billion.** Rain's family owns 40% and has zero interest in money; they just want to keep going. Many small companies never become big because capitalism is brutal. _[Sunteck Realty, Rain Industries]_ — [2019-05-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kax8XnBU1ik)
- **Buybacks are just another investment: do them heavily when the stock is severely undervalued and never when overvalued, but most CEOs are great salespeople and lousy capital allocators.** Coca-Cola buys back stock formulaically regardless of whether the P/E is 10 or 1,000, and MasterCard's buybacks at 2019 prices are 'very stupid'; dividends would be smarter for both. Poor allocation shows up as overpriced acquisitions and mistimed buybacks, and many CEOs outsource their personal portfolios while pumping billions into buybacks. _[Coca-Cola, MasterCard]_ — [2019-05-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N0TwWxGxYs0)
- **Owning a business alongside a prudent capital allocator like Brookfield, which owns 80% and understands buybacks, means excess cash flow will likely be returned efficiently.** Three Brookfield people sit on the GrafTech board; Brookfield also cut six plants to three and drove manufacturing efficiencies, and the company is moving work from Monterrey to Pennsylvania to lower costs further. _[GrafTech, Brookfield]_ — [2019-11-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kdGltV0eomU)
- **Don't trust projections; judge managers by long track records, and rockstar executors like Marchionne, Tavares, Mittal and Sehgal keep making it work.** Marchionne had an eight-year auto record and Harvard cases before 2012, having fixed a Fiat losing $100-150 million a month; Carlos Tavares turned GM Europe profitable (north of $1 billion a year) in nine months after GM lost money there for 20 years; Ajay Banga's Citibank record preceded MasterCard. _[Sergio Marchionne, Carlos Tavares, Lakshmi Mittal, ArcelorMittal, Fiat Chrysler, PSA Peugeot, GM Europe, Ajay Banga, MasterCard]_ — [2019-11-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kdGltV0eomU)
- **Look for Jim Collins' level-five leader traits: ambitious for the organization, not themselves, low ego and servant leadership, and avoid Chainsaw Al types.** Tavares wears off-the-rack suits, flies coach while peers use private jets, and buys his own deli sandwich when visiting plants; Al Dunlap at Sunbeam blew up spectacularly. Philip Fisher's book also lists traits of great leaders. _[Carlos Tavares, Al Dunlap, Sunbeam, Jim Collins, Philip Fisher]_ — [2019-11-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kdGltV0eomU)

### Markets, cycles & macro (5)

- **The 9% long-run US equity return is a half-truth: markets go through roughly 17-year stretches of nothing followed by equally long spectacular runs, because 17 years is about the length of human memory.** The Dow was about 870 in 1965 and again in 1981 while the economy grew a lot; from 1982 to 1999 it went from under 900 to over 12,000 (about 15% a year); from 2000 to 2012 it was flat again. Businessweek ran 'the death of equities' near the 1981 bottom, and extreme bearishness sets the foundation for a bull run. _[Maggie Mahar, Bull]_ — [2019-02-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_0XPurSI9cQ)
- **Cycles of euphoria and pessimism will continue forever because markets are driven by humans who vacillate between fear and greed.** The pattern is global, not limited to the Dow: the NASDAQ did 20% a year from 1980 to 2000, then fell 75% from 5,000 to 1,250 and took 16 years to recover even with Amazon, Apple and Netflix inside it. India's Sensex was flat for 12 years after the 1992 liberalization, and the German DAX was flat for the last 11 years. _[NASDAQ, Sensex, DAX]_ — [2019-02-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_0XPurSI9cQ)
- **He pays no attention to macro because forecasting one business is hard enough and forecasting markets is nearly impossible, but it helps to know where you are in a cycle when things reach extremes.** Markets only get to obvious extremes once every 15-20 years. Japan and Korea are clearly cheap; in the US he can't find much to buy, which means fully valued rather than necessarily overvalued since companies could grow into their prices. — [2019-02-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_0XPurSI9cQ)
- **Markets will keep vacillating between fear and greed no matter how much AI or algorithmic trading exists, because human nature does not change and valuation is part art.** Bubbles are far more common than people think (he recommends Ron Insana's Trend Watching); index funds already beat 90-95% of managers after fees. Stock picking gets hard in euphoric markets and easy in depressed ones. _[Bitcoin]_ — [2019-05-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N0TwWxGxYs0)
- **Markets move in roughly 17-year cycles because human memory fades after 17 years: the Dow was flat at 873 from 1965 to 1981, then rose to ~12,000 by 1999.** He knew when starting Pabrai Funds in 1999 that he was entering a headwind period through about 2016, and it still worked out fine. Maggie Mahar's book Bull chronicles the 1982-99 run. — [2019-05-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N0TwWxGxYs0)

### Stock case studies (7)

- **Rain Industries in India was a $200 million market cap on $2 billion of revenue where the market gave no value to 90% of the assets; after two years of going straight down, earnings hit $200 million and the market cap went to $2 billion.** Bought roughly four years before 2019, the stock fell to about $160 million market cap before the third-year earnings arrived; the position was 12x at the peak and about 2.5x after a subsequent earnings correction. Uncertainty lasting only six or nine months still gets punished by markets. _[Rain Industries]_ — [2019-02-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_0XPurSI9cQ)
- **A 12-year contest started October 14, 2018 pits Guy Spier's MasterCard ($204/share, $212B cap, 42x trailing PE) against Sunteck Realty (under $700M cap).** Guy's $1 million in MasterCard became $12 million but will not become $144 million in the next 12 years. Through May 2019 MasterCard was up 25% and Sunteck up 38%. He runs about 10 such contests to shake up people who conflate great companies with great investments. _[MasterCard, Sunteck Realty, Guy Spier]_ — [2019-05-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kax8XnBU1ik)
- **Sunteck Realty was bought at about 100 rupees after India's 2016 demonetization when its market cap of under $200M was below the $500M value of a single project of 60 finished Mumbai apartments.** Demonetization, RERA and GST wiped out 90% of Indian developers, leaving clean operators like Sunteck among only 8-10 players who will rebuild Mumbai over 30-40 years. He bought 9.999% (the maximum allowed) and the stock rose almost 5x to 460-500 in three years. _[Sunteck Realty]_ — [2019-05-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kax8XnBU1ik)
- **Rain Industries was bought at 35 rupees in 2015 for a $200M market cap when he judged it would earn $200M a year within three or four years; it hit 450 rupees in 2018.** A stranger in Vancouver emailed a 20-page PDF; three hours later he told his broker to buy every share and reached 9.999%. Rain supplies coal tar pitch and calcined coke to aluminum smelters in a two-or-three-player oligopoly with long-term contracts. Even after the fall it is a 3x, at 6x earnings. _[Rain Industries]_ — [2019-05-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kax8XnBU1ik)
- **Discussing a current position like GrafTech avoids the selection bias of only teaching past home runs, and even the best analyst is wrong one in three times.** He picks GrafTech because the valuation is near his purchase price and the facts are current; quotes John Templeton that investing is a game of probabilities, and cites Johnson & Johnson talc and PG&E as examples of unpredictable trajectories, which is why you own a few businesses rather than one or two. _[GrafTech, Johnson & Johnson, PG&E, John Templeton, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2019-11-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kdGltV0eomU)
- **GrafTech's edge is captive, hedged needle coke at about $2,750/ton versus $4,500-7,000/ton for competitors, so its next five years of cash flow roughly equal its market cap.** Of ~180-190k tons of UHP electrode capacity, ~145k tons carry the low-cost advantage; selling near $10,000/ton yields north of $1 billion in margin, and after ~$300 million of overhead, capex and debt service plus taxes, $500-600 million a year is locked in for several years. _[GrafTech]_ — [2019-11-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kdGltV0eomU)
- **Motherson Sumi's flywheel is getting paid by OEMs to take over distressed suppliers, compounding at 30% a year for 25-30 years in the auto parts business.** They never solicit or answer acquisition calls; only when an OEM like BMW asks them to rescue a loss-making mirror supplier do they act, receive $50-75 million to take it over, never relocate plants to China, replace the top executive with a young insider, and turn it profitable within about six months. _[Motherson Sumi, Vivek Chaand Sehgal, BMW]_ — [2019-11-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kdGltV0eomU)

### Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US (7)

- **Japan is among the cheapest equity markets in the world 29 years after its 1990 bubble, but its cash-rich balance sheets are an illusion because Japanese companies put shareholders last and will not release the cash.** The Nikkei peaked at 40,000 in 1990 and sits at about half that in 2019; at the peak the Tokyo Imperial Palace was valued above all real estate in California. Many Japanese companies trade below net current assets, Ben Graham style, but the value can't be unlocked. _[Nikkei]_ — [2019-02-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_0XPurSI9cQ)
- **South Korea is probably the most fertile hunting ground in the world: 30 years of incredible growth and the KOSPI went only from 1,000 to 2,000, with plenty of businesses at three times earnings.** Since 1989 the KOSPI has compounded at a little over 2% a year despite the rise of Samsung and Hyundai. He has one Korean investment, is visiting Seoul and Busan next month, and says the impediments are language, culture and circle of competence; something like the Moody's of Korea would be easier to get his arms around. _[KOSPI, Samsung, Hyundai]_ — [2019-02-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_0XPurSI9cQ)
- **He has not found a US stock to buy in four years except one, and his portfolio has shifted to India and other geographies purely bottom-up, not from a macro view.** He used to be 100% US; he holds less than 10% cash; he thinks the US is fully priced or possibly overpriced but could grow into it, and India investments of the last few years were better than anything available in the US. — [2019-02-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_0XPurSI9cQ)
- **In India he never invests without kicking the tires because of fraud risk, whereas in the US he never meets management.** He has sat in meetings with Indian companies that were obvious frauds; India's promoters often ignore outside shareholders, so clean accounting, honest auditors and governance must be verified. The same adjustment likely applies to China. _[Micron]_ — [2019-05-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kax8XnBU1ik)
- **India offers more gaps between price and value because companies are under-followed, while the US shrank from 8,000 to 3,600 public companies with far more analysts.** It is much harder to find value gaps in the US than in India, so the tool set must be adjusted per market. — [2019-05-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kax8XnBU1ik)
- **In countries with deteriorating institutions or crazy inflation, own bulletproof businesses that transcend geography and currency, like the Coke bottler or the dominant credit rating agency.** Growing up in socialist India, the Coke bottler still did fine; people will trade a certain amount of labor for a Coke even if the currency is seashells. In Turkey he told his Graham-overdosed local friend to skip the PE-of-0.1 stocks and visit the Coke bottlers, where paying three times earnings is fine. _[Turkey, India, Coca-Cola bottlers]_ — [2019-11-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kdGltV0eomU)
- **Don't focus on discounted pies; what you really want are growing pies, and South Korea offers more growing pies than Turkey.** His single Turkish bet is a young entrepreneur with great assets bought at a ridiculous discount, but the whole pie was ~$40 million (probably worth north of $500 million) so he cannot deploy $100 million there. Korea's market has done nothing for three decades, governance is improving, the chaebols are losing power, and much more capital can be deployed there. _[Turkey, South Korea]_ — [2019-11-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kdGltV0eomU)

### Psychology & temperament (7)

- **Extreme patience is the single most important trait, because real business change takes years while stock prices change by the second and activity tends to hurt you.** A Fidelity study of self-directed accounts found the top 10% performers were overwhelmingly people who were dead or had forgotten they had the account. The two best performing criteria were being dead or having forgotten. _[Fidelity]_ — [2019-02-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_0XPurSI9cQ)
- **Everyone needs a 'rope' to climb out of the well of a deep drawdown; it is a mistake to sell things just because they became cheaper unless you are convinced the value is below the price.** His bankrupt father paid an astrologer for rosy forecasts as a rope. Down 70% in the financial crisis, Pabrai broke his own 'thou shalt not use Excel' rule to build a spreadsheet of his portfolio at much higher 2009-2011 prices, and that was his rope. Otherwise be like the Fidelity dead clients and do nothing. _[Fidelity]_ — [2019-02-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_0XPurSI9cQ)
- **Be unreasonable and a harsh grader: if everything is not perfect, say no and toss it.** One of his 10 commandments; with governance issues you should just pass because you are fighting an uphill battle. He is not only a small-cap investor, having recently bought Micron (over $40B cap) and Fiat Chrysler (over $20B). _[Micron, Fiat Chrysler]_ — [2019-05-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kax8XnBU1ik)
- **In investing there are no called strikes: you can let 95% of great ideas go by, and being right two out of three times will make you wealthy.** Buffett's baseball analogy; there are always more balls being pitched, so be a very harsh grader on stocks. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2019-05-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N0TwWxGxYs0)
- **Our brains are a mishmash of ancient and modern and were never designed to pick stocks, so understanding the psychology of human misjudgment is a massive advantage in life and investing.** Poor Charlie's Almanack is worth '10 LBS degrees'; he rereads it every year, and the final essay on the Psychology of Human Misjudgment (pages 440-498) should be read 50 times. Cialdini's Influence is the other key book. _[Charlie Munger, Robert Cialdini]_ — [2019-05-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N0TwWxGxYs0)
- **Reciprocation tendency is hard-coded but uncalibrated, so a small gift creates a disproportionate sense of obligation; he exploits it deliberately in his fund's marketing.** Prospective investors get a $20-plus box with a $25-30 Cross pen and his book; only about 1 in 200 returns it to avoid the obligation. 'I give you a $30 pen, you wire me 2 million.' _[Pabrai Investment Funds]_ — [2019-05-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N0TwWxGxYs0)
- **To persuade humans, focus on interest, not reason, as Ben Franklin advised; logical arguments make no headway with relatives, trade partners or North Korea.** He switched from reason to interest in family disagreements and was shocked at the breakthroughs; the US-China trade war will be settled by interest, not reason. _[Ben Franklin]_ — [2019-05-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N0TwWxGxYs0)

### Buffett & Munger lessons (6)

- **Charlie Munger is the gold standard of patience: after 50 years and roughly 25,000 stock tips from Barron's he acted on one, Tenneco, in 2003 and turned $10 million into $80 million in three years, then gave it to Li Lu where it became about $800 million.** Munger was 80 when he made the Tenneco bet; an 80x in 15-16 years would rank in the top 1% globally. The willingness to wait for a really fat pitch is the lesson. _[Charlie Munger, Tenneco, Li Lu, Barron's]_ — [2019-02-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_0XPurSI9cQ)
- **Investment teams are an oxymoron: value investing is an individual pursuit, and 80% of the industry's participants subtract value, so the industry would be better if smaller.** A 2-and-20 firm with $100 million has a guaranteed $2 million to fund payroll, whereas a zero-fee structure can produce years with no revenue at all. Pabrai Funds has no full-time employees other than him. John Bogle said in investing you get what you don't pay for. _[John Bogle]_ — [2019-02-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_0XPurSI9cQ)
- **Run an empty calendar like Buffett and Munger and be very good at saying no.** Peking U was the only item on his calendar that week; he has about 400 investors and cannot remember his last call or email with any of them, copying Buffett's partnership practice of being available one day a year with semi-annual letters. _[Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger]_ — [2019-05-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kax8XnBU1ik)
- **Buffett's personal portfolio outside Berkshire was always concentrated in two or three stocks, sometimes with options or leverage, and grew from under $20M in 1970 to over $2B.** Learned from Munger over their regular bridge lunches; he also listens to 30 minutes a day of the Berkshire annual meeting archive at buffett.cnbc.com going back to 1994, often the biggest learning of the day. _[Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2019-05-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N0TwWxGxYs0)
- **Unlike Buffett's Swiss Army knife, most investors have only one to three tricks, and one trick is more than enough.** Buffett's breadth of experience lets Berkshire do deals like the $10 billion Occidental financing at 8% with warrants, like 2009; ordinary investors may never develop that range and don't need to. _[Warren Buffett, Berkshire Hathaway, Occidental]_ — [2019-11-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kdGltV0eomU)
- **Even Buffett makes lots of mistakes: equal-weighted, Berkshire's acquisitions have a poor record, but dollar-weighted he was right on the big ones.** Wedgewood Partners' letter listed IBM, Precision Castparts, Lubrizol, not enough Apple, and missing Microsoft and Google; nearly all Berkshire retail investments other than Borsheims and Nebraska Furniture Mart failed. Mistakes are par for the course. _[Berkshire Hathaway, Wedgewood Partners, IBM, Precision Castparts, Lubrizol, Apple, Borsheims, Nebraska Furniture Mart]_ — [2019-11-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kdGltV0eomU)

### Mistakes & lessons learned (5)

- **His biggest recurring trouble area is levered institutions, where several picks went to zero, so he now tells himself to stay away even when they look good.** He believes there is some mis-wiring in his brain that makes him miss the issues with leveraged companies, and the fix is to know where to hunt and where to avoid rather than try to get better at it. — [2019-02-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_0XPurSI9cQ)
- **Even the best investor makes mistakes, and in investing you can be wrong 40% of the time and still do very well.** Cited in the context of Buffett not selling Coke in 2001. _[Warren Buffett, Coca-Cola]_ — [2019-05-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kax8XnBU1ik)
- **As a cheapskate at the core, my unwillingness to pay up for great businesses is a huge disadvantage, and paying up for huge-runway compounders is probably worth it.** Munger told him the failed Costco-Walmart merger terms would not have mattered because the pie would have been so much larger; Costco doesn't look cheap today but could be very cheap on a 20-year view. He names two lessons he has yet to learn: paying up and holding on. _[Costco, Walmart, Charlie Munger]_ — [2019-11-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kdGltV0eomU)
- **I should never, ever have sold Moutai: bought under 150 RMB four or five years ago, sold at an average of 800-900, and it now trades around 1,200.** He calls Moutai the deepest moat on the planet, a thousand-year-old brand entrenched in over a billion minds that, unlike Costco, does not have to execute brilliantly every day; he captured 5-6x but was fully out before 1,000. _[Kweichow Moutai, Costco]_ — [2019-11-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kdGltV0eomU)
- **Learn from your mistakes but don't learn too much; you have to move on quickly, as Munger told me in his only phone call to me after I overanalyzed Horsehead in my letters.** Horsehead Holdings, a zinc processor, went to zero after a large gain. Munger's concern was that dwelling on it would mess with his mind; Guy Spier got so absorbed in the Horsehead bankruptcy committee that he couldn't hear Pabrai pitching Moutai and only bought ~$100,000 of it. _[Horsehead Holdings, Charlie Munger, Guy Spier, Kweichow Moutai]_ — [2019-11-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kdGltV0eomU)

### Career, entrepreneurship & life (12)

- **Starting a fund in July 1999 at the peak of a bubble still worked because all the money was flowing into a small sliver of equities, leaving lots of opportunity in lesser-known names for anyone who didn't join the euphoria.** NASDAQ peaked at just over 5,000 on March 9, 2000, the same day Berkshire Hathaway hit a multi-year low as people moved money from Berkshire to Pets.com. Pabrai Funds was up north of 70% in its first year and 15-20% or more annually for several years after with small capital. _[Berkshire Hathaway, Pets.com, Pabrai Investment Funds]_ — [2019-02-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_0XPurSI9cQ)
- **Choose your first jobs by the people you would work for and with, someone you like, admire and trust, not by the highest offer or the biggest brand name.** Compensation takes care of itself. Buffett says laying out a plan like three years of banking, then an MBA, then a business is like saving sex for old age; go directly at your goals. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2019-02-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_0XPurSI9cQ)
- **A genuinely good investor should already be wealthy by their forties from compounding small sums at 30-40%, and doesn't need a 1% management fee.** Munger asks why give money to a manager who isn't already wealthy. Pabrai's own $1 million from selling part of his business in 1994 grew to $12 million by 1999 at about 70% a year. A 1% fee on $2 million is $20,000, which pays for coffee but makes fundraising harder and puts you out of alignment with the universe. _[Charlie Munger]_ — [2019-02-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_0XPurSI9cQ)
- **If you have the skills of a good investor you can generate your own capital with some chutzpah, as Li Lu and Desmond D'Souza did.** Li Lu arrived at Columbia with no English, did three degrees simultaneously, invested his student loans and graduated with about $250,000; Munger gave him money because 'there was nobody else'. Desmond D'Souza, a back-bencher from Pabrai's Dubai high school, bought a house near campus with his tuition money, rented it to 40 students, then flipped 20 foreclosed homes to Haitian contractors and was worth millions a few years after graduation without a job. _[Li Lu, Charlie Munger, Desmond D'Souza]_ — [2019-02-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_0XPurSI9cQ)
- **Keep an empty calendar with no meetings, take an afternoon nap, and leave large chunks of every day for reading widely; finding two or three ideas a year is doing well.** He has a nap room off his office and picked up the empty-calendar habit from Warren and Charlie; a podcast request gets scheduled in whatever week has nothing on the calendar. _[Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger]_ — [2019-02-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_0XPurSI9cQ)
- **Take the job you would do if you were not getting paid; choosing a career for pay or prestige is the wrong decision.** His trainer Jason said that after winning a $500 million Powerball he would still come to the club; Pabrai runs an $800 million fund in shorts and Nike sneakers because he would do it unpaid. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2019-05-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Kax8XnBU1ik)
- **Copy Buffett's empty calendar: the most important thing money cannot buy is time, and an empty calendar is a side effect of being great at saying no.** Buffett had 80+ CEOs reporting to him and a $200B portfolio with an almost empty calendar; Pabrai takes no meetings without a compelling agenda and funnels all requests to 5:30 AM at the south entrance before the Berkshire meeting. The LBS talk was the only item on his calendar that week. _[Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger]_ — [2019-05-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N0TwWxGxYs0)
- **Read only on paper, get freedom from devices, and limit email to 900 seconds a day.** He reads the FT, WSJ and NYT in physical form daily; his assistant handles nearly all email and hands him a folder at 11:00 AM that he finishes with handwritten replies by 11:15. Munger has never used a mobile phone or computer and reads ~20 books a week. _[Charlie Munger]_ — [2019-05-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N0TwWxGxYs0)
- **Before starting a fund, prove you are a good investor with an auditable track record in a separate brokerage account; Munger's first criterion for picking a manager is that he must already be rich.** Li Lu turned ~$20,000 of student-loan float into $950,000 by graduation from Columbia and has compounded north of 20% for 20+ years, which is why Munger picked him. Pabrai himself grew $1M to over $11M from 1994 to 1999 before friends asked him to manage money. _[Li Lu, Charlie Munger]_ — [2019-05-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N0TwWxGxYs0)
- **Raise capital from the three F's, friends, family and fools, and if you deliver above-average returns investors will swim to you through shark-infested waters.** Pabrai Funds started in 1999 as a hobby with eight or nine friends and $1M; 15 months in he decided to build it into a real business despite SEC limits on soliciting. _[Pabrai Investment Funds, Warren Buffett]_ — [2019-05-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N0TwWxGxYs0)
- **Take the job you would do if you weren't paid, and work for people you like, admire and trust; choosing on brand name or compensation is stupid.** Most firms violate the core principles, so the next best thing is Buffett's advice on choosing bosses and peers you respect. His own life would be almost identical with or without outside money. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2019-05-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=N0TwWxGxYs0)
- **You can be a successful part-time investor with a passionate non-investing career; being comatose on trading and finding roughly one idea a year is enough.** He spent 15-20 hours a week on investing while running his IT company; his radiation oncologist college roommate makes ~$1 million a year but his investing wealth dwarfs it, so oncology is now 'a hobby'. _[Guy Spier]_ — [2019-11-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kdGltV0eomU)

### Philanthropy & Dakshana (2)

- **Philanthropy is the opposite of entrepreneurship and value investing: you must swing for the fences and be willing to lose everything, because safe approaches to hard problems have already been tried and failed.** Entrepreneurs minimize risk and hunt for offering gaps, while charities face five or six intractable problems governments have spent billions on. The Gates Foundation's vaccine moonshots mostly fail, but one polio or malaria success has a huge impact on humanity. _[Gates Foundation]_ — [2019-02-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_0XPurSI9cQ)
- **Charities lack the brutal feedback loop of capitalism, so Dakshana inverted the problem and refuses to engage in any charitable activity that cannot be measured, throwing away 99% of possible activities.** A billion-dollar foundation spending the legally required 5% a year never goes out of business no matter how bad its 'haircuts'. He tells Dakshana staff 'we are not a charity, we are a business' without a profit motive but with tight outcome measurement; the blankets-versus-housing homelessness example shows why most charity can't be measured. _[Dakshana Foundation, Rockefeller Foundation, Ford Foundation]_ — [2019-02-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_0XPurSI9cQ)
