### Cloning & learning from great investors (13)

- **Cloning is one of the most powerful mental models: lift what smart people have already figured out rather than inventing everything yourself.** He calls himself the shameless cloner; he stumbled on Buffett via a Peter Lynch book about 26 years earlier and cloned many aspects of Buffett, including the idea of owning an insurer with float, which led to buying Stonetrust. _[Warren Buffett, Peter Lynch, Berkshire Hathaway, Stonetrust]_ — [2020-04-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iW0Mv9zVt0o)
- **Most investors should index (S&P 500 or the Chai with Pabrai free lunch portfolio) because valuing businesses years out is extremely complicated and indexing is like watching paint dry.** The free lunch portfolio mixes Uber Cannibals, spinoffs and shameless-cloning ideas, is back-tested and updated annually; zero-commission brokers make stock picking look easier than it is. — [2020-04-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iW0Mv9zVt0o)
- **Heroes should not be limited to the living; most of his learning from Buffett and Munger came from reading, not from knowing them, and one's parents are the greatest heroes.** Munger says the eminent dead are some of the best heroes; Pabrai got a tremendous head start from both parents and picks up different things from many people. _[Charlie Munger, Warren Buffett]_ — [2020-05-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_2aFw40NqP8)
- **Nick Sleep returned all investor capital rather than keep charging fees on a three-stock portfolio of Amazon, Berkshire and Costco, and that portfolio turned out to be Corona-proof.** Sleep ran north of a billion dollars, held the three stocks for over 10 years, told investors to buy them directly, and gave up hundreds of millions in future fees; only Buffett has otherwise shut down a partnership, and he did it because prices were too high. _[Nick Sleep, Amazon, Berkshire Hathaway, Costco, Warren Buffett]_ — [2020-05-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_2aFw40NqP8)
- **Li Lu is a Swiss-army-knife investor with unusual wiring who, like Buffett and Munger, focuses first on what can go wrong, then on long runways and entrepreneurs, and holds for 15-20 years.** Munger introduced them 11 years ago and insisted they lunch monthly. Li Lu, a Tiananmen leader smuggled out of China, did three Columbia degrees in four years and made his first million investing the float on his student loans. _[Li Lu, Charlie Munger, Warren Buffett]_ — [2020-05-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_2aFw40NqP8)
- **The Buffett partnership 0/6/25 fee structure is the fair one: no management fee, a quarter of gains above 6%, and he went a decade (2007-2017) without a fee rather than resetting the high-water mark.** A $5 billion fund charging 2% collects $100 million a year for breathing even when down 10%; he earned $30+ million in 2007, the funds fell about 65-67% by 2009, and he collected over $50 million in 2017-18 after regaining the high-water mark plus 6% a year. If the industry adopted this structure, 80% of it would disappear. _[Buffett Partnership, Pabrai Investment Funds, Charlie Munger, Daily Journal]_ — [2020-05-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w2hnOllfpwI)
- **Book recommendations: Greenspan's 'Capitalism in America' (from Munger, with lessons for India) and Richard Koo's 'The Other Half of Macroeconomics' (from Li Lu) on why money printing did not cause inflation.** Munger recommended the Greenspan book at their last dinner on March 7, 2020, a week before US lockdowns. _[Charlie Munger, Li Lu, Alan Greenspan, Richard Koo]_ — [2020-05-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nogBvLWB6cU)
- **Once you find great compounders, let them run for decades, as Nick Sleep and Chuck Akre do.** Nick Sleep returned about $3 billion in 2015 holding just Amazon, Costco and Berkshire, telling investors to buy the three stocks themselves; it did not matter what else he owned as long as he owned Amazon. Pabrai notes this approach would not have worked buying compounders at 50 times earnings in 2000-2016. _[Nick Sleep, Amazon, Costco, Berkshire Hathaway, Chuck Akre]_ — [2020-10-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ANn907GgLPs)
- **Hack the 50,000-stock universe by looking at what great investors have bought, then filter by circle of competence.** DataRoma is free and cuts the universe by 90-98%; categorize investors like Chuck Akre, David Tepper and Jeff Ubben by pattern, favoring larger holdings. Buffett instead went page by page through the Moody's manual and Japan Company Handbook and refused Capital IQ. _[DataRoma, Chuck Akre, David Tepper, Warren Buffett, Li Lu]_ — [2020-10-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ANn907GgLPs)
- **Humans and companies are bad at cloning, which creates a big window for businesses that embrace copying.** Microsoft copied everything after its 1976 BASIC compiler (Excel from Lotus, Word from WordPerfect, Teams from Slack); Walmart copied Kmart and Sears for its first 15 years; Costco copied everything from Price Club; Starbucks brought the Italian cafe to Peoria. Markets do not recognize the power of great cloning. _[Microsoft, Walmart, Costco, Price Club, Starbucks, NVR]_ — [2020-10-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ANn907GgLPs)
- **Pabrai Funds started in July 1999 as a hobby for eight friends, structured as a Buffett-style 0/6/25 partnership with no management fee, a 6% hurdle and 25% of the profits above it.** He photocopied pages of a Buffett biography describing the fee structure and had a non-securities lawyer create the LP, later spending a few thousand dollars fixing mistakes. Because the investors were close friends he personally guaranteed their principal and 6% a year; when scaling required dropping the guarantee, he closed the fund and reopened without it and all investors followed. _[Warren Buffett, Pabrai Investment Funds]_ — [2020-11-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iJII3_CyUvo)
- **Useful idea sources are Value Investors Club, SumZero and thoughtful write-ups people email him, because buy-side authors actually want to own the businesses.** Sell-side material is only for entertainment; these venues contain somewhat thoughtful write-ups. _[Value Investors Club, SumZero]_ — [2020-11-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iJII3_CyUvo)
- **Nick Sleep's Nomad shut down in 2014 with 90%+ in Amazon, Costco and Berkshire and told investors to just hold those three without paying fees.** Nomad managed about $3 billion in 2013 with maybe 60-70% in Amazon near $300 a share; Sleep first bought Amazon at $30 in 2002 and kept buying at $100, $200, $300. One great spawner made up for everything else in a dozen-stock portfolio. _[Nick Sleep, Nomad Investment Partnership, Amazon, Costco, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2020-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pUiwBs_N5cE)

### Circle of competence & checklists (14)

- **Circle of competence: if you have to ask whether a business is in it, the answer is that it isn't.** Munger's 'to ask the question is to answer it'; MasterCard, American Express and Carnival are easy to understand, pass quickly on the ones where you're scratching your head. _[Charlie Munger, MasterCard, American Express, Carnival Cruise Lines]_ — [2020-04-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iW0Mv9zVt0o)
- **Don't aim to broaden your circle of competence; being an inch wide and a mile deep beats a mile wide and an inch deep.** Munger's friend John Arriaga became a billionaire investing only in real estate within one mile of Stanford; Buffett and Gates both name focus as the key trait. Read business biographies like Ken Iverson's Plain Talk on Nucor to stay curious. _[John Arriaga, Nucor, Ken Iverson, Bill Gates]_ — [2020-04-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iW0Mv9zVt0o)
- **His checklist was built from post-mortems of great investors' losing investments, asking whether the failure was obvious beforehand; the biggest categories are leverage, moats and management.** With interns he studied hundreds of failures across 15-20 investors like Ackman, Einhorn, Buffett and Munger via 13Fs; in most cases the weak link was visible in advance, e.g. US Airways was not the low-cost provider when Southwest came in. _[Bill Ackman, David Einhorn, Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger, US Airways, Southwest Airlines]_ — [2020-04-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iW0Mv9zVt0o)
- **If you don't understand how a business makes money, you don't need to go there; there are 30,000 other stocks.** He never seriously looked at Enron since energy is outside his circle, and he still can't figure out how Amazon's first-party retail makes money on Prime shipping, though AWS, Google and Apple he understands. _[Enron, Amazon, Google, Apple]_ — [2020-04-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iW0Mv9zVt0o)
- **He is an anomaly-based, bottom-up investor who never picks a sector first and then hunts for the best play within it.** He always looks at what an individual business can do, and the same holds for real estate investors finding the mispriced house. — [2020-05-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w2hnOllfpwI)
- **The first question about any investment is 'How would I lose money on this?'; focus on the downside and the upside takes care of itself.** The checklist comes later to ensure nothing is missed; the aim is investments where the downside is very muted. — [2020-05-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nogBvLWB6cU)
- **Valuation yardsticks differ by business; the key is identifying the two or three variables that drive the outcome and seeing the business the way the CEO does.** Moutai has a $3-4 cost per bottle selling for $150 and went up 6-7x in 4-5 years (he sold it because of the 50/90 rule); Fiat Chrysler in 2012 had $130-plus billion revenue at a $5-6 billion market cap where even 2-4% margins meant a multi-bagger; for NVR all that matters is shares outstanding and cash flow at the end point. NVR builds no speculative homes and owns no land, only options. _[Moutai, Fiat Chrysler, NVR]_ — [2020-10-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ANn907GgLPs)
- **Investing is a business of no called strikes, so you can dump entire industries like retail with no penalty.** He hates retail because it is the most transparent business with no trade secrets and no customer contract, so it is a graveyard; he dumps Costco, Amazon and Walmart along with it and admits he does not understand Amazon's last-mile economics. There are infinite good things, so throwing away good stuff costs nothing. _[Costco, Amazon, Walmart, Sam Walton, Kmart]_ — [2020-10-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ANn907GgLPs)
- **He never builds Excel models because precision leads you astray; a ~160-question checklist before investing exposes questions he cannot answer and counters greed.** Typically he finds he does not know the answers to about 10 questions and goes back to do the work. Almost no business other than Costco passes with no blemishes; the judgment call is whether a given issue is the one that kills it. _[Costco]_ — [2020-10-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ANn907GgLPs)
- **The size of your circle of competence does not matter; what matters is not stepping outside it and playing at its epicenter.** John Arrillaga became a billionaire investing only in real estate within a couple of miles of Stanford. Be a harsh grader; the most obvious ideas come from things you consume, like Shimano bike parts, which he passed on at double-digit earnings. _[John Arrillaga, Shimano]_ — [2020-10-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ANn907GgLPs)
- **Sell-side research is mostly garbage because analysts focus one or two quarters ahead and set price targets only 30-40% above the current price, ratcheting up as the stock rises.** A Mumbai broker's report valued Satyam at 60 rupees when it was 40, though its real estate alone was worth twice the price and the business was growing 50% a year; the analyst told him a 600-rupee target was not allowed. Owners don't need next-quarter precision, only long-term trajectories and probabilities. _[Satyam Computer Services]_ — [2020-11-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iJII3_CyUvo)
- **Spawning cannot be screened for quantitatively; you have to study the business, but a few hours of history usually make the DNA obvious.** He holds three spawners below $1 billion market cap and recently found a fourth below $400 million with a long history; his holy grail is a portfolio of only apex spawners, five to ten names, and finding one a year is enough. — [2020-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pUiwBs_N5cE)
- **Missing a spawner like Alibaba or Google is fine; the real error is calling something a spawner when it is not, so it must be obvious.** Like baseball, there are no called strikes for passing; spawning is a continuum from extreme non-spawner to extreme spawner, and you want only strong spawning DNA. Li Lu's early BYD bet was not a spawner call, but once BYD entered cars it became a keeper. _[Alibaba, Google, McDonald's, BYD, Li Lu]_ — [2020-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pUiwBs_N5cE)
- **The size of your circle of competence is irrelevant; what matters is staying inside it, and running a business first is a huge advantage for investors.** He could not have built the spawner framework without having done adjacent spawning at his own IT company. Munger's friend John Arrillaga became a billionaire investing only in real estate within two miles of Stanford; Sam Walton, Ray Kroc and Jim Sinegal had very narrow expertise. _[John Arrillaga, Sam Walton, Ray Kroc, Jim Sinegal, Costco]_ — [2020-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pUiwBs_N5cE)

### Valuation & margin of safety (10)

- **He has moved from discounted pies to growing pies: '5x is for losers', the bar is now 10x in five years with a deep moat, which makes most things fail the cut and simplifies life.** In 2008-09 he required at least a 5x on any bargain regardless of quality; in 2019 he made three investments and in 2020 one, which he sees as a straight 10x in five years with a nice moat. — [2020-04-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iW0Mv9zVt0o)
- **It is dangerous for individuals to act on stock names; a great business is not necessarily a great investment because the entry price determines investor returns.** Amazon will do well but buying at a trillion-dollar cap is a different question; Jio is an incredible dominant business but returns from today differ from 10 or 20 years ago. He declined to disclose his portfolio for this reason. _[Amazon, Reliance Jio]_ — [2020-05-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_2aFw40NqP8)
- **Gold is a non-productive asset, an 80-foot cube that stays the same size for 100 years; buy jewelry to enjoy but do not invest family assets in it.** He recounts Buffett's Martian analogy; gold and real estate have not been the straight rides Indians assumed, and Indian women are moving toward equity markets, a shift he expects to continue. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2020-05-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_2aFw40NqP8)
- **Microsoft in 2000 shows that a great business bought at an egregious price returns almost nothing: $600 billion market cap on under $10 billion of cash flow became about a 3% annual return over 21 years with a rough ride.** He told Microsoft executives holding 80-90% of their net worth in the stock that it was going nowhere but down; it fell to less than a third and took 13-14 years to recover, reaching $1.3 trillion only by 2020. _[Microsoft]_ — [2020-05-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w2hnOllfpwI)
- **The FANGs are unbelievable businesses with moats and pricing power, but it is all baked into ridiculous trailing P/Es, so the odds are against investors buying them today.** Facebook, Apple, Amazon, Google and Netflix are driving the S&P; you could buy Amazon and look great in 10 years, but it is not a good bet. _[Facebook, Apple, Amazon, Google, Netflix, S&P 500]_ — [2020-05-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nogBvLWB6cU)
- **Growth and value are joined at the hip; all intelligent investing is value investing.** Growth just means more and higher coupons in the future to discount; whether coupons grow 20%, 0% or decline 5%, each yields a valuation. Given a choice he wants to invest in growth and long runways without paying up too much. — [2020-10-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ANn907GgLPs)
- **Markets dislike messiness and wide outcome ranges, so embedded optionality remains mispriced for investors who appreciate that businesses do not move in straight lines.** When he bought Fiat Chrysler in 2012 Ferrari made under $150 million a year and he dismissed it; they paid about $16 a share for Ferrari inside FCA and it went to $190-200, delivering a third of the total value. Starbucks Reserve is another example of optionality outside the model. _[Fiat Chrysler, Ferrari, Starbucks, Costco]_ — [2020-10-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ANn907GgLPs)
- **He is not wired to pay up for a great business, so his universe is compounders that are unrecognized or hit by a temporary hiccup and therefore cheap, but with a genuinely long runway.** Other investors are wired to pay up and that is fine for them; he is limited to buying the growing pie cheap and then, unlike in the past, running it for a while. Finding one or two such ideas a year is plenty. — [2020-11-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iJII3_CyUvo)
- **Pabrai's spawning rules: assume no business exceeds $50 billion market cap, so buy below $5 billion for a 10x and below $500 million for a 100x.** Of 3,700 US IPOs in the last 20 years, only nine now exceed $100 billion. Most 100x returns are captured while a company is private; Alibaba at $800 billion cannot plausibly reach $80 trillion, and Uber, public at $50 billion, is unlikely to be a 100x. _[Alibaba, Uber, Walmart]_ — [2020-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pUiwBs_N5cE)
- **The spawner framework changes valuation: instead of valuing 'other bets' at zero, he now pays something extra for the spawning DNA.** Previously he treated Alphabet's other bets as free upside worth zero; now he would value the core pieces and add maybe $5-10 billion for the DNA, since zero is too extreme, and would have wanted Google at under $5 billion or $500 billion market cap. _[Alphabet, Google, Android, YouTube]_ — [2020-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pUiwBs_N5cE)

### Portfolio concentration & selling (7)

- **The Kelly formula is the mistake in The Dhandho Investor and should be ignored, because investing offers one-off bets, not thousands of sequential ones.** Kelly works for a 51/49 coin flipped 2,000 times; in investing you get a single 70/30 or 90/10 opportunity, so the formula doesn't fit the format. — [2020-04-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iW0Mv9zVt0o)
- **Don't be single-stock since anything can go to zero, but 20 stocks is also not bright; he caps positions at 10% and ideally holds about 10 bets.** In his daughters' UGMA accounts with $15k-30k a year and a very long runway he went down to two or three highest-conviction ideas and it worked out; only exceed a tenth if you can't see a downside. — [2020-04-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iW0Mv9zVt0o)
- **Make 8-10 carefully selected long-runway bets at careful valuations and you end up very wealthy even if 40% of them fail.** Equal-weighted, easily a third of Berkshire's acquisitions did not work, though dollar-weighted 80-90% did. If one of ten 10% bets becomes a 30-bagger and some are 5-10 baggers over 20-30 years, you do fine. _[Berkshire Hathaway, ADP, Visa, MasterCard]_ — [2020-10-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ANn907GgLPs)
- **Set the hurdle for switching positions very high because the mistress always looks hotter than the wife.** You know all the blemishes of what you own and none of the new shiny thing's; do not switch on 60:40. Guy Spier's inaction saves him: he refused to sell Nestle or buy Moutai until badgered into $100k, then regretted missing a 5x. _[Guy Spier, Nestle, Moutai]_ — [2020-10-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ANn907GgLPs)
- **The Kelly criterion does not apply to investing and was a mistake to put in The Dhandho Investor.** Kelly works when you can make many similar-odds bets like 100 coin tosses at 51/49; investing is one bet at a time without the luxury of repeats, so he ignores it completely. _[The Dhandho Investor]_ — [2020-10-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ANn907GgLPs)
- **A portfolio of 5-10 spawners at 10% each can tolerate several duds because two or three home runs pay for all the mistakes.** His hypothesis is that with careful selection three or four may not work and that is fine; the approach tolerates being wrong, and duds are relatively easy to avoid by checking the track record. — [2020-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pUiwBs_N5cE)
- **The first rule of compounding is never to interrupt it; only exit when it is absolutely clear a secular decline has started, even if you give up 50% from the peak.** Businesses do not go up in a straight line, so ignore temporary headwinds; after a long run, being a little late getting off the bus does not hurt returns, but getting off for a temporary hiccup does. _[Charlie Munger]_ — [2020-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pUiwBs_N5cE)

### Compounding & long-term holding (10)

- **Compounding has three variables (capital contributed, runway length, rate of return) and starting early matters most; even a 5-10% return with maxed 401k/IRA builds spectacular sums over decades.** Buffett started at 20 with $10,000 and has compounded 70 years; Rick Guerin was levered in 1973-74 and sold Berkshire shares to Buffett at $40 that were recently $300,000. There's no minimum age for an IRA, so a 14-year-old with a part-time job should open one. _[Warren Buffett, Rick Guerin, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2020-04-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iW0Mv9zVt0o)
- **Compounding has three variables, capital, length of runway and rate of return, and a long runway makes a high return unnecessary.** 50% a year for five years and 5% a year for 50 years give almost interchangeable results, so starting very early matters more than heroic returns or even the amount of capital. — [2020-05-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_2aFw40NqP8)
- **Ordinary families do not need to understand companies; consistent long-term index investing and dollar-cost averaging over decades will deliver great returns.** He strongly encourages the Millennium Mams to index, since most of their wealth sits in their families' future earning power; wealthy Indian families should also use the $250,000 annual remittance allowance to get S&P 500 exposure to the Amazons and Microsofts of the world. _[S&P 500, Amazon, Microsoft]_ — [2020-05-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_2aFw40NqP8)
- **Investors do themselves a disservice through hyperactivity; you make money by waiting.** High frictional costs plus hyperactivity hurt investor results both in the US and India. — [2020-05-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nogBvLWB6cU)
- **The 2020 lesson is that the flat-curve period is over and the goal now is to find great compounders or cannibals at reasonable prices and set them and forget them, bringing portfolio velocity to zero.** He is no longer looking for a 50-cent dollar bill but for very long runways at reasonable prices with a lot of stability; one to three such ideas a year is enough. Munger does not sell businesses that go somewhat above intrinsic value, and Berkshire has not touched Coke in 32 years even at 40-plus times earnings in 2000. _[Coca-Cola, Berkshire Hathaway, Charlie Munger]_ — [2020-10-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ANn907GgLPs)
- **The big epiphany of 2020 is that if you were lucky enough to buy a great compounder with a long runway at a reasonable price, do not sell it just because it reaches 100 or 120 cents on the dollar; hold until it is egregiously overvalued.** He calls 2020 his biggest learning year since the mid-1990s. For 20 years he had bought 50-cent dollars and sold at 90 cents, a fine 20%-plus return but one that requires constantly finding the next idea and paying taxes; the better model is to stay on the train and get off only when it gets egregious. — [2020-11-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iJII3_CyUvo)
- **From 2020 onward he is no longer interested in discounted dollar bills; the pie has to be a growing pie, bought cheap and then held.** He hopes to have 25-35 more years of runway to apply the lesson of 2020 rather than repeat the Moutai and Ferrari exits. — [2020-11-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iJII3_CyUvo)
- **Investors face two options, growing pies and discounted pies, and growing pies are the better path because they allow set-it-and-forget-it and 10x-100x outcomes.** Discounted 40-50 cent dollars put you on a tax-inefficient treadmill of buying and selling and rarely deliver more than a double or triple; growing pies with long runways can be held indefinitely even at optically expensive prices. — [2020-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pUiwBs_N5cE)
- **There are five paths to 10-100 baggers: focused mouse traps, great capital allocators, uber cannibals, deeply undervalued players, and spawners.** Examples: Moutai and McDonald's as focused players; Berkshire, Danaher and Exor as allocators; NVR bought back 82% of shares since 1996 for a 70x+ return with little business growth; Teledyne under Henry Singleton bought back 80%+ of stock for 125x from 1960-1980; Teck Cominco was a 10-bagger from 2009 and Fiat Chrysler from 2012. _[Moutai, McDonald's, Berkshire Hathaway, Danaher, Exor, NVR, AutoZone, Teledyne, Henry Singleton, Teck Cominco, Fiat Chrysler]_ — [2020-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pUiwBs_N5cE)
- **Every sale is a confession of error; the goal is to be a silent minority partner with a great entrepreneur and ride as long as they ride.** He cites Thomas Phelps and Nick Sleep's line that 'truly brilliant investors weren't investors, they were entrepreneurs that didn't sell', invoking Jack Ma, Sam Walton and Jeff Bezos. _[Thomas Phelps, Nick Sleep, Jack Ma, Sam Walton, Jeff Bezos]_ — [2020-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pUiwBs_N5cE)

### Moats & business quality (8)

- **Insurance's great attributes are customers paying you upfront (float) and sticky recurring revenue; lending is the opposite and one of the worst businesses because money leaves the door on every sale.** Workers' comp is legally mandatory and renews year after year like the barbershop example; recurring revenue is one of the most beautiful aspects of any business. _[Stonetrust]_ — [2020-04-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iW0Mv9zVt0o)
- **Insurance is 'good from far but far from good': you make a sale without knowing your cost of goods for years, and it takes exceptional people to run, unlike a Coke bottler your idiot nephew could run.** Berkshire's real edge, which he only understood recently, is that its AAA rating and overcapitalization let regulators treat a railroad bought for $30B (now worth over $100B) as if it were a bond, a freedom almost no other insurer has. _[Stonetrust, Berkshire Hathaway, BNSF, Coca-Cola]_ — [2020-04-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iW0Mv9zVt0o)
- **Investments fall into three categories: discounted pies, obvious growing pies (which cheap value investors can't bring themselves to buy), and hidden moats, which is where the action is.** The whole planet knows Google, Amazon, Microsoft and Salesforce are great, so the edge lies in growing businesses with moats that very few humans can see. _[Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Salesforce]_ — [2020-04-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iW0Mv9zVt0o)
- **Recurring revenue streams (RRS) are the holy grail of business.** He hates ADP's prices but keeps trying and failing to leave because switching payroll is not worth the hassle; Broadridge gets paid per investor for filings that cost nearly zero to send digitally. Retailers like Walmart, Costco and Home Depot must win back customer loyalty every day against constant erosion. _[ADP, Paychex, Broadridge, Costco, Walmart, Home Depot]_ — [2020-10-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ANn907GgLPs)
- **A moat should be obvious before you look at the numbers, and businesses with recurring revenue are more resilient than those that must earn customer trust daily.** He knows ADP and Visa are great before seeing any numbers; Chipotle has widened its moat with its app and delivery but is harder because it has no recurring revenue. Boeing looked like an incredible duopoly moat with no white tails and then all hell broke loose. _[ADP, Visa, Chipotle, Starbucks, Boeing]_ — [2020-10-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ANn907GgLPs)
- **Spawners, companies whose DNA is to continuously incubate related and unrelated businesses, are the focus of his 2020 investing renaissance.** Very few companies have spawning DNA; they expect many bets to fail and take failure in stride, as in Bezos's 'experiment patiently, accept failures, plant seeds, protect saplings, double down when you see customer delight'. _[Amazon, Jeff Bezos]_ — [2020-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pUiwBs_N5cE)
- **Spawners come in types: adjacent, embryonic (buy and nurture), cloner (copy successful products), non-adjacent, and rare apex spawners that do all four.** Amazon adding categories beyond books is adjacent; Microsoft buying Forethought (PowerPoint) is embryonic; Microsoft cloning Windows, Word, Excel, Explorer, Azure, Teams is cloner; BYD entering N95 masks is non-adjacent. Apex spawners like Amazon, Alphabet, Alibaba, Tencent, Baidu and Berkshire have many roads to Nirvana, like a Swiss Army knife. _[Amazon, Microsoft, BYD, Starbucks, Facebook, Google, Alphabet, Alibaba, Tencent, Baidu, Berkshire Hathaway, GEICO]_ — [2020-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pUiwBs_N5cE)
- **Most businesses lack spawning DNA and some, like McDonald's and Ford, deliberately divested good adjacent businesses as distractions.** McDonald's took a 20-30% stake in Chipotle at 20-30 stores and sold it as a distraction; Alan Mulally sold Land Rover and Jaguar in 2009 to focus on the Ford brand. Costco and Moutai are also classic focused non-spawners, whereas Walmart has spawned many formats. _[McDonald's, Chipotle, Ford, Alan Mulally, Land Rover, Jaguar, Costco, Moutai, Walmart]_ — [2020-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pUiwBs_N5cE)

### Management & capital allocation (5)

- **A diehard cannibal with a stable business can deliver non-linear returns regardless of index headwinds.** NVR, a home builder with no intellectual property, spent 100%-plus of owner earnings on buybacks every year since 1994 except 2008-09; top line up 3-4x in 20 years, share count down 56%, and the stock up 55x over the same 20 years. _[NVR]_ — [2020-10-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ANn907GgLPs)
- **Judge leaders by what they have done, not what they say; public markets give you track records venture investors lack.** Sergio Marchionne was obviously unusual in 2012 and kept exceeding his assessment; GM had competent but far lesser leadership so he sold it after 40-50% gains. Elon Musk understands first principles of physics unlike other auto CEOs, so he would neither go long (too expensive) nor short Tesla. _[Sergio Marchionne, Fiat Chrysler, GM, Elon Musk, Tesla, Sam Walton]_ — [2020-10-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ANn907GgLPs)
- **Spawning is more capital-efficient than cannibalizing because reinvesting cash flows reduces reported income and taxes, an interest-free loan from the government.** Cannibals must pay tax on earnings before buying back shares; Amazon reported almost no earnings for most of its history while its profitable core funded new bets, and 30-40% of that money would otherwise have gone to the government. _[Amazon]_ — [2020-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pUiwBs_N5cE)
- **A great spawner never bets the farm; bets are small relative to the mothership, scaled up only as traction appears, and killed quickly when they fail.** BYD's N95 mask entry would be a rounding error if it failed; Amazon buried the Fire Phone when it got no traction. Elon Musk's indifference to money bothers him because he could make a huge unproven bet, which Bezos would not do. _[BYD, Amazon, Tesla, Elon Musk, Jeff Bezos]_ — [2020-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pUiwBs_N5cE)
- **Spawners must be founder-led or have a leader with 10-15 years of studyable history; spawning that happened under a founder and then passed to professional management is a red flag.** All his spawner holdings are founder-led with 10-30 years of history (the Japanese one founded in 1985, public around 2003, founder now 55). Reliance Industries is a case where the second generation is better than the founder, but that takes time to see. _[Reliance Industries, Amazon]_ — [2020-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pUiwBs_N5cE)

### Markets, cycles & macro (21)

- **In April 2020 markets were nowhere near 2008-09 bargain levels; he had found only one business he was excited about and was buying it, versus an avalanche of 5-10x basket bets in 2008-09.** In 2008-09 he made five 2% bets instead of one 10% bet because everything looked cheap and every investment was a winner; the 2020 fiscal and monetary response was much faster, with 10% unemployment reached far quicker than the 15 months it took in 2008-09. — [2020-04-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iW0Mv9zVt0o)
- **Diversify across 8-10 bets within your circle of competence because 100-year events happen every 10 years; don't sweat whether the odds are 70% or 90%.** Guy Spier's view is 100-year events happen every 10 years and 50-year events every 7; nobody projected Vegas going to zero customers for weeks. Three REITs or three casinos is not diversification; prioritize low odds of losing money. _[Guy Spier, Wynn Las Vegas, Encore Boston]_ — [2020-04-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iW0Mv9zVt0o)
- **Never count America, the world or humans out: the COVID shock is intense and many fragile businesses will fail, but a few years on the scars will be barely visible.** GM's supply chain took ventilator maker Vintech from 150 to a planned 20,000 units a month in days; airlines will survive but equity holders may not do well since the government only cares that planes fly. _[GM, Vintech]_ — [2020-04-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iW0Mv9zVt0o)
- **There is a huge disconnect between the real economy and equity markets, so building cash is not a bad idea even if the gloom scenarios never play out.** More than 33 million Americans, over 20% of the workforce, filed for unemployment, possibly surpassing the Great Depression's 25% peak, yet markets brushed it off; Buffett noted the real 1929 decline of 85% came over the following two years after an initial rebound. On a desert island hearing only the economic news he would have guessed the Sensex and Dow were down 50-70%. _[Sensex, Dow Jones, Warren Buffett]_ — [2020-05-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_2aFw40NqP8)
- **Most businesses are extremely fragile creations that cannot pay staff for even 30-45 days without revenue, so the small-business damage from the pandemic is huge and warrants caution.** Businesses earn a few percentage points of profit under brutal competition; Bill Gates wanted Microsoft to hold enough cash to pay staff for two years with no revenue, which almost no business can do. _[Microsoft, Bill Gates]_ — [2020-05-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_2aFw40NqP8)
- **The pandemic differs from other crises in having a definitive end date, perhaps 15-18 months away, but the have-nots lose first and wealth polarization will worsen.** The have-nots have the least staying power and savings and were the first to lose jobs, globally and in India. — [2020-05-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_2aFw40NqP8)
- **A rising power has never challenged an incumbent peacefully, and US-China relations are at a multi-decade low, so the range of outcomes is wide with ugly outliers.** The US has valid grievances since trade with China was unfair, but it benevolently allowed it (Marshall Plan, favorable deals) to help the world rise; countries will now rebuild medical supply chains and stockpiles so US dependence on China and India for medicines falls within 10 years. Long run, the world needs China and China needs the world. — [2020-05-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_2aFw40NqP8)
- **Richard Koo's 'The Other Half of Macroeconomics', recommended by Li Lu, is the only credible explanation for why Fed money printing did not cause inflation, and it may not this time either.** He thinks the Fed printing money now is the right thing to do and it is unclear inflation will follow; most books could be 10 pages and the first 30-40 pages of Koo's suffice. _[Richard Koo, Li Lu]_ — [2020-05-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_2aFw40NqP8)
- **US stimulus must be seen against household wealth: America is a $100 trillion family that can spend $5-10 trillion without feeling it.** Global household wealth is about $400 trillion, $100 trillion of it in the US versus $22 trillion GDP; US household wealth was 50-55 trillion in 2009. Jerome Powell may go down as one of the greatest Fed governors for unprecedented actions like buying commercial paper directly. _[Jerome Powell]_ — [2020-05-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_2aFw40NqP8)
- **The COVID lockdown was an overreaction that deliberately took a rockstar economy off the rails; the medicine is far worse than the disease.** A three-week shutdown followed by contact tracing and distancing would have sufficed; nearly 40 million unemployment claims bring suicides, depression, divorce and abuse that nobody counts, and natural experiments in Sweden, Northern Italy and New York (20%+ already infected) argue against continued lockdown. _[Sweden, New York]_ — [2020-05-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w2hnOllfpwI)
- **Businesses are fragile; few can survive losing 60 or 90 days of revenue, so the shock will cause multiples of the normal 1,600 weekly US business failures and the economy will not be back to January 2020 levels even in five years.** Normal creative destruction replaces 1,600 failures a week with better businesses; he expects unemployment to settle at 7-9% and says a 3% unemployment economy is unlikely even by 2025, though he would never bet against America or against Las Vegas as a town. _[Las Vegas, Japan]_ — [2020-05-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w2hnOllfpwI)
- **In May 2020 the equity markets do not reflect economic reality and there is a bubble broader than the 1999-2000 one, because prices of FANG-type businesses are disconnected from any discounted cash flow.** Nasdaq was flat on the year and the S&P down less than 15% while bargains were hard to find far above the March 23 lows; in 2000 the bubble was a sliver (Nasdaq 5,000 to 1,200), whereas today everything is built around a kernel of truth but every great business has a finite price. _[Nasdaq, S&P 500, FANG, Amazon, Facebook]_ — [2020-05-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w2hnOllfpwI)
- **If long-term rates stay at 1-2% for years, equity markets and even FANG valuations are not expensive, but he cannot handicap rates with the printing presses running far beyond 2008-09.** Fed and Treasury actions were the right thing and helped both Main Street and Wall Street, but they make 2008-09 look like nothing. _[Federal Reserve]_ — [2020-05-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w2hnOllfpwI)
- **Forget the macro; the micro always trumps the macro, and the investor's job is judging individual businesses, like a house bought for $250,000 with $25-30,000 of rent.** It is not our job to figure out unemployment or interest rates; if the unlevered return from rent is known and the area is known, you do that deal all day long. — [2020-05-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w2hnOllfpwI)
- **History will judge leaders poorly for COVID shutdowns because nobody analyzed the cost of 35 million lost US jobs against 100,000 deaths.** Suicide, depression, divorce, domestic violence and child abuse will rise; India's mass migrations made social distancing impossible; masks and distancing are good, but wholesale shutdowns were the wrong call. — [2020-05-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nogBvLWB6cU)
- **Businesses are fragile creations, and the shutdown destroyed hundreds of thousands that will never return, causing permanent damage to the global economy.** The US normally loses 1,600 businesses a week (100,000 a year) and creates more; from 3% unemployment and 160 million employed in January 2020, it may take five to ten years to get back, not this year, not next, not when everyone is vaccinated. — [2020-05-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nogBvLWB6cU)
- **US markets have brushed off COVID and are not pricing in the bad news; the polarization between FANGs/Tesla and languishing brick-and-mortar resembles 1999-2000.** Markets assume a vaccine in finite time (historically vaccines have never come this fast) and no further shutdowns; he guesses 7-8% US unemployment two years out. The US is a superhuman economy that will bounce back, and some brick-and-mortar businesses are decent values. _[Tesla]_ — [2020-05-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nogBvLWB6cU)
- **Markets go through very long flat periods and equally long euphoric periods, roughly 17 years each, because human memory does not go past 17 years.** The Dow was flat from 1965 to 1982 (about 870) then went from under 1,000 to over 12,000 from 1982 to 1999, then flat again from 1999 to 2011; after the 1929 crash it took a quarter century to recover. Cites Maggie Mahar's book recommended by Buffett. _[Dow Jones, S&P 500, Maggie Mahar]_ — [2020-10-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ANn907GgLPs)
- **When valuations get extreme enough, even incredible business growth cannot rescue the stock for 15 years or more.** In 2000 Microsoft and Cisco were each around $600 billion with Microsoft earning under $10 billion at 70-plus times trailing earnings; Microsoft delivered zero returns until 2015-16 with violent drops. The NASDAQ took 16 years to get back to 5,000. The Nikkei peaked in 1990 and has done minus 2% a year for 30 years; the Imperial Palace in Tokyo was valued above all California real estate. Korea, by contrast, is now a cheap market he is interested in investing in. _[Microsoft, Cisco, NASDAQ, Nikkei, KOSPI]_ — [2020-10-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ANn907GgLPs)
- **The current party will end in extreme euphoria, his best guess somewhere between the late 2020s and early 2030s.** As long as humans are involved, markets go from extreme undervaluation to extreme overvaluation; he does not know whether the cycles will be 10, 17 or 30 years but says extreme binges produce longer periods. — [2020-10-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ANn907GgLPs)
- **In bubbles the market splits in two: a frenzied sliver and boring businesses nobody wants, and the day the NASDAQ peaked in March 2000 Berkshire hit a multi-year low; today (2020) looks somewhat similar.** Berkshire was around 40,000 down from 70,000 as the NASDAQ hit 5,000. In 2020 he sees a small sliver that is egregiously overvalued, a large portion probably overvalued but not egregiously, and many businesses people aren't interested in. _[Berkshire Hathaway, NASDAQ]_ — [2020-11-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iJII3_CyUvo)

### Stock case studies (7)

- **In 2000 he warned Microsoft's Indian executives that holding the stock at a $600 billion cap earning under $10 billion would end badly, and it went nowhere for 15 years despite the business growing.** They had 95% of net worth in Microsoft and had never seen it decline; the stock fell 50-60% and was flat until 2013-14, and the money they put in Pabrai Funds did far better. _[Microsoft, Pabrai Investment Funds]_ — [2020-05-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_2aFw40NqP8)
- **Auction-driven markets produce strange pricing, which is the reason investors can make money in equities: Live Nation lost all 35,000 concerts but fell only about 40%, while Carriage Services fell 30% though its funeral business went up.** A private funeral company worth $1 billion in January would laugh at a $700 million offer in April since revenues rose; funeral services has the lowest failure rate of any SIC code, people never shop quotes for a burial, and Live Nation's top line is gone for 2020 and most of 2021 yet its valuation was not compelling. _[Live Nation, Ticketmaster, Carriage Services]_ — [2020-05-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w2hnOllfpwI)
- **Microsoft in 1999 at a $600 billion cap and 75x trailing earnings was obviously a bad investment despite being a great business, and stayed flat for 14-15 years with a 50%-plus drawdown.** He told Microsoft employees with 90% of net worth in the stock to trim; paying $600 billion for $6-7 billion of earnings takes too long to earn back at any growth rate. Twenty years later at $1.2 trillion the return was about 3.5% a year ex-dividends, 5% with. _[Microsoft]_ — [2020-05-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nogBvLWB6cU)
- **When an idea hits you over the head like a two-by-four, that is when you act; ignore anything that merely seems okay.** IPSCO at $45 had $15 cash and two years of $15 contracted earnings, so plant and inventory were free; a Swedish buyer offered $160 in 2006 for a 4x. A Turkish warehouse operator with 12 million square feet and tenants like IKEA, Carrefour and Amazon had a market cap under $30 million versus liquidation value of $300 million to $1 billion and went up 7-8x in 13-14 months; micro trumps macro at the right price. _[IPSCO, Turkish warehouse company, Value Investors Club, DataRoma]_ — [2020-10-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ANn907GgLPs)
- **Satyam Computer Services was a $10,000 bet in the mid-1990s that became about 140x because it traded below the liquidation value of its Hyderabad real estate while growing 50% a year with Fortune 500 recurring revenue.** He knew the company through shared US clients. He sold within two weeks of the 2000 peak when a spun-out dotcom subsidiary inflated the valuation; the stock then lost 60-70%. _[Satyam Computer Services]_ — [2020-11-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iJII3_CyUvo)
- **CMGI, a Boston incubator spawning dotcoms, was bought at a modest valuation as a way to own the internet without knowing which company would win, and a $100,000 10% bet became over $10 million.** He compares it to owning Tencent or Alibaba today: businesses that throw many things at the wall, most of which don't stick, but the ones that do stick do very well. _[CMGI, Tencent, Alibaba, Amazon]_ — [2020-11-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iJII3_CyUvo)
- **He bought Seritage in Q2 2020 after it fell 70-80% in weeks; it is an 'unspawner' selling assets to stay afloat, bought before the framework, but he is happy with it.** His two reported US holdings are Micron, held for a couple of years, and Seritage; the steep drop is the clue to his interest. _[Seritage, Micron]_ — [2020-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pUiwBs_N5cE)

### Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US (8)

- **India dropped the ball big time on capturing manufacturing leaving China; Vietnam is running out of labor while almost no work moved to India.** Red tape and bureaucracy make India hard for multinationals despite a favored US relationship and Trump-Modi rapport; passive investments by Facebook, Silver Lake and the Saudis in Reliance Jio are exceptions, not the holy grail of a bicycle maker relocating production to India. Rule changes after Walmart's Flipkart deal illustrate the problem. _[Reliance Jio, Facebook, Silver Lake, Walmart, Flipkart, Vodafone]_ — [2020-05-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_2aFw40NqP8)
- **India grows while the government sleeps; the private sector delivers (Jio, aviation, mobile) but the government fails on physical infrastructure like rail and power.** India's rail track has barely grown since 1947 while China laid tens of thousands of kilometers of high-speed track; Dakshana Valley in Pune lacks three-phase power four days a week while power plants sit idle. A benevolent dictatorship would be better but the odds are against a dictator being benevolent. _[Reliance Jio, Dakshana]_ — [2020-05-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_2aFw40NqP8)
- **The Chinese people gave the Communist Party a long rope and it has delivered growth impossible in a democracy, but tension will rise as prosperity makes citizens want more than economics.** Most Chinese would agree the growth would not have happened under democracy; society has so far accepted the price in freedom of speech. — [2020-05-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_2aFw40NqP8)
- **His entry into India has been unwise so far, with far better outcomes in China and the US, but he expects his Indian investments to do very well over five to ten years.** India's positives are a great class of entrepreneurs, improving governance, pent-up demand and a demographic dividend (average age 28), which he also expects to blunt COVID mortality; the big 'if' is government-provided infrastructure and education. — [2020-05-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_2aFw40NqP8)
- **India inflicts self-wounds: it captured almost none of the manufacturing exodus from China that Vietnam picked up because its rules defy Ricardo and Adam Smith.** The mantra for making a country rich is well known from Lee Kuan Yew, Pinochet's Chicago School economists, Adam Smith and Ricardo; vote-bank politics prevents it, and India could be lifting tens of millions from poverty every year but is not. _[Lee Kuan Yew]_ — [2020-05-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nogBvLWB6cU)
- **In India, look for businesses with long runways and aligned management that can do well assuming the government does nothing.** India grows at night while the government sleeps; the mantra is the same anywhere, great moat plus great management with the right incentives. Jio's execution in taking share and resetting pricing has been amazing, though he is not recommending the stock. _[Reliance Jio]_ — [2020-05-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nogBvLWB6cU)
- **Indian asset and wealth management has incredible multi-decade tailwinds as money moves out of gold, real estate and fixed deposits into equities.** US frictional costs have fallen through technology and scale while India's remain high; buy a home to live in, not for price appreciation. He is a shareholder of Edelweiss and its wealth and asset management franchises excite him most. _[Edelweiss]_ — [2020-05-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nogBvLWB6cU)
- **He would rather invest in the US, where governance and language are easier, and the hurdle for overseas investments is higher, but his portfolio is full of foreign names simply because that is where value is.** Overseas he has to meet the company and get past language and cultural issues to understand the nuances. In 2020 he found only one US business to buy, during the April-May COVID selloff; most recent finds have been outside the US. — [2020-11-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iJII3_CyUvo)

### Psychology & temperament (9)

- **There are no called strikes: if something about a business bothers you, take a pass and never regret it, but do regret understanding a good business and failing to pull the trigger.** Carnival bothers him because much revenue comes from captive casinos past 12 miles and cruise lines skirt labor laws; it could be a 10-bagger but he doesn't need to spend more time on it. _[Carnival Cruise Lines]_ — [2020-04-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iW0Mv9zVt0o)
- **Bitcoin has no long-term value; he sold the one Bitcoin a VC friend gifted him at $4-5,000 when it reached $19,000 and the rest at $12-13,000.** Two hours with a Forbes-profiled Bitcoin billionaire did not change his view; he told the friend to unload his billion and put an end to the ride, and files Bitcoin in the too-hard pile. _[Bitcoin, Coinbase]_ — [2020-05-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_2aFw40NqP8)
- **He received a lifetime blackjack ban from a Vegas casino on New Year's Eve 2019 because his non-card-counting system beat the house consistently.** He visited every two or three months playing up to a few hundred dollars a hand and made a solid six figures; the casino had watched for over a year, could not find card counting, and said the trajectory plus the money behind him did not bode well for them. _[Edward Thorp]_ — [2020-05-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w2hnOllfpwI)
- **The first rule in blackjack, as in investing, is choosing which game and where to play so the odds are in your favor; he has zero interest in any bet where he lacks the edge.** BJ21.com publishes the odds of every blackjack table in North America monthly for about $100 a year; blackjack is a fight for 50.1% versus 49.9%, whereas in equities he can make bets with 80% odds in his favor. _[BJ21.com, Edward Thorp]_ — [2020-05-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w2hnOllfpwI)
- **You can optimize fun or optimize dollars, but not both.** His friends find the way he plays blackjack extremely boring; he is all about optimizing dollars. — [2020-05-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w2hnOllfpwI)
- **Being far from financial epicenters like New York is an advantage because investing is a solitary activity of reading and thinking with less noise.** Munger told Chris Davis that merely moving his operation from New York to Santa Barbara would add about half a percent a year to returns; Davis considered it but stayed. _[Chris Davis, Davis Funds, Charlie Munger, Omaha, Irvine]_ — [2020-05-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w2hnOllfpwI)
- **Once you have a roof and three meals, it is dumb to get hyperactive about wiggles in the stock market; if wealth is lost, nothing is lost.** The drivers of happiness and good health are not brokerage balances; keep perspective except for those truly without food. — [2020-05-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nogBvLWB6cU)
- **Bridge and investing are both games of probabilities, which is why so many value investors play; COVID showed there are no sure things, only fat tails.** He plays five to six hours a week on Bridge Base, Buffett more than 10; he once played online with Buffett. _[Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger]_ — [2020-05-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nogBvLWB6cU)
- **Stocks drop 20% after he buys them and that never bothers him, because auction-driven markets swing wildly and you are buying a business, not a stock.** Any Shanghai stock's 52-week range is like 70-150 while home prices move 5-15% a year; if you understand what the business is worth you should be happy to buy more when it drops. 'If wealth is lost, nothing is lost; if character is lost, everything is lost.' — [2020-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pUiwBs_N5cE)

### Buffett & Munger lessons (12)

- **Be a harsh grader of people, as Buffett is: let in only the exceptional 4% and give no benefit of the doubt to the 92% you can't judge.** From his 2008 lunch, Buffett said he isn't a great judge of people but simply culls; Munger adds there are enough nice people that you needn't make exceptions. Small signals like how someone treats a waiter suffice, and there's a gravitational effect from who you spend time with. Buffett's swap test: the classmate you'd trade half your lifetime income with has integrity, intelligence and energy. _[Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger]_ — [2020-04-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iW0Mv9zVt0o)
- **Have a trusted peer with different life experience to bounce investments off, not a subordinate, because you can't see everything through your own filters.** Munger told him he has always had someone to talk to about investments; Buffett and Munger worry they think so alike that an idea passing one filter passes the other. He uses Guy Spier and others who don't work for him. _[Charlie Munger, Guy Spier]_ — [2020-04-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iW0Mv9zVt0o)
- **The biggest lesson from the 2020 Berkshire meeting was that Buffett did not go shopping and even said Berkshire's cash cushion is not that high given the range of outcomes.** Munger described them as a ship captain in the worst tempest whose objective is to get to the other side safely; Berkshire was a net seller of equities over four months and exited the airlines, which Pabrai calls a no-brainer. _[Berkshire Hathaway, Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger]_ — [2020-05-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_2aFw40NqP8)
- **When Buffett, Munger and Li Lu are all bearish, the right response is to pay attention even if you do not fully understand their reasons.** Their intellect is beyond human intellect; second- and third-order effects of the pandemic (hospitals laying off staff as elective procedures stop, CVS prescriptions down, finely tuned auto supply chains breaking) are hard to forecast. _[Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger, Li Lu, CVS]_ — [2020-05-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_2aFw40NqP8)
- **Poor Charlie's Almanack, especially the Psychology of Human Misjudgment on pages 440-494, is the number one book because understanding human quirkiness gives a leg up in life and relationships.** He rereads that talk every year; Munger took 50-60 years to distil that wisdom and is endlessly curious about how humans work, even Pabrai's dysfunctional relatives at their last dinner on March 7, 2020. _[Charlie Munger, Poor Charlie's Almanack]_ — [2020-05-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_2aFw40NqP8)
- **Buffett is 'just a kid': he barely uses a cell phone, eats what he ate at five, and plays the game like Monopoly, which is the most accurate description of him.** Lunches with his assistant Debbie were more revealing than lunch with Buffett; he keeps his phone in her drawer, and on an impromptu tour of Berkshire headquarters he showed memorabilia and a foot-high strawberry milkshake lunch. _[Warren Buffett, Berkshire Hathaway, Guy Spier]_ — [2020-05-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_2aFw40NqP8)
- **Berkshire's actions in the crisis read as bearish: net sellers of equities, out of all airlines and Goldman Sachs, not buying back stock near book value, and Buffett saying $130 billion of cash is not that much.** Munger described them as the captain of a ship in a tempest wanting to ride out the storm rather than roll the dice; Buffett had been willing to buy back Berkshire at 1.2x book before but was not buying now. _[Berkshire Hathaway, Goldman Sachs, Airlines, Charlie Munger]_ — [2020-05-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w2hnOllfpwI)
- **He bid for the Buffett lunch purely as guru dakshana to thank Buffett for intellectual property that made him tens of millions, and it paid dividends through friendships with Buffett and Munger.** Buffett set no time limit and the lunch ran over three hours with his daughters aged 10 and 12 and Guy Spier; it led to many bridge games and dinners with Munger. Buffett wants winners to feel they got a bargain. _[Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger, Guy Spier]_ — [2020-05-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nogBvLWB6cU)
- **Munger won't sell Costco at 40 times earnings even though he wouldn't buy it there, admitting there is no intellectual way to justify it; give great businesses with intact DNA room to run.** From a socially distanced dinner on Munger's LA patio a week earlier. Pabrai guesses Munger would hold Costco at 50 or 60 times but not at 100 or 200. Costco has one store in China and is in a small number of countries, so outcomes include a thousand-plus Chinese stores. _[Charlie Munger, Costco]_ — [2020-11-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iJII3_CyUvo)
- **Keep the team size at one: 21 years in, Pabrai Funds is as exciting as day one because the numbers got larger but the team never did.** The psychologists told him he does not do well in team sports; he plays bridge four or five hours a week (Buffett plays 10-12) as a near-single-player math game, and investing is a rational, analytical game of the same kind. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2020-11-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iJII3_CyUvo)
- **To avoid the man-with-a-hammer problem, bounce investment ideas off a candid peer, not an employee, as Munger advised.** Munger told him he did not always have Warren to talk to but always discussed ideas with a peer; hierarchy blocks candid sharing, and you are the easiest person to fool. _[Charlie Munger, Warren Buffett]_ — [2020-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pUiwBs_N5cE)
- **Investors buy stocks for one reason but sell for a hundred, so nothing can be inferred from Berkshire selling Costco.** The Costco sale surprised him since Munger loves Costco and talks about it at every dinner; Buffett's actions show he deeply loves Bank of America and less so Wells Fargo now. _[Berkshire Hathaway, Costco, Bank of America, Wells Fargo, Charlie Munger]_ — [2020-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pUiwBs_N5cE)

### Mistakes & lessons learned (14)

- **You only truly understand a business after you own it with real money; paper portfolios don't make the learning sink in.** Before the ink was dry on the $65M Stonetrust purchase in 2014 he realized he'd made a mistake; there is no way to avoid that tuition bill. _[Stonetrust, Dhandho Holdings]_ — [2020-04-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iW0Mv9zVt0o)
- **When you know you've made a mistake, change the mission like Shackleton: stop chasing the original goal and get your investors' capital back at 100 cents on the dollar.** He decided not to run Stonetrust from a board level because of the opportunity cost, hired bankers and aimed simply to recover roughly the $65M paid; if you get all your money back on a mistake, that's a good place to be. _[Stonetrust, Ernest Shackleton]_ — [2020-04-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iW0Mv9zVt0o)
- **Leverage is the number one reason investments and businesses fail; great businesses like Google, Amazon and Microsoft don't need leverage to earn high returns.** Delta Financial went to zero in the financial crisis and another holding was nearly a zero; in a concentrated portfolio zeros are hard to recover from, and this made him cut back sharply on leveraged institutions. _[Delta Financial, Google, Amazon, Microsoft]_ — [2020-04-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iW0Mv9zVt0o)
- **Philip Fisher-style scuttlebutt (talking to ex-employees, customers, vendors) beats armchair investing; he was wrong to avoid it for most of his career.** He had followed the Graham view that CEOs are super salesmen who sway judgment, but investing internationally forced him to get on a plane to eliminate fraud risk, which he found invigorating. _[Philip Fisher, Benjamin Graham]_ — [2020-04-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iW0Mv9zVt0o)
- **Leverage is the number one reason value investors' investments fail; he now avoids levered businesses and financial institutions and uses no margin.** In 2008-09 with 10 positions making up 80% of assets, a mortgage lender went to zero and another finance company nearly did, taking a while to recover from. The other big failure causes are management/ownership ethos and misunderstanding the moat. — [2020-05-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nogBvLWB6cU)
- **He used two different models in two different periods: set-and-forget in the 1990s, then 'buy at 50 cents, sell at 90 cents' from 1999 to 2020, and he forgot he was supposed to switch back.** In 1994-99 he captured more than one hundred-baggers: Satyam Computers in India ($10-12k into $1.5 million, physical shares stuck in a drawer) and CMGI ($100k into about $10 million). Starting his fund in 1999 facing headwinds he switched to buying dollar bills for 50 cents and selling at 90, which worked well through 2011 but ideally he would have switched back two or three years before 2020. _[Satyam Computers, CMGI, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2020-10-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ANn907GgLPs)
- **The number one reason his investments failed was leverage.** He had a few zeros and near-zeros from over-leveraged businesses: Delta Financial, a mortgage lender, went to zero in 2008-09 and CompuCredit produced a significant loss. He admits he still owns some businesses with more leverage than he would like. _[Delta Financial, CompuCredit]_ — [2020-10-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ANn907GgLPs)
- **In the pandemic he exited Fiat Chrysler at a significant discount because auto operating leverage made outcomes unknowable, and doing nothing would have been better.** Capitalism is brutal and most businesses are fragile; his unlevered Indian real estate companies could handle the overhead so he kept them. He made two new investments in late March 2020 that did very well. _[Fiat Chrysler]_ — [2020-10-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ANn907GgLPs)
- **Selling Moutai after a 6-7x because it looked optically expensive at a high-20s/low-30s multiple was a mistake; it more than doubled afterward and will keep going.** Moutai is the most valuable liquor company on the planet at over $200 billion market cap, with a cost of goods of about $5 per bottle sold for $150 and pricing power to reach $300 or $500. Volume is constrained by local sorghum acreage and a single annual water draw at the autumn full moon; 80% of Moutai sold in China is counterfeit. _[Moutai]_ — [2020-11-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iJII3_CyUvo)
- **Selling Ferrari at $70-100 a share when it looked expensive on trailing earnings was another mistake; it has more than doubled since, and it has never spent a dollar on advertising in 70-plus years.** Ferrari came public via the Fiat Chrysler spin-out in the $40s around 2016 and the position exceeded $100 million. Neither Moutai nor Ferrari was egregiously overvalued, only optically so for a cheapskate; as Munger says, we are old too soon and wise too late. _[Ferrari, Fiat Chrysler, Charlie Munger]_ — [2020-11-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iJII3_CyUvo)
- **He switched from growing pies to discounted pies around 2000 because of the bubble, but should have switched back three to five years ago.** He captured a 200-bagger in the 1994-99 boom, then saw froth by late 1999; the day NASDAQ peaked in March 2000 Berkshire hit a multi-year low near $40,000. NASDAQ was flat from 2000 to 2016 and the S&P flat till about 2012, so discounted pies worked, but he stayed too long. _[Berkshire Hathaway, NASDAQ, S&P 500, pets.com, eToys]_ — [2020-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pUiwBs_N5cE)
- **Kotak Mahindra was a spawner he bought in 1995 and dumbly sold in 2000 with almost no return; $3,000 held would be about $600,000 today.** He put $25,000 into Indian stocks in 1995; one became 140x ($10,000 to $1.4 million) in the dotcom boom, and he sold the other three including Kotak for no good reason. Kotak's 2003 banking license and adjacent spawns drove it to one of India's largest private banks. _[Kotak Mahindra, Goldman Sachs]_ — [2020-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pUiwBs_N5cE)
- **Beware fake spawners: CMGI, Satyam and the 1999-2000 internet incubators, and the 2020 SPAC wave looks similar.** He bought CMGI in 1995 for little more than cash, made 100-140x ($100,000 to $10 million) and got off near the peak because valuation was ridiculous, not because he could tell the spawns were failing. When everyone has a SPAC, it is likely a bubble; set a high bar that spawning must be obviously real. _[CMGI, Satyam, Internet Capital Group, Idealab, Safeguard Scientifics, Chamath Palihapitiya, Opendoor]_ — [2020-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pUiwBs_N5cE)
- **His biggest source of investing mistakes over 26 years has been companies with too much debt or inherent leverage; a good business should not need debt.** Many failed investments were leveraged companies or financial services firms; he still holds some leveraged names, 'like an alcoholic who has not given up alcohol yet', but wants to minimize it. — [2020-12-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=pUiwBs_N5cE)

### Career, entrepreneurship & life (12)

- **You cannot write a good contract with a bad person; the most important thing in life is that everyone in your orbit is a high-quality individual.** The Stonetrust sale closed with $45M cash and a $26M note from Chou, $16M of which was adjustable for reserves; both sides waived the annual actuary review and there were no price adjustments in over two years, saving an estimated $2-5M in fees. _[Francis Chou, Stonetrust]_ — [2020-04-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iW0Mv9zVt0o)
- **Start your business while employed: do just enough not to get fired, let the employer pay the rent, and switch full-time once there's revenue and traction.** He ran TransTech for nine months on evenings and weekends while at Tellabs, then left at 25 with $70,000 in credit card debt and an emptied 401k; his boss offered him his job back anytime, so the risk was low. Many ideas today need intellectual capital, not money. _[TransTech, Tellabs]_ — [2020-04-07](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iW0Mv9zVt0o)
- **At the charity lunch Buffett told his daughters the single most important decision in life is whom you marry.** The lunch ran over three hours with more than 50 questions; his daughters, then 10 and 12, still remember the advice, and it makes a massive difference for women who often get the shortest straw. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2020-05-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_2aFw40NqP8)
- **He became a value investor by accident after reading Peter Lynch, which led him to Buffett and the idea that a stock is a fraction of a business to be analyzed as if buying the whole thing.** Never went to business school; realized he could analyze businesses well and quickly using the same analytics as running a business, and started Pabrai Investment Funds in 1999 with $1 million as a hobby for friends. _[Peter Lynch, Warren Buffett, Pabrai Investment Funds]_ — [2020-05-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w2hnOllfpwI)
- **Each person's inner map is hardcoded by age five and never changes; the sliver of humans who align their outer life with it go very far.** Two industrial psychologists gave him his 'owner's manual' in 1999 at age 34, three months before Pabrai Funds launched, and said they could not understand how he functioned running a 160-person IT company; one became an original investor. He now keeps his calendar with no scheduled calls or meetings. _[Pabrai Investment Funds]_ — [2020-05-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nogBvLWB6cU)
- **Entrepreneurs do not take big risks; ignoring venture-backed startups (under 0.1% of all startups), they seek low-risk arbitrage with limited downside.** A dry cleaner opening a small, short-lease drop-off shop in a new town between two existing towns can scale if it works and pull back if it does not; Dhandho, his Gujarati roommate's word, means an approach to business with upside and no downside. — [2020-05-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nogBvLWB6cU)
- **Success means leading an aligned life daily, being happy, and being liked, admired and trusted, not just the financial output.** He cites Buffett's test of whether friends would hide you like the Jewish girl in World War II; bridge, blackjack, investing and even Dakshana are math games he wants to play elegantly. _[Warren Buffett, Dakshana]_ — [2020-05-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nogBvLWB6cU)
- **Graduates in an advanced economy will never be homeless, so they should pursue their passion directly rather than a circuitous 20-year plan.** The problem for elite graduates is opportunity cost since the world pays more than passion does; he started his first business part-time on credit cards while employed, and it is easiest when young, single and childless. The Staples founder stocked grocery shelves after Harvard Business School because he loved retail. _[Staples, Warren Buffett]_ — [2020-10-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ANn907GgLPs)
- **Investing his own $1 million from 1994 on Buffett-Munger principles returned more than 70% a year through 1999, taking his net worth to about $10 million before the fund launched.** The fund was up about 70% after fees in its first year to June 2000, including the NASDAQ crash, because he had completely sidestepped the bubble and owned no Pets.com-type names. _[Pets.com]_ — [2020-11-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iJII3_CyUvo)
- **Someone starting a fund today should keep expenses near zero, run it from home, amortize setup costs over five years, and raise from friends, family and fools, especially the fools.** He ran the fund from his house for 18 months, then rented one room from his wife's business for about $400 a month with a 10-hour-a-week assistant. A $25,000 legal setup can be repaid by the fund at $5,000 a year. Good performance brings more money and introductions from the initial group, as it did for Buffett. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2020-11-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iJII3_CyUvo)
- **Humans arrive without an owner's manual; who you are is hard-coded by genetics and the first five years, so align your outer map to your inner map rather than conform to the world.** Two industrial psychologists (firm named Conquest, after Genghis Khan, who was a tyrant inside and out and therefore effective) tested him in 1999 with 360 interviews and produced a 20-page personality template he rereads every year. Their advice: don't try to be Gandhi outside if you're a villain inside. _[Jack Skeen, Conquest]_ — [2020-11-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iJII3_CyUvo)
- **The profiling told him to get rid of his 160-employee IT company within six months because managing people was off his map, and that his calling was a single-player mathematical game he believed he could win, which is exactly what Pabrai Funds is.** He loved the business for its first four or five years when it was a math game of leads and closes, and hated it once his role became managing politics among vice presidents. Two of the psychologists each invested $100,000 in the fund, saying 'I cracked your brain open, I know exactly what's in there'. He recommends everyone get their manual (about $10,000 a person now versus $25,000 for 12 people then) and have the intestinal fortitude to read it. _[Jack Skeen, Pabrai Investment Funds]_ — [2020-11-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=iJII3_CyUvo)

### Philanthropy & Dakshana (4)

- **Financially literate women are the cornerstone of household wealth because 'spend less than you earn' is largely in their hands, which is why Dakshana is more excited to support a girl than a boy.** Supporting a girl impacts the whole family and several generations, the same reason Grameen Bank went with women; savings driven by women become the foundation for compounding. _[Dakshana, Grameen Bank]_ — [2020-05-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_2aFw40NqP8)
- **Large inheritances are a disservice to kids and grandkids, so the real answer is giving the money back to society efficiently, measured by social return on invested capital.** Trust fund kids and welfare kids are both on an IV drip; he did not want to start thinking about giving in his seventies, so Dakshana was set up about 14 years earlier and got traction right away despite fears of corruption. _[Dakshana Foundation, Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger]_ — [2020-05-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w2hnOllfpwI)
- **Dakshana has taken on about 5,000 kids at roughly $3,000 each, with about 800 in the program at any time, preparing very poor students for IIT and medical entrance exams.** Parents are mostly illiterate laborers earning under $100 a month; graduates work at Google, Amazon, Microsoft and Samsung, and one at Google earns over a quarter million a year while his father was a tailor making $50-60 a month. The 110-acre campus in Pune is on robust financial footing. _[Dakshana Foundation, IIT, Google, Amazon, Microsoft, Samsung]_ — [2020-05-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w2hnOllfpwI)
- **Capitalism maximizes wealth but not balanced wealth, so government and philanthropy must redistribute without damaging the engine, which India gets backwards.** India clobbers its wealth-creation engine and then redistributes a pie that is not growing; Americans are the most generous people on earth and private foundations like Gates do far better work than governments. _[Bill and Melinda Gates Foundation]_ — [2020-05-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nogBvLWB6cU)

### Cloning & learning from great investors (12)

- **2020 was his second-biggest year of learning after 1994-95, because Nick Sleep's partnership letters and Thomas Phelps's '100 to 1 in the Stock Market' caused him to make significant changes to how he invests.** Sleep ran a fund from 2001 to 2014 and his 13 years of letters are 'like the Dead Sea Scrolls'; read them oldest to newest. Phelps's 1972 book is 48 years old but timeless. _[Nick Sleep, Thomas Phelps]_ — [2021-01-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QIUH0IzoV6E)
- **Unable to find undervalued stocks in the US in 2018-2019, he expanded his circle by visiting the portfolios of trusted Graham-style investors in Korea and Turkey who had already applied a first filter.** He asked a Korean investor named David and his friend in Istanbul to walk him through every company they owned, relying on them for local knowledge about honesty and auditors, while nudging them from deep value toward compounders. In 2019 the Coke bottler in Turkey, partly owned by Coca-Cola, traded at seven times earnings with better growth than the US bottler. _[Coca-Cola Icecek, Korea, Turkey]_ — [2021-02-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NXxIQfVIzVU)
- **Reading Nick Sleep's Nomad letters in 2020 caused a significant change: think about ownership stakes the way a founding family would, which stretches time horizons and is more tax efficient.** Instead of buying discounted pies at 50-60% off intrinsic value, he now focuses on growing pies, long-term compounders that can scale, even if they require paying a bit more. He recommends Googling 'Nick Sleep Nomad letters'. _[Nick Sleep, Nomad Investment Partnership, Zak Zakaria]_ — [2021-03-04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V_djW_RGPGA)
- **Buffett's principles are the 'laws of investing', like gravity; the mutual fund industry ignores them, so simply following them gives an edge.** After reading Peter Lynch's two books on a 1994 London-Chicago flight he discovered Buffett; mutual funds held 200 stocks and turned over half the portfolio yearly, the opposite of concentration and buy-and-hold. He put his first $1 million into equities using Buffett's frameworks and it became $13 million in five years, leading to Pabrai Investment Funds in 1999. _[Peter Lynch, Warren Buffett, Pabrai Investment Funds]_ — [2021-03-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NEB2RfRgBSQ)
- **Book recommendations: Suneel Gupta's 'Backable' and William Green's 'Richer, Wiser, Happier', especially the chapters on Nick Sleep and Zak Zakaria and on himself.** Green spent hundreds of hours with each subject, including nights on Indian trains with Pabrai; he predicts the book will become a classic. _[William Green, Nick Sleep, Suneel Gupta]_ — [2021-03-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NEB2RfRgBSQ)
- **Nick Sleep and Qais Zakaria showed that a handful of great businesses held with almost no activity can beat nearly every fund manager.** Nomad managed about $3 billion in 2014 with Amazon near a third of capital; under regulator pressure they returned capital, each with roughly $100 million, and Nick put everything into Amazon, Costco and Berkshire while Zak spread across six stocks and never traded since. Amazon went from about $300 to $3,300 a share. The Nomad letters are freely available online and chapter six of 'Richer, Wiser, Happier' is worth reading. _[Nick Sleep, Qais Zakaria, Nomad Investment Partnership, Amazon, Costco, Berkshire Hathaway, Marathon Asset Management, William Green]_ — [2021-05-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9JYXICM3RSo)
