- **He has not abandoned deep value but added four or five knives to the Swiss army knife; he overdosed on Graham for 20 years and should have switched back to compounders around 2013-14.** He was Buffett/Munger in the mid-90s, Graham for close to 20 years, and is now moving back toward Nick Sleep, Buffett and Munger. The best way to invest is a stake in a high-return-on-capital business with a long runway run by great management, even if you pay up. Most of the time compounders do best, but sometimes deep value wins, so stay flexible. _[Nick Sleep, Ben Graham, Charlie Munger, Amazon]_ — [2021-07-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cJGkrSFVnns)
- **When 20 years of Tencent transcripts and annual reports said nothing, the cliff notes came from an outside shareholder, Naspers' Koos Bekker, who repeatedly called Tencent the best management team on the planet.** He read 18 years of Naspers letters and transcripts to understand Tencent; Naspers IR told him they would never sell Tencent, which compelled him to dig in. The lesson is to go to different sources when the company itself is not helping you. _[Naspers, Prosus, Koos Bekker, Tencent]_ — [2021-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_7UfqjD3IEg)
- **Cloning is a hugely powerful and under-appreciated mental model; the small sliver of companies with cloning DNA have a massive advantage because most humans and companies look down on it.** Almost all of Microsoft's success came from cloning (Word from WordPerfect, Excel, Azure) while most R&D was burned; Burger King used two guys to site stores across from McDonald's; Jim Sinegal said nothing he knows wasn't taught by Sol Price, and Costco later acquired Price Club; Sam Walton cloned Sears and Kmart. You can have two or three coffee players succeed, not thirty. _[Microsoft, Burger King, McDonald's, Costco, Jim Sinegal, Sol Price, Price Club, Walmart, Sam Walton, Starbucks]_ — [2021-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_7UfqjD3IEg)
- **Cloning is a powerful mental model most humans have an aversion to, but in investing it is only a funnel: once you have a shortlist from a great investor's portfolio, turn your own brain on.** He has studied cloning for 33-34 years. With 50,000 public stocks nobody can master even 100, so following five or ten great investors' positions is a far better way to cull the data set than darts or quantitative screens, regardless of whether those investors later lose their edge. — [2021-10-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PN3f668IKO0)
- **Everything you need to learn from Buffett and Munger is already in the public domain; you don't need to know them personally because they are open books.** He recommends the Berkshire letters, the CNBC annual meeting archive, the Buffett and Munger biographies and Poor Charlie's Almanack. _[Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2021-10-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-etUrauRHgE)
- **Shameless cloning remains a big advantage: use Dataroma's top holdings of 10-15 great investors as a 50-stock universe instead of 50,000 global stocks.** Anything in Chuck Akre's or Bill Ackman's concentrated portfolio has passed many filters; then screen for what you understand, which are great businesses, and finally valuation. _[Dataroma, Chuck Akre, Bill Ackman]_ — [2021-11-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wT1m8J4hdpA)

### Circle of competence & checklists (22)

- **Separate capitalism from doing good: you cannot optimize two variables, so focus investing on returns and create impact through philanthropy.** He personally would not invest in tobacco and is not eager on casinos, sports betting or lotteries, but has invested in a liquor company and in carbon-heavy car companies, and would not argue much with others who draw different lines. — [2021-01-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QIUH0IzoV6E)
- **He would not hold Bitcoin: money is a medium of exchange valued by what we ascribe to it, and a Bitcoin worth $5 million defies logic, though 99% of the world he does not need to understand.** He cites people losing hundreds of millions in Bitcoin to forgotten passwords and a UK hard drive with $280 million in a landfill (the owner offered $70 million to dig). He does not need to go long or short. _[Bitcoin]_ — [2021-01-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QIUH0IzoV6E)
- **You do not need a large circle of competence, only to know its boundaries and stay inside them, as John Arrillaga did by investing solely in real estate within two miles of Stanford.** Arrillaga will not let you finish a sentence about a strip mall in Sacramento or a Turkish warehouse; he knows the rent and value of every building near campus, sells when euphoric and buys back when pessimistic, and became a billionaire. Students should start with products they use, like Amazon or Peloton, and ask how the company makes money, its runway and price. _[John Arrillaga, Stanford, Amazon, Peloton]_ — [2021-02-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NXxIQfVIzVU)
- **He invests bottom-up rather than top-down: first ask whether you understand the business, then what it is worth, though there are a hundred ways to get to Mecca.** On the streaming and ad-dollar shift, he notes platforms like Twitter and Google under-monetize and could get more eggs from the goose without killing it; Netflix raising prices to $17.99 will not see disconnects anywhere near the 15% price increase because it is like an IV drip. _[Twitter, Google, Netflix]_ — [2021-02-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NXxIQfVIzVU)
- **The best lessons come from losers, so his pre-investment checklist, built about 13 years ago from great investors' mistakes, clusters around leverage, misunderstood moats, and management/ownership issues.** Leverage was the largest category of mistakes where visible pre-investment data should have given pause. He has had multiple 100% losses from leverage and is much leerier of heavily indebted companies. — [2021-03-04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V_djW_RGPGA)
- **You need no opinion on 99% of securities; look only at what is inside your circle of competence, products you use and things around you.** If you understand a business you know what it is worth and can see the delta to price. Before buying, you should be able to explain to a nine-year-old in five sentences why you will be drowning in wealth and cannot lose money. _[Apple]_ — [2021-03-04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V_djW_RGPGA)
- **Low disclosure in emerging markets does not preclude conviction if you understand the product, moat and economics and the track record shows it; otherwise have the discipline to pass.** Disclosure and understanding are not directly correlated; he does not invest without great conviction, and the range of alternatives is large enough to walk away. — [2021-03-04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V_djW_RGPGA)
- **The first filter on any pitch is whether it is inside the circle of competence, and about 99% of ideas fall outside his.** Many student pitches were 'straight over my head'; they become hard until more time is spent. He also noted that a $1 billion minimum market cap and 10-year horizon 'took away all the fun', since 10x is easier to find sub-billion, though tiny caps may trade by appointment. — [2021-03-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NEB2RfRgBSQ)
- **You need a system to eliminate large swaths of companies in seconds; the goal is to be really good at saying no, and the business must convince a deep skeptic it deserves a place in the portfolio.** He passes on all of US healthcare (corrupt, no market forces), defense contractors and high-flying tech on valuation; Snowflake takes him 15 seconds to dismiss. Sources include Value Investors Club, Value Line, SumZero and ideas emailed daily. _[Snowflake, CVS, Walgreens, Value Investors Club, SumZero, Value Line]_ — [2021-04-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XNtWcAag9as)
- **If you are asking whether something is in your circle of competence, or what the business is worth, it is not; stay dead center because competence fades gradually from the center outward.** Within the circle you know the two or three variables driving the long-term outcome and the valuation is apparent; he says he does not understand 99% of stocks and is not breaking out in hives about it. — [2021-04-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XNtWcAag9as)
- **The three new moat-checklist questions are: Is it a cinch? Are the feet on the desk? Is the destination awesome? His portfolio should eventually be a museum of only such businesses.** Costco just opened its first China store and got mobbed; it could have 1,000 China stores and enter 10 more of the 160-170 countries where it has no presence in 20 years. He candidly says only two of his current holdings are cinches with feet on the desk and hopes the 'Mickey Mouse moat' businesses get replaced. _[Costco, Frontline]_ — [2021-04-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XNtWcAag9as)
- **A checklist is built by studying how great investors lost money and asking what was knowable beforehand; his has about 170 questions.** Buffett's Dexter Shoe loss to cheap Chinese labor produced the question 'could this business be hurt by cheap overseas labor?', which is a no for Amex and Costco but relevant for US manufacturers. _[Dexter Shoe, American Express, Costco]_ — [2021-04-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XNtWcAag9as)
- **He is always bottom-up and never starts from a sector or country; the first question is whether a business is in your circle of competence, and Covid is opportunity because trouble creates uncertainty.** Jio is largely unaffected or helped by Covid while private hospitals face murky mandates and airlines were uninvestable in 2020; he quotes John Templeton that trouble is opportunity, since babies get thrown out with the bathwater. _[Jio, Zoom, John Templeton]_ — [2021-05-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9JYXICM3RSo)
- **Mechanical filters make him cringe because the real world and individual businesses are messy; statistical cheapness is only the beginning of the hunt.** A stock well below book value may be worth far more or far less than book, and a P/E of 2 may be deserved if the company is gone in year three. After finding something cheap, the first question is whether it's within your circle of competence and you can figure it out. — [2021-08-02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p5xt09gAi-U)
- **Because monopolists won't explain their edge, reading annual reports alone is diluted; you must treat the moat as a jigsaw puzzle and back into it from the numbers and from being a customer.** Rain Industries has been in his portfolio for more than six years and is a low-cost producer whose plants stay profitable when competitors bleed red ink; he can see it in the numbers but after meeting the CEO twice still cannot explain how or why. A great business cannot mask its economics in required reporting. _[Rain Industries, Nick Sleep, Qais Zakaria, Costco]_ — [2021-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_7UfqjD3IEg)
- **He doesn't get ideas from talking to people and is against analyst teams generating ideas; his two colleagues only help with deep dives on businesses he is already looking at.** He makes one or two investments a year, so an idea-generating analyst would be frustrated by constant no's. Free Value Investors Club, a paid SumZero subscription (roughly $10-15k a year) and Value Line are enough; one could do really well with just Value Line and one or two investments a year. _[Value Investors Club, SumZero, Value Line]_ — [2021-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_7UfqjD3IEg)
- **In investing there are no called strikes; you can let a thousand pitches go by and only need opinions on a tiny sliver of the planet.** Unlike baseball, investing is like cricket where you can let 100 balls pass; one can live a healthy and wealthy life without ever shorting a stock. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2021-10-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PN3f668IKO0)
- **Less can be more: narrow focus, even to a single state's companies, can give a big edge because you know the businesses intimately and can easily kick the tires.** The Mairs and Power Fund in Minnesota mostly invested in Minnesota companies and did really well; you do not need to look globally. _[Mairs and Power Fund]_ — [2021-10-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-etUrauRHgE)
- **If you find yourself asking whether a business is in your circle of competence, the answer is no; you would not have asked the question if you understood it.** He gives the example of asking yourself 'Do I understand Apple?' as proof that you don't. _[Apple]_ — [2021-10-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-etUrauRHgE)
- **The size of your circle of competence doesn't matter; what matters is staying at its epicenter, and if you're wondering whether something is in it, it isn't.** He cites John Arrillaga's tiny circle; for students, the most likely circle is the products and services they use daily (YouTube, Facebook, Google, iPhone, toothpaste), since becoming a trusted brand is a very high bar. _[John Arrillaga, Facebook, Google, Apple]_ — [2021-11-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wT1m8J4hdpA)
- **Personally, finance depreciating assets and your home but never carry margin debt or play with options; in businesses, the ideal is very high ROE with no borrowed money.** Fair Isaac (FICO scores, ~a penny per score) is his example of a hugely profitable business that needs no leverage; refusing to invest in levered businesses would still let you live a blissful, profitable life, though leverage occasionally creates opportunities when the market misreads it. _[Fair Isaac]_ — [2021-11-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wT1m8J4hdpA)
- **Greed can mislead you, so build circuit breakers: a 160-170 question pre-investment checklist and a trusted peer investor to discuss ideas with.** Munger told him to discuss ideas with a peer who cares about him rather than an analyst who works for him. On a first pass the checklist typically surfaces 10-20 unanswered questions, which means the work isn't done; focus on what could cause permanent loss of capital and the upside takes care of itself. _[Charlie Munger]_ — [2021-11-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wT1m8J4hdpA)

### Valuation & margin of safety (19)

- **He no longer does precise intrinsic-value calculations; he owns 4 million of Reysas's 12 million square feet through his funds and intends to keep the business for a long time rather than sell when it reaches full price.** Before 2020 he viewed the Turkish investment as a temporary undervaluation to exit after a good run; now the mindset is ownership of a well-managed business. _[Reysas]_ — [2021-01-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QIUH0IzoV6E)
- **Value and growth are two sides of the same coin: any business is worth its future cash flows discounted to present value, and paying meaningfully less than that is value investing regardless of the growth rate.** Whether a business grows 10%, 50% or declines 5%, the cash flows drive what it is worth; paying anything for future cash flows has led to poor long-term results. He would love to see 20-year cash flow projections for Snowflake to judge whether it is overvalued. _[Snowflake]_ — [2021-02-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NXxIQfVIzVU)
- **A great business can be a terrible stock if overvalued: Microsoft in 2000 produced under $10 billion of cash flow on a $600 billion valuation and was a bad holding until 2015-2016 even though the business kept doing well.** Visiting Redmond in early 2000, Microsoft employees with nearly all their assets in the stock told him it had only gone straight up for 24 years; the market cap later dropped 70-80%. Cisco had the same issue; these were not Pets.com businesses with no model. _[Microsoft, Cisco, Pets.com]_ — [2021-02-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NXxIQfVIzVU)
- **P/E is an inadequate metric; a portfolio at 23x forward earnings is not expensive if the businesses grow 20-30% a year for 5-10 years, and market trends and macro should be ignored.** Per Nick Sleep, you could have paid 100x earnings for Walmart in the 1970s or even 1980s and still beaten the market; Walmart's public runway has lasted 51 years and only the Walton family held it throughout. _[Walmart, Nick Sleep]_ — [2021-03-04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V_djW_RGPGA)
- **Focus on the downside; if the downside is solidly protected the upside almost takes care of itself.** The ideal equation is: if it does not work I end up with roughly what I started with, and if it works it is a multi-bagger. A significant probability of a zero coupled with a high probability of a multi-bagger is not of much interest. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2021-03-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NEB2RfRgBSQ)
- **He never deliberately enters binary-outcome situations; every business has a non-zero probability of going to zero, so the aim is to maximize home-run odds while minimizing permanent capital loss.** Before investing he tries hard to figure out what could go wrong and what would happen to the position if it did; sometimes an investment becomes binary only after it has gone south. — [2021-03-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NEB2RfRgBSQ)
- **Margin of safety has evolved from Graham's hard-asset protection to protection from brands, culture and customer relationships, and investors must be flexible about this.** Graham was scarred by the 1930s; buying a crappy business at a third of liquidation value protects the downside but crimps the upside. See's Candies (paid over $25 million for under $5 million of book) led to Coca-Cola and later Apple, where the downside protection was the brand; Munger notes Graham made most of his money on GEICO because it was a great business, not because it was cheap. You rarely get hard-asset protection and 100-bagger potential together. _[Ben Graham, See's Candies, Coca-Cola, Apple, GEICO, Copart, Charlie Munger]_ — [2021-03-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NEB2RfRgBSQ)
- **Even for a great compounder he will not pay up: Costco at 36x trailing earnings loses him, though he would look at low double digits.** He jokes he wants his cake and to eat it too, ideally Costco at three times earnings; at 15 times, 'you lost me'. _[Costco]_ — [2021-04-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XNtWcAag9as)
- **Thou shall not use Excel: if you need a DCF to know whether an investment works, there is a problem.** For Costco you need a rough range of future stores, members and profit per store in your head; if he could buy Costco at nine times earnings he would not need Excel to know he would make money. _[Costco]_ — [2021-04-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XNtWcAag9as)
- **Growth and value are two sides of the same coin: every business is worth its discounted lifetime cash flows, so a rapidly growing stream deserves a higher price.** Buying Amazon does not make it a non-value stock and buying a company at one-fifth of book does not make it a great value stock. He admits he shifted to a Grahamian approach before the dotcom bubble, was up about 70% a year in 1999-2000 with no losses, but 'forgot to switch back' to his original preference for high-ROE growth businesses. _[Amazon]_ — [2021-05-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9JYXICM3RSo)
- **Graham and Munger approaches use the same part of the brain: what does a dollar put out today return in five or ten years, via convergence to value or growth in value.** In the Graham way you buy a $2 bill for a dollar and results depend on how long convergence takes; in the Munger way the dollar grows and results depend on the rate and duration. It is 'orgasmic' when the two worlds meet. — [2021-07-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cJGkrSFVnns)
- **Holding company discounts like Prosus/Naspers are very common; the market pays less when a Picasso and a Matisse are shoved down its throat together.** Koos Bekker's analogy from a Naspers call: roughly $200 billion of Tencent stock plus $40 billion of other investments trading at maybe under $150 billion. Sometimes the market gives you things on a platter. _[Prosus, Naspers, Tencent, Koos Bekker]_ — [2021-07-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cJGkrSFVnns)
- **A small investor should set an absolute target such as doubling every three years (about 26% a year), which rules out buying at 80% of intrinsic value and requires buying a dollar for 30 cents.** Sources can include distressed or high-yield bonds yielding over 30% to maturity when mispriced; Munger bought Tenneco common and bonds at 20-30 cents on the dollar around 2002 and turned $10 million into $80 million in three or four years. _[Charlie Munger, Tenneco]_ — [2021-08-02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p5xt09gAi-U)
- **He has shifted from a bias toward low-P/E bargains to a bias toward compounders, and doubts he would place his Seritage-vs-MasterCard bet with Guy Spier today.** He guesses MasterCard is probably ahead, though Seritage is just hitting its stride and the outcome will play out over five to seven years. _[MasterCard, Seritage, Guy Spier]_ — [2021-08-02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p5xt09gAi-U)
- **He invests bottoms-up and opportunistically rather than picking sectors; basket bets only work when the world goes to extremes, like commodities in 2009.** Most of the time so much capital chases good businesses that they get fully or overpriced, so you need an understanding of the business that differs from the world's to get a valuation gap. — [2021-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_7UfqjD3IEg)
- **Finding great businesses is easy; finding great investments, where the price does not reflect the great economics, is the hard part.** Amazon, Alphabet and Microsoft are obviously great; the harder second step is finding the aberration where the market has not figured it out, and as Munger says, 'Why should it be easy to get rich?' _[Amazon, Alphabet, Microsoft, Charlie Munger]_ — [2021-10-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PN3f668IKO0)
- **Deep mispricings like Reysas persist because tiny market caps are below institutional radar and historic-cost lira accounting hides the asset value.** He first suspected fraud and spent an afternoon touring warehouses with the founder; the company does a poor job educating investors, and depreciated 30-year-old lira book values bear no relation to market value. _[Reysas]_ — [2021-10-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PN3f668IKO0)
- **A DCF of future cash flows is the only way to truly value any asset; the difficulty is not the model but the uncertainty of the cash flows, and most of the value sits in the next five to seven years.** A business certain to grow 50% a year for five years would be at 12-13x earnings in five years even if bought at 100x, so paying 100x could be wise; a business shrinking 5-10% a year may be too expensive at 10x. He uses Facebook at 20-30x as the example. _[Facebook, Tesla, McDonald's]_ — [2021-10-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-etUrauRHgE)
- **Intrinsic value need not be precise: Coke is clearly worth more than 15x trailing earnings, so at 5x it's a no-brainer and at 12x you don't know and pass, since there are no called strikes.** You can let a thousand balls go by; keep saying no until something like Facebook at 12x earnings shows up and hits you like a two-by-four. _[Coca-Cola, Facebook]_ — [2021-11-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wT1m8J4hdpA)

### Portfolio concentration & selling (15)

- **Buying dollar bills for 30-50 cents and selling near a dollar turned every $1 in Pabrai Funds into about $14 after fees over 21 years, but it is an inefficient treadmill compared with holding great businesses with long runways.** A really good business will periodically look optically overvalued, maybe for a long time, and that should not by itself prompt a sale. The shift makes life easier, improves returns and cuts taxes. _[Pabrai Investment Funds]_ — [2021-01-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QIUH0IzoV6E)
- **Nick Sleep's model: when you find exceptional businesses with high returns on equity, long runways, great managers and deep moats, go all in, ideally find them small, then set it and forget it.** In 2013 Sleep ran about $3 billion with 40% ($1.2 billion) in Amazon and 90% across Amazon, Costco and Berkshire, defying UK regulators. He compounded about 20% a year for 14 years, returned capital in 2014 with Amazon at $300 (now over $3,300), kept his own stake, and has since outperformed almost any manager while working perhaps 100 hours a year. _[Nick Sleep, Amazon, Costco, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2021-01-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QIUH0IzoV6E)
- **Repositioning the portfolio toward great compounders is like turning an aircraft carrier and will take a few years, after which the job is monitoring; his job has always been reading and thinking as a 'gentleman of leisure'.** New positions were started in 2020 but the fund is 'pregnant with a bunch of positions' that must play out before the carrier is positioned correctly. — [2021-01-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QIUH0IzoV6E)
- **Think of yourself as a partner and co-owner of the business, not an investor, and like great entrepreneurs be extremely non-diversified.** Sam Walton, Steve Jobs and Bill Gates often had 99% of wealth in one illiquid business. Buffett says it is madness to put money in your 25th best idea; Munger says three stocks are enough. Pabrai's personal accounts rarely hold more than two or three stocks, sometimes one, while the funds cap positions at 10% at cost although one or two positions have grown to 60-70% and he was reluctant to trim. _[Sam Walton, Steve Jobs, Bill Gates, Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger]_ — [2021-02-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NXxIQfVIzVU)
- **It is very hard to beat the index with a 20-stock portfolio capped at 5% per name; when a business you understand extremely well is also very undervalued, step up to the plate: when it is raining gold, put out a bucket, not a thimble.** He distinguishes between businesses one understands extremely well and not so well, and says the convergence of deep understanding and deep undervaluation is the moment to concentrate. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2021-02-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NXxIQfVIzVU)
- **Don't trim or sell a great business because it hits or exceeds intrinsic value; the only question is whether the business is getting better.** Worth 100 and trading at 120 is an irrelevant data point; 20x fair and 30x actual is not a reason to sell into a 12x alternative given taxes. Only something egregious like Snowflake at 80x sales is a different conversation. He used to sell at intrinsic value and buy something else, and no longer does. _[Snowflake, Walmart, Nick Sleep]_ — [2021-03-04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V_djW_RGPGA)
- **Be comfortable with 95% of the portfolio in one stock if it is a great business that keeps getting better, like Amazon held for 15 years.** Amazon is getting better by the day and is not egregiously overvalued; Jeff Bezos says it is still day one, so he would wait until day two to reconsider. _[Amazon, Jeff Bezos]_ — [2021-03-04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V_djW_RGPGA)
- **Four or five stocks is enough for your own money, per Munger; with other people's money he caps positions around 10%, and 10 stocks is plenty.** Nobody should own 20 or 30 stocks. Pabrai Funds rarely puts more than 10% into anything because it is other people's money. _[Charlie Munger, Pabrai Investment Funds]_ — [2021-03-04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V_djW_RGPGA)
- **Diversification is overrated; do not compromise the circle of competence to get diversified, and even two or three stocks is fine if the competence is solid.** Sam Walton and most entrepreneurs had no diversification and no sleepless nights; John Arrillaga became a billionaire investing only in real estate within two miles of Stanford. _[Sam Walton, John Arrillaga]_ — [2021-04-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XNtWcAag9as)
- **Pabrai Funds never puts more than 10% of assets into a position at cost, but he refuses to trim winners and has let two stocks become 70% of the portfolio.** He is not a proponent of cutting the flowers and watering the weeds and will not sell purely for 'risk management'; his personal portfolio rarely has more than three stocks and often just one. _[Pabrai Investment Funds]_ — [2021-04-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XNtWcAag9as)
- **He will not discuss positions he is still building, such as Alibaba, but if he is buying he must like it.** He says Alibaba is a fascinating business worth studying and will discuss it, like Graphtec, once he no longer owns it. _[Alibaba]_ — [2021-05-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K4mggdrMHVo)
- **If you know what you are doing, owning 20 or 30 stocks is insanity; four carefully selected stocks is enough, and if you do not know what you are doing, index.** Munger's Peoria example: owning the Ford dealership, McDonald's franchise, best office building and best apartment tower would do extremely well; Buffett asks why put money in your 27th best idea instead of your third. Pabrai Funds uses a 10x10 portfolio, his personal account sometimes holds one stock, and Dakshana's $20-23 million is mostly in three positions. _[Charlie Munger, Warren Buffett, Dakshana Foundation]_ — [2021-05-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K4mggdrMHVo)
- **With $20-30 million of capital he would put a quarter or a third of it into his best idea like the Turkish company; concentration is what makes small-capital returns meaningful.** At his fund size the Turkish position could only be 4% of NAV because he could only invest $7 million. _[Reysas]_ — [2021-07-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cJGkrSFVnns)
- **If you make 10 bets and one is a hundred-bagger with an enduring moat that the rest of the world hasn't figured out, it doesn't matter what happens to the other nine.** Finding even one such business a year is plenty; the game is the willingness to dive deep and solve the jigsaw puzzle when companies aren't helping you, which also gives conviction to hold through temporary headwinds. _[Koos Bekker]_ — [2021-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_7UfqjD3IEg)
- **Shorting is one of the dumbest activities: the most you can make is 2x and the most you can lose is everything.** Roaring Kitty, GameStop and AMC showed there is no limit to how far a stock can rise; no short sellers appear in the Forbes top 10 because 'they lost their shorts'. He sent Ben Mezrich's 'The Antisocial Network' to Buffett and Munger. _[GameStop, AMC, Roaring Kitty]_ — [2021-10-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PN3f668IKO0)

### Compounding & long-term holding (14)

- **Nick Sleep's question: if you owned Walmart in 1970 or 1980, what facts caused you to sell, and if you owned Kmart, what caused you to keep it?** The Walton family has held Walmart since its 1970 IPO but almost no public investor held it even 20 years. Kmart was cheap on many metrics but in decline; Walmart looked expensive but was going from strength to strength. _[Walmart, Kmart, Nick Sleep]_ — [2021-01-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QIUH0IzoV6E)
- **'The best investors weren't investors at all; they were entrepreneurs who never sold' (Nick Sleep): think of yourself as the founder or owning family and ignore valuation as long as the moat is widening.** The exception is egregious cases: a family owning GameStop right now should have sold a while ago. He has gradually begun shifting his portfolio to this mindset. _[Nick Sleep, GameStop]_ — [2021-01-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QIUH0IzoV6E)
- **In 2020 he changed his thinking from buying dollar bills for 40-50 cents and selling at 90 cents to buying great compounders with long runways, even at small discounts, and holding them for 10x or 100x.** The old approach was tax-inefficient in taxable accounts, especially in Massachusetts and California, and he would sell compounders once they reached full price. With 10 carefully chosen compounders not bought at ridiculous valuations, one or two winners suffice even if four fail. — [2021-02-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NXxIQfVIzVU)
- **The Nifty 50 lesson: a single 2% position in Walmart, a $30-40 million market cap company when it came public in 1970, made the entire richly priced basket beat every index by a mile despite a 98% error rate.** The Nifty 50 (McDonald's, Coca-Cola, Polaroid, Xerox, Kodak) traded at 70-100x earnings and got crushed in 1973-74 when the market lost two-thirds; without Walmart it performed terribly. Yet nobody but the Walton family held Walmart from 1970, 1980 or even 1990 to now, which only an owner mindset makes possible. _[Walmart, Nifty 50, McDonald's, Coca-Cola, Polaroid, Xerox, Kodak, Walton family]_ — [2021-02-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NXxIQfVIzVU)
- **Three variables drive wealth: capital invested, length of runway, and rate of return; for young people the runway is 70-80 years, and $5,000 at 15% (doubling every five years by the rule of 72) becomes $5 million in 50 years.** He put his 18-year-old daughter's $5,000 summer earnings into a Roth IRA: 10 doubles is 2^10, about 1,000x, tax-free. At 10% and seven-year doubles a 70-year runway gives the same result, so great stock picks are not where the game is. — [2021-02-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NXxIQfVIzVU)
- **Reading Nick Sleep's Nomad letters in 2020 convinced him he had been 'barking up the wrong tree'; the Holy Grail is finding long compounders and not sweating modest overvaluation.** Because markets were so euphoric in 1999-2000 he defaulted to classic Graham, buying 50-cent dollars and selling at 90 cents. Owning a business the way a founder does means you do not need a fine exact value and, as long as it is not in secular decline, you let it ride, with tax efficiencies as a bonus. _[Nick Sleep, Nomad Investment Partnership, Ben Graham]_ — [2021-03-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NEB2RfRgBSQ)
- **Every sell decision is an investing mistake; the holy grail is a compounder you can hold for decades while you sit on your ass and the company kicks ass for you.** Citing Thomas Phelps' '100 to 1 in the Stock Market' (1972), he says he went through a significant change in thinking in 2020: the buy-at-half-off-sell-at-double approach is tax-inefficient and a treadmill, so he now asks what a business looks like in 10 or 20 years. _[Thomas Phelps, Frontline]_ — [2021-04-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XNtWcAag9as)
- **With a buy-and-hold-forever approach the hurdle rate changes: if a business bought at 9x reaches 40x, leave it alone as long as the moat is deepening, just as the founding family would.** The key questions are whether the business is getting better and more valuable, not what forward return the current multiple implies. _[Costco]_ — [2021-04-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XNtWcAag9as)
- **Ask the Walmart question: if you owned a great compounder in 1980 or 1990, what would make you sell, and if you owned K-Mart, what would make you keep it?** Walmart has been public 51 years and only the Walton family has held it the whole time, collecting dividends through three generations. Nick Sleep's insight is that answering those two questions well is the core of long-term investing. _[Walmart, K-Mart, Nick Sleep]_ — [2021-05-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9JYXICM3RSo)
- **Think of yourself as the promoter, or the junior partner of the promoter, of a business rather than as an investor, and hold as long as the trajectory keeps improving.** Indian promoters commonly own 50-70% of listed businesses and keep their wealth concentrated there because they know the business best. His new model is not to sell at 90-100% of intrinsic value but to keep owning for 10, 20 or 30 years while the business gets better. — [2021-05-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9JYXICM3RSo)
- **Naspers' 8,000x on Tencent, from $32 million in 2001 to about $200 billion, shows that extreme patience and stepping up with a meaningful bet matter more than being right often.** Naspers bought the 43% stake from Li Ka-Shing, who would be worth $230 billion instead of $30 billion had he held, and resisted pressure to sell at $1 billion, $10 billion and $100 billion. Pabrai believes Tencent is deeply undervalued even at $700 billion with too many ways to win and too few to lose, and that 'the story has just begun'. _[Naspers, Tencent, Li Ka-Shing]_ — [2021-05-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9JYXICM3RSo)
- **Nick Sleep's three questions: What is the destination in 10-30 years? Is the business getting better and the moat wider? Is the valuation reasonable, not egregious?** Reading Sleep in 2020 added an explicit layer on lessons that were implicit in Buffett and Munger; the 10 Commandments need cutting down, as God reduced everything to 'do unto others'. _[Nick Sleep]_ — [2021-05-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K4mggdrMHVo)
- **Koos Bekker is 'Nick Sleep on steroids': a hired-gun CEO who turned a $32 million bet on Tencent in 2001 into a position worth hundreds of billions and did not sell a single share until 2018.** Bekker joined Naspers in 1998 asking for zero salary, zero bonus and no contract in exchange for 3% of value created, and took the company from under $200 million to over $200 billion in about 20 years, a thousand-x. Even when Tencent became 97% of Naspers' assets he took no chips off the table, and the 2018 sale proceeds were used to buy back Naspers stock. _[Koos Bekker, Naspers, Tencent, Nick Sleep]_ — [2021-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_7UfqjD3IEg)
- **Nick Sleep and Qais Zakaria outperformed everyone after hanging up their boots simply by keeping large stakes in Amazon, Berkshire and Costco untouched.** If you kept Amazon at one-third of your portfolio from around 2013 and didn't touch it, you beat everybody without doing much real work. _[Nick Sleep, Qais Zakaria, Amazon, Berkshire Hathaway, Costco]_ — [2021-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_7UfqjD3IEg)

### Moats & business quality (24)

- **Moats show up in the numbers over long periods, and the challenge is that great businesses are usually fully priced, so wait for misunderstanding or temporary headwinds to decimate the price.** Picking up MasterCard's numbers is enough to see it is a great business; sifting great from not-great is not hard. _[MasterCard]_ — [2021-03-04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V_djW_RGPGA)
- **Capitalism is brutal creative destruction: most businesses will not make it, and by the time a company enters the S&P 500 the elements of its decline are usually already in place.** Very few businesses last 50 years and almost none last 100. Looking at the 25 student pitches, ten years from now the list will show a high mortality rate, with many not even where they are today; a great brand alone (e.g. Twinkies) does not guarantee survival because brands need constant nurturing. _[Twinkies]_ — [2021-03-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NEB2RfRgBSQ)
- **Retail is a terrible business, but 'recycling and funeral services' retailers like Ollie's and TJ Maxx are great because mismatched inventory always needs an honorable burial.** Manufacturers will always have too much or unwanted inventory, so there is a continuous need; the treasure-hunt aspect adds a Costco-like element. The caveat is that, unlike Costco, they must keep feeding the machine as they scale. eBay and Big Lots are in the same category, and TJ Maxx is a strong tenant for his Seritage investment. _[Ollie's Bargain Outlet, TJ Maxx, Costco, eBay, Big Lots, Seritage]_ — [2021-03-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NEB2RfRgBSQ)
- **Funeral homes are a great business because nobody aspires to enter it, customers do not take the low bid, and deaths per year are highly predictable recurring revenue.** From the out-of-print Mosaic (chapters free on ChaiwithPabrai): you do not call 10 funeral homes for the cheapest quote when your grandmother dies, and you say yes to flowers; 'I don't know who's going to die in Peoria in 2022, but I know how many'. — [2021-03-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NEB2RfRgBSQ)
- **Look for the exceptional business that is not fragile, then find it at a cheaper price; putting the pieces together is why investing is not easy.** Businesses are very fragile creations, and even short periods of neglect can be detrimental to great brands. — [2021-03-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NEB2RfRgBSQ)
- **If the CEO or CFO can run the business with his feet on the desk, it is generally a kickass business to invest in.** An American Tower CFO sat idle because every tower owner already had his number and knew his price; Chuck Akre found the Bandag tire-retreading CEO with feet up decades ago. Most businesses would fail in three months if the boss did that. _[American Tower, Bandag, Chuck Akre]_ — [2021-04-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XNtWcAag9as)
- **Scaled economies shared, where a business gives the benefits of scale back to customers, produces very long runways and is one of the most powerful business models.** MasterCard keeps the spoils of its 20-25 basis point take rate, but Costco caps markups at 15% versus 25-30% at Walmart or Amazon, treats itself as a buying agent for members, and earns essentially only the membership fee; its wine buyers guarantee vineyards 20 years of output at fair prices. Each new Costco makes all Costcos stronger; Amazon and Berkshire's insurance follow the same track. _[Costco, MasterCard, Amazon, Berkshire Hathaway, Walmart, Nick Sleep]_ — [2021-05-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9JYXICM3RSo)
- **The key question for a great business is its destination: what will it look like in 10 or 20 years and with what probability?** Capitalism is so brutal that most businesses cannot be forecast that far, but some, like Costco, give comfort; Costco's first China store had mile-long lines and could have 1,000 stores in 20 years, so a shareholder need make no decisions and just hold. _[Costco]_ — [2021-05-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9JYXICM3RSo)
- **A Covid-hit business is only worth buying if it has great capital allocation, a balance sheet that easily survives two or three bad years, and a great core business; some businesses you should only be a customer of, never an owner.** He hates hotels and airlines because price transparency means your dumbest competitor sets the price, though he respects IndiGo as the lowest-cost operator. _[IndiGo]_ — [2021-05-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9JYXICM3RSo)
- **Businesses in the 'death' or 'rebirth' business, funeral services, asset reconstruction, off-price retail, are really good businesses with pricing power that nobody questions.** US funeral home roll-ups never go bankrupt because deaths are predictable and no one shops six funeral homes for the lowest price; TJ Maxx flourishes buying others' inventory mistakes at one-third of cost; Seritage redevelops shuttered Sears stores; Piramal buying DHFL's debt is a funeral-services business. _[TJ Maxx, Seritage Growth Properties, Piramal, DHFL, Oaktree]_ — [2021-05-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9JYXICM3RSo)
- **Tencent contains a 'Sequoia Fund on steroids': a biz dev arm that redeploys roughly $15 billion of annual free cash flow into mostly private, post-traction businesses with a record that rivals the best VCs, and with no carry.** They avoid large stakes to preserve team incentives and have backed 15-20 companies that became unicorns; this redeployment engine is extremely rare among even great businesses. _[Tencent]_ — [2021-08-02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p5xt09gAi-U)
- **US payment systems are archaic with extremely high frictional costs, so Visa and MasterCard's 2-3% take is a moving target globally even though their US moat, reinforced by airline-mile kickbacks, is very hard to disrupt.** China and Korea are far more advanced; using a bank or other rails would cut a small merchant's cost by over 95%. Alipay and Tencent Pay built great moats, but payments can shift rapidly so one must be careful. _[Visa, MasterCard, Alipay, Tencent]_ — [2021-08-02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p5xt09gAi-U)
- **Some businesses are so good an idiot can run them, like a Coke bottler with a monopoly territory, while most of capitalism is dog-eat-dog where you must be amazing at execution.** The dying bottler's advice to his kids: 'whatever you do, don't let them change the contract'. Businesses that must be well managed to survive end up well managed; those that can tolerate slack generally have it, so most Coke and Pepsi bottlers are undermanaged. _[Coca-Cola, Pepsi]_ — [2021-08-02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p5xt09gAi-U)
- **Real monopolies go to great lengths to convince you they are not monopolies, while the 99% of businesses in hypercompetitive spaces try to convince you they have unassailable advantages, so what companies present is mostly backward.** Drawn from Peter Thiel's 'Competition is for Losers' Stanford lecture (2015 or 2016); Google says 'poor me, I'm a tiny part of global advertising' to deflect attention from its search monopoly, and maybe 1% or less of capitalism has such moats. _[Peter Thiel, Google, Facebook]_ — [2021-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_7UfqjD3IEg)
- **A whale only gets harpooned after it surfaces, so the best operators scale in stealth; once Amazon disclosed AWS around 2015-2016, Microsoft and Google immediately pounced.** Buffett told him this line in the context of Ajit Jain, who has no desire to ever surface. Bezos accepted competitors cannibalizing Amazon's retail so it could sell 'pickaxes in the gold rush', rebuilt spaghetti code into APIs, and hid the cloud business for years; today it is a three-horse race with AWS leading, Microsoft a strong second, and Google a distant third. _[Amazon, AWS, Microsoft, Google, Ajit Jain, Warren Buffett, Jeff Bezos]_ — [2021-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_7UfqjD3IEg)
- **In software the productivity gap between an incredible engineer and a good one can be a thousand to one, so a company like Tencent would rationally pay $50 million a year to a true superstar versus $100,000 for a run-of-the-mill engineer.** Pony Ma is very good at sifting out the rockstars and making sure they are well taken care of; this army is a bazooka he can point wherever he wants. _[Tencent, Pony Ma]_ — [2021-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_7UfqjD3IEg)
- **Low-cost provider status gives many businesses a long-term enduring competitive advantage.** He cites GEICO, Berkshire Hathaway, Costco, Walmart and Nucor's mini-mills alongside the Patel motels. _[GEICO, Berkshire Hathaway, Costco, Walmart, Nucor]_ — [2021-10-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PN3f668IKO0)
- **Capitalism is brutal and 99% of businesses are tough; per Peter Thiel's 'Competition is for losers', investors should seek the 1% with monopoly-like enduring edges at a reasonable price.** Even at 1% of 50,000 listed companies there are 500 awesome businesses; Thiel's Stanford lecture is on YouTube and worth watching. _[Peter Thiel]_ — [2021-10-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PN3f668IKO0)
- **Monopolies go to extreme lengths to convince you they are not monopolies, while competitive businesses beat their chests claiming secret sauce.** Facebook and Google do not want governments thinking they are monopolies; listing the products you use (iPhone, Amazon, your utility) reveals monopolies, and their financials scream it out even when they want you to walk on by. _[Facebook, Google, Apple, Amazon]_ — [2021-10-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PN3f668IKO0)
- **Levered businesses are significantly less likely to survive multiple decades because a downturn coinciding with rising rates lets lenders turn the screws.** Capitalism is brutal and most businesses don't survive more than a few decades even when successful; check gearing ratios and whether interest is a large share of earnings at low rates. — [2021-11-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wT1m8J4hdpA)
- **A horse that counts to ten is a smart horse, not a smart mathematician: the best company in a bad industry is only the smartest horse, so pick businesses with natural advantages and pricing power.** Fair Isaac may be a better business than the best steel company or oil refiner; investors have the choice to be patient and choose where to go. _[Fair Isaac]_ — [2021-11-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wT1m8J4hdpA)
- **Moats are usually obvious with some thought (network effects at Facebook/Instagram, low-cost at Costco); if you can't convince yourself it's a no-brainer, pass, because one decision every year or two is fine.** Moat is Buffett and Munger's shorthand for enduring competitive advantage, simpler than Porter's five forces; sometimes the advantage is hidden and you see it only in the profits or growth, which makes it a treasure hunt. _[Facebook, Instagram, Costco, 7up]_ — [2021-11-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wT1m8J4hdpA)
- **Identifying which high-return businesses can keep earning high returns for decades is the hard question that can make you insanely wealthy, and even GEICO shows advantages can erode.** GEICO's direct-writer model gives an 8-12% cost edge over State Farm and Allstate and took it from 2-3% to 8-12% share, but Progressive's early bet on telematics let it run circles around GEICO, which was not predictable 10-15 years ago; similar uncertainty applies to Coke's sugar issue and Visa/MasterCard/Amex in payments. That's why a margin of safety and aha moments are needed. _[GEICO, Progressive, State Farm, Allstate, Coca-Cola, Visa, MasterCard, American Express]_ — [2021-11-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wT1m8J4hdpA)
- **The definition of a great business is American Tower's CFO with his feet on the desk: sellers know his number and his price, no deals need negotiating.** The second tenant on a tower is nearly 100% margin and carriers keep paying because moving a tower disrupts their network topology, though a satellite disruptor like Elon Musk could change that. _[American Tower, AT&T]_ — [2021-11-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wT1m8J4hdpA)

### Management & capital allocation (11)

- **'Uber cannibals' that put 100% or more of net income into autopilot buybacks can compound spectacularly even if the business barely grows.** NVR, a capital-light homebuilder, bought back about 80% of its shares over 25 years and the stock rose more than 400-fold; AutoZone is an okay business where buybacks did the heavy lifting. Rebalancing annually to find future NVRs can produce a hockey stick when the multiple eventually takes off. _[NVR, AutoZone, Charlie Munger]_ — [2021-03-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NEB2RfRgBSQ)
- **Research is a jigsaw puzzle: form a thesis, then compare what management said five or ten years ago with what transpired to see whether they under-promise and over-deliver.** He is always looking for a flimsy reason to stop; recently he dropped a company after three days of digging but valued the learning about the industry and CEO. — [2021-04-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XNtWcAag9as)
- **Indian Hotels is a great place to stay but he would not put a penny in at any price because of horrible capital allocation.** It overpaid for the Pierre Hotel in New York after 60-65% of the best-view rooms had been sold as apartments, and guaranteed those owners free twice-daily turndown service at New York labor rates; Taj Boston was similar. Bombay House-run businesses like Corus, Tetley, TISCO and TELCO fared poorly while TCS and Titan, which it left alone, did extremely well. _[Indian Hotels, Tata Group, TCS, Titan, Corus Steel, Tetley]_ — [2021-05-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9JYXICM3RSo)
- **Invert the problem: you only need one or two bets a year, so with an empty calendar you can dismiss most ideas in five minutes and go deep only on the interesting ones.** Buffett and Munger used no analysts and he had none for over 20 years; he now has a couple of researchers by accident who do narrowly directed probing. _[Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger]_ — [2021-05-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9JYXICM3RSo)
- **Avoid being swayed by management meetings: CEOs are super salesmen with a huge knowledge edge, so judge them by what they said 10 years ago versus what transpired.** Buffett said at the 2021 Berkshire meeting that a personable but incompetent CEO is an unlisted risk factor; it took Pabrai 15 months to realize one CEO was not that great, and Jeff Immelt 'checked all the boxes' yet snowed even Jack Welch (see the books 'Lights Out' and 'Hot Seat'). Lack of access can be an advantage for individual investors. _[Jeff Immelt, General Electric, Jack Welch, Al Dunlap, Jeff Bezos]_ — [2021-05-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K4mggdrMHVo)
- **The Agnellis will hold Ferrari forever but Exor will move more capital out of mass-market autos over time, because Ferrari's 10,000 cars a year are worth more than Stellantis's millions.** John Elkann is a learning machine and good capital allocator; the economics of Ferrari versus Stellantis are night and day. Pabrai's mistake was not holding Ferrari himself. _[Exor, Ferrari, Stellantis, Fiat Chrysler, John Elkann]_ — [2021-07-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cJGkrSFVnns)
- **The best use of capital is an internal spawning engine with a high hit rate, second is buying or investing in other businesses at valuations that yield high ROE, and third is dividends or buybacks, which work best at modest valuations.** Amazon redeploys mostly through internal spawns while Berkshire mostly acquires externally; MasterCard, despite very high net margins, must buy back stock at 40x earnings because it has no other option, and buying at 10x would be far better. Spawners sit at the apex of the pyramid. _[Amazon, Berkshire Hathaway, MasterCard]_ — [2021-08-02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p5xt09gAi-U)
- **Among the seven or eight big US and Chinese tech giants, only Amazon and Tencent truly understand capital allocation, which shows up in the fact that they alone carry no cash while the others drown in it.** Microsoft, Apple, Google and Alibaba sit on $50-150 billion earning under 1%; it doesn't bother Sundar, Satya or Apple, but it bothers Pony Ma, who spends slightly more than the cash he generates and borrows at 1% rather than leave money in a checking account. _[Tencent, Amazon, Microsoft, Apple, Alphabet, Alibaba, Pony Ma]_ — [2021-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_7UfqjD3IEg)
- **There is no single template for great management; there are many ways to Nirvana and different styles fit different people.** Reed Hastings has no office, wanders around and boasted of going three months without making a decision, yet that produced Squid Game; Bloomberg and Bruce Flatt sit in bullpens; Andy Grove managed by walking around. Buffett's baseball analogy: hitters stand differently but all can hit. _[Netflix, Reed Hastings, Michael Bloomberg, Bruce Flatt, Brookfield, Andy Grove, Jeff Bezos]_ — [2021-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_7UfqjD3IEg)
- **Study business biographies of underappreciated leaders like Ken Iverson of Nucor, Reed Hastings of Netflix and Sol Price of Price Club, whose 'buying agent for the consumer' philosophy is the source of everything that makes Costco great.** Sol Price didn't think of Price Club as a retailer but as being on the consumer's side against manufacturers, keeping a small sliver. Reed Hastings has no office or desk and said the longer he goes without making a decision, the better Netflix runs. _[Nucor, Ken Iverson, Netflix, Reed Hastings, Sol Price, Price Club, Costco, Home Depot, Michael Dell]_ — [2021-10-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-etUrauRHgE)
- **Not being able to meet management is an advantage because you won't be sold; judge management by comparing what they said 10-20 years ago to what they delivered.** Buffett and Munger don't care about projections, only track record; going back 10-15 years shows whether managers under-promise and over-deliver and whether they're competent. — [2021-11-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wT1m8J4hdpA)

### Markets, cycles & macro (22)

- **Auction-driven markets overshoot and undershoot: a random NYSE stock shows at least a 2-to-1 range between its yearly low and high while an apartment building near Clemson would be quoted at nearly the same price all year.** Intelligent buyer facing intelligent seller yields rational prices; faceless auction pricing does not. Ben Graham: markets are voting machines short term and weighing machines long term. Without these distortions he could not make a living. _[Ben Graham]_ — [2021-01-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QIUH0IzoV6E)
- **The GameStop squeeze is unprecedented: a Reddit crowd that does not know each other is not illegal collusion but has broken market mechanisms, and the SEC is torn about the right response.** GameStop's short thesis was justifiable given the secular shift from physical stores to downloads. The stock was at $303 during the talk, with online chatter aiming for $1,000 to wipe out hedge funds; one argument is to let the dumb hedge funds face the music. _[GameStop, BlackBerry]_ — [2021-01-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QIUH0IzoV6E)
- **In January 2021 there are bubbles in SPACs, heavily shorted stocks and 10-15 Robinhood names including Tesla, but beyond those it is not clear the broader market is overvalued if rates stay low.** GameStop has gone beyond a bubble to a mega bubble; Tesla is clearly in bubble territory in his view. The rest of the market seems richly valued but justifiable under low interest rates. _[Tesla, GameStop]_ — [2021-01-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QIUH0IzoV6E)
- **Micro trumps macro: with 80% of the portfolio in six or seven positions, what matters is how those businesses perform, not who is president, which party controls Congress, or what the market does in 12 months.** Buying a McDonald's in Clemson, you would look at its past cash flows and local demographics, nothing else. He has no idea what markets will do next year and does not care. _[McDonald's]_ — [2021-01-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QIUH0IzoV6E)
- **Auction-driven markets overshoot and undershoot constantly, with almost every stock showing a 100% gap between its 52-week high and low, so volatility is part and parcel of investing and a 50% drawdown is par for the course.** Munger says Berkshire has dropped 50% or more from a high three times in his life. Pabrai's funds lost two-thirds in 2008-09 while intrinsic value was much higher, then rose over 110% in 2009 because they were so undervalued, not because the businesses did better. _[Berkshire Hathaway, Charlie Munger, Pabrai Investment Funds]_ — [2021-02-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NXxIQfVIzVU)
- **Market crashes are the best times to improve a portfolio by swapping lesser businesses for better ones that got thrown out more deeply.** In 2008-09 commodity stocks fell to prices that made no sense, so he built a basket of seven or eight commodity bets at 2% each without time to drill down; every one at least doubled and some rose seven or eight times. _[commodity basket 2008-09]_ — [2021-02-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NXxIQfVIzVU)
- **Focus on the micro, not the macro: 99% of what happens on the planet he does not understand, and Walmart and Bezos did fine through oil shocks, wars, price controls and sky-high rates.** Negative-yielding debt, the Fed balance sheet, Bitcoin and the GameStop short squeeze are all popcorn entertainment; the real opportunity is where no one is paying attention. _[Walmart, Jeff Bezos, GameStop, Bitcoin]_ — [2021-02-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NXxIQfVIzVU)
- **The stock market is a theater where every seat must always be occupied, so when someone yells fire the ticket clears at whatever price gets a new buyer to sit down.** Seritage traded at $35-40 before COVID and instantly went to $6-9; Pabrai bought a bit more than one-eighth of all the seats and says the movie is great even if it is a little warm under his seat. He will discuss it fully once he no longer owns it. _[Seritage Growth Properties]_ — [2021-03-04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V_djW_RGPGA)
- **Market inefficiency is not tied to a specific country; in 2021 the US inefficiency is in overheated sectors, not in bargains, so he looks for businesses worth 10 selling for 4, which mostly exist outside the US.** Different markets are at different points in the cycle; some whole markets are very cheap. He is not interested in something worth 10 selling for 8. — [2021-04-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XNtWcAag9as)
- **Shorting makes no sense: there are no short sellers in the Forbes 400, which is dominated by long-only, non-diversified people.** Short sellers must cut positions as a stock rises and are chained to the quote machine; Buffett and Munger say they were almost always right on the company but wrong on timing. A short seller who loses 3% a year while the S&P makes 9% calls it 6% alpha, which only makes money via fees. _[Tesla, Sam Walton, Bill Gates, Jeff Bezos]_ — [2021-04-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XNtWcAag9as)
- **Indian unicorns will produce a few outlier winners and many disappointments, but there is no need for envy; every investment must be a no-brainer before you make it.** Friends dismiss food delivery as heavy logistics with restaurants resenting 30% cuts, yet cloud kitchens and dense delivery could make the top two or three players incredible businesses in 10-20 years. You can be a very successful investor without ever making any of those bets. _[Zomato, Groww, Zerodha]_ — [2021-05-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9JYXICM3RSo)
- **Food delivery is at an embryonic stage and will be 'Amazonized' over the next 10-20 years, and such reconfiguration of industries creates efficiencies and investment opportunities.** Pizza Hut was dine-in only when he arrived in Clemson in 1983 and is now almost all delivery; DoorDash's one-to-one deliveries are 'ridiculous' compared with pooled routes, and cloud kitchens with 30-50 kitchens per warehouse, pre-positioned drivers and drones are coming. _[Pizza Hut, Domino's, DoorDash, Chipotle]_ — [2021-05-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K4mggdrMHVo)
- **Microsoft in early 2000 was a great business but a bad investment: over $600 billion market cap, under $10 billion cash flow, 60-70x earnings, and zero returns for 13-14 years despite huge revenue growth.** Microsoft, GE and Cisco were the only three $600B+ companies; he told Microsoft employees holding 80-90% of their wealth in the stock that it looked like a bad investment. Even holding from 2000 to 2021 yielded only about 3x. Pabrai Funds was up over 70% in its first year (mid-1999 to mid-2000) by sidestepping the euphoria. _[Microsoft, GE, Cisco, NASDAQ]_ — [2021-07-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cJGkrSFVnns)
- **He is not a market timer; undervalued businesses exist at all times, only the geographies and industries change, so investing is a treasure hunt among 50,000 businesses.** A company hitting a temporary air pocket gets taken out back and shot by the market, and that deserves attention. Ten-baggers are few and far between in any market. — [2021-07-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cJGkrSFVnns)
- **GameStop, AMC and Bitcoin are in bubble territory in 2021, but large US and Chinese tech are exceptional businesses that are merely not deeply discounted, not bubbles.** Ron Insana's book TrendWatching shows bubbles exist all the time because humans vacillate between fear and greed. Being right about Bitcoin is irrelevant if you are neither long nor short; what matters is being right on what you own. _[GameStop, AMC, Bitcoin]_ — [2021-07-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cJGkrSFVnns)
- **Successful investors are forced to move up the capital chain, leaving the low end permanently open to young, enterprising entrants.** Per Joel Greenblatt, a $1 million investor earning 50% soon has $10 million and can no longer use the small opportunities; managing about $750 million, Pabrai won't research a business where he can only deploy $2 million even if he'd love the hunt. _[Joel Greenblatt]_ — [2021-08-02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p5xt09gAi-U)
- **China regulatory risk is real and rules can change the economics of a business overnight, which is exactly why you don't have only one bet.** He doesn't know whether Tencent will do well in the future; there is nothing like a sure bet in investing and capitalism is just hard. _[Tencent, Alibaba]_ — [2021-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_7UfqjD3IEg)
- **Everything about COVID unfolded opposite to what he expected, and it created secular, permanent shifts in behavior worth studying for investment opportunities.** In March 2020 he never imagined indices at all-time highs in October 2021; he sees business travel and business hotels permanently impaired, delivery businesses like DoorDash becoming 'whatever you need in 30-60 minutes' businesses, and housing prices up because everyone wants more space at once. _[DoorDash, Marriott]_ — [2021-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_7UfqjD3IEg)
- **The bottom of the market is continuously emptied out as good small investors get wealthy and move up the chain, so obscure opportunities for small capital are always available.** Citing Joel Greenblatt: a $10,000 position matters to a beginner but Buffett can't touch it; Pabrai himself can't justify investments where only $50,000 could be put to work. _[Joel Greenblatt, Warren Buffett]_ — [2021-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_7UfqjD3IEg)
- **As long as humans vacillate between fear and greed there will always be mispricings in both directions, so bargains always exist somewhere, though they are rarely comfortable to buy.** The ones fitting the criteria are usually the hardest to convince yourself to buy, as with Turkey where everyone wants to exit because of Erdogan and backwards macro policy. — [2021-10-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PN3f668IKO0)
- **Micro trumps macro: as a bottoms-up stock picker he cares little about geography, currency or who runs the country because long-term returns depend on how the business does.** Some markets are still cheaper than others: Turkey is very undervalued due to macro noise, Japan because of decades of terrible returns, and pockets of India and China may be undervalued, but plenty of undervalued businesses exist in the US too. — [2021-10-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-etUrauRHgE)
- **Don't overlay macro assumptions on investing; most people are wrong about everything and it may not matter in the end.** He was wrong about COVID in March 2020 and would never have guessed all-time highs after half a million US deaths or that remote work would raise productivity. — [2021-11-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wT1m8J4hdpA)

### Stock case studies (17)

- **In July 2019 Turkey's largest warehouse operator could be bought for about $40 million, under $3.50 per square foot for 12 million square feet leased 99% long-term to blue-chip tenants, against a liquidation value of $50-60 a foot.** With about $17 a foot of debt, $3 of equity per foot would return about $33 in liquidation, 11x. Tenants include Amazon, Alibaba, Carrefour and IKEA; multinational leases are in euros with 2-3% escalators, Turkish leases inflation-indexed. He spent an afternoon visiting all the warehouses to rule out fraud and now owns one-third of the company, his largest percentage ownership ever. _[Reysas, Amazon, Alibaba, Carrefour, IKEA]_ — [2021-01-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QIUH0IzoV6E)
- **In 2019 he bought a third of a Turkish company (Reysas) for under $7 million at a $19 million market cap versus at least $500 million liquidation value, less than 5 cents on the dollar, run by exceptional capital allocators, and plans to do nothing but check on it in 2030.** The company owns 12 million square feet of warehouses and Turkey's largest truck fleet; it is up seven or eight times in about 20 months. He expects the father-son team, who own about 40%, to at least triple intrinsic value in 10 years to perhaps $1.5 billion by 2030, and the 35-year-old son gives a three- or four-decade runway. It was 1.5% of assets at purchase. _[Reysas, Turkey]_ — [2021-02-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NXxIQfVIzVU)
- **Copart is an exceptional business with a tailwind: sensor-laden bumpers mean minor damage totals five- or six-year-old cars, sending more vehicles to salvage.** He liked the founder's book 'From Junk to Gold' and the company's principles; students pitched it at a $25 billion market cap with ~45% US share, 30%+ ROE and 26% earnings growth over six years. _[Copart]_ — [2021-03-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NEB2RfRgBSQ)
- **Long gestation periods for new supply create violent booms and busts, and VLCC shipping is the office-tower cycle on steroids.** Office towers take 4-6 years so supply arrives all at once; VLCCs take about three years from Korean yards, day rates swing from $5,000 to $200-250,000, and when rates collapse Greek owners scrap single-hull ships (post-Exxon Valdez rules) so the fleet shrinks from 400 to 350 and rates then spike within weeks when demand returns. _[Frontline, Exxon Valdez]_ — [2021-04-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XNtWcAag9as)
- **D-Mart succeeds because its model blends Costco and Walmart, which is why nobody in India can touch it.** He says Avenue Supermarts took many lessons from Costco, and counts D-Mart among good businesses alongside MasterCard, Costco and Berkshire. _[D-Mart, Avenue Supermarts, Costco, Walmart]_ — [2021-05-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9JYXICM3RSo)
- **In 2019 he bought one-third of Turkey's largest warehouse, truck and rail operator for $7 million at a $19 million market cap against $300 million to $1 billion of liquidation value.** The company traded at roughly 2-7% of liquidation value with 12 million square feet of fully leased warehouses; his only question was whether the promoters were crooks. Turkey is one of the best markets because local investors have extremely short holding periods, expecting to buy at 10am and sell at noon for 10%. _[Reysas]_ — [2021-05-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9JYXICM3RSo)
- **Rain Industries was a no-lose deep-value bet that went 10x, but it is a good business with a great capital allocator, not the great business a Nick Sleep framework would target.** In 2015 he bought the 9.99% foreign-investor maximum at 35-40 rupees when Jagan Reddy had grown revenue from $200 million to $2 billion through two non-recourse, fully debt-financed acquisitions (a US business for $600-650 million and Rutgers in Europe for $900 million) that the market valued at zero. Earnings hit $200 million in 2017-18, the stock went to 450, fell to 50 in Covid, and sits around 170-180; he still holds because Reddy spends about $10 million a year extra on pollution control and thinks long term. _[Rain Industries, Jagan Reddy, Rutgers]_ — [2021-05-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9JYXICM3RSo)
- **When the nature of a bet changes, exit even at a small profit or loss rather than watch the story unfold in slow motion.** Graphtec's dominant EAF electrode position with take-or-pay contracts made cash flows knowable, bought at $7-9 and trading at $14-15 pre-pandemic; in March 2020 force majeure claims and falling steel output made the contracts questionable, so he sold at a small profit and would not change that decision even though the stock recovered. _[GrafTech, Brookfield]_ — [2021-05-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K4mggdrMHVo)
- **His 2019 Turkish investment was bought at 4-5% of liquidation value ($20M market cap vs $500-600M liquidation value) with two great capital allocators, making it 'Nick Sleep on steroids'.** He owns a third for about $7 million; the free float turned over every 15-17 days because Turkish investors trade for hours. In two years liquidation value rose to $800-900 million and market cap to over $100 million. The Sleep lesson: set it and forget it as long as the capital allocators are in place, even if the discount closes. _[Reysas, Nick Sleep]_ — [2021-07-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cJGkrSFVnns)
- **Rain Industries, bought in 2015 at a 'future PE of one', went from a $200 million to over $2 billion market cap by 2018 when the expected earnings arrived.** The company had close to $2 billion of revenue and he expected a year with $200 million of earnings within three or four years; not a cigar butt and not a great business, but a good business with a great capital allocator. He fell in love with the management. _[Rain Industries]_ — [2021-07-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cJGkrSFVnns)
- **Indian Energy Exchange is an effective monopoly with 80% operating margins whose share of India's electricity has grown from under 3% to over 6.5%, but like most great businesses it cannot redeploy its cash and can only dividend or buy back.** IEX collects about 1.5% of the amount transacted; $100 of revenue becomes about $80 pre-tax and about $60 after 25% tax. Its first spawn, Indian Gas Exchange, also needs almost no capital. _[Indian Energy Exchange, Indian Gas Exchange]_ — [2021-08-02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p5xt09gAi-U)
- **Tencent's real business model is two 'bazookas': an army of software engineers earning about 65% annualized return on capital and 20-30 'digital Warren Buffetts' who invest the leftover cash at about 35% a year.** On roughly $15 billion of cash flow, the engineering arm can absorb only about $1 billion (5,000 engineers at $200,000 each), so the remaining $14 billion goes into minority stakes in companies like PDD, JD.com and Meituan that do the heavy lifting off Tencent's payroll. He thinks this model runs circles around Amazon's and that Tencent could be the most valuable business on the planet in 10-15 years. _[Tencent, Pony Ma, PDD, JD.com, Meituan, Amazon]_ — [2021-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_7UfqjD3IEg)
- **Reysas in Turkey was bought in 2019 at 4 cents on the dollar of liquidation value: 12 million square feet of prime warehouses against a $20 million market cap.** Warehouses 99% leased to Amazon, Ikea and Carrefour on 10-year inflation-indexed leases, under $200 million debt, worth $75-80 a square foot or about $1 billion. He ended up owning a third of the company; two years later it is up 6x in dollars (10x in lira), still only 24 cents on the dollar, and rooftop solar of about 50 MW added roughly $200 million of value. _[Reysas, Amazon, Ikea, Carrefour]_ — [2021-10-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PN3f668IKO0)
- **Indian Energy Exchange was the highest-quality business of 200-plus Indian management teams he met, but he dumbly sold his 4.99% stake during COVID.** In 2018-19 IEX handled 3% of India's electricity with a 1% fee and about 70% net margins, foreigners capped at 5%; Guy Spier bought about 4.4 million shares near $2 for roughly $9 million, now a $50 million-plus position up five to six times. Pabrai rebought and holds a similar position. _[Indian Energy Exchange, IEX, Guy Spier]_ — [2021-10-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PN3f668IKO0)
- **Leverage that hurts operators can create opportunities for investors, as with Teck Cominco, which fell from $45 to $4 in early 2009 when a one-year bridge loan could not be refinanced and was back at $45 within a year.** Teck had a dominant, oligopoly-like metallurgical coal footprint with long-term contracts tied to specific coal chemistry. He reasoned banks would not want to run coal mines, so they would extract a pound of flesh and extend the loan, while Teck sold assets and forward-sold production, which is exactly what happened. _[Teck Cominco]_ — [2021-10-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-etUrauRHgE)
- **A Turkish warehouse operator with $600-800M of net asset value and a $20M market cap was a no-brainer where the only remaining question was whether management was honest.** 12 million sq ft at $70-80/sq ft replacement cost, 99% leased to Amazon, Carrefour and Ikea on ~10-year leases, a couple hundred million of debt; you don't need to weigh a huge bull to know it's big. He met the father and son and checked with trusted locals. _[Reysas]_ — [2021-11-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wT1m8J4hdpA)
- **Indian Energy Exchange is his American Tower: 95-98% share of spot power trading, 1% take rate, 75% of revenue is net income, and share of India's electricity went from 3% to 7.5% in three years with policy pointing to 20-35%.** Invested about three years earlier, up 5-6x; an 80-person company that could 10x revenue with only 50% more staff. It's now 40% of his India fund and he'll let it ride and simply disclose even if it reaches 95%. _[Indian Energy Exchange, American Tower]_ — [2021-11-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wT1m8J4hdpA)

### Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US (16)

- **The Turkish lira fell 40% after he invested, yet the position is up six or seven times in dollars because prime warehouses have a global value regardless of whether the local currency is seashells, dollars or lira.** Currency instability, poor leadership and mass foreign exit were the macro backdrop in 2019, and none of it mattered. The exceptional father-son capital allocators have since done value-adding things he never had on his radar; he has no plans to sell. _[Reysas]_ — [2021-01-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QIUH0IzoV6E)
- **Currency risk was irrelevant for the Turkish warehouses because he was buying hard assets for one year's rent, $3 a square foot to buy versus $3 a square foot of inflation-indexed rent.** In July 2019 foreigners were fleeing Turkey, and the lira fell 40% within six months of his investment, yet the position was up 7x in dollars and 12x in lira; a weaker lira raises cement prices and therefore replacement cost of existing warehouses. Tenants included Amazon, Carrefour and IKEA at 100% occupancy. _[Reysas, Turkey, Amazon, Carrefour, IKEA]_ — [2021-02-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NXxIQfVIzVU)
- **With US stocks priced to perfection in 2019-2021, he broadened to entire markets that were cheap and unloved like Japan, Korea and Turkey, visiting portfolios of trusted local Graham-Munger investors.** Week-long trips to Seoul cover 15-20 businesses from a friend's portfolio; cloning such ideas is powerful because they have already passed one set of filters. He now has investments in Turkey and Korea, and a China trip was cancelled by COVID. — [2021-03-04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V_djW_RGPGA)
- **In very cheap markets the temptation is to buy anything at 3x earnings rather than the better businesses at 8-9x, and he is trying to move his Turkish friend from Graham to Munger.** Cultural nuances about how owners and managers think are an overlay, but a business is a business anywhere: discount future cash flows. — [2021-03-04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V_djW_RGPGA)
- **India is a minefield where the truly great businesses generally trade at very elevated valuations, with only occasional dislocations.** HDFC Bank is not just a great Indian bank but probably one of the best banks in the world, and through that lens it may be value-priced even though it never looks cheap on normal metrics. _[HDFC Bank]_ — [2021-05-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9JYXICM3RSo)
- **India grows at night while the government sleeps; market-distorting regulations still shackle natural entrepreneurs, which makes him somewhat skeptical.** India and Singapore had the same per-capita GDP 70-75 years ago and the difference now is night and day; India could grow fast for a long time if the shackles were removed, but he never picks sectors top-down. — [2021-05-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9JYXICM3RSo)
