- **80% of Mumbai is a tear-down and the city will be completely rebuilt over the long haul because the land is so valuable, in fits and starts.** Mumbai real estate is terrible value for money; redevelopment laws protect apartment owners (rent allowances, larger replacement flats) and now require slum dwellers to be rehoused on the same site, but slum redevelopment is a dirty, political, mafia-involved business that organized developers avoid. — [2021-05-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K4mggdrMHVo)
- **He spends almost no time on macro or exchange rates because he has no competence there and, for the right businesses, those factors mostly do not matter.** The Turkish Coke bottler, which also bottles for Pakistan and is partly owned by Coca-Cola and indirectly by 3G, can raise prices even if the currency devalues 100%; cases sold grow with GDP, and it trades far cheaper than any other Coke bottler despite nearly identical economics. _[Coca-Cola Icecek, Coca-Cola, 3G Capital]_ — [2021-05-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K4mggdrMHVo)
- **You cannot paint a country with one brush; within the chaos of emerging markets like India or Turkey there are great teams and businesses that transcend currency, inflation and leadership problems.** Growing up in India he saw well-organized operations like Coca-Cola inside the chaos, which gives him comfort diving into Turkey when friends dismiss it for its currency and leadership. _[Coca-Cola]_ — [2021-07-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cJGkrSFVnns)
- **Most of China is outside his circle of competence, but Alibaba and Tencent are understandable because they had Western investors early and are multinational in DNA despite being based in China.** Munger's view that the Chinese are natural capitalists trapped in a socialist system; capitalism there is still embryonic but developing quickly. He recently bought Alibaba. _[Alibaba, Tencent, Charlie Munger]_ — [2021-07-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cJGkrSFVnns)
- **He sides with the Chinese government on cracking down on for-profit tutoring, calling the equivalent Indian industry 'rootless capitalists' after 14 years of studying it at Dakshana.** With 10-15,000 IIT seats and half a million to a million aspirants, capitalism creates toll bridges that don't add seats; in China the cost and effort made couples decide not to have more kids, which is why the government stepped in. A blogger he follows says China is innovation then regulation, Europe regulation then no innovation, and the US innovation and no regulation. _[Dakshana]_ — [2021-08-02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p5xt09gAi-U)
- **China's large tech players are high quality and operated in a wild west where rules were undefined, so government tweaks may ultimately produce a better, more competitive ecosystem.** He says very little that has happened in China recently makes him scratch his head, and a robust competitive environment is healthy for the country. He declined to comment on current portfolio holdings. _[Tencent]_ — [2021-08-02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p5xt09gAi-U)
- **Chinese government action on video games is a 'pimple on a camel' for Tencent because less than 5% of its video game revenue and profit comes from inside China, and the engineering army can be redirected anywhere.** He says you could ban video games globally and Tencent would still prosper; in the absence of clear rules from the CCP, Pony Ma has pointed both bazookas outside China. What Tencent wants is for the CCP to state all the rules at once instead of dribbling them out. _[Tencent, Pony Ma]_ — [2021-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_7UfqjD3IEg)
- **He agrees with the CCP's crackdown on Chinese for-profit education because test-prep companies are win-lose businesses that don't create seats, they only decide who gets the limited ones.** In India roughly 1 million kids compete for about 15,000 IIT seats, so only about 1.5% succeed and 95% of paying customers end up disappointed; he contrasts this with Costco where every participant in the ecosystem wins. His 15 years running Dakshana gave him a front-row seat. _[Costco, Dakshana, Guy Spier]_ — [2021-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_7UfqjD3IEg)
- **The biggest wealth in China over the next 10-20 years will come from businesses that are private or worth under $1 billion today, not from Tencent or Alibaba which can hardly go up more than 10x.** He admits this is outside his own circle of competence, but tells students to roll up their sleeves and find the Tencents and Alibabas of tomorrow. He thinks Alibaba's model is not as good as Tencent's but both can do well. _[Tencent, Alibaba, JD.com, PDD]_ — [2021-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_7UfqjD3IEg)
- **Inflation and currency collapse are a non-event when you own hard assets bought far below replacement cost.** The lira went from under 5 to over 9 per dollar between 2019 and 2021; if inflation rises, cement and land prices and warehouse replacement cost rise too, so the properties appreciate in lira and hold value in dollars. Turkey remains one of the cheapest markets in the world with many mispriced businesses. _[Reysas]_ — [2021-10-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PN3f668IKO0)

### Psychology & temperament (17)

- **Shorting is a very dumb activity: maximum gain is a double and maximum loss is infinite, so he has never shorted a stock and will go to his grave without doing so.** He finds many things overvalued but has no ability to predict when or how overvaluation corrects; nothing prevents an overvalued stock from becoming more overvalued. Shorting heavily shorted stocks is playing with fire; an index or basket would be safer. _[GameStop]_ — [2021-01-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QIUH0IzoV6E)
- **Never use leverage, because it becomes lethal in large drawdowns when the broker asks for cash at the moment you have none.** He also keeps the saying 'if wealth is lost nothing is lost, if health is lost something is lost, if character is lost everything is lost'; a portfolio drop is only a temporary loss of wealth and has never bothered him. — [2021-02-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NXxIQfVIzVU)
- **The stock market is a mechanism to transfer wealth from the active to the inactive, and the number one skill an investor needs is extreme patience: if you love watching paint dry, this is the business for you.** Turkish retail investors hold stocks for hours or days, creating the volume that let him buy; his main job now is sitting on his ass while the operators work, like Rip Van Winkle waking up in 2030. _[Warren Buffett, Reysas]_ — [2021-02-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NXxIQfVIzVU)
- **He refuses to give stock picks because there is only downside: even the Turkish bet could go to zero, and buying something because someone else told you about it is a bad starting point.** A tip runs out of steam in two or three years and the tipster is nowhere to be found; a know-nothing investor should dollar-cost average into the S&P 500 and own Apple, Amazon and the other great businesses. _[Apple, Amazon]_ — [2021-02-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NXxIQfVIzVU)
- **You only truly understand a business after you own it with real money, so starting small and adding as the price rises, as Li Lu and Nick Sleep do, is a valid approach.** Li Lu believes risk goes down the longer you own a business because knowledge grows. Nick Sleep ran about 30 stocks with seven or eight making up 70-80% and a 'farm team' of small positions that might be promoted. _[Li Lu, Nick Sleep]_ — [2021-03-04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V_djW_RGPGA)
- **What happens in the market is irrelevant; even when his portfolio fell two-thirds in the financial crisis his demeanor did not change, because panics are when tickets get discounted.** 'If wealth is lost nothing is lost, if health is lost something is lost, if character is lost everything is lost.' Businesses go on sale either from company-specific hiccups or when a hundred theaters are on fire at once. — [2021-03-04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V_djW_RGPGA)
- **The single most important trait for an investor is extreme patience, because business change takes years while the brain processes in seconds.** Someone who loves to watch paint dry, like Seinfeld's Puddy staring at the seat back, is ideally suited to investing. — [2021-04-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XNtWcAag9as)
- **As Munger says, why should it be easy to get rich? Be patient and act only when something is mispriced and fully understood, which may happen two or three times in two or three years.** Answering a former Shree Cement CFO who never owned his own 5,000x stock, he says if an insider cannot forecast cash flows the outsider's job is harder, but you only need to be right on one such business in a 50-year investing life. _[Charlie Munger, Shree Cement]_ — [2021-05-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9JYXICM3RSo)
- **Do not overdose on conspiracy theories; the feared Brookfield 'take-under' of Graphtec was a low-probability event that would still have delivered a decent return.** Brookfield's PE funds had 10-year lives and needed to sell down, which is why they IPO'd Graphtec; a take-under at $15 would have had to be around $18 against a $7-9 cost basis. _[GrafTech, Brookfield, Teekay Offshore]_ — [2021-05-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K4mggdrMHVo)
- **Drawdowns are irrelevant if you have no leverage and know what your portfolio is worth rather than what the auction market prices it at every second.** Munger's Berkshire lost more than half its value three times and it did not bother them. Any NYSE stock's yearly price range might be 50 to 100 while a home on Zillow moves 5-10%; auction-driven markets overshoot and undershoot and that is what makes money. 'If wealth is lost, nothing is lost; if health is lost, something is lost; if character is lost, everything is lost.' _[Charlie Munger, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2021-07-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cJGkrSFVnns)
- **There will always be winning tickets on the ground; the only question is whether you'll bend down and pick them up, as with a Turkish company at a $20 million market cap and $500-600 million liquidation value in 2019, or Rain Industries in 2015.** Neither 80 million Turks nor 1.3 billion Indians were interested, so 'the guy from Bandra' had to do the job. These sit in plain daylight but you must be passionately focused on the hunt. _[Reysas, Rain Industries]_ — [2021-08-02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p5xt09gAi-U)
- **Investing does not need a high IQ or Oxford grades, just basic common sense, a calculator and Excel.** The Reysas math was simple: sell the warehouses for a billion, repay 200 million of debt, and compare 800 million to a 20 million market cap. _[Reysas]_ — [2021-10-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PN3f668IKO0)
- **Live by an inner scorecard: when the outer and inner scorecards diverge, follow the inner one, which makes you more trustworthy and gives a huge edge in life.** Buffett asked at lunch whether you'd rather be the greatest lover known as the worst, or the worst known as the greatest. If his fund is up 30% he asks internally what risk he took and whether it was the best opportunity cost; the easiest person to fool is yourself. _[Warren Buffett, Guy Spier]_ — [2021-10-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PN3f668IKO0)
- **Humans are hardcoded by age five or six and do not change between six and 96, so be extremely picky about friends because you drift toward the people you spend time with.** Hanging out with better people makes you better; wishful thinking that someone will change is futile once you know their nature. — [2021-10-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PN3f668IKO0)
- **Making as few decisions as possible is a huge edge; Guy Spier takes in lots of data but hardly acts on it.** Spier told him 'I don't trust myself to make decisions, so I try to make as few decisions as possible.' _[Guy Spier]_ — [2021-10-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PN3f668IKO0)
- **Read like a gentleman of leisure, curious about how businesses work, and wait for the two-by-four 'aha moment' where you see an insight the market doesn't; once a year is enough.** He reads several physical newspapers daily and biographies; he was still learning about Fiat Chrysler from a Reid Hoffman podcast with John Elkann nine years after that investment. _[Fiat Chrysler, John Elkann]_ — [2021-11-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wT1m8J4hdpA)
- **Investing is permanently thrilling because even a simple business like Coca-Cola requires multidisciplinary thinking, such as psychology of association and celebrity endorsement.** He references his UC Irvine Coca-Cola talk; the factors affecting a business are wide-ranging so you must hone in on what is likely to happen and its impacts. _[Coca-Cola]_ — [2021-11-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wT1m8J4hdpA)

### Buffett & Munger lessons (15)

- **The $650,000 Buffett lunch (2008) 'continues to pay dividends endlessly' even though his only motive was to say thank you.** Buffett, competitively, arranged a lunch with Munger, which led to regular dinners at Munger's home and bridge games with Munger and Rick Guerin at the LA Country Club; he and Guy Spier have been invited to the Sunday Berkshire managers' brunch for about 10 years. His wife said it was the best thing he did other than marrying her. _[Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger, Rick Guerin, Guy Spier]_ — [2021-03-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NEB2RfRgBSQ)
- **Buffett and Munger barely use mobile phones; Buffett's sits in his assistant's desk and Munger has never used one, despite being among Apple's largest shareholders.** Learned over Thursday lunches with Buffett's assistant Debbie, which he says were '10x better than the lunch with Warren' for insight into how Buffett functions. _[Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger, Apple]_ — [2021-03-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NEB2RfRgBSQ)
- **For long-term compounders you need a fanatical focus on near 'cinches', Munger's term for businesses whose franchise is almost impossible to destroy.** After dinner with Charlie that weekend: Amex was a cinch 20 years ago but is not now, while Costco is a cinch because every new store and member deepens the moat; 99% of businesses do not last 10 years and even Fortune 500 companies die within decades. _[Charlie Munger, American Express, Costco]_ — [2021-04-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XNtWcAag9as)
- **The Buffett lunch was about saying thank you for the intellectual property, and it led to a 13-year friendship with Warren and a relationship with Charlie.** Buffett cleared his afternoon and told Pabrai's daughters, then 9 and 11, that the most important decision in life is whom you marry; they asked him about 55 questions. _[Warren Buffett, Guy Spier]_ — [2021-04-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XNtWcAag9as)
- **The 2007 Buffett lunch was 'guru dakshina' for the intellectual property that built most of his $80 million net worth, and it led to a close friendship with Charlie Munger.** Buffett works to make lunch winners feel they got a bargain, gave unlimited time, and, when told Harina preferred Munger, competitively arranged a Munger lunch. Pabrai went on to play bridge with Munger and Rick Guerin every few weeks and calls Munger the smartest, most humble person he will ever meet. _[Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger, Guy Spier, Rick Guerin]_ — [2021-05-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9JYXICM3RSo)
- **Live by an inner scorecard: the world often miscalibrates how good or useless you are, so set an internal true north and measure yourself against it.** Buffett at the 2008 lunch asked whether you would rather be the best lover known as the worst or the worst known as the best; Nick Sleep's Nomad, shaped by 'Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance', cared about how well the job was done, not just turning $1 into $10, and Zach ran a $3 billion fund reading in a lazy boy without a desk. _[Warren Buffett, Nick Sleep, Nomad Investment Partnership, Alice Schroeder]_ — [2021-05-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K4mggdrMHVo)
- **50% a year on small capital is possible with a dogged Graham approach and no more than three stocks, but it requires Buffett's intensity of going through every stock one at a time.** Buffett went through the Moody's Manuals at least twice, looking for anomalies like a business earning $25 million trading for $15 million, and told a questioner to 'start with the A's'. Upanishad: your deepest desire is your destiny. Buffett's 1% outside Berkshire, often one stock, has compounded faster than Berkshire itself. _[Warren Buffett, Moody's Manual, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2021-07-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cJGkrSFVnns)
- **Munger is far more well-rounded than Buffett: investing is just one interest alongside designing dormitories, boats and caravans, and he does not obsess over his annualized compounding rate.** Most of what Pabrai learned from Munger came from observing him with friends, family and grandkids rather than from anything Munger said. _[Charlie Munger]_ — [2021-07-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cJGkrSFVnns)
- **Berkshire never paid a dividend from 1965 onward (except once, when Buffett jokes he was in the bathroom) and didn't even buy back shares for over 40 years because it could redeploy all cash, until recently when it ran out of opportunities.** See's Candies has been a money spinner that can't use its own cash, but the Berkshire engine took See's cash flow and bought a hundred other businesses; the stock is now over $400,000 a share. _[Berkshire Hathaway, See's Candies, Warren Buffett]_ — [2021-08-02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p5xt09gAi-U)
- **Who you are is hard-coded by age five, so the best life comes from aligning your behavior with your inborn traits; Buffett at 80 with the Japan Company Handbook was doing exactly what he did at 12 with racetrack tickets and at 25 with Moody's manuals.** Young Buffett picked up discarded Ak-sar-ben tickets and had Aunt Alice cash the winners; later he read every company in Moody's manuals twice from 7 AM to 11 PM, finding things like an insurer with a $15 million market cap and $25 million earnings. He couldn't help himself with Korean stocks either. The Upanishads: 'your deepest desire is your destiny'. _[Warren Buffett, Moody's Manual, Japan Company Handbook]_ — [2021-08-02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p5xt09gAi-U)
- **Lunches with Buffett's assistant Debbie Bosanek gave more of the real lowdown than lunch with Buffett himself, because Buffett has a veneer of diplomacy.** For several years he and Guy Spier took Debbie to lunch on the Thursday before the annual meeting; one year Buffett met them at the 14th-floor elevator and gave a headquarters tour. _[Warren Buffett, Debbie Bosanek, Guy Spier]_ — [2021-08-02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p5xt09gAi-U)
- **Humans are hard-coded by age five or six, and Buffett's treasure hunt at 11 picking up discarded racetrack tickets, at 26 with Moody's manuals, and today with the Japan Company Handbook is the same activity.** Buffett refused to spend $10-15k on Capital IQ but happily spends $150 on the Japan Company Handbook, and told Pabrai 'all the good stuff is always at the back of the book'. The edge comes not from slicing data faster (NLP or otherwise) but from the analytics you apply; Buffett has no computer on his desk and became the richest guy. _[Warren Buffett, Moody's Manual, Japan Company Handbook, Capital IQ, Tracy Britt]_ — [2021-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_7UfqjD3IEg)
- **Buffett at nine, 25 and 80 was doing the identical activity: sifting discarded racetrack tickets, Moody's Manuals, and the Japan Company Handbook for needles in haystacks.** At Ak-Sar-Ben he sent Aunt Alice to collect winning tickets; in his twenties he found companies with $15 million caps earning $25 million; at over 80 with $100 billion-plus in Berkshire cash he was still reading the Japan handbook, where Pabrai dog-eared pages for him and Buffett said 'all the good stuff is in the back'. _[Warren Buffett, Berkshire Hathaway, Moody's Manual, Japan Company Handbook]_ — [2021-10-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PN3f668IKO0)
- **The biggest lesson from Charlie Munger is not what he says but what he does: stoic behavior to the power of stoic behavior, never engaging in self-pity no matter what life deals him.** Munger, turning 98, lost his wife after a fall down the stairs and nearly lost sight in his one good eye; his only comment was that he might have to learn Braille. He also says he never spent an hour working out and added those hours to reading, while the doctors who advised otherwise are all dead. _[Charlie Munger]_ — [2021-10-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-etUrauRHgE)
- **He attributes nearly all of his 2007 net worth (~$80M) to using Buffett's intellectual property without paying royalties, which is why he bid $650,100 with Guy Spier for the 2008 charity lunch.** Buffett's mental model for the lunch is that the winner must feel they got a bargain; he said he had nothing going on all afternoon and told Pabrai's daughters (10 and 12) to call him Warren. The lunch led to a free second lunch with Munger, then years of Friday bridge at the LA Country Club with Munger and Rick Guerin. _[Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger, Guy Spier, Rick Guerin]_ — [2021-11-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wT1m8J4hdpA)

### Mistakes & lessons learned (19)

- **Delta Financial, a sensible mortgage underwriter, went to zero in late 2007 when securitizations stopped and it was caught with mortgages on its warehouse lines, costing about $50-60 million.** The originate-securitize-repeat model needed little equity and was very profitable until the music stopped; he has not touched a mortgage company since and does not plan to. _[Delta Financial]_ — [2021-03-04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V_djW_RGPGA)
- **Horsehead taught him never to assume management's ambitious new plants will go as planned; the size of a project relative to the mothership must be survivable.** Horsehead's new plant kept getting delayed with cost overruns while the old plant was shut, then zinc prices collapsed and it ran out of runway. Rain Industries in India also has plant delays and overruns, but even if those plants were worth zero the business would survive and thrive. _[Horsehead, Rain Industries]_ — [2021-03-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NEB2RfRgBSQ)
- **Buying at a discount to liquidation value with non-recourse ship debt meant he could not lose on Frontline, but selling at his double meant missing the run to $150.** Frontline had about 80 of the world's 350-400 VLCCs all on the spot market; stock was $4-5 versus $8-9 liquidation value, he put 10% of the fund in, exited around $10-11 and the stock later exceeded $150. Extreme compressions usually pop the other way, so he could have kept a small position. _[Frontline]_ — [2021-04-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XNtWcAag9as)
- **The Kelly formula in The Dhandho Investor was a mistake and should be disregarded for stock picking because you never get to make the same bet 10,000 times.** The 10% position size simply felt comfortable; he is fine with higher concentration in his own money but keeps 10% with other people's money. _[The Dhandho Investor]_ — [2021-04-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XNtWcAag9as)
- **Losing money is par for the course: of 10 investments, four to six will work out worse than expected, and zeros happen.** Delta Financial (a $50-60 million investment in 2006-07) and Horsehead Holdings both went to zero; he says if wealth is lost nothing is lost, and it does not rattle him. _[Delta Financial, Horsehead Holdings]_ — [2021-04-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XNtWcAag9as)
- **Dhandho Holdings, the 2014 insurance holding company, was a mistake, but a mistake with no loss of capital is a home run.** He raised over $150 million, bought an insurer, realized the plan would not work, sold the insurer for slightly more than he paid and is returning more capital than was raised; sitting in board meetings and reviewing claims gave him a great understanding of insurance. _[Dhandho Holdings]_ — [2021-04-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XNtWcAag9as)
- **His biggest mistake was spending too many years on Graham's discounted pies instead of Munger's growing pies, and Nick Sleep goes further: think of yourself as the founding family and hold for the long haul.** He urges the students to get Nick Sleep, who is in their London backyard, to do a webcast. _[Nick Sleep, Ben Graham, Charlie Munger]_ — [2021-05-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K4mggdrMHVo)
- **Buy great businesses run by great management and don't sweat intrinsic value; the entrepreneur is not selling, so why are you?** In 1995 he put $40,000 of his $1 million into four Indian stocks; one went up 140-160x by 2000 and he sold the other three. Kotak (bought for $2,400 because he was impressed dealing with them as his broker; banking license came eight years later) is up 500x and Blue Dart, the FedEx of India, is up 150x, requiring a 26-year hold; Skypack fell 90%. _[Kotak Mahindra, Blue Dart, Skypack, FedEx]_ — [2021-05-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K4mggdrMHVo)
- **Selling his 1%-plus of Ferrari because it traded at 30-40x earnings is a deep regret: the funds made about $100 million but would hold about $300 million of Ferrari stock today.** He owned 1.3-1.4% of Fiat Chrysler after putting about $70 million in at a $5 billion market cap, and received 1.3 million Ferrari shares in the spin-off. He thinks Exor under his friend John Elkann is a good capital allocator with a long runway. _[Ferrari, Fiat Chrysler, Exor, Stellantis, John Elkann]_ — [2021-08-02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p5xt09gAi-U)
- **He retreated into Ben Graham bargains during the 1999-2000 dot-com bubble, which worked well until about 2012-2014, but he missed the turn back to great compounders and is now shifting to buying great businesses with long runways at reasonable prices.** Reading the chapter on Nick Sleep and Zak in 'Richer, Wiser, Happier' during COVID crystallized that the holy grail is finding great businesses early, not paying too much, and riding them. Investing knowledge is cumulative, so unlike Tom Brady an investor keeps getting better with age. _[Ben Graham, Nick Sleep, Qais Zakaria]_ — [2021-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_7UfqjD3IEg)
- **Without failure there is no success; learning from others' mistakes is less painful but our own mistakes get seared in deeper.** Peeling the onion on any successful person reveals many failures along the way; Munger says 'we are old too soon and wise too late'. _[Charlie Munger]_ — [2021-10-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PN3f668IKO0)
- **His biggest regret is abandoning long-runway compounders for Ben Graham cheap stocks after the 1999-2000 bubble and not switching back around 2012-2014.** Bargain hunting became a comfortable habit; reading chapter six on Nick Sleep in 'Richer, Wiser, Happier' in 2021 showed him Sleep won by identifying long runways and doing nothing, so he began his journey back to great compounders. _[Nick Sleep, Ben Graham, Berkshire Hathaway, Costco, Amazon, Coca-Cola, American Express]_ — [2021-10-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PN3f668IKO0)
- **In 2002 he put 10% of his fund into Amazon at $10 a share after a Harvard case on CFO Joy Covey, sold at $14, and blew away a 330x.** With $70-80 million under management, roughly $5 million at 300x would have been $1.5 billion and nothing else in the portfolio would have mattered; 'there can't be dumber than that'. _[Amazon, Joy Covey, Jeff Bezos]_ — [2021-10-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PN3f668IKO0)
- **Even the best investors are right only two out of three times, and asymmetric payoffs mean investing can tolerate a very high error rate.** John Templeton put the top batting average at about 65%; most of Berkshire's roughly 100 acquisitions and Buffett's retailer and airline bets did not work while his bank record is perfect. Had he kept his 5% Amazon position, the other 95% could have gone to zero and the outcome would still be incredible. _[John Templeton, Warren Buffett, Berkshire Hathaway, Amazon]_ — [2021-10-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PN3f668IKO0)
- **Capitalism is brutal and almost all businesses are fragile, so a levered business that hits a headwind may not get to play out its hand; operators should avoid the leverage path.** This applies whether you are a startup or a Fortune 100 company; his daughter's startup carries no debt and has income from the founders' other jobs. — [2021-10-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-etUrauRHgE)
- **Buying the Stonetrust insurance company was a mistake because insurance at its core is a terrible business: you sell a product whose cost you don't know, and pricing is set by your dumbest competitor.** Bought and sold at roughly $60M book value for a small gain; the buyer, a better operator and fixed-income investor, has since grown book value to almost $140M. Workers' comp buyers treat premiums as a tax and shop on price alone, unlike Patek Philippe or Tiffany where higher prices raise demand. _[Stonetrust, Costco, Patek Philippe, Tiffany]_ — [2021-10-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-etUrauRHgE)
- **Failures teach, winners only feel good; keep a real brokerage account because you must feel the pain and you will lose money at least one in three times.** He quotes John Templeton on being wrong one out of three times; Delta Financial, a subprime lender, took $60-70M to zero in 2008 in his concentrated portfolio. _[John Templeton, Delta Financial]_ — [2021-11-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wT1m8J4hdpA)
- **Everyone has SIC codes they excel at and ones they fail in; after repeated losses he no longer looks at banks or finance companies, but low-cost commodity producers have worked well for him.** Buffett has apparently never been wrong on a bank (Forrest Rockford, Wells Fargo, JPMorgan, Bank of America, M&T) but Berkshire's dozens of retail acquisitions have mostly done terribly apart from Nebraska Furniture Mart and Borsheims, because retail is so hard. _[Warren Buffett, Illinois National Bank Rockford, Wells Fargo, JPMorgan, Bank of America, M&T Bank, Nebraska Furniture Mart, Borsheims]_ — [2021-11-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wT1m8J4hdpA)
- **He made a mistake trimming IEX from the 5% ownership cap when COVID hit because it always looked expensive; spectacular compounders like IEX or Fair Isaac will never trade at 8x earnings.** IEX might trade at 80-100x trailing earnings; you only need to find one IEX or one American Tower and, if right about a 30-40 year runway, sit and let it rip. _[Indian Energy Exchange, Fair Isaac, American Tower]_ — [2021-11-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wT1m8J4hdpA)

### Career, entrepreneurship & life (31)

- **Savings rate matters more than stock picks, and it is fully in your control, as Mr. Money Mustache showed by retiring at 30 on a generic programmer's salary.** He lives on about $8,000-10,000 a year, would never buy a new car or a $4 latte, bikes everywhere and uses maybe 15 gallons of gas a year; the one-third-of-income-on-housing rule is for the uneducated majority. It is important to find a Mrs. Money Mustache who is even more frugal. _[Mr. Money Mustache]_ — [2021-02-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NXxIQfVIzVU)
- **Entrepreneurship is the neglected engine that built the United States, ignored by business schools because entrepreneurs are too cheap to hire professors as consultants and practitioners lack the credentials for tenure.** He praises Babson's focus on entrepreneurship as unique; at the core of the nation's wealth is an entrepreneur chasing an impossible dream. _[Babson College]_ — [2021-02-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NXxIQfVIzVU)
- **Pabrai Funds started accidentally as a hobby in July 1999 with $1 million from eight friends, cloning the Buffett partnership rules of the 1950s.** No management fee, a 6% hurdle and annual redemptions; the fund was up over 70% the first year, reached about $2.5 million by late 2000, and he then decided to treat it as a real business. _[Pabrai Investment Funds, Warren Buffett, Buffett Partnership]_ — [2021-03-04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V_djW_RGPGA)
- **Investing knowledge is cumulative, so you must be a continuous learning machine and can keep improving into your seventies and eighties.** Unlike athletes, investors get better as they pile on years, learning especially from mistakes and from other investors, and the model changes periodically. — [2021-03-04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V_djW_RGPGA)
- **Start a fund with the 0/6/25 structure from day one, and first prove yourself by building your own wealth, because Munger's first criterion for a manager is financial independence.** Li Lu turned the float on his student loans into over $1 million by graduation. Pabrai sold part of his business for about $1 million in 1994 and had over $10 million by 1999, and investors came to him. Many of his investors refuse managers who charge 1-2% fees. _[Li Lu, Charlie Munger, Warren Buffett]_ — [2021-03-04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V_djW_RGPGA)
- **Your fund's rules act like a McDonald's sign: no investor calls, no quarterly calls, just a website, which filtered his base to principals and first-generation entrepreneurs rather than agents.** University endowments moved on quickly when given only a website login. Investors in New Zealand wired several million dollars without ever meeting or calling him; the fund has 350-400 families and one annual meeting. _[Pabrai Investment Funds]_ — [2021-03-04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V_djW_RGPGA)
- **Non-venture-backed entrepreneurs are not risk-takers; they do everything possible to minimize risk, and investors should think the same way.** At 24 he started TransTech with $30,000 from his 401k and $70,000 of credit-card debt after researching personal bankruptcy law; Visa and MasterCard were venture capitalists who took no board seats. His old boss promised a job with a 20% raise 'when your business fails', so there was little downside; he ate $7 of Subway sandwiches a day and the business was sold for about $20 million in 2000. _[TransTech]_ — [2021-03-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NEB2RfRgBSQ)
- **Venture-capital 'IV drips' are bad for you; it is better to spend your time getting customers than getting a VC to fund you.** Venture-backed startups are perhaps 1% of all startups; non-venture-backed businesses are what drive the US economy. For students without money, substitute what is between your ears for capital, and use Li Lu, who invested student-loan float at Columbia and graduated with over $1 million, as a role model. _[Li Lu]_ — [2021-03-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NEB2RfRgBSQ)
- **To start a fund, first get independently wealthy with a real track record; then friends and family come, and after that assets are almost automatic.** He turned $1 million into $12-13 million from 1994-99, started Pabrai Funds in 1999 as a hobby guaranteeing friends' principal plus 6% with a one-quarter carry above that, and had to launch a second fund to drop the guarantees at about $3 million of assets. _[Pabrai Investment Funds]_ — [2021-04-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XNtWcAag9as)
- **Learn investing with a real brokerage account holding a meaningful portion of your assets, not hypothetical spreadsheets; make mistakes and learn from them.** Career advice: work for someone you like, admire and trust rather than a name brand, and optimize for learning rather than the resume. — [2021-04-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XNtWcAag9as)
- **Run an empty calendar like Buffett and Munger: no scheduled calls, only two talks a month, emails handled in 20 minutes at 11am, then reading, naps, bridge and cycling.** He sleeps late, gets a printed folder of emails at 11am and is done by 11:20, naps most afternoons, plays 5-7 hours of bridge a week, rides 20 km on weekdays and 40 km on weekends, and plays racquetball and tennis. _[Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger]_ — [2021-05-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9JYXICM3RSo)
- **Having met a payroll and won customers makes you a better investor; entrepreneurs do not run businesses through spreadsheets but through the three or four variables that drive 80-90% of the outcome.** He quotes Buffett: 'I'm a better businessman because I'm an investor and a better investor because I'm a businessman', and 'talking to a fish about walking on land for a hundred years is not the same as walking on land for five minutes'. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2021-05-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K4mggdrMHVo)
- **The brain is optimized to specialize between roughly ages 11 and 20, and Western education wastes that window by forcing generalism; pursue your passion and take the job you would do for free.** Michelangelo, Bill Gates and Buffett all specialized intensely as teenagers; Germany separates kids at 13-14 and becomes a manufacturing powerhouse despite high wages. A lemonade stand at age 10 has a huge impact 20 years later. _[Bill Gates, Warren Buffett]_ — [2021-05-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K4mggdrMHVo)
- **Per Munger, you should already be independently wealthy before starting a fund, having proven you can compound your own money.** Buffett, Munger and Graham have freely shared their frameworks in letters, books and biographies; having the right framework is three-quarters of the battle. _[Charlie Munger, Ben Graham]_ — [2021-05-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K4mggdrMHVo)
- **Having run a business is a huge edge for an investor because entrepreneurs manage three or four variables in their heads, not spreadsheets, and an investor must get to those same variables.** Buffett: 'I'm a better investor because I'm a businessman and a better businessman because I'm an investor', and a thousand years of telling a fish about land is not worth one day walking on it. Projecting a trajectory through Excel is dangerous because nothing goes in a straight line. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2021-07-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cJGkrSFVnns)
- **Traits that make a great investor can be at odds with those that make a great marriage, and Buffett's singular focus was compensated for by his wife Susie until she left in the 1970s.** Buffett worked from an office off his bedroom from 7 AM to 10 PM engrossed in the Moody's Manual; Peter Buffett said his dad would not throw baseballs but was home for dinner every day. With the right partner it can work. _[Warren Buffett, Susie Buffett, Peter Buffett]_ — [2021-07-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cJGkrSFVnns)
- **Before starting a fund you should already be independently wealthy from 10 years of 30-50% annual returns on your own small capital; if you have a great record, investors will 'swim to you in shark-infested waters'.** He started with $1 million from eight investors who had done well on his stock tips; since the SEC bars solicitation but not talking to existing investors, he told them their 'mission in life' was to bring in assets, and went from 8 to 17 to 25 investors. _[Pabrai Investment Funds, Warren Buffett]_ — [2021-08-02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p5xt09gAi-U)
- **Business biographies and autobiographies are his favorite genre because they let you see through founders' lenses across many industries.** He recommends Sam Walton's book, Sol Price's biography by his son (Jim Sinegal: 'there's nothing I know that did not come from Sol Price'), Lowenstein's 'Buffett: The Making of an American Capitalist' and Bezos's 'Invent and Wander'. He found Zen and the Art of Motorcycle Maintenance hard going and didn't get what Nick Sleep got from it, though Audible helped. _[Sam Walton, Sol Price, Price Club, Jim Sinegal, Costco, Jeff Bezos, Nick Sleep]_ — [2021-08-02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=p5xt09gAi-U)
- **He got into investing in 1994 after reading Peter Lynch on a flight, then Buffett biographies, and realized Buffett spent 80% of his time on the strategy work that was only 3% of his time running an IT company.** He had about $1 million after tax from selling part of his company in 1994-95 and began investing it using Buffett's approach of buying a business, not a stock. Herding cats was not fun; he wanted to be like 'that guy'. _[Peter Lynch, Warren Buffett]_ — [2021-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_7UfqjD3IEg)
- **Buffett-style public equity investing is lower risk than startups because you see plenty of history to extrapolate and can spread bets, whereas 98-99% of startups are non-venture-backed and inherently high risk.** Entrepreneurs minimize risk by limiting what they can lose and keeping the option to go back and get a job; venture-backed founders play a different game because it's not their own capital. — [2021-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_7UfqjD3IEg)
- **Investing is like bridge: you can learn the game in 20 minutes but never master it in a lifetime, which makes it one of the broadest and most continuously challenging disciplines.** Recent books he found useful: The Antisocial Network (skimmable, on GameStop/Robinhood), Ace Greenberg's autobiography (recommended by Munger, good on learning from failure) and Red Roulette. _[Ace Greenberg, Bear Stearns, GameStop, Robinhood]_ — [2021-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_7UfqjD3IEg)
- **The Patels came to dominate 70% of US motels from 0.2% of the population by becoming the low-cost provider, a framework that maps directly onto value investing.** Expelled from Uganda by Idi Amin in the 1970s with $5-15,000, they bought $50-75,000 motels with $5-10,000 down, lived on site, eliminated payroll, priced rooms below competitors, saved at high rates and cascaded family members into more motels. _[Patels, The Dhandho Investor]_ — [2021-10-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PN3f668IKO0)
- **You cannot add on Buffett's personality; it is binary, so understand who you are and build behaviors that maximize your own talents.** Sam Walton, Buffett, Howard Schultz and Bezos are intensely singular in their pursuits; if you would not enjoy picking up tickets at Ak-Sar-Ben you will not become Buffett. _[Warren Buffett, Sam Walton, Howard Schultz, Jeff Bezos]_ — [2021-10-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=PN3f668IKO0)
- **Most entrepreneurs go low risk, high return, not high risk, high return; venture-backed startups are an irrelevant anomaly making up well under 1% of startups.** His daughter's four-person beauty product startup muted the downside with no debt, no burn, and founders keeping their day jobs, giving it a long runway even though scaling remains a low-probability uphill climb. — [2021-10-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-etUrauRHgE)
- **A beginner should open a real discount brokerage account (not Robinhood, which is too much like a video game), study the products they already use, and hold no more than three high-conviction stocks.** Commission-free trading means you can start with $100; gains and losses must be real rather than in Excel. Buffett's 20-punch card means you get only 20 picks over 70 years, so don't blow 10 in one year. _[Warren Buffett, Apple, Alphabet]_ — [2021-10-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-etUrauRHgE)
- **Early-stage companies make lots of hiring mistakes because they have no brand and exceptional people see career risk, but a great business model can transcend team incompetence if you keep improving the team over time.** He made many hiring mistakes at TransTech in 1991 without 90% of the frameworks he has now; in the famous early Microsoft photo, only Bill Gates and Paul Allen stayed on, and even Gates, a great hirer, made many errors. _[TransTech, Microsoft, Bill Gates]_ — [2021-10-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-etUrauRHgE)
- **Startup success comes from attacking the right market with the right product at the right price and knowing how to sell; usually a disruption or an unaddressed offering gap lets new entrants gain traction.** Amar Bhide's The Origin and Evolution of New Businesses studied 10 years of Inc. 500 CEOs and found common tactics like putting 'Global' in the company name to look bigger; Pabrai carried a 'VP Marketing' business card instead of 'CEO' in sales situations for the same reason. Tesla could enter because electric cars were new. _[Amar Bhide, Tesla]_ — [2021-10-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-etUrauRHgE)
- **Before managing money for others, you should be independently wealthy from compounding your own capital; if you're truly good, investors will find you.** $10,000 compounded at 25% doubles every three years: seven doubles in 21 years is 128x, so a 20-year-old would have over $1 million by 41 and over $1 billion by 71 without ever adding to it or managing outside money. — [2021-10-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-etUrauRHgE)
- **Fund assets are a temporary pool of capital that can all leave in any year; there's one reason people give you money and many reasons they take it back, so it's not worth worrying about.** He stumbled into the investment business by accident with a plan only to invest his own money; if all outside capital left he would still consider it a blessed life. _[Pabrai Investment Funds]_ — [2021-11-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wT1m8J4hdpA)
- **Running a business (meeting payroll, losing customers, hiring) teaches more than reading about one; analyzing a company through spreadsheets is dangerous.** Buffett's line that one day walking on land beats a thousand years explaining it to a fish; put yourself in the CEO's seat and identify the three or four variables that drive most of the outcome. _[TransTech]_ — [2021-11-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wT1m8J4hdpA)
- **He would not change the Buffett partnership fee structure if starting over: investors get the first 6%, then a 25/75 split above that with high-water marks.** At 20% gross returns the manager earns 3.5% on other people's money while investors still net 16.5%, so it's lucrative and aligned. _[Buffett Partnership, Pabrai Investment Funds]_ — [2021-11-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wT1m8J4hdpA)

### Philanthropy & Dakshana (12)

- **Large inheritances are a disservice to your gene pool, so surplus wealth should be recycled to society seeking a high social return on invested capital.** Buffett's line: Jesse Owens's son does not become a great sprinter by starting at the 40-meter line, though the 5-meter line is fine. Dakshana, started in 2006 with his wife, gives free prep to very poor bright Indian kids, and several thousand have entered the IITs and top medical schools. _[Dakshana, Warren Buffett]_ — [2021-03-04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=V_djW_RGPGA)
- **Beyond a certain number, wealth cannot buy happiness, and the only two choices are giving it to your gene pool or recycling it to society; a large inheritance is a disservice.** A second home would reduce his happiness. Buffett: Jesse Owens's son is not helped by starting the 100-yard dash at the 40-yard line; give kids enough to do anything but not enough to do nothing. By 2005-06 he could see wealth would keep growing with no way to use it, so at $50 million he committed to giving away 2% of wealth per year. _[Warren Buffett, Dakshana Foundation]_ — [2021-03-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NEB2RfRgBSQ)
- **Dakshana was designed by inverting the problem: only pursue charitable initiatives where results are easily measured by an independent third party.** Most charities spend 60% of money on fundraising and run 10 initiatives with no measurement. Training poor kids for the IIT and medical entrance exams gives an external test as a feedback loop, so if numbers drop they go back and fix it; non-profits otherwise never pay the penalty capitalism imposes for being stupid. _[Dakshana Foundation, Rockefeller Foundation]_ — [2021-03-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NEB2RfRgBSQ)
- **Philanthropy needs both heart and head; most charities have huge hearts and no heads, which does not work.** Wonderful people can be useless at running charities; you need a big heart coupled with horsepower. — [2021-03-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NEB2RfRgBSQ)
- **Philanthropy lacks capitalism's feedback loop, so Dakshana only runs programs that lend themselves to easy measurement and gets an independent report card every year.** A billion-dollar foundation can spend 5% stupidly for 50 years and survive, run by agents who care mainly about being paid; Dakshana inverted the problem, chose education for its multiplier effect, and now ties a significant portion of faculty compensation to results. _[Dakshana Foundation, Rockefeller Foundation]_ — [2021-04-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=XNtWcAag9as)
- **Dakshana exists because large inheritances are a disservice to children, leaving society as the only other place for the money.** Citing Buffett's Jesse Owens analogy, a son should not start the 100-meter dash at the 40-meter line. He started Dakshana at 42 so as not to begin giving at 75 with no energy, and aims to die with $1 left. _[Dakshana Foundation, Warren Buffett]_ — [2021-05-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9JYXICM3RSo)
- **Philanthropy must be high-risk, high-return and willing to fail, because it tackles problems society has not solved, and giving money away well is harder than making it.** He expected ten years of spinning wheels but Dakshana got traction within weeks. R.K. Damani of D-Mart gives about seven crores a year and Prem Watsa about $1 million a year; the model can absorb only $7-8 million annually versus $3-4 million currently spent, so the engine must grow as his compounding grows. _[Dakshana Foundation, R.K. Damani, Prem Watsa]_ — [2021-05-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=9JYXICM3RSo)
- **In investing never swing for the fences, take singles; in philanthropy go for sixers every time because only a willingness to fail moves the needle on hard problems.** Dakshana is very willing to fail when it spends money, while its investment portfolio of three or four well-selected stocks is not that risky. _[Dakshana Foundation]_ — [2021-05-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=K4mggdrMHVo)
- **Dakshana is exploring a joint venture to train high-school graduates for two years in software engineering and entrepreneurship, cutting four years off the current path through university.** Universities are bloated aircraft carriers; if the new model works he is willing to abandon the existing one. Philanthropy needs head as well as heart: measure money in against good to society out, and be willing to fail. _[Dakshana Foundation]_ — [2021-07-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=cJGkrSFVnns)
- **Nonprofits must be businesslike about how their endowments are invested, because investment returns directly determine the wellbeing of students; decision by committee is subpar.** Grinnell College, with under 1,000 students, put Buffett on its endowment advisory board with Joe Rosenfield, invested early in Intel, and grew the endowment past $1 billion, about $10 million per student. Yale's endowment covers roughly a third of total expenses. _[Grinnell College, Warren Buffett, Joe Rosenfield, Intel, Yale]_ — [2021-10-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-etUrauRHgE)
- **Dakshana succeeded because it cloned a great model, got lucky with a high-quality leadership team, took a businesslike approach demanding extremely high social return on invested capital, and said no to almost everything.** After almost 15 years it has exceeded his wildest dreams; most charities have too much heart and too little head, whereas foundations run by business leaders like Gates, Dell and Zuckerberg are likely to do well. Dakshana does only one or two things and does them better than any nonprofit he knows. _[Dakshana Foundation, Bill Gates, Michael Dell, Mark Zuckerberg]_ — [2021-10-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-etUrauRHgE)
- **Philanthropy is harder than making money and requires the opposite of investing: go high risk, high return, swing for the fences and be willing to completely lose.** Most philanthropic organizations are meek and unwilling to fail, a recipe for disaster; the Gates Foundation's vaccine bets have had no home run yet but are the right place for the money because a malaria vaccine or polio eradication would be enormous. _[Gates Foundation, Dakshana Foundation]_ — [2021-10-26](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-etUrauRHgE)

### Cloning & learning from great investors (16)

- **To find investors worth cloning, use DataRoma and follow people like Josh Tarasoff and Rob Vinall of RV Capital.** He found GM by seeing that a couple of investors had bought it. _[DataRoma, Josh Tarasoff, Rob Vinall, RV Capital, GM]_ — [2022-01-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b9ioA0J-p2M)
- **Study and clone Chuck Akre, a one-trick pony whose three-legged stool (high ROE without leverage, great people, ability to reinvest at high rates) has produced 200-baggers.** The third leg is the hardest: MasterCard under Ajay Banga has high ROE but cannot reinvest, while Starbucks has all three legs. Pabrai admits it is 'so stupid' that he still doesn't own Starbucks. Akre sells when something compounds at only 7%. _[Chuck Akre, MasterCard, Ajay Banga, Starbucks]_ — [2022-01-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dzfjw0ZXVm4)
- **Buffett's approach of few, big, infrequent bets was diametrically opposite to how mutual funds operated, so anyone who actually executed it would have a clear advantage.** He discovered Buffett in 1994 via a Peter Lynch book and the first biographies; mutual funds had 100% annual turnover and dozens or hundreds of positions. He tested the idea with $1 million from selling part of his IT business, grew it past $10 million at about 70% a year by 1999-2000, and started Pabrai Funds in 1999 as a hobby for eight friends with $1 million. _[Warren Buffett, Peter Lynch, Pabrai Investment Funds]_ — [2022-02-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0SbspUlZW8A)
- **Shameless cloning is bowling with bumpers: start from the highest-conviction bets of investors you admire, then apply your own circle-of-competence filter.** With over 50,000 listed companies, circle of competence removes 90-95% and cloning cuts the rest dramatically while guaranteeing each idea already passed a great mind's filter with real money behind it. He names Munger, Buffett and Bill Ackman as investors to clone. _[Charlie Munger, Warren Buffett, Bill Ackman]_ — [2022-02-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0SbspUlZW8A)
- **He found his Turkish ideas by cloning a local value-fund manager who had already filtered the market, spending a week visiting every company in that portfolio.** The friend, a Graham-trained investor who attended Pabrai's 2014 meeting, gave decades of history on the families behind each business. 'Bowling with bumpers in Istanbul is awesome.' _[Reysas]_ — [2022-02-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0SbspUlZW8A)
- **The Free Lunch portfolio is a free, fee-less 15-stock quasi-index built from cloned ideas, spawners and cannibals, rebalanced only once a year.** It is not a stock-picking or money-making product for him; low activity lets the businesses run, and it does reasonably well. — [2022-02-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0SbspUlZW8A)
- **Be a shameless cloner: nobody is smart enough to invent everything, so ride on the shoulders of Graham, Buffett and especially Munger.** Microsoft's research labs spent tens of billions for almost nothing while Word came from WordPerfect, Excel from Lotus 1-2-3, Teams from Zoom and Edge from Chrome; Burger King's two guys follow McDonald's site selection; the only airlines that thrived (e.g. Ryanair) cloned Southwest. Something in the human psyche looks down on cloning, which is why it gives a massive edge. _[Microsoft, Burger King, McDonald's, Ryanair, Southwest Airlines, Charlie Munger]_ — [2022-04-04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hQsP8ogUp8k)
- **Idea generation should start from lists that have already passed through a good brain: a Graham investor's Turkish portfolio, Dataroma, or Bill Ackman's 13F.** In Turkey he visited only the companies his friend had already put money behind rather than a hundred at random; Ackman's picks have perhaps a 50% batting average, still better than throwing darts. _[Bill Ackman, Dataroma]_ — [2022-04-04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hQsP8ogUp8k)
- **Cloning is the great shortcut in a universe of 50,000 stocks: start with what investors you admire have already put their own money into.** Munger endorses cloning; a great investor's portfolio has already passed one filter. His Turkish investments came from spending a week visiting every company a Ben Graham-style friend in Istanbul owned. _[Charlie Munger]_ — [2022-06-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y2zu_8w_2H0)
- **Being an outsider taught by Buffett, Munger and Graham through the public domain was a gift; he would have done worse in the professional investment industry.** He never worked under anyone in investing. Becoming an investor was luck: picking up a Peter Lynch book in London in 1994 while running an IT company led him to Buffett biographies. Nick Sleep is miles ahead of him as an investor. _[Peter Lynch, Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger, Ben Graham, Nick Sleep]_ — [2022-06-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y2zu_8w_2H0)
- **For a know-nothing investor, passive index investing with low frictional costs is a great baseline, especially with decades ahead; pick stocks only if you understand specific businesses.** Being a passive investor is certainly a great way to go for most people. — [2022-06-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qBdieWfouZM)
- **Limiting yourself to businesses written up on Value Investors Club is a hack that trims the universe to a well-curated set better than throwing darts.** Membership is difficult and requires submitting decent ideas each year. DataRoma's 13F filings and Barron's are other sources; his assistant shows him all VIC ideas posted in the last month, and Value Line arrives weekly. _[Value Investors Club, DataRoma, Barron's, Value Line]_ — [2022-09-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zw5B7F5IUV4)
- **His most helpful resources are Poor Charlie's Almanack (reread yearly), Thomas Phelps' 100 to 1 in the Stock Market, the Berkshire letters and the archived Berkshire meetings on buffett.cnbc.com.** He listened to all the archived meetings in the shower over six months, twice, and has attended every meeting since 1998. _[Poor Charlie's Almanack, Thomas Phelps, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2022-09-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zw5B7F5IUV4)
- **Given a choice among Guy Spier, Buffett, Munger, Li Lu and Cathie Wood to manage his money, he would choose Li Lu.** He joked it was very close between Li Lu and Cathie Wood. He also notes the baton is not being passed to him; Buffett and Munger have many great students and their writings remain forever. _[Li Lu, Cathie Wood, Guy Spier]_ — [2022-09-20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rzXG8pUg4sM)
- **Cloning is a core mental model most humans think is beneath them; Dakshana was built by cloning Anand Kumar's Super 30 and running it on an industrial scale.** Super 30 got 27-30 of 30 poor kids into IIT each year; Anand declined funding to scale to 300 but happily let Pabrai replicate the model, and Dakshana sourced students through the government's Navodaya magnet school system. _[Anand Kumar, Super 30, Dakshana Foundation]_ — [2022-10-11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QJNB_CC-PDk)
- **The best way to learn is to teach; he does AMA sessions because he comes out wiser from the pushback and because teaching is part of the credo Graham, Buffett and Munger laid down for value investors.** He admits an ulterior motive: comments and questions in these sessions make him feel wiser afterwards. _[Ben Graham, Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger]_ — [2022-12-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W--321tO12M)

### Circle of competence & checklists (30)

- **He looks at hundreds of businesses a year but spends under five minutes on most, discarding anything outside his circle such as pharma, healthcare and health insurance.** US healthcare and health insurers do not operate under market forces; it becomes obvious quickly when there is no moat, no growth or no durability. — [2022-01-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b9ioA0J-p2M)
- **There are no called strikes in investing: you pay a penalty only for bets that fail, never for passing on Amazon at $10.** Buffett's baseball analogy; you can be sloppy about what you let go, and he has let many awesome businesses go because he could not see them. _[Amazon, pets.com, Warren Buffett]_ — [2022-01-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b9ioA0J-p2M)
- **Value investors have no information edge, only an analytics edge.** He had no inside knowledge of funeral businesses; the edge was concluding it was a great business with a bad capital structure and doing the work to see it could transcend it. _[funeral services companies]_ — [2022-01-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b9ioA0J-p2M)
- **He no longer invests in levered financial institutions because he has suffered permanent losses in them and thinks he is bad at them.** Captive finance arms are the exception he understands; John Deere Finance's earnings are a smooth straight line while the equipment business is cyclical. _[John Deere]_ — [2022-01-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dzfjw0ZXVm4)
- **You cannot connect the dots looking forward, only backward; observations stored for 30 years can suddenly become actionable.** The JI Case captive-finance insight from the early 1990s drove his Fiat Chrysler analysis in 2012 and his recent look at John Deere. _[JI Case, Fiat Chrysler, John Deere]_ — [2022-01-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dzfjw0ZXVm4)
- **Anomalies are the trigger for digging in, and a funeral services company at a PE of 2 was an anomaly that made no sense.** With 50,000 stocks you need a shortlisting method; he scans Value Line's lowest-PE list weekly, where 2-3x PE names are usually dogs whose earnings are gone, but in 2002 Stewart Enterprises (PE 2) and Service Corp (PE 2.3) stood out since deaths are predictable and the business deserved 10-30x. _[Stewart Enterprises, Service Corp, Value Line]_ — [2022-01-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dzfjw0ZXVm4)
- **Never invest top-down by asset class; it is a bottom-up treasure hunt driven by anomalies and serendipity.** He never decided to invest in tech, blockchain or Turkey; he went to Turkey in 2018 for the tea and baklava and to meet his Ben Graham-style friend's portfolio companies. Templeton said being wrong 30-40% of the time is still okay. _[John Templeton]_ — [2022-01-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dzfjw0ZXVm4)
- **The first question is always whether a business is within your circle of competence; only then can you value it and compare price to worth.** A Des Moines apartment investor knows a good local deal instantly but may have no edge in London or Florida real estate. If the gap between price and value is large, step in; if negative or minuscule, move on. — [2022-02-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0SbspUlZW8A)
- **His brain does not try to figure out the economy; it starts with a single business and asks what it looks like 5, 10 or 15 years out, which is only possible for a small sliver of businesses.** Within his circle he expects a 50-60% success rate, which with 'two-by-four' no-brainers produces great results; he does not waste time on questions that full-time macro experts cannot answer. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2022-04-04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hQsP8ogUp8k)
- **His checklist, built about 14 years ago from great investors' losing bets (via 13F filings), shows the biggest causes of failure are leverage, misjudged moats and management or ownership issues, all visible beforehand.** For each loss he asked why it failed and whether the data was visible before the investment, e.g. Buffett's US Air, where Southwest's low-cost attack on the Pittsburgh hub was a misread moat. The list now has about 170 questions and typically surfaces 7-10 unknowns that force another month or two of research before a go/no-go decision, since every business has issues. _[US Air, Southwest Airlines, Warren Buffett, Fiat Chrysler Automobiles]_ — [2022-04-04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hQsP8ogUp8k)
- **Whatever criteria you set among 50,000 global stocks (net-nets, PE of one, 100-baggers) you will find if you stay focused; he has chosen the multi-bagger game.** Real net-nets can still work, but dot-com era net-nets were illusions because they were bleeding cash daily. Net-nets are no longer an area of interest for him. — [2022-06-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y2zu_8w_2H0)
- **The value-investing tent is wide (50-cent dollars, spinoffs, cannibals, spawners, net-nets, special situations, P/E of 1), and with 50-100,000 stocks globally almost any criterion can work if you focus on it with clarity.** Quoting the Upanishads, your deepest desire is your destiny: if you want 20-cent bills you will find them, and if you want 100-baggers you will find those too, as long as you sift company after company with your framework. _[Joel Greenblatt, Ben Graham]_ — [2022-06-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qBdieWfouZM)
- **First ask whether the business is in your circle of competence; if you can bound its 10-20 year cash flows, valuation is straight math, and if you can't, take a pass.** Even at 100x trailing earnings, DMart could be judged over- or undervalued by discounting cash flows, but only if you understand the business well enough to estimate them. _[DMart]_ — [2022-06-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qBdieWfouZM)
- **Venture capital is not a game where the odds are in my favor: no downside protection, no historical track records, and returns dominated by deal flow that unknown investors lack.** Top-quartile venture funds beat bottom-quartile by multiples while bond funds differ by 100-200 bps; VC friends say access to Sequoia's trash can would triple their returns. By contrast, in public markets the small investor with 10 lakhs to 5 crores has a huge advantage over institutions because they can look at nano caps. _[Sequoia, Andreessen Horowitz, Y Combinator]_ — [2022-06-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qBdieWfouZM)
- **Look at every investment through the CEO's shoes: find the two or three variables that drive the outcome and ask whether they are predictable.** Buffett says he is a better investor because he is a businessman. No CEO runs a business through a spreadsheet; they hold simple models in their head, and if the investor can reach the same models he has a basis for forecasting. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2022-07-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E0_K-eFC8bQ)
- **There are no called strikes in investing: you pay no penalty for ignoring a great business you don't understand, only for buying a bad one.** Skip the chemical company you can't explain; MasterCard, Visa and Amex are obvious monopolies or oligopolies. Louis Vuitton's after-tax margins above 20% make it obviously great, but whether it is a great investment depends on whether it trades at 3x or 50x earnings. _[MasterCard, Visa, American Express, LVMH]_ — [2022-08-30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wz8N5CkTA2w)
- **If you need Excel or a DCF to decide whether something is a good investment, it is a pass; you should be able to explain it to a 10-year-old in five to seven sentences.** IPSCO in 2004-2005 traded at $45 with $15 a share of cash and two years of announced $15 a share earnings from pipeline contracts; he put 10% of the fund in, a third $15 year was announced with the stock at $90, and a Swedish buyer offered $160, at which point he sold at $155 immediately. _[IPSCO, Reysas Logistics, Apple]_ — [2022-08-30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wz8N5CkTA2w)
- **Start with an open canvas rather than targeting an industry like education, although a focused hunter like Tom Russo can succeed by living only in luxury brands and premium liquor.** Chinese tutoring companies went from hero to zero when banned, but they were not win-win businesses since they fought over limited elite seats rather than expanding education; governments' mandate to educate cheaply works against education companies. He never went looking for a Turkish warehouse company. _[Tom Russo, Reysas Logistics, Chinese tutoring companies]_ — [2022-08-30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wz8N5CkTA2w)
- **First hack: do not aspire to know the intrinsic value of everything; ignore anything outside your circle of competence such as biotech or technology you do not understand.** Large swaths of equities fall outside any individual's circle; if you cannot identify the main factors that drive an industry, move on. — [2022-09-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zw5B7F5IUV4)
- **If you need Excel to figure out intrinsic value, there is a problem; you should be able to do it in your head.** For Starbucks or McDonald's the odds of lower earnings in 5-10 years are very low; the complication is how much higher, e.g. China going from 5,000 to 10,000 stores in 5 years, which requires more assumptions than Reysas or Rain. _[Starbucks, McDonald's]_ — [2022-09-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zw5B7F5IUV4)
- **Scuttlebutt, as Phil Fisher advocated, is a wonderful add-on and he admits he should do more of it.** He tries to think about whom to call among users, competitors, customers and suppliers, or to be a user himself. _[Phil Fisher]_ — [2022-09-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zw5B7F5IUV4)
- **If you are wondering whether something is in your circle of competence, the answer is that it is not.** Inside the circle you would know how to value the business, how it makes money and its likely trajectory within ranges. The same hack applies to crypto: outside the circle, no opinion needed. — [2022-09-20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rzXG8pUg4sM)
- **His research process starts by looking for a reason to stop: first who the admired shareholders are, then all Value Investors Club write-ups and comments, then 20-30 years of shareholder letters, then transcript Q&A, then proxies, and only then the financials.** Reading old letters with hindsight (2005-07 before the 2008 tsunami, 2018-19 before the pandemic) shows how resilient the model is and whether management underpromises and overdelivers. Transcript Q&A is valuable because it is not written by a PR firm; proxies reveal dilution and comp plans. _[Value Investors Club]_ — [2022-09-20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rzXG8pUg4sM)
- **He will not invest in crypto because he does not understand it and does not need an opinion on everything; a productive life with plenty of returns is possible with no crypto.** Crypto is like one of the 96 people at the cocktail party you do not need to figure out; he does not even understand blockchain well. _[Bitcoin]_ — [2022-09-20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rzXG8pUg4sM)
- **He skips entire sectors like US healthcare, pharma and defense because they don't run on market forces and he would be late to the party; the first question is always whether it's in your circle of competence.** Billionaire John Arrillaga only ever invested in real estate within two miles of the Stanford campus, knew every building cold, went to cash when cap rates hit 3% and bought back in downturns. Better to be an inch wide and a mile deep than a mile wide and an inch deep; he makes only about two investments a year. _[John Arrillaga, Charlie Munger]_ — [2022-10-11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QJNB_CC-PDk)
- **Companies that have never made money go straight into Buffett's 'too hard' pile - 99% of ideas belong there and there's no point wasting brain cells.** Story from a 2010-11 Berkshire HQ tour with Debbie Bosanek: the famous 'too hard' box on Buffett's desk was empty, so he filled it with paper on the spot. Once in a while a Turkish warehouse company shows up that isn't too hard. _[Warren Buffett, Debbie Bosanek]_ — [2022-10-11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QJNB_CC-PDk)
- **If you have to open Excel there is a problem; start with an honest circle-of-competence check and stay in its center.** He avoids biotech, defense (few customers), US healthcare (non-market forces) and blockchain. Quotes Buffett that the size of the circle matters less than staying in the center; then assess trajectory, ROE, capital needs and the capital allocator. — [2022-10-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_h10aNEQK50)
- **You do not need to sweat expanding your circle of competence; it grows organically from reading and thinking, but you must be intellectually honest and pass on anything outside it.** Young investors start with the brands and companies they consume. Many of his mistakes came from thinking he knew something he did not. — [2022-11-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m606MaKujq4)
- **ESG produces strange results (screens including Exxon but excluding Tesla); he does not exclude industries but peels the onion one layer deeper on what kind of corporate citizen a company is.** Exxon is essential to our quality of life. His oldest holding, owned about eight and a half years, supplies inputs to the aluminum industry with heavy gas discharge, yet spends several million dollars a year on scrubbers beyond legal requirements that competitors skip; an ESG overdose would have passed on it. _[Exxon, Tesla]_ — [2022-12-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W--321tO12M)
- **His checklist was built by using 13F filings to identify great investors' realized losses and asking what was visible at the time that they missed; leverage is the biggest category with about 30 questions, then moat misjudgment with 20-30, then management and ownership.** Buffett's IBM loss came from relying heavily on IBM's honest five-year guidance on cash flows, revenues and buybacks while there were visible tread marks in the business. Unions, environment and other items rank lower. There is no secret sauce and he may publish it someday. _[IBM, US Air, Warren Buffett]_ — [2022-12-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W--321tO12M)

### Valuation & margin of safety (23)

- **The best place to invest is a great growing business, but buying at 80 times earnings is not a way to get rich; every business has a value and you buy well below it.** He is resetting his frameworks toward compounders while remaining careful about price. — [2022-01-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b9ioA0J-p2M)
- **When you find very high uncertainty combined with very low risk, the result is usually a very high return, because Wall Street confuses the two.** Markets hate uncertainty and would not give IPSCO a 10x multiple because they feared peak earnings; Silicon Valley Bank's undisclosed warrant basket was the same setup. _[IPSCO, Silicon Valley Bank]_ — [2022-01-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dzfjw0ZXVm4)
- **He has no interest in a $10 stock worth $13-17; he wants wild mispricing, and you need an analytics edge rather than an information edge.** With SVB he had no information edge about the warrant basket but could analyze from a high level that he couldn't lose. _[Silicon Valley Bank]_ — [2022-01-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dzfjw0ZXVm4)
- **All intelligent investing is value investing; growth and value are two sides of the same coin and anything else is speculation.** Buying a dollar for 25 cents gives 4x, but a business like Starbucks that recovers store investment in 18-24 months in the US and 12-15 months internationally with 60-70% unlevered ROEs and near-infinite store runway is the holy grail, and you need not pay much below a dollar if you are right about growth. _[Starbucks]_ — [2022-01-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dzfjw0ZXVm4)
- **Value investing is simply buying things for well below what they are worth; you either get it in five minutes or never.** A rental apartment netting $12,000 a year is worth no more than $100-120k to someone wanting 10% and no more than $60k to someone wanting 20%; stocks are the same, with the added question of how long the market takes to converge on value. Go for no-brainers where the math can be done in your head without a spreadsheet. — [2022-02-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0SbspUlZW8A)
- **A fully built asset base with inflation-indexed rents cannot lose value in high inflation, which is why he invested knowing Turkish inflation would run 50% a year.** From 2019 to 2022 Reysas cut debt from $200 million to $90 million at a 14% blended rate while receiving 20-25% CPI rent increases; leases reset to market only every 10 years, only 15-20% of the footprint is at market rent, and a spawned solar business added about $200 million of intrinsic value. Despite the lira falling from 5 to nearly 14 per dollar, dollar intrinsic value is higher than in 2019 and the market cap is over $100 million yet still deeply undervalued. _[Reysas]_ — [2022-02-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0SbspUlZW8A)
- **PE ratios are not very useful: a 4x company can be overvalued and an 80x company undervalued; value is future cash over 5-15 years discounted back.** A melting ice cube with earnings falling 50% a year may not be worth one times earnings, while a business growing 40% a year with long tailwinds can deserve a 100 multiple. Investors should look for no-brainers where no DCF is needed. — [2022-02-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0SbspUlZW8A)
- **Ben Graham's three cornerstones remain the foundation: stocks are fractional ownership of a business, insist on a margin of safety, and make Mr. Market work for you.** Graham's portfolio was clobbered from 1929 to 1938, which produced Security Analysis and the net-net approach of paying two-thirds of net current assets; those bargains are very hard to find today. _[Ben Graham, Warren Buffett]_ — [2022-04-04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hQsP8ogUp8k)
- **He does not invest top-down from hot sectors; he looks for anomalies where value is so compelling that returns come even without growth.** Indian IT services and cloud will do well, but knowing a sector grows does not mean you can make money. The Turkish bet would return 30x just from reaching fair value even if management did nothing, and they are good capital allocators. _[Reysas]_ — [2022-06-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y2zu_8w_2H0)
- **Well-known moats get priced to perfection, but if the runway truly lasts decades, an expensive-looking price can still be a great value investment, though keep a dose of skepticism.** DMart, with a Costco/Aldi-like model, is embryonic in India relative to its 10-30 year potential and trades at huge multiples (around 100x trailing); private sector banks may go from a third to half or two-thirds of a growing Indian banking pie. _[DMart, Costco, Aldi]_ — [2022-06-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qBdieWfouZM)
- **Value investing is a huge tent that includes merger arbitrage and below-liquidation buys, but the most money is only made through partial ownership of a business with tremendous economics and a tremendous runway.** Buffett bought Activision Blizzard purely as merger arbitrage on the Microsoft deal, and the Twitter/Elon Musk spread is similar; with a great business you only need to be right once or twice in a lifetime and it covers a lot of sins. _[Activision Blizzard, Microsoft, Twitter, Elon Musk, Warren Buffett]_ — [2022-08-17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MYR0tWgstMI)

### Portfolio concentration & selling (17)
