- **His approach is not scalable; all investors do worse as assets grow, and Berkshire now needs $30-50 billion positions to move the needle.** With $500 billion he could not be the same investor; the universe shrinks to companies over $20-30 billion in market cap where a 10% stake is possible. _[Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2022-06-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y2zu_8w_2H0)
- **In the multibagger framework you don't sell when a position becomes fully valued or even overvalued; you sell only when it is egregiously overvalued.** This is a departure from Graham, who taught selling as price approaches fair value; the investor must learn to distinguish overvalued from egregiously overvalued. _[Ben Graham]_ — [2022-06-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qBdieWfouZM)
- **Every sell decision is an investing mistake, per Thomas Phelps: if you bought it right, it never needs to be sold.** He and Li Lu sold Maotai at 700-900 RMB after Li Lu called with concerns; Monsoon, who had visited the distillery in 2017 and saw a business with under $2 cost of goods and a ~$1,200 selling price, ignored both of them and still holds it above 2,000 RMB. _[Kweichow Moutai, Li Lu, Thomas Phelps, Monsoon Pabrai]_ — [2022-07-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E0_K-eFC8bQ)
- **Ben Graham did value investors a disservice with his edict never to hold a stock above intrinsic value; the right question, per Chuck Akre, is whether the business is getting better.** There is an asymmetry between the price at which you would buy and the price at which you would sell: you would not buy Titan at 30-50x trailing earnings, but you should not sell it either if the moat deepens with every store opened. _[Benjamin Graham, Chuck Akre, Titan Industries, Costco, Walmart]_ — [2022-08-17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MYR0tWgstMI)
- **Hold an overvalued great business, but sell when it becomes egregious; Costco at 40-50x earnings should be held, but at 200x normalized earnings you have left the reservation.** If a great, growing business is run by honest managers and you can see the runway, hang on for life; only egregious valuation justifies selling. _[Costco]_ — [2022-08-17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MYR0tWgstMI)
- **A concentrated basket of compounders tolerates an extremely high error rate: even if 96% of Jhunjhunwala's portfolio had gone to zero, Titan alone made it a home run.** Make 10 bets of 10% each in carefully studied businesses like NVR and AutoZone, then go to sleep despite Ukraine, inflation, Fed hikes and business hiccups. Jhunjhunwala had four screens in front of him all day and still never touched Titan for decades. _[Rakesh Jhunjhunwala, Titan, NVR, AutoZone]_ — [2022-08-30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wz8N5CkTA2w)
- **Position sizes below 5% make little sense and above 20% is the ceiling; his psyche fits a 10-by-10 portfolio of ten 10% bets.** Twenty stocks should be the upper limit and fewer than 5-10 is imprudent without strong picking skills; beginners hell-bent on stock picking can start with 20 and whittle down as confidence grows, though indexing is right for most. _[Warren Buffett, Apple]_ — [2022-08-30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wz8N5CkTA2w)
- **Selling is much harder than buying, and the mistake of most of his career was selling great businesses because they looked too richly valued.** Ask whether the business is getting better; if so, keep it even if expensive, and only consider selling when the valuation becomes egregious, like 100x normalized earnings after buying at 15x, or when there is conclusive proof of permanent secular decline. Think like a family that has owned the business for 50 years. _[Rakesh Jhunjhunwala, Titan]_ — [2022-08-30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wz8N5CkTA2w)

- **Getting out is much harder than getting in - like Abhimanyu in the chakravyuha - and Phil Fisher's view is that if the job is done right you never need to sell.** You only really understand a business after you own it, and especially when it drops 30-40%. - **Sell only for three reasons: the valuation becomes extreme, you realize you made a mistake about the business, or a clearly better opportunity exists, and the last is dangerous because 'the mistress always looks better than the wife'.** Quotes Phil Fisher: 'if the job is done right, every sell decision is a mistake.' His Turkish friend sold Reysas after a 100% gain despite believing it was worth 40X more, prompting Pabrai to tell him to triple his Munger worship time. _[Phil Fisher, Reysas, Charlie Munger]_ — [2022-10-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_h10aNEQK50)
- **Make very few bets with extremely asymmetric odds; even with a 30-40% error rate the winners do so well that the losers do not matter.** He looks for low-risk, high-reward bets that auction-driven markets offer only from time to time; the rest of the time risk is high and reward low, so discipline and patience are needed. — [2022-11-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j3U0tb-1zSU)
- **He never puts more than 10% of fund assets into a bet at cost, ideally a 10-by-10 portfolio, but if the job is done right the portfolio ends up very concentrated as winners grow.** Rakesh Jhunjhunwala started with under $500, never managed outside money, and died in his early sixties worth over $6-7 billion; a 4% bet in Titan Industries decades ago became more than half his portfolio. Even if the other 96% had gone to zero he would still have had about $3 billion. _[Rakesh Jhunjhunwala, Titan Industries]_ — [2022-11-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m606MaKujq4)
- **Trimming winners at 15% or 17% is cutting the flowers and watering the weeds; a manager who has done the job right ends up with 80-90% of net worth in one stock.** Smart investors bought MasterCard after its IPO as a 5% position and trimmed every time it grew, so it never reached 20%. The Waltons, who no longer run Walmart, keep 90%+ of their wealth in it; Nick Sleep retired with three stocks and Amazon grew to 80%, outperforming Berkshire and Costco. Think of a great business you own like a founding family would and leave it alone. _[MasterCard, Walmart, Nick Sleep, Amazon, Berkshire Hathaway, Costco]_ — [2022-11-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m606MaKujq4)

### Compounding & long-term holding (17)

- **Value and growth are two sides of one coin; all intelligent investing is value investing, and the only thing that changed in his framework is holding above perceived intrinsic value.** Two $1 billion businesses, one paying $100 million flat for 50 years and one growing 10% for 25-30 years, both have a discountable value per John Burr Williams; you invest where the gap between price and value is greatest. - **Inactivity wins: the Fidelity study found the best-performing self-directed accounts belonged to customers who were dead.** Accounts with hardly any activity did best, and many of the very best had owners who were no longer alive. _[Fidelity]_ — [2022-06-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y2zu_8w_2H0)
- **He is not interested in doubling his money; he wants businesses he can hold 10-20 years for 30x, 50x or 100x, which he cannot find in the US in 2022 but can in a sliver of Turkish companies.** He invested this way in 1995, switched to cheap stocks in 1999-2000 when things got euphoric, and should have switched back to compounders in 2009. In the US even after corrections he finds it hard to see 5-10x in 5-10 years. — [2022-06-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y2zu_8w_2H0)
- **Three variables control eventual wealth, in order of importance: length of runway, rate of return, and starting capital; 7-9% returns over a long runway are nothing to look down on.** Buffett's Manhattan Indians example: $20 in 1622 at 7% becomes $20 trillion by 2022, and $0.02 in 1522 would do the same. Buffett's one wish is that people look at his corpse and say 'man, he was old'; he started at 11 and is 91. The S&P has returned about 9% for 100+ years. _[Warren Buffett, S&P 500]_ — [2022-06-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y2zu_8w_2H0)
- **If there is a best approach, it is focusing on multibaggers: businesses that can be 10x in 10 years or less, or 100x in 20 years or less.** Advantages: unrealized gains go untaxed for decades (an interest-free loan from the government where rates can be 40-50%), and you escape the treadmill of finding undervalued stocks, selling at fair value and starting over. — [2022-06-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qBdieWfouZM)
- **One decision can trump all others: 90% of Enam's value came from keeping the unwanted Infosys shares it was stuck with as underwriter.** Whatever else the Nariman Point investment bank did over 30 years is irrelevant; had it sold the Infosys stock it would be a shadow of itself. _[Enam, Infosys]_ — [2022-06-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qBdieWfouZM)
- **If you are even a slightly above-average investor, spend less than you earn and use no leverage, you cannot help but get very wealthy.** Rick Guerin was forced by 1973-74 margin calls to sell his Berkshire shares to Buffett at $40, shares now worth over $400,000. Take out leverage, be patient, go one day at a time. _[Rick Guerin, Berkshire Hathaway, Warren Buffett]_ — [2022-07-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E0_K-eFC8bQ)
- **Rakesh Jhunjhunwala's $4 billion fortune came mostly from never selling two great businesses, Titan and Lupin, even as he day-traded everything else and even when they looked optically overpriced.** He started 40 years ago with a $25,000 loan at 18% interest secured only by his signature; Titan was 3-4% of his portfolio 20-25 years ago, compounded at 30-35% for two decades and was about $2 billion of the $4 billion at his death; Titan, backed by the trusted Tata group, is consolidating fragmented Indian jewelry and still has a 50-year runway. _[Rakesh Jhunjhunwala, Titan Industries, Lupin, Tata]_ — [2022-08-17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MYR0tWgstMI)
- **Only 4-5% of companies generate almost all index returns, and the index beats stock pickers because it is too dumb to know it owns Google, Microsoft or Costco and too dumb to ever sell them.** Picking one of 20 great businesses while wearing a cheapskate hat is very hard; the holy grail is that when you do own a great business, the biggest thing you must do is nothing, as Jhunjhunwala did as $25-50 million became $2 billion. _[Google, Microsoft, Costco, Rakesh Jhunjhunwala]_ — [2022-08-17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MYR0tWgstMI)
- **The holy grail of investing is partial ownership of businesses that can grow and compound intrinsic value for very long periods, then never touching them.** Rakesh Jhunjhunwala started by borrowing about $20,000 at 18% and died a multi-billionaire; a 4% position in Titan bought roughly 30 years ago grew to about half his net worth, compounding at over 30% a year, and he never visited a single Titan plant. He regretted selling CRISIL until the end. _[Rakesh Jhunjhunwala, Titan, Lupin, CRISIL]_ — [2022-08-30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wz8N5CkTA2w)
- **Knowing your exit date is a huge advantage because you can plan backwards; life is all about how many doubles you get.** Life expectancy calculators moved his expected death from June 11, 2044 to 2054-2056; the extra 10-12 years mean two to four more doubles. Buffett's genie wish: 'when they look at my corpse, they say, man, he was old', purely to maximize the compounding runway. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2022-09-20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rzXG8pUg4sM)
- **The Native Americans who sold Manhattan for $24 got a good deal; they just lacked a competent trust officer to compound it.** $24 (60 guilders) in 1626 at 7% a year doubles every 10 years, giving 1,000x per century: $24 trillion by 2026, or roughly $16-17 trillion in 2022, versus US total wealth of about $130 trillion and Manhattan land worth at most a few hundred billion. His daughter's $5,000 internship savings at 18 in an IRA compounding at 15% becomes $5 million at 68, and each year's savings adds another $5 million. — [2022-10-11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QJNB_CC-PDk)
- **85% of money managers lag the index because of 1-2% fees and because the index is 'too dumb' to ever sell Apple, Microsoft or Starbucks, while managers turn over 80-100% a year.** An index costs 5-10 basis points; a manager charging 1-2% must earn 10-11% just to match a 9% index. Book value times a multiple ignores what happens when a great capital allocator runs the company for 50 years. ### Moats & business quality (21)

- **Enduring, durable moats are rare in capitalism and almost happen by accident; he wants durability of growth plus a great price, which lines up only a couple of times a year.** Most startups disappear in 5-10 years and few survive 20-30. American Express, Visa and MasterCard have produced great returns on capital for decades; Costco and Amazon are almost bulletproof. Private equity instead involves levering up and putting lipstick on a pig. _[Microsoft, Amazon, Berkshire Hathaway, Snowflake, Carvana]_ — [2022-11-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m606MaKujq4)
- **Inflation is generally bad for equities, but a small sliver of Turkish businesses with euro or dollar revenues or pass-through pricing benefit from or are neutral to it, and they were thrown out with the bathwater.** A juice exporter (not owned) has all costs in lira and revenues in euros, so every 10% lira decline lifts profits 3-4% because wages lag inflation (as in the US with 8-9% inflation and 4-5% wage growth). His airport operator runs 15 airports in eight countries with euro revenues; his warehouse company's assets are priced off international steel, concrete and Istanbul real-estate prices with inflation-indexed leases. _[Turkish airport operator, Reysas]_ — [2022-12-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W--321tO12M)
- **The US market is quite efficient and picked over; passive flows create occasional overvaluation but he sees no undervaluation mispricing that helps the active investor.** On how much passive share distorts markets, he cites John Bogle's view that we are still far from the point of distortion and admits the question is above his pay grade. _[John Bogle]_ — [2022-12-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W--321tO12M)
- **Ignore the index; focus on individual businesses, because auction-driven markets give random stocks 52-week ranges of 50-100% even in benign years while a house across the street would move 5-10% at most.** Google is the same kind of business six months ago and six months from now, so a 50-60% value swing makes no sense when value comes from discounting long-horizon cash flows. These wide ranges are why people like him can make a living. _[Google]_ — [2022-12-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W--321tO12M)

### Stock case studies (36)

- **Funeral services at a PE of 2 was a great business with a bad capital structure: stable, protected, tradition-bound recurring demand where nobody shops for the low bid.** About 20 years ago he spotted two funeral companies at a PE of 2 on the Value Line lowest-PE list; a 25-30-year-old roll-up had over-leveraged them. The question was whether they could withstand the debt, and the investment worked well. _[Value Line, funeral services companies]_ — [2022-01-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b9ioA0J-p2M)
- **Fiat Chrysler in 2012 traded at 3-4% of revenue ($140 billion revenue, $5 billion market cap) after the 2009 crisis had removed much of what people hated about autos.** He first looked at GM because a couple of investors had bought it, then found Fiat Chrysler. - **Ferrari, obtained at about $13 a share inside Fiat Chrysler in 2012, went to about $270 (20x) and he sold at $60, $100 and $130 because a 40-times IPO multiple was above his pay grade.** Ferrari can earn whatever net income it decides and has never spent a dollar on advertising in 70-plus years since 1950, unlike any other top-10 brand such as Coke. He only understood the business after buying a Ferrari car, post-sale, and buying back higher is too painful for his brain. _[Ferrari, Fiat Chrysler, Coca-Cola]_ — [2022-01-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b9ioA0J-p2M)
- **Moutai, bought when the stock tanked during China's corruption crackdown, is the world's most valuable liquor company at about $700 billion with under $3 cost per bottle selling for $1,200-5,000.** 80-90% of Moutai sold in China is counterfeit and special editions at 40,000-70,000 sell out in 15 minutes; he sold it too early. Officials photographed with Moutai on the table ended their careers, which is why sales collapsed and he bought. _[Moutai]_ — [2022-01-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b9ioA0J-p2M)
- **Micron is his largest position because the memory industry consolidated to three rational players, a change the market refused to believe after decades of boom and bust.** About 30% of the cost of an Amazon data center goes to memory makers, a 30% tax on streaming and e-commerce that he is collecting. His thesis dates from three or four years earlier; the industry changes rapidly but he likes the upside-downside. _[Micron, Amazon, Nvidia]_ — [2022-01-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b9ioA0J-p2M)
- **Fiat Chrysler in 2012 was a cleansed post-bankruptcy auto business at 4% of revenues, with Sergio Marchionne as the main reason to invest.** $5 billion market cap on $130 billion revenue; bankruptcy removed pension liabilities and reset union contracts so Detroit went from one of the worst places to build a car in 2007 to one of the best by 2009; modest profits of $5-7 billion implied a PE under 1. The stock was a 10x from 2012 to 2022 though he captured 4-5x after Marchionne's death. _[Fiat Chrysler, Sergio Marchionne, John Elkann]_ — [2022-01-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dzfjw0ZXVm4)
- **A great business with a bad balance sheet can be fixed, and Stewart Enterprises was such a case that doubled and doubled again.** Over-levered roll-ups had bought thousands of mom-and-pop funeral homes at 8-12x earnings; Stewart could sell a few hundred back to founders at 5x to cover debt, had 18 months of breathing room, and instead sold its cash-flow-negative European homes for $400-500 million, after which the stock took off. _[Stewart Enterprises]_ — [2022-01-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dzfjw0ZXVm4)
- **IPSCO in 2004 was a case of high uncertainty but low risk: cash plus two years of contracted earnings equaled the stock price, with all plants and equipment free.** Stock ~$42-43, $14/share cash, no debt, $14/share of earnings guaranteed for each of the next two years by pipeline contracts; he put 10% of the fund in. A third $14 year was announced, the stock went to $60, then $85-90, and a Swedish acquirer bid ~$155; he sold immediately at $148. _[IPSCO]_ — [2022-01-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dzfjw0ZXVm4)
- **Silicon Valley Bank, his first fund investment on July 1, 1999, gave dotcom upside without downside via a free basket of undisclosed warrants.** He knew from his own private dotcom that a bubble was underway; SVB is like a captive lender to VC-backed startups, recycling repossessed servers and software licenses, and collected warrants on every loan with no disclosure. Bought at 10x earnings, he made about 3x in 14 months and exited by August 2000; the bank has since compounded ~20% a year for 20 years. _[Silicon Valley Bank, Sequoia, Andreessen Horowitz, Greylock]_ — [2022-01-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dzfjw0ZXVm4)

### Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US (22)

- **China will keep rising because naturally entrepreneurial people were artificially kept in a non-capitalist system and the genie is out of the bottle.** Chinese per capita GDP will double, triple or quadruple over coming decades, and hundreds of millions of newly rich people have few ways to express wealth, as LVMH's Chinese-origin sales show. _[Moutai, LVMH]_ — [2022-01-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b9ioA0J-p2M)
- **He switched most of his large Alibaba position into Prosus (which owns Tencent) as a somewhat better bet, while acknowledging CCP risk.** Both Alibaba and Tencent are amazing businesses; the CCP could kibosh them but he doesn't think it wants to. - **In Turkey he limits himself to businesses with lira costs and euro or dollar revenues, where devaluation is a tailwind rather than a risk.** A Turkish packaged-juice exporter sends 98% of output duty-free to Europe with lira costs and euro revenue, so its input costs fall as the lira depreciates. Every professional investor has exited Turkey over its fiscal policies, and mass exodus creates mass mispricing; he is 'buying every day'. _[Reysas]_ — [2022-02-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0SbspUlZW8A)
- **Turkey is the cheapest market in the world because everyone has exited, and spending time on 50 Turkish companies is more worthwhile than anything in the US.** He is 'most orgasmic' about Turkey; he has only one US holding (bought 2018) plus a 2020 purchase already sold, because he cannot find obvious investments in the US that his 'little brain' can understand. — [2022-04-04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hQsP8ogUp8k)
- **India has strong long-term tailwinds and is a good place to be, but red tape and constraints on free enterprise leave obvious low-hanging fruit unpicked compared with China.** He noted at the 2022 Berkshire meeting that Buffett and Munger see non-zero, perhaps 1-5%, odds of a Russian nuclear event, an example of why macro is too hard; global dollar-cost averaging over a long runway is probably the best default. _[Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger]_ — [2022-06-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y2zu_8w_2H0)
- **In 2019 in Istanbul I found a dollar bill trading for 3 cents: a $20 million market cap with liquidation value over $600-700 million, and I bought a third of it for about $8 million.** Turkey is the cheapest market in the world with crazy inflation and policies, reminiscent of India in the early 1990s; reaching fair value alone would be a 30-33x, it is already up 5-6x in three years, and if the phenomenal capital allocators triple its value it becomes a 100-bagger. Having learned from Kotak and Blue Dart, his job is to do nothing and still own it in 20 years. _[Turkey, Reysas]_ — [2022-06-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qBdieWfouZM)

- **97-98% of listed Turkish businesses are uninvestible because of inflation, but a 2-3% sliver of great businesses transcend the macro and are extremely cheap because people fled.** Since 2018 he has visited every holding of a hard-core Graham-style Turkish friend, and spent three weeks in an Istanbul Airbnb in early 2022. If starting with small capital today he would put all his time into Turkey. _[Turkey]_ — [2022-07-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E0_K-eFC8bQ)
- **Turkey's market is a casino: 80% is held by insiders and foreigners and the 20% held by locals turns over every nine days, which is why a $20M company had massive volume.** A Turkish CFO explained the national game is Backgammon, pure luck, versus chess in Russia and poker in the US; locals buy at 10 and sell by 2. Buffett: the stock market transfers wealth from the active to the inactive. _[Turkey, Warren Buffett]_ — [2022-07-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E0_K-eFC8bQ)

Only 2-3% of listed Turkish companies have this dynamic, and there is always a bull market somewhere among 50,000 stocks. _[Turkey, Turkish fruit juice exporter]_ — [2022-08-17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MYR0tWgstMI)
