- **He went to Turkey in 2018 because the currency was unstable, everyone was leaving and the market looked optically cheap, visiting only companies already in a trusted friend's portfolio.** The 2019 follow-up trip is when he visited Reysas at 3% of liquidation value; a geography under stress can be a funnel input. _[Reysas]_ — [2022-09-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zw5B7F5IUV4)
- **Turkey is the most interesting geography because it is the most dislocated market with the most extreme valuations; what matters is how the business does long term, not the country.** He has spent time in South Korea, China, India and increasingly Turkey, with only a few Latin American investments; crazy leadership and policies in Latin America can mask really good companies. — [2022-09-20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rzXG8pUg4sM)
- **In Turkey 95-97% of stocks are uninvestible due to inflation, so a Turkish ETF is unhelpful; filter for companies with revenue in euros or dollars and Lira costs, which cuts 200 listed companies to about 10.** Example: a listed juice company with 98% of revenue exported to Europe, where Turkey has duty-free access, does really well under heavy inflation because Lira costs fall while euro revenue is stable. — [2022-09-20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rzXG8pUg4sM)
- **Turkey is an extreme case of wealth transferring from the active to the inactive: 80% of the market is static insider and foreign holdings while the retail 20% turns over every nine days.** Turkish retail 'investors' aim to buy at 10am, sell at 3pm and make 10%. With 85% inflation, a collapsing lira and foreign investors gone, it is a good time to enter; Buffett compares it to playing bridge with people told it does no good to look at the cards. _[Turkey]_ — [2022-10-11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QJNB_CC-PDk)
- **In high-inflation countries, buy businesses where inflation is a tailwind, not a headwind - euro revenues or hard assets like land, cement and steel.** The airport operator's revenues and costs are in euros, so lira devaluation is irrelevant, and the warehouse operator's assets are automatically inflation-indexed. The number one skill is patience: let the game come to you. _[TAV Airports, Reysas]_ — [2022-10-11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QJNB_CC-PDk)
- **China will always be difficult because of government policy risk, so he will not put much energy there now despite admiring Tencent and Pony Ma.** He previously invested in Moutai (a Li Lu idea), Alibaba and Tencent, all well run with good governance, but the unknown of the state is too large. He accessed Tencent through Prosus because the look-through discount was at times over 40% and Prosus was acting to close it. _[Tencent, Alibaba, Moutai, Prosus, Pony Ma, Li Lu]_ — [2022-10-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_h10aNEQK50)
- **Turkey deserves more of his energy: 95-97% is uninvestable but the 3-5% with euro or dollar revenues is sold to him at great prices by gamblers and fleeing institutions.** 80% of the Turkish market is held by insiders and foreigners and doesn't trade; the local-held 20% turns over every nine days. Templeton funds sold him Reysas at 2.5% of liquidation value. He also owns a Coke bottler and the VW importer/dealer group in Turkey. The market is like a burning theater where every seat must be occupied. _[Reysas, Coca-Cola Icecek, Dogus Otomotiv, Templeton]_ — [2022-10-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_h10aNEQK50)
- **His Turkey approach combines cloning and asymmetry: he visits only the companies a high-quality local fund manager has real money in, so the ideas have already passed one filter, and the downside is just an airfare.** A Turkish fund manager who attended his annual meeting hosted him for a week in Istanbul visiting every portfolio company; he had no plan to invest but has repeated the trip several times and will again in March 2023. — [2022-11-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m606MaKujq4)
- **Turkey has been his most productive fishing ground: 85% inflation, foreign investors gone, and the 20% of market cap held by locals turning over every nine days.** 80% of Turkish market cap is held by insiders or foreign institutions and hardly trades; retail investors want to buy at 10 am, make 10% and exit by 2 pm, so nobody looks at fundamentals. Quoting Buffett, the market transfers wealth from the active to the inactive. About 95% of the market is uninvestible, but he only needs a couple of ideas a year. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2022-12-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W--321tO12M)
- **Outside the US, fraud and governance risk must be eliminated first; inside the US you protect against your own stupidity, not fraud.** Starting in 2018 he visited only the companies his Graham-overdosed Turkish fund-manager friend already had money in, because the friend had 20 years of history on the managements; running screens in a place like Turkey would be a recipe for disaster. _[Reysas]_ — [2022-12-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W--321tO12M)

### Psychology & temperament (25)

- **Be like Puddy from Seinfeld: the biggest mistake investors make is being too active, and inaction is a tremendous skill.** Getting Guy Spier to trade anything is like a root canal; he focuses on extreme durability and refuses swaps. Valuations can take many years to reflect reality, completely out of sync with watching a screen. _[Guy Spier, Fiat Chrysler]_ — [2022-01-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b9ioA0J-p2M)
- **Your deepest desire is your destiny: if you truly put everything into a wish and a will, it will happen.** From the Upanishads, written 2,500-3,000 years ago. Buffett at 24 told his wife he wanted to be the wealthiest person; Bill Gates wanted a desktop on every desk. _[Upanishads, Warren Buffett, Bill Gates]_ — [2022-01-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b9ioA0J-p2M)
- **Auction-driven markets swing between extreme greed and extreme fear, and that fluctuation, not private negotiation, is what makes value investing possible.** Reysas could sell one or two of its 82 warehouses to private buyers for $70-80 million each and retire all its debt, yet the whole company traded at $20 million; a stock's 52-week range might be 50 to 120 while a house moves under 5% a year. If he had to negotiate directly, the owners would say it is not for sale below a billion. _[Reysas, IBM, New York Times]_ — [2022-02-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0SbspUlZW8A)
- **You make money by waiting, not by buying or selling; when things do not make sense there is no compulsion to act and it is fine to pass on 99%.** In a typical year he finds zero to three things to buy and zero to three to sell. The job description is to read and think, not to act; investors who expect weekly activity invested with the wrong guy. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2022-04-04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hQsP8ogUp8k)
- **He is unconcerned about assets under management or investors leaving; if all outside money left he would manage his own and make Reysas half the portfolio.** Much of his reading is unrelated to investments, e.g. 'The CEO Factory' about Hindustan Unilever, which has compounded at 16% a year for 65 years. _[Hindustan Unilever, Reysas]_ — [2022-04-04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hQsP8ogUp8k)
- **Never use leverage and never short, because auction-driven markets swing wildly and you must be able to play the next day.** Any NSE/BSE stock's 52-week range may be 100 to 300 rupees while a Mumbai flat barely moves 10% in a year. Shorting caps the upside at a double and the downside at bankruptcy; the hedge funds shorting GameStop and AMC analyzed correctly but are gone. _[GameStop, AMC]_ — [2022-06-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y2zu_8w_2H0)
- **Investing is not a game where the highest IQ wins; temperament and patience matter most, and holding periods are the lesson he is still learning.** The Turkish company needed only a 100-120 IQ to see it was cheap; what was needed was willingness to buy when others would not and to hold for a very long time. — [2022-06-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y2zu_8w_2H0)
- **Templeton said the best analyst is wrong one in three times; multibagger investing tolerates being wrong half the time, and two or three 100-baggers in a lifetime are all you need.** A brain surgeon with a 3% error rate would have no patients, but he has been wrong close to half the time with a phenomenal record; you may only need to find one 100-bagger. _[John Templeton]_ — [2022-06-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qBdieWfouZM)
- **To survive 50-90% drawdowns you need conviction, and conviction comes from a thesis you can explain to a 10-year-old in 5-10 sentences without a spreadsheet.** His Turkish company has 12 million square feet of 99%-leased prime Istanbul warehouses on 10-year inflation-indexed leases, worth $1-2 billion against ~$80-100 million of debt, bought at ~$80 per square foot that may reach $200 but won't fall to $30. For Starbucks the two pieces that matter are unit economics and store count (5,000 stores could be 25,000 in 20 years). _[Turkey, Reysas, Starbucks]_ — [2022-06-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qBdieWfouZM)
- **Women are temperamentally better investors, and his daughter Monsoon's approach is superior to his own because she hates to sell and is biased toward very high quality.** Temperament is hard-coded by age five or six; a hyperactive person who needs action will not do well in value investing. He never pushed either daughter toward investing, only toward finding their natural calling. _[Monsoon Pabrai]_ — [2022-07-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E0_K-eFC8bQ)
- **His psyche will not pay up even 20x earnings for a MasterCard, so he waits for great businesses on the operating table with a temporary hiccup; in investing you can let a thousand balls go by.** Buffett took about 40% of GEICO when bad underwriting had wiped out its surplus and fear was rampant; the market overweighs short-term factors, so patience over longer periods is the edge, and with 50,000 stocks some are always on the operating table. _[MasterCard, Microsoft, GEICO, Warren Buffett]_ — [2022-08-17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MYR0tWgstMI)
- **Turkey's retail float of 20% turns over every nine days, so the market is a game of pure luck like backgammon, and the stock market transfers wealth from the active to the inactive.** 80% of the Turkish market is held statically by insiders and foreigners; a typical US stock turns over once or twice a year versus 35-40 times in Turkey, Turks say they 'play' the market, and retail investors ask CFOs for a carpet-style price on shares. _[Turkey, Warren Buffett]_ — [2022-08-17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MYR0tWgstMI)
- **Investing is not a game where the highest IQ wins; the hardest part is doing nothing after you own great businesses, being content to watch paint dry.** Paraphrasing Pascal, all investment manager misery stems from the inability to sit quietly in a room and do nothing. He and Buffett each play 10-15 hours of bridge a week and he does student sessions partly to absorb time that might otherwise cause action. _[Warren Buffett, Pascal]_ — [2022-08-30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wz8N5CkTA2w)
- **He waits for an idea to hit him like a two-by-four; two investments a year is a good year, and in the first eight months of 2022 he found one and a second just appeared.** Future years could bring zero or four ideas; basic questions like circle of competence and 'what is it worth' eliminate most of the 50,000 stocks. — [2022-09-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zw5B7F5IUV4)
- **He directs 80-90% of his horsepower to one business at a time and compares any new candidate against it on a risk-adjusted basis.** He still reads several newspapers daily and scans other ideas, most of which are discarded quickly. — [2022-09-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zw5B7F5IUV4)
- **Buffett and Munger's people hack: bring only the obvious top 3-4% into your circle and treat the unknown 92% the same as the bad ones, because 3% of infinity is still infinity.** Buffett told him he is not a great judge of humans; at a party of 100 he could identify 3-4 great and 3-4 bad and could not rank the rest. Excluding a great person carries no penalty, like passing on a great company, but including a bad one does. Pabrai's own hack: every friend of Charlie is a friend of mine. _[Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger]_ — [2022-09-20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rzXG8pUg4sM)
- **Investing is a forgiving business: even the best investors are wrong one in three times and you can be wrong half the time and still do well.** He cites John Templeton's one-in-three error rate and contrasts it with a brain surgeon. Roughly 4% of stocks - 1 in 25 - produce the index's 9% return, which is another reason active managers struggle. _[John Templeton]_ — [2022-10-11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QJNB_CC-PDk)
- **Never short and never use leverage: shorting doubles your money if right and bankrupts you if wrong, and 'to finish first you have to first finish'.** Notes Bill Ackman recently said he is done with shorting. Retail investors should think like the Walton family, holding an unhedged, unlevered concentrated position for decades; a dozen carefully chosen long positions can do well even if half don't work. _[Bill Ackman, Walmart, Walton family]_ — [2022-10-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_h10aNEQK50)
- **Investing carries a very high error rate, at least 40% and maybe 50%, and one can still do well because the winners dominate.** Micron was a 10% bet that peaked near 25% of the fund and is now around 20%; he will not know if it worked until the dust settles. Of ten non-correlated bets, five or six working, one or two losing and one or two flat still produces a massive home run. _[Micron]_ — [2022-11-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j3U0tb-1zSU)
- **Asymmetry, doing things where the downside is muted or non-existent and the upside is unknown, is a great mental model alongside cloning, and you should go for it whenever you can identify it.** Jeff Bezos and Amazon throw many small bets against the wall; most fail but the few that work pay hugely. Satyam not working would have cost 1% of his portfolio. His first business risked only $30,000 from his retirement account plus $70,000 of credit card debt that bankruptcy would wipe out, with millions of upside. His recent insurance company acquisition did not work but capital was returned and nothing was lost. _[Amazon, Jeff Bezos, Satyam Computer Services]_ — [2022-11-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m606MaKujq4)
- **Investing is not a team sport; it must be a dictatorship because a team can never reach consensus on distressed, hated or unloved ideas.** He has been visiting Turkey for four years and pitched its great businesses, management and moats to everyone he admires, including Munger and Guy Spier, and no one is interested. Teams end up in non-controversial names because 'you don't get fired for buying IBM'. Analysts and helpers are fine, but the decision must be one person's. _[IBM]_ — [2022-11-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m606MaKujq4)
- **Temperament is largely genetic; you cannot convert a hyperactive trader into a happy long-term value investor, so it is important to know yourself.** Some traits can be learned, but you will struggle doing something far from your natural tendency or bias. — [2022-11-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m606MaKujq4)
- **Reading 'Power vs. Force' convinced him that you cannot get away with lying, so he eliminated even white lies; pure candor makes you trustable, which is one of the most important things in life.** Body language eventually gives lies away, whereas constant truth-telling makes people stronger around you: 'we want to hang out with the Dalai Lama, not used car dealers'. Guy Spier adds that 99% truthful gets you halfway; the last 1% gets you all the way. — [2022-11-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m606MaKujq4)
- **Everything he buys goes down after he buys it, which is par for the course; don't let the stock price instruct you, let it serve you, and let the fundamentals decide whether to add.** John Templeton said the best analyst is wrong one in three times, and more likely you are wrong half the time, yet a 50% error rate still allows well-above-market returns. After a decline, investigate whether there is a long-term secular issue; if it is temporary, ignore it. _[John Templeton]_ — [2022-12-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W--321tO12M)
- **He peeks at prices about once a day but does not fixate; with only eight or nine stocks per fund it is easy to tell what is going on.** When traveling he may go one or more days without looking at prices or valuations at all. — [2022-12-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W--321tO12M)

### Buffett & Munger lessons (17)

- **Buffett is a Swiss Army knife who can invest 20 different ways, but figuring out 3% of what he knows within a narrow circle is enough to do very well.** Buffett is an open book: 20+ years of Berkshire meetings on CNBC's site and the annual reports. Understanding only captive auto finance and investing there alone could still do very well. _[Warren Buffett, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2022-01-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dzfjw0ZXVm4)
- **Buffett's Japanese trading house bet, financed entirely with yen debt at 0.5% against 7-8% dividend yields, is a way to soak up excess brain horsepower without harming Berkshire.** About $6-7 billion in 5-10% stakes, up 50-70% in three years, with infinite return on equity invested. Munger told him Buffett's large brain must stay active in ways not detrimental to Berkshire: bridge, Korean stocks bought one Saturday afternoon, negative-rate bonds. Pabrai plays 8-10 hours of bridge a week and has Dakshana for the same reason. _[Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger, Berkshire Hathaway, Japanese trading companies]_ — [2022-06-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y2zu_8w_2H0)
- **Buffett's advice to his 10- and 12-year-old daughters at the 2007 lunch, that whom you marry is the most important decision in life, was alone worth many times the $650,000 price.** Buffett said he had nothing going on all afternoon and let them end the 2h45m lunch; Pabrai noted 54 questions. Buffett's ethos is that the winner must feel they got a bargain, which he contrasts with a lunch with Eric Schmidt; the final auction went for ~$19M in 2022. _[Warren Buffett, Eric Schmidt, Johnny Rockets]_ — [2022-07-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E0_K-eFC8bQ)
- **The Buffett lunch was 'buy one get one': Buffett set up a lunch with Munger, which he found even more interesting because Charlie has no diplomatic filters.** He then had dinner with Munger every few months and became a Friday Bridge substitute at the LA Country Club, where Rick Guerin was a partner. His then-wife said it was the smartest thing he ever did besides marrying her. _[Charlie Munger, Rick Guerin, Warren Buffett]_ — [2022-07-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E0_K-eFC8bQ)
- **Munger says he and Buffett could not do today what they did then because far more brainpower now chases fewer stocks, so you must zag when others zig and go where it is hated and unloved.** They used to shoot fish in a barrel after letting the water out; in 2022 Pabrai owns one US stock and a few in Turkey, which smart value investor friends dismiss outright because of 80%+ official inflation. _[Charlie Munger, Warren Buffett, Turkey]_ — [2022-08-17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MYR0tWgstMI)
- **Munger told him in 2009 it is really important to have someone to talk to about investments, and seeking unbiased opinions helps lower the error rate.** Munger said it was not always Warren; Pabrai deliberately began seeking out differing opinions after that second meeting. _[Charlie Munger, Warren Buffett]_ — [2022-09-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zw5B7F5IUV4)
- **The 2008 Buffett lunch, bid simply to say thank you for his public-domain IP, delivered unbelievable value because Buffett's mindset is to make the winner feel they got a bargain.** It ran almost three hours and covered about 54 questions. A question about Rick Guerin became a lesson: Rick had margin calls in 1973-74 and sold Berkshire to Buffett at about $40; 'if you are slightly above average, spend less than you earn and don't use leverage, you cannot help but get rich'. The introduction to Munger was the gift that kept giving. _[Warren Buffett, Rick Guerin, Charlie Munger, Guy Spier, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2022-09-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zw5B7F5IUV4)
- **The $650,000 Buffett lunch in 2007 was a tuition bill for the $84 million he had made from Buffett, Munger and Graham, and it turned out to be 'buy one, get infinite free'.** He was prepared to bid $2 million; Guy Spier was capped at $250,000 for a third. The lunch led to years of lunches and Friday bridge with Munger at the LA Country Club and annual invitations to Buffett's Sunday brunch in Omaha from 2007 to 2022. _[Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger, Guy Spier]_ — [2022-09-20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rzXG8pUg4sM)
- **Buffett turned an innocent question about Rick Guerin into a lesson on leverage: Rick was levered in 1973-74 and had to sell Berkshire to Buffett at $40 a share, now over $400,000.** That is 10,000x in under 50 years. Buffett's mindset at the lunch is that whoever paid should feel they got a bargain, so he works hard to deliver value. _[Rick Guerin, Berkshire Hathaway, Warren Buffett]_ — [2022-09-20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rzXG8pUg4sM)
- **The one book to read is Poor Charlie's Almanack, especially 'The Psychology of Human Misjudgment', which took Munger 50 years of wisdom to write and gives a huge advantage in life.** He rereads it every year and finds new things. Munger's edge is horsepower plus 400-500 books a year for 80 years (about 40,000 books) plus the third hack of mental models. _[Charlie Munger, Poor Charlie's Almanack]_ — [2022-09-20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rzXG8pUg4sM)
- **Buffett's only wish is that when he dies people say 'man, he was old' - he wants runway because he just wants to compound.** Buffett bought his first stock at 11 and says he wasted his time until then; he had about $10,000 saved at 18 (about $120,000 today) and has now compounded for 74 years, having just turned 92. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2022-10-11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QJNB_CC-PDk)
- **Buffett's lesson from Rick Guerin: if you are even a slightly above-average investor who spends less than you earn, you cannot help but get rich over a lifetime - but never use leverage.** In the 1973-74 crash, more severe than 1929 but in slow motion, Guerin was leveraged with margin loans and had to sell Berkshire shares to Buffett at $40; they now trade above $400,000, a 10,000x in 48 years. _[Rick Guerin, Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2022-10-11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QJNB_CC-PDk)
- **Bidding $650,000 for lunch with Buffett in 2007 was 'tuition' for intellectual property used for free, and it paid off through an unexpected friendship with Charlie Munger.** With a net worth of $85 million he was willing to bid up to $2 million; his only agenda was to say thank you (and touch Buffett's feet). Buffett introduced him to Munger, leading to dinners every two or three months, bridge twice a month, and invaluable non-investing life advice. _[Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger, Guy Spier]_ — [2022-10-11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QJNB_CC-PDk)
- **Buffett's ethos differs from Singleton's: Buffett treats shareholders as partners and refuses to 'play gin rummy' with them, so Berkshire resisted buybacks and now only buys back with full disclosure.** Singleton saw shareholders as faceless counterparties and made money off them; Buffett wants to make money with his partners. Pabrai notes John Malone does not seem to share Buffett's scruples. _[Berkshire Hathaway, Warren Buffett, Henry Singleton, John Malone]_ — [2022-10-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_h10aNEQK50)
- **Warren Buffett is the best investor because he is a learning machine who has continuously evolved over an unmatched span.** Buffett moved from buying fractions of businesses to whole businesses to leading an empire with over 80 CEOs reporting directly; Lowenstein's biography and 'The Snowball' are the books to read. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2022-11-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j3U0tb-1zSU)
- **Echoing Buffett, go to work for people you like, admire and trust; pay and brand are secondary.** You spend such a large portion of your life with the people you work with that who you work for and with should excite you more than money or recognition. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2022-11-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j3U0tb-1zSU)
- **The Buffett lunch was a tuition bill for lifted intellectual property, and it turned out to be 'buy one, get infinite free'.** In 2007 his net worth was over $80 million, almost all from following Buffett, Munger and Graham, so a couple of million (about 2.5%) seemed a reasonable tuition; Guy paid a third, leaving Pabrai about $400,000. His only aim was to thank Buffett, but it led to friendships with Buffett, a deeper one with Munger, and with Buffett's assistant Debbie, plus Munger's high-quality bridge friends whom he deliberately made his own friends. _[Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger, Guy Spier]_ — [2022-11-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m606MaKujq4)

### Mistakes & lessons learned (18)

- **He started in 1994 as a Munger-style compounder investor, switched to Graham deep value in 1999 because of the dotcom bubble, and stayed on that path nearly 20 years too long.** The day the NASDAQ peaked in March 2000 Berkshire hit a multi-year low as money moved into pets.com; he was buying funeral homes and compounded at mid-30s percent a year from 1999-2000 to 2007 while the S&P did low single digits. The ideal time to switch back to compounders was 2009-2012; reading about Nick Sleep and Zak in William Green's book in 2020 finally triggered the switch. _[Berkshire Hathaway, pets.com, Nick Sleep, William Green]_ — [2022-01-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b9ioA0J-p2M)
- **Starbucks and Chipotle are incredible businesses he understood for 20 years but never bought because they looked expensive.** A US Starbucks store pays back in 18-24 months and an international one in a year; opening a second and third store diagonally across a New York intersection did not dent the original's sales because demand is convenience-driven. _[Starbucks, Chipotle]_ — [2022-01-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b9ioA0J-p2M)
- **His two big mistakes are being too cheap to pay up for great businesses and being too cheap to keep holding them after they re-rate.** Some businesses looked optically overpriced at 30-40 times earnings and still did well; others bought at 10 times were sold at 20-30 times and kept going. He hammers into his head daily that capitalism is brutal and if you own a truly exceptional business, do not worry about valuation. — [2022-01-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b9ioA0J-p2M)
- **Ben Graham led him astray for most of his career: the mistake was treating intrinsic value as a red line for selling, when the most money is made by holding businesses with long growth runways well above intrinsic value.** A Graham investor in Walmart in the 1970s would have exited at 40-50x earnings and missed the forest for the trees. He figured this out only two or three years ago and reckons he has '22 years of runway left' to make amends. _[Ben Graham, Walmart]_ — [2022-04-04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hQsP8ogUp8k)
- **He exited Seritage after admitting he underestimated how hard redeveloping properties across a hundred different municipalities would be; the real mistake was opportunity cost in Q2 2020.** Bought at $6-9 after it fell from $30+ pre-pandemic, sold for a 20-40% gain, but many other cheap companies were available then. Templeton said the best analysts are right two out of three times, and realistically it is about half; being honest with yourself and taking chips off the table when a thesis is flawed is essential. _[Seritage Growth Properties, John Templeton]_ — [2022-04-04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hQsP8ogUp8k)
- **Selling Kotak, Blue Dart and Sky Pack in 2000 for no reason was the biggest lesson of his career: Kotak went up 500x and Blue Dart 300x after he sold.** In 1995 he put $20,000 in India: $10,000 in Satyam at 40 rupees, which he sold near 6,000-7,000 rupees for $1.3-1.5 million within 10% of the top, and $3,000 each in Blue Dart, Sky Pack and Kotak, which were flat and he sold anyway. Sky Pack fell 90%, but three of four were 100-baggers or more. 'The most important skill is to be patient.' _[Kotak Mahindra, Blue Dart, Sky Pack, Satyam, Falguni Nayar]_ — [2022-06-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y2zu_8w_2H0)
- **Silicon Valley Bank, his first Pabrai Funds purchase on July 1, 1999, was sold after 2.5x in a year, but it compounded at about 26% a year from 1999 to 2022 because he failed to appreciate how well run the franchise was.** SVB traded near book value with an undisclosed basket of warrants from venture-backed borrowers; he put 10% of the $1 million fund in. 'Old too soon and wise too late', but investing is a forgiving business where things work out despite many mistakes. _[Silicon Valley Bank, HDFC, Kotak Mahindra]_ — [2022-06-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y2zu_8w_2H0)
- **My journey has been sloppy; if I had focused purely on 10- and 100-baggers from 1994-95 my results would have been vastly better.** Starting with ~$1 million in 1995, he had two 100-baggers in the first five years (one turned $100,000 into ~$10 million and the US portfolio went from $980,000 to ~$13 million by 1999-2000), but none from 2000 to 2022; the two 100-baggers drove 80-90% of returns. — [2022-06-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qBdieWfouZM)
- **Satyam turned $10,000 into ~$1.4 million (150x) from 1995 to 2000, but I sold Kotak and Blue Dart in 2000 for no good reason and missed a 500x and a 300x.** He put 2% ($20,000) of his portfolio into India via an NRI account at Kotak: half in Satyam (then an honest company that went wayward 10-12 years later), and ~$3,300 each in Kotak, Blue Dart and Sky Pack; Sky Pack fell ~90% and went bankrupt, but the lesson is that selling winners was the error. _[Satyam Computers, Kotak Mahindra, Blue Dart, Sky Pack Courier]_ — [2022-06-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qBdieWfouZM)
- **Investing is a very forgiving business: Templeton said the best investor is wrong one in three times, most of us are wrong half the time, and you can still do well.** The key is to recognize when you are in the happy position of owning a great business and then set Ben Graham aside. _[John Templeton]_ — [2022-08-17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MYR0tWgstMI)
- **Per John Templeton the best analyst is wrong one in three times, and Pabrai expects 40-50% of his own picks to not work, so the error rate is baked in like a law of physics.** Berkshire bought 80-90 businesses in 50 years and at least 30 did not work, including almost all furniture retailers except Nebraska Furniture Mart, jewelers and retail; weighted by size Buffett is right about 90% of the time. Failures usually flatline or drop 20%, not go to zero. _[John Templeton, Warren Buffett, Berkshire Hathaway, Nebraska Furniture Mart]_ — [2022-08-30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wz8N5CkTA2w)
- **Expect at least one-third of bets to fail, even for Buffett: more than a third of Berkshire's 70-80 acquisitions did not work on an equal-weighted basis.** Templeton's rule means two or three of six bets over three years will do far worse than expected. Every Berkshire furniture retailer except Nebraska Furniture Mart and every jeweler except Borsheims failed, and many would have gone under in the financial crisis without the parent; dollar-weighted, Buffett's larger bets worked. _[John Templeton, Berkshire Hathaway, Nebraska Furniture Mart, Borsheims]_ — [2022-09-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zw5B7F5IUV4)
- **Beginners must make real investments with real money rather than paper portfolios, expect a 33-50% error rate even if very good, and learn from their own and others' mistakes.** Cites John Templeton's one-third to one-half error rate for really good investors; trading costs are low so even $5,000-10,000 is enough to start after doing the work. _[John Templeton]_ — [2022-09-20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rzXG8pUg4sM)
- **The holy grail of investing is a small ownership of a great growing business held for a very long time; his drift into cigar butts after 2000 was a mistake he is correcting.** He was buy-and-hold in 1994-2000 (a 200-bagger), switched to Ben Graham cigar butts at the 2000 NASDAQ peak and did ~36% a year for eight or nine years and +130% in 2009 in commodities, but should have switched back around 2012. Reading William Green's 'Richer, Wiser, Happier' manuscript in 2020 made him realize he had 'screwed up'. _[William Green, Nick Sleep, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2022-10-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_h10aNEQK50)
- **Following Marcus Aurelius, to encounter misfortune and overcome it is good fortune; every setback has produced exponential learning paybacks he could not see at the time.** His serial-entrepreneur father went bankrupt every three or four years, and as a college junior on a student visa the family's bankruptcy left him helpless until an uncle stepped in. The fund's 65-70% drop in the financial crisis seared in mistakes that improved later performance; 'we don't learn from success, we learn when we stumble'. _[Marcus Aurelius]_ — [2022-11-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j3U0tb-1zSU)
- **Selling about 1% of Ferrari from his funds was an idiotic mistake; 'we are old too soon and wise too late', but he still has perhaps 32 years to apply the lesson.** He has deep regrets about many great businesses he sold. Guy Spier kept his Ferrari (selling only half at the start of lockdown) and Guy's own regret is selling Crisil, the 'Moody's of India', which is up 50-100x since. _[Ferrari, Crisil]_ — [2022-11-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m606MaKujq4)
- **Learn from mistakes but not too much: the best investors are wrong one in three times and mere mortals half the time, so be intellectually honest, move on, and don't try to win the money back the same way you lost it.** Quoting Munger's advice to 'learn but not learn too much'. Jhunjhunwala only needed to be right on 4% of his portfolio. Once a loss of capital reveals a better understanding of the business, it may make sense to simply exit. _[Charlie Munger, Rakesh Jhunjhunwala]_ — [2022-11-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m606MaKujq4)
- **When you are at the bottom of a deep well you need a rope: in 2008-09 his rope was a spreadsheet of what the businesses were worth rather than the market value.** Pabrai Funds fell 65-67% from the 2007 peak to March 2009, from about $600 million under management to under $200 million, while his valuation showed the portfolio worth over $600 million. From March to December 2009 the funds rose about 135%. With Reysas at $20 million he did every check for fraud, visited all the warehouses and met management before concluding nothing was wrong. _[Pabrai Investment Funds, Reysas]_ — [2022-12-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W--321tO12M)

### Career, entrepreneurship & life (28)

- **Dhandho means smartly doing business so that risk is lowered and return is high; entrepreneurs like the Patels minimize downside rather than take big risks.** Non-venture startups (99.99% of all startups) structure things so downside is limited and upside asymmetric; the Patels entered motels with tiny capital outlays, leveraged the cash flows and now own 70-80% of US motels. The same approach was used by Graham, Buffett and Munger. _[Patels, Ben Graham, Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger]_ — [2022-01-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b9ioA0J-p2M)
- **Venture capital is a much harder game than public markets because deal flow depends on brand and there are no track records to judge.** Top and bottom quartile bond managers differ by basis points, but Sequoia has been top 3-5% for decades and VCs say Sequoia's rejects would triple returns; a no-name VC is the 301st person to see a deal. Public businesses like Starbucks, Chipotle, Moutai and Ferrari have history; in VC you cannot tell Theranos from Apple since both wore turtlenecks. _[Sequoia, Andreessen Horowitz, Y Combinator, Theranos, Apple]_ — [2022-01-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b9ioA0J-p2M)
- **He wandered aimlessly until 34, when a 360 analysis by industrial psychologists at a YPO retreat gave him an 'owner's manual' showing he is a single-player game player who needs an edge.** He loved his company at one person and hated it at 170 people running HR and politics; they told him to sell or hire a CEO, and within six months he was gone and starting Pabrai Funds, which they said was perfect. One psychologist, Dr. Jack Skeen, became an early investor and has a 16x so far. Myers-Briggs is the poor man's version. _[Jack Skeen, YPO, Pabrai Funds]_ — [2022-01-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=b9ioA0J-p2M)
- **Taking outside money without a track record is somewhat dishonest; build a record first, because compounding a modest sum at mid-20s returns doubles every three years.** If you must, go to friends, family and fools. At mid-20s returns you have 1,000x in 30 years, so in 10-15 years you can have a decent sum and a legitimate reason for others to invest. — [2022-01-19](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dzfjw0ZXVm4)
- **Index investing is a great way to go for almost everyone; venture into individual stocks only if the business is in your circle and you have the time.** An ER doctor might understand Walmart, Costco or Apple as a customer, but without time to dig in, better not to go there. The S&P 500, Berkshire Hathaway and his Free Lunch portfolio are all valid starting points. _[Walmart, Costco, Apple, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2022-02-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0SbspUlZW8A)
- **The bottom of the market is continuously cleared of great talent as successful managers outgrow small bets, so emerging managers always have nooks and crannies available.** Per Joel Greenblatt, a $5 million manager can make $100,000-$500,000 bets that move the needle; once $5 million becomes $500 million they must leave the bottom. Managers worth studying include Josh Tarasoff and Andrew Wilkinson of Tiny Capital. _[Joel Greenblatt, Josh Tarasoff, Andrew Wilkinson, Tiny Capital]_ — [2022-04-04](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=hQsP8ogUp8k)
- **The investor's job description is reading and thinking, not acting; actions should be very infrequent and curiosity makes it a great life rather than work.** Tom Murphy of Capital Cities said he never worked a day in his life; visiting 15 businesses in a week in Turkey is more fun than sightseeing. _[Tom Murphy, Capital Cities ABC]_ — [2022-06-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y2zu_8w_2H0)
- **Investing is an endeavor where you can keep getting better throughout your life, unlike basketball or cricket.** Continuous improvement and learning are both possible and desirable in this business. — [2022-06-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=qBdieWfouZM)
- **Sitting on his father's de facto board from age 11-12 and doing sales calls at 15-16 gave him several MBAs before 19, during the years the brain is wired to specialize.** His father was brilliant at starting businesses from zero after each bankruptcy but grew them with heavy leverage and no savings, so they crumbled at the first headwind. Brain connections are culled from ~10 to 20, so Buffett, Gates and Michelangelo, who specialized at 10-11, got an edge that 20s or 30s cannot replicate even with 5x the time. _[Warren Buffett, Bill Gates]_ — [2022-07-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E0_K-eFC8bQ)
- **Engineers who ignore the economics of what they build make no sense; he switched to the business side after 2.5 years and found he could crack business models faster than most.** At a telecom equipment company 200 engineers had no interest in how the product made money; his boss told him it was not their concern. — [2022-07-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E0_K-eFC8bQ)
- **Businesses can be started with nothing: his father's first venture in 1962 turned a 250-rupee magazine ad for mail-order magic kits into 1,400 rupees of profit, then reinvested.** His father joked he could be put naked on a rock and start a business. Pabrai started TransTech in 1991 with $30,000 from his 401k and $70,000 of credit-card debt and sold it nine years later for $20M. _[TransTech, Illustrated Weekly of India]_ — [2022-07-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E0_K-eFC8bQ)
- **Investing converts the 2-3% of entrepreneurship spent on strategy into 80% of the job, with none of the operational heavy lifting.** He discovered Buffett in 1994 via Peter Lynch's books, then the first two biographies and the Berkshire letters; the aha was that the mental models he and his father used to run businesses were the same ones Buffett used to evaluate investments. _[Warren Buffett, Peter Lynch]_ — [2022-07-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E0_K-eFC8bQ)
- **The best way to learn is to teach; student sessions improve him and, like bridge, keep him from making sell decisions.** He would be blissfully happy in a prison cell with three bridge players for life; investing is a great activity for gentlemen and ladies of leisure who can refrain from acting on their portfolio. — [2022-08-30](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=wz8N5CkTA2w)
- **Large inheritances do more harm than good; his father's bankruptcy when he was 20 was one of the best things that happened to him because it made clear no inheritance was coming.** Buffett's Jesse Owens analogy: start the son at the 10-meter line, not the 40-meter line. A large inheritance is an IV drip, the same as welfare for 'trust fund babies'. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2022-09-20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rzXG8pUg4sM)
- **He funded UGMA accounts of $10,000 a year for each daughter, managed them with three or four stocks, and gave full control at 18 on the theory that 18 years is enough to transfer values.** The accounts compounded to seven figures; he told his daughters at 12-13 that nothing else was coming and to pursue passion rather than pay. Inheritances should arrive before 30-35 when trajectory changes are still possible. Daughter Monsoon used the money as confidence to quit her job and launch a fund. _[Monsoon Pabrai]_ — [2022-09-20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rzXG8pUg4sM)
- **His job description is reading, thinking and talking; as an introvert he finds drilling into a company's VIC reports and letters an 'orgasmic experience'.** His favorite genre is biographies and autobiographies of business leaders, because they show what drove them and the long history of the business. — [2022-09-20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rzXG8pUg4sM)
- **Life and investing payoffs are asymmetric: many ventures fail, but the ones that work make up for the rest, so take any asymmetric bet whose downside you can tolerate.** He bought an insurance company two years earlier, realized within three months it was a mistake and sold it for about what he paid. He cites Teddy Roosevelt's man in the arena. — [2022-10-11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QJNB_CC-PDk)
- **Everyone should get their 'owner's manual': who you are is hard-coded by age six, and knowing it lets you pick games you can win.** In 1999 two industrial psychologists did a 360 on him and told him he likes single-player games he can win with no people; they urged him to leave his 170-person company (he hated herding cats past 20-30 people) and start Pabrai Investment Funds. He now works 100% from home and stays out of Dakshana's operations. _[Pabrai Investment Funds, Dakshana]_ — [2022-10-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_h10aNEQK50)
- **Running a business makes you a better investor; the goal is to identify the three or four variables the CEO actually runs the business on.** Quotes Buffett: 'I'm a better businessman because I'm an investor and a better investor because I'm a businessman' and the fish-walking-on-land analogy. Bezos and Jassy make small bets with asymmetric upside and don't run Amazon through spreadsheets. _[Amazon, Jeff Bezos, Andy Jassy, Warren Buffett]_ — [2022-10-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_h10aNEQK50)
- **Go to work for people you like, admire and trust rather than for brand names, and hang out with people better than you.** He did not know who he was until 35 and wishes he had his owner's manual at 20; graduates should choose workplaces where they move up in quality of people, not pay or Thanksgiving-table prestige. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2022-10-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_h10aNEQK50)
- **Entrepreneurs are not risk takers; over 99.9% of startups are non-venture-backed and their founders do everything possible to reduce risk while capturing asymmetric upside.** In 1991 at 25 he funded TransTech with about $70,000 of credit-card debt plus $30,000 from his 401(k), having researched that bankruptcy would wipe the cards and even make him a good credit for seven years; his bosses promised a promotion 'when' the business failed. Amar Bhide's 'The Origin and Evolution of New Businesses' found Inc. 500 founders think the same way. _[TransTech, Amar Bhide]_ — [2022-11-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j3U0tb-1zSU)
- **Not starting a business was the high-risk path, because once married with kids in your thirties or forties there is far more to lose.** Single and bankrupt at 25 means nothing and you bounce back, so he felt he had one open clear shot and took it. _[TransTech]_ — [2022-11-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j3U0tb-1zSU)
- **A hedge fund has tremendous economics because one person can run hundreds of millions or billions, and his early investors served as unpaid analysts.** His first investors were entrepreneurs whose businesses sometimes overlapped with what he was studying; he lost interest in the IT business as investing became a profitable pursuit he was passionate about. _[Pabrai Investment Funds]_ — [2022-11-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j3U0tb-1zSU)
- **Hedge funds cannot publish returns to non-accredited investors under SEC rules, which is why his letters are not public.** Guy Spier's Aquamarine also checks accreditation before sharing; mutual funds are open because they are built for the public with daily NAVs, whereas hedge funds must keep a curtain from the general public. _[Guy Spier, Aquamarine Fund]_ — [2022-11-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j3U0tb-1zSU)
- **His career rule: if on Monday morning he is not fired up to go to work, he does not go to work and hits the reading.** He left his employer when it grew from 8 to 800 people and his undefined job became narrow; he started TransTech around opportunities he saw because the risk was low. _[TransTech]_ — [2022-11-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j3U0tb-1zSU)
- **Cloning Munger's habit of introducing randomness into life, he hosts strangers for afternoon tea in Austin a couple of times a month because there is no downside and occasionally a great friendship results.** Munger pulls letters from his coat pocket and picks strangers to have breakfast with, which has led to friendships and business partnerships. Since moving to Austin eight or nine months earlier he has still met Munger three times, including a catamaran cruise in Santa Barbara. _[Charlie Munger]_ — [2022-11-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m606MaKujq4)
- **Elite universities add value mainly as a selection filter that opens employer doors, not through the education itself; most people get only two or three impactful courses out of a degree.** From his engineering degree, an elective in public speaking had the biggest long-term impact. The IITs have probably the world's most objective undergraduate admissions filter (no legacies or donors) with great talent in and out despite mediocre or pathetic professors; graduates land at Amazon, Salesforce or Google because of horsepower and hard work, not the teaching. _[IIT, Amazon, Google, Salesforce]_ — [2022-11-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m606MaKujq4)
- **To build a fund, start with any small amount in a brokerage account you never draw on, build an auditable track record, then raise from friends, family and fools; do well for them and the world shows up.** Buffett says if you are even slightly above average, investors will swim to you through shark-infested waters in the middle of the Atlantic. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2022-11-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=m606MaKujq4)

### Philanthropy & Dakshana (17)

- **Large inheritances are a disservice to your gene pool, so the only choice is to give the money back to society, and to do it thoughtfully while you still have energy.** Around 2006-07 at age 42 he saw his wealth would exceed his ability to spend it and followed Buffett's line about giving kids enough to do anything but not enough to do nothing; he did not want to be writing Red Cross checks at 85 'drooling with half my brain gone'. _[Warren Buffett, Dakshana Foundation]_ — [2022-02-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0SbspUlZW8A)
- **Most charities are all heart and no head; philanthropy needs a Bill Gates-style balance and a focus on social return on invested capital.** Comparing housing a homeless person versus needle exchanges versus climate change is nearly impossible to measure, so following Munger's 'invert, always invert' he chose to fund only causes where measurement is easy, which led to education and poverty alleviation in India. _[Charlie Munger, Bill Gates, Dakshana Foundation]_ — [2022-02-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0SbspUlZW8A)
- **Dakshana lifts a family permanently out of poverty for about $3,000 by coaching poor, gifted students into nearly free government engineering and medical schools.** Two years of free coaching yields a 70-80% admission rate; students from families earning under $100-200 a month go on to earn $1,000-2,000 a month. Results are verified by third parties and published at dakshana.org, and Buffett has called the Dakshana annual reports the best nonprofit reports he has ever read. _[Dakshana Foundation, Warren Buffett]_ — [2022-02-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0SbspUlZW8A)
- **Large inheritances do more harm than good, so surplus assets must be recycled back to society rather than given to the gene pool.** Bestowing large amounts on children is like an IV drip that puts them in a welfare state; Buffett's line that Jesse Owens' son should start at the 10-meter line but not the 40-meter line. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2022-06-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y2zu_8w_2H0)
- **Philanthropy inverts the investing rule: you must go high risk, swing for the fences and be fully willing to fail, because that is the only way to move the needle.** In investing he goes low risk, high return and can let 99.9% of the market go by; in philanthropy you are forced to confront tough problems like poverty and education. He started giving 2% of assets a year, modelled on Buffett giving 5% of his Berkshire shares annually. _[Dakshana Foundation, Warren Buffett]_ — [2022-06-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y2zu_8w_2H0)
- **Dakshana was cloned from Anand Kumar's Super 30 and scaled from 30 kids to over 1,000 a year, with 60-80% admitted to IITs, AIIMS or medical schools at $2,500-3,000 per kid.** Students come from illiterate rural farming families earning under $100 a month; alumni now work at Microsoft, Amazon and Google, in the IAS, and as VC-funded founders. He started Dakshana at 42 because waiting until 70 or 80 would leave no energy to do more than write checks. _[Dakshana Foundation, Anand Kumar, Super 30, IIT]_ — [2022-06-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y2zu_8w_2H0)
- **Large inheritances do more harm than good, and most charities have great hearts but not great heads, so he had to build Dakshana himself to learn how to give well before he loses his marbles.** Buffett's line: Jesse Owens's son can start the 100m at the 10m line but not the 40m line. Dakshana is a lab for social return on invested capital that can scale as wealth grows. _[Dakshana Foundation, Warren Buffett]_ — [2022-07-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E0_K-eFC8bQ)
- **Dakshana levels the playing field for gifted poor kids to enter the IITs, achieving a 70-80% admit rate versus ~1-1.5% overall.** About 1,000 kids a year, 700-800 reach IIT and the rest good second-tier colleges. One scholar, son of a slum tailor in Hyderabad whose family sometimes went to bed hungry and could not pay a 20-rupee school fee, ranked 63 of 1.3M, went to IIT Bombay CS and now earns $300-400K at Google. _[Dakshana Foundation, IIT, Google]_ — [2022-07-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=E0_K-eFC8bQ)
- **Large inheritances do more harm than good, so beyond a head start the money should go to society; Dakshana was started about 15 years ago in his early forties.** Modest lifestyle plus compounding plus fees on other people's money meant sums well beyond need; putting heirs on an IV drip is counterproductive. _[Dakshana]_ — [2022-09-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zw5B7F5IUV4)
- **Most charities have great hearts but not great heads and cannot quantify impact, so Dakshana's hack is to do only things that are easy to measure, just like the intrinsic value hack.** Dakshana coaches gifted 16-18-year-olds from very poor families for IIT and medical entrance exams; an independent external report card each year shows admissions that the team cannot fudge, with cost per kid and lifetime benefit extrapolations. _[Dakshana, IIT]_ — [2022-09-16](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=zw5B7F5IUV4)
- **Charities need to be good at capital allocation, so Dakshana only pursues endeavors where outcomes can be measured easily, which biased it toward education.** In 2006-07 he found most charities had good hearts but no business sense, and 97-98% of causes (e.g. needle distribution for the homeless) cannot be measured. Following Munger's 'always invert', he limited himself to measurable outcomes. _[Dakshana Foundation, Charlie Munger]_ — [2022-09-20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rzXG8pUg4sM)
- **Dakshana takes over the education of very poor 16-18 year olds and gets 70-80% into the IITs or top medical schools, versus a 1-2% base rate.** Over 1.4 million apply for 15,000 IIT seats and 2 million for 10-15,000 medical seats; once in, the schools are nearly free. After 15 years the oldest alumni are approaching 30 with flourishing careers. _[Dakshana Foundation, IIT]_ — [2022-09-20](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=rzXG8pUg4sM)
- **Giving money away effectively is far harder than making it, so start early - he began Dakshana at 43 by committing 2% of assets a year and accepting he might lose it while learning.** Investing is low risk, high return; charity must be high risk, high return - only go for sixers, because that is the only way to move the needle. Dakshana is about 15 years old. _[Dakshana Foundation]_ — [2022-10-11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=QJNB_CC-PDk)
- **Philanthropy should invert the investing rules: go high risk, high return, concentrate on a single cause, and only pick causes where outcomes are measurable.** Buffett told him to 'swing for the fences' in charity. Dakshana spends $2,000-3,000 per bright poor Indian kid from families earning $30-100 a month; some alumni now earn over $500,000 a year at Google. Most charities optimize for what feels good, and in some cases 90% of funds raised go to fundraising. _[Dakshana, Gates Foundation, Warren Buffett]_ — [2022-10-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_h10aNEQK50)
- **Charities need heart and head; a charity with ten initiatives should measure them, cut to eight, then six, and pour money into the highest social return on invested capital.** He found most charities run by good-hearted people who do not understand capital allocation and keep spreading money to appeal to donors or make annual reports look nice. _[Dakshana Foundation]_ — [2022-11-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j3U0tb-1zSU)
- **Dakshana cloned Anand Kumar's Super 30 because education has a massive multiplier: about $3,000 per student yields near-infinite payback by transforming a family for generations.** In 2006 in Bihar, Super 30 spent about $700 per kid from families earning under $2 a day and got 90-100% into the IITs, whose graduates get hired by Microsoft, Alphabet and Apple; Kumar would not take money but endorsed cloning. He has not found a higher SROI and would switch if he did. _[Dakshana Foundation, Super 30, Anand Kumar]_ — [2022-11-08](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=j3U0tb-1zSU)
- **Giving money away is harder than making it, so he started at 42 committing 2% of net worth a year rather than waiting until 80 to write checks, and plans to scale toward a quarter of net worth.** He expected to get his head handed to him in India for 10 years as tuition, but Dakshana got traction within weeks and its social ROI is 10x better than he thought possible over 15-16 years. Google and the MetLife tables say he departs June 11, 2054 (recently revised from 2044); on the Chuck Feeney plan he should have $100 left on June 10, 2054. _[Dakshana, Chuck Feeney]_ — [2022-12-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=W--321tO12M)
