### Cloning & learning from great investors (27)

- **Business biographies are his favorite genre, and he is currently reading Roy Thomson of Fleet Street.** Thomson went broke and ended up owning some 300 newspapers and TV stations; Pabrai tripled the size of his library after moving to Austin about a year earlier. He also praised the Hero Honda family book as a classic Dhandho story. _[Roy Thomson, Hero Honda]_ — [2023-01-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5P1c9bhhYPo)
- **Idea sourcing needs no team: 13F filings in the US and public disclosure of what great Indian investors like RK Damani own feed the hopper.** He can see what Buffett bought last quarter and what many great investors have bought, then study those; RK Damani owns VST Industries, a tobacco company. _[RK Damani, VST Industries, Warren Buffett]_ — [2023-01-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5P1c9bhhYPo)
- **Buffett's 'start with the A's' is real: he thumbed the Moody's Manual in 1956-57 finding companies earning $15M with $25M market caps, and was still thumbing the Japan Company Handbook around 2010-11.** The 12-year-old collecting discarded winning tickets at Aksarben racetrack is the same person at 26 and 82; personality is die-cast by age five. When Pabrai dog-eared Buffett's Japan Company Handbook, Buffett said the good stuff is always at the back, so maybe start with the Z's. _[Warren Buffett, Moody's Manual, Japan Company Handbook, Guy Spier, Debbie Bosanek]_ — [2023-01-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c7Oyv-Echa0)
- **You only get ~1,500 months of life and could study maybe 600-700 businesses, about 1% of the universe, so use hacks like Value Investors Club, Dataroma and Berkshire's portfolio.** VIC gives digested qualitative and quantitative write-ups from a rigorous membership; Dataroma lists holdings already filtered by smart investors. One good investment a year is a year well spent; he is a shameless cloner. _[Value Investors Club, Dataroma, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2023-01-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c7Oyv-Echa0)
- **The value investing community from Graham to Buffett and Munger has an ethos of selfless knowledge sharing, and nobody gets poorer by teaching.** He claims no original ideas, only cloned ones from earlier masters, and notes Buffett wants just one line on his gravestone: 'Was a teacher.' _[Ben Graham, Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger]_ — [2023-01-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c7Oyv-Echa0)
- **Chuck Akre's three-legged stool is a simple, repeatable filter: great economics with high ROE, a long runway to redeploy cash flows, and high-integrity management with skin in the game.** Akre, 80, manages $14-15 billion from one-traffic-light Middleburg, Virginia, and calls himself a slow learner who does one thing, unlike Buffett and Munger who are Swiss Army knives. Pabrai cold-wrote him and visited in 2022. High ROE without leverage is the hallmark of a great business. _[Chuck Akre]_ — [2023-02-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UcJB1m3cXKw)
- **He has nothing homegrown in his philosophy; everything is cloned from Buffett, Munger, Graham, Akre and others, made possible by value investing's culture of sharing knowledge.** He never went to business school and self-educated via Buffett biographies, Berkshire letters, partnership letters and Munger. He recommends buffett.cnbc.com, where he listened to every annual meeting since the mid-1990s twice, in the shower, over seven or eight months. _[Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger, Ben Graham, Chuck Akre]_ — [2023-02-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UcJB1m3cXKw)
- **His answer to Peter Thiel's question about a truth most of the world disagrees with is cloning: humans have an aversion to cloning just as they do to Turkish stocks, and irrational aversions are where to go all in.** Stand on the shoulders of the giants who came before rather than trying to rise on your own. Cloning has helped him in many areas, including Dakshana. _[Peter Thiel]_ — [2023-02-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UcJB1m3cXKw)
- **Buying the Buffett lunch for $650,000 in 2007 was 'buy one, get infinite free' because it led to friendships with Buffett and Munger; he viewed it as a 2% tuition fee on a net worth built by cloning Buffett.** His net worth was north of $80 million in 2007, mostly from cloning Buffett, so about $1.6 million seemed a fair tuition; Guy Spier capped his share at $250,000. The lunch ran three hours and about 54 questions; Buffett introduced him to Munger, whom he now sees four or five times a year and used to play bridge with on Fridays at the LA Country Club. _[Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger, Guy Spier, Glide Foundation]_ — [2023-03-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=miqfRmUDwFQ)
- **Rakesh Jhunjhunwala died worth about $7 billion with half of it in Titan Industries, a position he put 4% of net worth into 25-27 years earlier and never touched despite being a hyperactive trader.** He started by borrowing about 10,000 rupees at 18% with the stocks held in the lender's name as collateral and never managed outside money. Torch 96% of his mid-1990s portfolio and Titan alone still leaves $3.5 billion, the same math as the Nifty 50. _[Rakesh Jhunjhunwala, Titan Industries]_ — [2023-03-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=miqfRmUDwFQ)
- **Buffett's 20-punch-card approach is night and day from a mutual fund with 100 stocks and 80% turnover — following Buffett should beat the professionals.** After reading Peter Lynch's One Up On Wall Street and Beating The Street in 1994 he discovered Buffett; he tested the theory with $1 million in 10% bets starting in 1994 and turned it into $13 million in about five years, roughly 70% annualized. _[Peter Lynch, Warren Buffett]_ — [2023-04-11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ibsxgKdJNpA)
- **Nick Sleep's Nomad could have been wrong 80% of the time and still won: the 20% Amazon position from 2004 alone would have beaten the S&P by six points if everything else went to zero.** Investors left Nomad over concentration; when Nomad closed in 2014 with ~$3B, Sleep told LPs to put money equally in Amazon, Costco and Berkshire for 10 years, but a large university endowment said it was not allowed to buy stocks; Sleep himself trimmed Amazon at 70% of his portfolio to buy ASOS, which has not done well. _[Nick Sleep, Nomad Partnership, Amazon, Costco, Berkshire Hathaway, ASOS]_ — [2023-05-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SP6kKi2nMz4)
- **Ben Graham's biggest success was buying a great business, GEICO, and never applying his sell-at-intrinsic-value rule to it, though he never wrote about that.** He put 25% of the portfolio into half of GEICO for $712,000 in 1948; by his death in 1976 it was $95 million excluding dividends and more than half his net worth; GEICO alone would have delivered 12.9% versus 6.9% for the S&P. _[Ben Graham, GEICO]_ — [2023-05-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SP6kKi2nMz4)
- **Poor Charlie's Almanack, the Buffett biographies, the archived Berkshire meetings and the partnership letters are the core body of work for a beginner.** He also recommends Pulak Prasad's What I Learned About Investing from Darwin, Where the Money Is, and Munger's book list at the back of the Almanack; buffett.cnbc.com archives 25-30 years of five-hour meetings. _[Pulak Prasad, Charlie Munger]_ — [2023-05-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Qgtb7LnvP6Y)
- **Humans have an inexplicable aversion to cloning, so great ideas like the Buffett partnership structure or the Chipotle format go unreplicated for decades, leaving huge opportunity for the shameless cloner.** Buffett ran his partnerships from 1956 to 1969 with no management fee and one-fourth of the upside over 6%; nobody visible replicated it until Pabrai in 1999, 30 years later, and Munger confirmed only a couple of obscure people had. Chipotle's user-directed assembly format is not rocket science yet took years before CAVA and others copied it. _[Buffett Partnership, Chipotle, CAVA, Charlie Munger]_ — [2023-09-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MDuPszGThmE)
- **Humans have an inexplicable aversion to cloning, so being a shameless cloner is a huge structural advantage.** Nobody has cloned Chipotle's customizable assembly line (Baja Fresh never scaled; CAVA applied the concept to different food), McDonald's fries or the Egg McMuffin, even though there is room for two to four players in anything already proven. _[Chipotle, Baja Fresh, CAVA, McDonald's]_ — [2023-09-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kfgbTNWLMJE)
- **When a smart investor buys something you hate, study it to understand 'what drugs they were smoking'; Berkshire's and Einhorn's 2012 GM purchases led him to Fiat Chrysler.** He hated autos (high capex, unions, consumer taste risk) but read Steve Rattner's 'Overhaul' and the 2009 UAW contract signed without changing a comma under threat of no bailout, and realized Detroit had become the best place to build cars again. _[General Motors, Berkshire Hathaway, David Einhorn, Ted Weschler, Steve Rattner, Fiat Chrysler]_ — [2023-09-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kfgbTNWLMJE)
- **Cloning is a powerful mental model precisely because most humans have an inexplicable aversion to it and think it is beneath them.** People wrongly assume that because Starbucks or SoulCycle has been done there is no room for more. Microsoft Research has produced nothing in four decades, while all of Microsoft's successes were clones: Word from WordPerfect, Excel from Lotus 1-2-3, Explorer/Edge from Netscape, Bing from Google, Windows from the Xerox PARC/Apple mouse. Walmart's first 15-20 years were entirely cloned from Kmart and Sears; Starbucks cloned Italian cafes. _[Microsoft, Walmart, Sam Walton, Starbucks, Howard Schultz, Apple, Xerox PARC]_ — [2023-10-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w9oC1rPV5yQ)
- **Pabrai Investment Funds and Dakshana are both clones: the fund copies the 1956-1970 Buffett partnership structure and fee model, which no one else had cloned in the three decades after Buffett shut it down.** He charges no management fee, copied from Warren, which attracts a demographic wanting aligned interests. Dakshana copied a model from a man who did not want to scale but was happy to help. 'I have no original ideas. I am just a shameless cloner.' _[Pabrai Investment Funds, Buffett Partnership, Dakshana Foundation]_ — [2023-10-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w9oC1rPV5yQ)
- **Cloning will never become too competitive because it only works for fanatics who go all in, and very few humans are willing to do that.** All Berkshire meetings are online at buffett.cnbc.com and millions listen, yet almost no company has cloned the Berkshire model. Sam Walton and Bill Gates were fanatics; the casual 'let me give this a go' approach fails. There are also so many greenfield areas to clone. _[Berkshire Hathaway, Sam Walton, Bill Gates]_ — [2023-10-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w9oC1rPV5yQ)
- **Nick Sleep's mistake was selling half his Amazon to buy ASOS; owning a mediocre business is a greater risk than a great one like Amazon going to zero.** Sleep returned client money after UK regulators questioned his Amazon weighting and put a third each into Berkshire, Costco and Amazon. When Amazon grew past 50-60% he trimmed. Pabrai would leave all three alone; if Amazon became 80% 'so be it', since Amazon is multiple businesses and even one survivor keeps him out of the poorhouse. _[Nick Sleep, Amazon, ASOS, Berkshire Hathaway, Costco]_ — [2023-10-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w9oC1rPV5yQ)
- **Owning great businesses like Ferrari, Amex and MasterCard with Guy Spier's lethargic no-sell approach will keep up with the S&P, but it is not the Mohnish way.** He repeatedly begged Guy to sell Nestle, which like ADP has no variance, and buy Reysas at 2-3% of liquidation value; Guy refused to buy anything in Turkey even after visiting Istanbul. _[Guy Spier, Nestle, Ferrari, American Express, MasterCard, Reysas]_ — [2023-10-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jZKOk-hlo8I)
- **Studying disconfirming evidence from smart investors turned his hatred of the auto business into a Fiat Chrysler no-brainer.** In 2012 he saw on Dataroma that Ted Weschler and David Einhorn had bought GM and set out to prove them wrong; reading the UAW contract Steve Rattner forced through in 2009 showed Detroit had become one of the best places to build cars. Sergio Marchionne guided to over $5 billion cash flow on a $5 billion market cap and nobody believed him. _[Fiat Chrysler, General Motors, Sergio Marchionne, Ted Weschler, David Einhorn, Steve Rattner, Dataroma]_ — [2023-10-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jZKOk-hlo8I)
- **13F filings of investors you admire are a form of investigative journalism: reverse-engineer why Ackman likes Chipotle or the railroads, then decide whether you agree and whether it is enough of an anomaly.** Often he has no interest in buying or selling, he just wants to understand why that person acted. _[Bill Ackman, Chipotle, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2023-11-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IJwOjG5gwAw)
- **A 'village idiot' who follows Buffett's basic laws of investing should beat most professionals, because mutual funds with hundreds of positions and 80% turnover violate the laws of physics of investing.** He discovered Buffett through a Peter Lynch book ~29 years ago while running an IT services firm, read the Berkshire and partnership letters, and tested the theory by putting $1M into a 10x10 portfolio in 1994-95; by early 2000 it was north of $13M, roughly 70% a year. _[Warren Buffett, Peter Lynch, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2023-11-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0qxxVBKd8CI)
- **Sourcing ideas from smart investors is fine, but remember they are also wrong half the time; Alibaba had wide moats yet fell on the wrong side of the Chinese government in a way no one could forecast five years earlier.** With Reysas he still has no idea when the market will close the discount; you place bets on hopefully conservative assumptions and move on. _[Alibaba, Reysas]_ — [2023-11-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0qxxVBKd8CI)
- **He runs Pabrai Funds without analysts because Buffett and Munger never had any, and because investing is not a team sport: the data set of 50,000 companies is too large for any team anyway, so you need hacks to shrink it.** Buying only the top two or three holdings of 20 admired investors (via Value Investors Club, SumZero, Dataroma) trims the universe to ~60 companies; discarding those outside his circle of competence leaves 10-12, which one person can handle. His two staff do deep dives and find blind spots but are told not to generate ideas. _[Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2023-12-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=A2vC2skCjCs)

### Circle of competence & checklists (29)

- **Circle of competence is the most important filter; you can get extremely wealthy with a circle an inch wide and a mile deep, and 98-99% of businesses should get a pass.** He passes on all biotech and healthcare, and dislikes defense contractors because a single government customer invites non-market forces. Missing a 100x or 1000x does not matter; avoiding what you do not understand does. — [2023-01-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c7Oyv-Echa0)
- **Take the path less traveled: a large company followed by 20 analysts is unlikely to be widely mispriced, so hunt obscure names.** He could not get his best investor friends to spend five minutes on Reysas ('Turkey, some nano cap'). Exceptions like Microsoft in the 1980s or Walmart in the 1970s would have worked at almost any multiple. _[Reysas, Belridge Oil, Microsoft, Walmart]_ — [2023-01-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c7Oyv-Echa0)
- **The law of large numbers is a mental block that keeps him out of $1-2 trillion market caps, because the death rate of giant businesses over 50-100 years is very high.** He can see nothing hurting Apple for 10 years but cannot make that call for 20-40 years, which buying at $2 trillion requires. Ferrari and Hermes will still be cranking in 20-80 years; LVMH has a much stronger chance of existing in 50 years than Amazon. Berkshire's railroad is an indestructible moat over 100-200 years, and Munger corrected him that its power business is pretty good too. _[Apple, Ferrari, Hermes, LVMH, Amazon, Berkshire Hathaway, BNSF, Charlie Munger]_ — [2023-02-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ncYdcZEnH7E)
- **In Turkey he only looks at businesses whose earnings are in euros or dollars or whose assets have international value, so lira collapse becomes a tailwind rather than a risk.** A Turkish fruit juice exporter with 90-98% of revenue from the EU (free trade under the customs union) sees euro earnings rise as lira costs fall; the baby got thrown out with the bathwater. — [2023-02-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UcJB1m3cXKw)
- **For a constrained US-only student fund, look for anomalies in the $1-2 billion cap range and merger arbitrage like Microsoft-Activision, and mine Value Investors Club and Dataroma rather than looking at Googles.** Running $20-30 million is an advantage because smaller names are more inefficient; a 30-50 position minimum is a handicap, since Buffett told Todd and Ted he wouldn't care if they put everything in one name. After five years and about 20 company visits per trip in Turkey he found only two investments. _[Microsoft, Activision, Value Investors Club, Dataroma, Todd Combs, Ted Weschler]_ — [2023-02-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UcJB1m3cXKw)
- **The size of your circle of competence is irrelevant; never stray outside it, because investing without conviction means you cannot hold through drawdowns or separate signal from noise.** He hates defense (one government client) and US healthcare (no market forces); Moderna might be a home run but it is outside his circle, and envy of a neighbor who got rich on Salesforce is pointless. John Arrillaga became a multi-billionaire investing only in real estate within two miles of Stanford, loading up in pessimism and unloading in euphoria. Entrepreneurs like Sam Walton succeed by being an inch wide and a mile deep; the circle expands naturally over time. _[John Arrillaga, Sam Walton, Moderna, Salesforce, Stanford]_ — [2023-03-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=miqfRmUDwFQ)
- **Start your circle of competence with the products you actually buy, because a company that can extract even a dollar from a careful human has a tremendous moat.** A 16-year-old with an Apple phone, Levi's jeans and Nike shoes already understands something about those businesses; very narrow circles are enough. _[Apple, Levi's, Nike]_ — [2023-05-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SP6kKi2nMz4)
- **The small investor has a huge advantage because investing is one of the only disciplines where size is a disadvantage.** Buffett needs to put tens of billions to work, exceeding almost every company's market cap, so his universe is tiny; a small investor can hunt anomalies among smaller names where mispricing is greater, if willing to roll up their sleeves. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2023-05-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Qgtb7LnvP6Y)
- **Jugaad in investing means cutting a huge data set down to the two, three or four factors that will drive the outcome.** The base path is reading historic annual reports, transcripts, industry and competitor reports; others' write-ups can accelerate learning if weighted correctly. Even then the error rate is 30-50%, and being right half the time while hanging on is fine. — [2023-06-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tYtG7ZvMSjM)
- **A simple rule to defeat the snake-oil salesmen of Wall Street is never to invest in IPOs or in companies with fewer than 5-10 years of public history.** Investors with poor outcomes have only themselves to blame; bankers and underwriters have packaged exciting stories for a hundred years and it is the investor's job to sift through them. — [2023-06-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tYtG7ZvMSjM)
- **Questions like who will win the AI race are too-hard-pile blue-sky thinking; he prefers simpler questions with a higher probability of being right.** After a two-and-a-half-hour dinner beside Bill Gates in Omaha in 2023, playing long/short/neutral on NVIDIA, AMD, Google and Salesforce, he would keep an existing Microsoft investment but as a cheapskate would hesitate to pay a rich price for it today. _[Microsoft, Bill Gates, NVIDIA, AMD, Google, Salesforce]_ — [2023-06-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tYtG7ZvMSjM)
- **Ask five or six competitors which companies in their industry they admire and which are bad; you will quickly learn who is best and worst in ways the numbers do not show.** A tool both Buffett and Munger use. He warns that falling in love with a company makes rationality go away, and that they study the past carefully to understand how the future will unfold. _[Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger]_ — [2023-06-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y0K1qVJdJxc)
- **A bank at a P/E of 0.1 with too much hair is a pass: even extreme cheapness doesn't justify sanctions-violation risk.** The first Turkish company his friend showed him was a large bank facilitating Iran transactions whose executive was jailed at Rikers; Pabrai told him to take it down a notch to at least a P/E of one. _[Halkbank]_ — [2023-07-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HhA8WfnEw9I)
- **Investing is a business with no called strikes: you can let 3,000 balls go and don't need an opinion on Tesla or Bitcoin.** Be an inch wide and a mile deep, like Munger's friend John Arrillaga who only did real estate within a mile of Stanford and died a billionaire. _[John Arrillaga, Tesla, Bitcoin]_ — [2023-07-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HhA8WfnEw9I)
- **Excel-based finance education, CAPM and efficient market theory fill your head with mush; you should detox and never need Excel again.** These models are beautiful to play with in Excel but have nothing to do with how the world works. Very few business schools (Columbia, Florida, Missouri, Jack McDonald at Stanford) teach Buffett's approach, and Harvard has no strong value investing program. — [2023-09-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MDuPszGThmE)
- **Keep a 'Swiss Army Knife' approach: compounders are plan A, but net-nets, merger arbitrage, convertibles and special situations are useful plans B, C and D while you wait.** Buffett's 2023 letter said 12 decisions in 58 years created 80-90% of Berkshire's value out of more than 300 stocks bought, roughly one great decision every five years, so even Buffett needs other tools. _[Warren Buffett, Berkshire Hathaway, GEICO, Coca-Cola, American Express, Burlington Northern, National Indemnity]_ — [2023-09-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kfgbTNWLMJE)
- **The hack for finding compounders: list every brand you spend money on, find which are public, and ask why you chose them over competitors.** Winning even a tiny part of a discerning consumer's spending is a huge accomplishment; as a consumer you already know much without the balance sheet. Peter Lynch advocated this. College students dropped landlines and cable first and used Facebook first, so Notre Dame students have a massive advantage over Buffett in Omaha, who changes nothing. _[McDonald's, Chipotle, Facebook, Peter Lynch]_ — [2023-09-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kfgbTNWLMJE)
- **After reading Pulak Prasad's 'What I Learned About Investing from Darwin' twice, he made leverage a far more important consideration: a business with no debt can play offense in bad times.** Prasad's rule is zero leverage. Pabrai previously would wave through $400-500M of debt on a $5B market cap; now he asks whether the business could run without debt and why it does not eliminate dividends to pay it off. Leverage juices returns but removes resilience; 'to finish first, you must first finish.' _[Pulak Prasad, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2023-10-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w9oC1rPV5yQ)
- **There is no systematic screening approach; idea sourcing is opportunistic, like reading Value Line's lowest-P/E and biggest-13-week-loser lists each week.** In October 2023 he flagged JetBlue at about $4 a share as a raw idea: consolidated industry, packed planes, pricing power, aircraft shortages from Boeing's troubles, though the Spirit deal and long-haul mix need digging. _[JetBlue, Southwest, Spirit Airlines, Value Line]_ — [2023-10-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jZKOk-hlo8I)
- **Don't use Excel: people calculate too much and think too little, and any real investment thesis should be explainable to a 10-year-old in five or six sentences.** For Level 3 bonds the only question was whether three coupons would be paid; Excel adds nothing but hocus pocus. A simple mental model becomes your North Star for filtering the noise that arrives after you invest. Pulak Prasad's rules of no leverage, no models, no projections also work. _[Pulak Prasad, Level 3 Communications, IPSCO, Reysas, JetBlue]_ — [2023-10-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jZKOk-hlo8I)
- **Before buying, the thesis must be explainable to a nine-year-old in four or five sentences - not a spreadsheet - and if those sentences stop being true, move on.** You only start learning a business after you own it; when it drops 50% you become an expert. Don't use the stock price to guide decisions, but within two or three years the writing on the real economics should be on the wall. — [2023-10-17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EzMWPRx9-CY)
- **Tune out macro, interest rates and economic growth forecasts entirely and focus on individual businesses within your circle of competence that are anomalies in the right direction.** The first question for any business is 'is it within my circle of competence?'; there is no point wasting time on questions nobody can answer. — [2023-11-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IJwOjG5gwAw)
- **The job description is reading and thinking, and you can sometimes proactively cause anomalies to show up, as when Turkey screened extremely cheap on P/E and price-to-book in 2018 and he went to visit his friend's portfolio companies.** His Turkish friend is a hardcore Ben Graham disciple he is trying to convert toward Munger; the 2018 trip was planned as a week of great dining and learning with no intention to invest. — [2023-11-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IJwOjG5gwAw)
- **Value Line's weekly lists of lowest P/Es, biggest 13-week losers, widest discounts to book and highest yields take under five minutes a week to scan and surface anomalies.** Over 20 years ago it flagged two funeral services companies at a P/E of 2; he bought at $2 a share and it was $10 about a year later, in and out within 12-18 months. _[Value Line]_ — [2023-11-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IJwOjG5gwAw)
- **Don't try to expand your circle of competence; it widens naturally by osmosis through curiosity and worldly wisdom, and the size of the circle is not correlated with investment success.** Start with products and services you already consume. Successful entrepreneurs often know nothing beyond their own industry and still do very well. _[Charlie Munger]_ — [2023-11-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0qxxVBKd8CI)
- **It is better to be an inch wide and a mile deep than a mile wide and an inch deep; the Arrillaga model of one rich rabbit hole is the model to follow.** John Arrillaga became a billionaire investing only in real estate within a mile of the Stanford campus, knowing every building's rents and value, selling in euphoria and buying back in pessimism. Nick Sleep and Qais similarly went deep into the Amazon rabbit hole after just reading annual reports. _[John Arrillaga, Nick Sleep, Amazon]_ — [2023-11-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0qxxVBKd8CI)
- **In a market with madness like Turkey, use one simple filter: buy the highest-quality business with the highest-quality management whatever the price, rather than the cheapest P/E.** In India you must compromise on business, management or governance quality to get a normal multiple; in Turkey you don't have to. He tells his Ben Graham-disciple friend Hayder to choose the 3x P/E business with better management over the 2x one. _[Anadolu Efes, Coca-Cola Icecek, TAV Airports]_ — [2023-12-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=A2vC2skCjCs)
- **In Turkey he filters out the 97-98% of businesses that high inflation would hurt within seconds, then hunts for the babies thrown out with the bathwater.** TAV's euro revenue and lira wages meant inflation actually helped it; CCI had 60-70% of business outside Turkey and Coke can always reprice, so neither volumes nor margins dropped. _[TAV Airports, Coca-Cola Icecek]_ — [2023-12-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=A2vC2skCjCs)
- **When meeting a company for the first time, the only goal is to build a picture in your head of how the business works and whether it is easy for you to understand.** For a Coke bottler you know the royalty, the capex, and that a strong brand creates pull once distribution exists, and there are bottler models worldwide showing what returns to expect. _[Coca-Cola Icecek]_ — [2023-12-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=A2vC2skCjCs)

### Valuation & margin of safety (25)

- **Auction-driven public markets overshoot and undershoot far more than the underlying asset changes, and that mispricing is what pays the bills.** A 10-crore Gurgaon apartment is quoted at 10 crores every day by a broker, but if listed its market cap would swing from 60 to 120 crores over a year; you can sometimes buy 100 crores of assets for 70 crores. — [2023-01-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5P1c9bhhYPo)
- **A simple path to a 100-bagger is buying a company that never grows at 1% of liquidation value.** If something worth $1B can be bought for $10M and the value holds, you have a 100x; not facetious, since Belridge and Reysas were exactly that kind of situation. _[Belridge Oil, Reysas]_ — [2023-01-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c7Oyv-Echa0)
- **Be very unreasonable about price: with 50,000 companies you can find 50%, 75%, 90% or even 95% off, and if you make 8-10 such bets and half fail you still do spectacularly.** If you truly understand a company you by definition know what it is worth; then demand a large delta to market price and wait for seven moons to line up. — [2023-01-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c7Oyv-Echa0)
- **Thou shall never use Excel: if you reach for a spreadsheet you do not have a Belridge or a Reysas; it should hit you over the head on first read that it is worth 10x the price.** Fine-tuning work may follow, but the no-brainer quality must be blindingly obvious up front. _[Belridge Oil, Reysas]_ — [2023-01-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c7Oyv-Echa0)
- **Valuation should be a no-brainer that needs no Excel: Reysas traded at less than 3% of liquidation value, a straight 30x even if liquidation value never grew, while reinvesting at 25-35% a year in dollars.** Turkey was the cheapest market he had ever screened, with 80% inflation and local investors whose average holding period is six hours. 12 million square feet at $80 replacement value is about $960 million, less $200 million debt, versus a $16-20 million market cap; tenants include Amazon, Carrefour, Ikea, Toyota, Mercedes and DuPont on 99% leased inflation-indexed leases. He got a third of the company for $7-8 million (about 1-1.5% of AUM); it is now a $350 million market cap and 25-30% of the portfolio, with liquidation value near $1.5 billion. _[Reysas, Turkey, Amazon, Ikea, Toyota, Mercedes, DuPont, Carrefour]_ — [2023-03-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=miqfRmUDwFQ)
- **Practice anomaly-based investing: invest in things that make no sense, because if it makes sense, don't invest in it; that is where you get a shot at greatness.** He cites Mark Twain: truth is stranger than fiction because fiction must make sense. Excel cannot make sense of something that does not make sense, and he jokes about an AA program for Excel addiction. He expects God gives him only one Reysas in a lifetime. _[Reysas, Mark Twain]_ — [2023-03-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=miqfRmUDwFQ)
- **The best approach is anomaly-based investing: look for things that make no sense and pass unless you are astonished.** Auction-driven markets throw up astonishing mispricings occasionally, not every year, but you only need one Titan, one Coke bottler, one Blue Dart. _[Titan, Blue Dart]_ — [2023-04-11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ibsxgKdJNpA)
- **Stick to auction-driven stock markets because they are the only asset class that gets depressed and euphoric enough to create mispricings.** A Mumbai flat appraised daily varies between 6 and 7 crores in a year, but inside a listed company it would trade between 3 and 9; private equity faces an intelligent seller and gets an intelligent price. The Turkish owners would have laughed at $25 million for the whole business, yet 30% was available in the market at that price. Gold and whole businesses don't offer this. _[Reysas]_ — [2023-04-11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ibsxgKdJNpA)
- **Avoid mega caps — at $100-300 billion the runway is in question, so I look for much smaller businesses with room to grow.** Alibaba was an exception that didn't help him; Apple going from $200 billion to $2.5 trillion happens, but such cases are few and far between and even a double from mega-cap size may not be easy. _[Alibaba, Apple]_ — [2023-04-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DtQVYvyO4Qg)
- **Value comes in many shapes — sometimes a mediocre business at 2x earnings worth 10x, sometimes a great business at a very high multiple that turns out even better.** Optically cheap stocks work if operations are stable or growing; Amazon-type stocks work because the multiple is not what it appears. _[Amazon]_ — [2023-05-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Qgtb7LnvP6Y)
- **In investing and in life, look for anomalies — Li Lu, Munger, Buffett and Amazon are all anomalies.** Be a student of business, be patient, and look for something that stands out and the market doesn't understand; out of thousands of listed companies you are looking for 2-4, one at a time. It's a treasure hunt. _[Li Lu, Amazon]_ — [2023-05-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Qgtb7LnvP6Y)
- **The law of large numbers is a real headwind for mega-caps like Tencent and Maotai: it is almost impossible for them to become 10x larger in a few years, so a smaller business can be the better investment.** Apple hovers around $3 trillion and $4 trillion market caps do not exist; there used to be no businesses above $500-600B. A small pool of capital can find companies that become 10, 20 or 50 times larger, while mega-caps are like aircraft carriers that are hard to navigate. _[Tencent, Kweichow Moutai, Apple]_ — [2023-06-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y0K1qVJdJxc)
- **In value investing the very first thing is downside protection; you don't even look at the upside until you have looked at the downside.** Like the barber who scrounges to keep risk down rather than signing a fancy lease, investors look for free lunches where downside is near zero and upside is massive. Auction-driven markets overshoot and undershoot, so hated and unloved things get mispriced in the right direction; 'we don't need to go buy Nvidia'. _[Nvidia]_ — [2023-09-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MDuPszGThmE)
- **If you are buying assets at pennies on the dollar you should not need leverage; avoid leverage in life and prefer businesses with zero debt so they can play offense in downturns.** Something at one-fifth of liquidation value gives great returns unlevered, and levered thinking clouds judgment. He recommends Pulak Prasad's 2023 book 'What I Learned About Investing from Darwin': Prasad's fund and all its portfolio companies carry zero leverage because leveraged businesses lose optionality in downturns. Non-recourse structures are the only acceptable exception when starting out. _[Pulak Prasad]_ — [2023-09-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MDuPszGThmE)
- **When a net-net basket has one winner and two laggards, do not rebalance mechanically; peel the onion to see if the laggards are structurally broken or melting ice cubes.** Small amounts of capital can do well in these 'Mickey Mouse games' on the side, but always keep an eye out for compounders. — [2023-09-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kfgbTNWLMJE)
- **Ben Graham's framework is bedrock, but far more money is made owning businesses that grow dramatically in value than buying static businesses at 40 cents on the dollar.** A business bought at 40 cents that never grows might return 2-3x, while paying 60-70 cents for one growing 10-20% a year is vastly superior and far more tax efficient because you are not paying Uncle Sam on every sale. _[Ben Graham]_ — [2023-10-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w9oC1rPV5yQ)
- **He has also adopted Prasad's practice of making no earnings or cash flow projections, since stacking four or five assumptions each off by 20% produces garbage.** Prasad's Nalanda buys and holds forever, treats every sale as a mistake, and publishes its entire portfolio including exits. If the holding period is forever, 'why are we messing around with DCFs?' _[Pulak Prasad]_ — [2023-10-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w9oC1rPV5yQ)
- **In 58 years only about 12 decisions built Berkshire, so the name of the game is finding rare anomalies, not merely cheap stocks.** Something worth $20 trading at $14 and growing 5-10% a year will not move the needle; per Buffett's 2022 letter, the dozen needle-movers include Ajit Jain, Washington Post, Amex, Coke, MidAmerican, BNSF and National Indemnity. In the last 10 years Apple and Japan stand out. _[Berkshire Hathaway, Apple, Washington Post, American Express, Coca-Cola, BNSF, National Indemnity, MidAmerican]_ — [2023-10-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jZKOk-hlo8I)
- **Wall Street confuses risk with uncertainty and punishes uncertain situations, so low-risk, high-uncertainty setups are where the mispricing lives.** Level 3 convertible bonds traded at 20 cents on the dollar with a 6% coupon in 2001-2002 while the balance sheet could pay interest for three years; Pabrai put 10% of his roughly $10 million fund in them, got his principal back in coupons and eventually a 5x when the bonds paid off at par. _[Level 3 Communications, Walter Scott Jr., Peter Kiewit and Sons]_ — [2023-10-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jZKOk-hlo8I)
- **A great, predictable business like ADP is of no interest because it is priced to perfection, whereas an unpredictable business like Exxon can be valued off a floor if you have an edge.** Twenty analysts would get within 5% of ADP's earnings, so there is no distress. For Exxon, if cost curves let you believe oil will not average below $60 for three years, you can build a floor valuation and buy when market cap is far below it, with upside if oil spikes. _[ADP, Exxon]_ — [2023-10-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jZKOk-hlo8I)
- **Most of the time the market is right that cheap things are cheap for good reason, so a high-conviction contrarian view will be rare, but even a 50% error rate works out fine.** Capitalism is brutal and almost everything declines eventually; he would not bet Apple's franchise is intact in 20 years even though it looks bulletproof for 10. Dig into hated industries from a learning perspective, and occasionally you find a rich vein like the 10x from the 'stupid auto business'. _[Apple, Fiat Chrysler, Ferrari]_ — [2023-10-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jZKOk-hlo8I)
- **Auction-driven markets can swing to extremes in both directions, unlike negotiated sales of homes or whole businesses, and the only time to act is when pricing is so extreme it makes no sense.** Euphoric bubble pricing means take a pass; extreme cheapness is when to act. If someone says Apple at $150 is worth $180-250 that is not an anomaly; if it's worth $1,000 and trades at $200, take a look. _[Apple]_ — [2023-11-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IJwOjG5gwAw)
- **Use Munger-style inversion to sanity-check growth assumptions: Varun Beverages compounding volume at 15% forever implies 700 servings per capita in India, which no comparable country supports.** Varun has ~900 million cases, $2B revenue, $250M net income and ~$16B market cap; his base case of 15% then 10% then 8% growth yields only ~1.3-3.2% annualized plus dividends. US is ~1,400 servings per capita, Saudi ~885, UK ~700, China ~337, while India is under 100 today. _[Varun Beverages, PepsiCo, Coca-Cola]_ — [2023-12-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=A2vC2skCjCs)
- **Great businesses bought at too high a price can produce zero returns for over a decade: Microsoft returned nothing from 1999 to 2015 and Coca-Cola nothing from 1998 to 2011.** Microsoft in 1999 had $22B revenue, $8-9B net income, a $600B market cap and a trailing P/E above 70; 16 years later revenue was 4x and the market cap half. Coke traded at 62x in 1998 and doubled its business by 2011 with shrinking market cap. Buffett: you pay a very high price for a cheery consensus. _[Microsoft, Coca-Cola, Warren Buffett]_ — [2023-12-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=A2vC2skCjCs)
- **The Kelly formula does not belong in value investing because you never get to make a thousand bets with known odds; if he rewrote The Dhandho Investor he would remove it.** John Burr Williams' intrinsic value definition is timeless, but the right approach is to never run a DCF and only act when the value is so obvious it needs no calculation, as with Reysas and TAV; Munger says he never saw Buffett run a DCF. _[Reysas, TAV Airports, Charlie Munger, Warren Buffett]_ — [2023-12-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=A2vC2skCjCs)

### Portfolio concentration & selling (30)

- **You only need one Reysas, not ten; his 2023 resolution is to deeply study 50 businesses in hopes of finding one.** Most candidates are discarded in five minutes; only those with high ROE, a runway and great management that survive two or three hours of screening count toward the 50. By January 10 he had studied and rejected one. _[Reysas]_ — [2023-01-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5P1c9bhhYPo)
- **Reysas was too small to become the 10% position he wanted, so he bought a third of the company for $7-8 million when the market cap was $16 million.** The fund managed ~$700 million; after the earthquake the market cap is $250-300 million against liquidation value now north of $1.5 billion, so it has moved from 2% to 20-25% of liquidation value. The lira went from 5 to ~19 per dollar (a 75% loss) yet the stock is up ~16x in dollars over 3.5 years. _[Reysas]_ — [2023-02-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ncYdcZEnH7E)
- **He will not lighten up even if two Turkish stocks reach 80% of his offshore fund; investors who dislike it can get off the bus.** Reysas and TAV Airports collectively make up about half the closed offshore fund through appreciation. He cites the Waltons, who keep 90%+ of their wealth in Walmart without controlling it and are perfectly comfortable. _[Reysas, TAV Airports, Walmart, Walton family]_ — [2023-02-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ncYdcZEnH7E)
- **Per Phil Fisher, if the job is done right every sell decision is a mistake; selling is much harder than buying and you can be sloppy on selling as long as you keep the crown jewels intact.** Chuck Akre's fund has about 1% annual turnover versus 70-80% for typical mutual funds. Sell candidates are only cases where you misjudged the moat, runway or future of the business. _[Phil Fisher, Chuck Akre]_ — [2023-02-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UcJB1m3cXKw)
- **You do not really know a business until you own it, and your analysis becomes amazing only after it drops 40%, so structure the portfolio as concentric circles with the rare tremendous business at the center and lower-conviction bets in outer rings.** The innermost circle needs a tremendous business with a long growth runway, high returns on equity without leverage, the ability to reinvest at high rates, and a modest price; the modest price is the deal killer and why Munger says fish where the fish are. He urged the students to sort their inherited portfolio into these circles. _[Titan Industries, Rakesh Jhunjhunwala, Charlie Munger]_ — [2023-03-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=miqfRmUDwFQ)
- **The tension of investing is circling the wagons around your crown jewel while creative destruction can still decimate it, so you must separate normal cyclicality from secular decline and only move the wagons when convinced the decline is permanent.** Be a little sloppy and careful on selling rather than trigger-happy to avoid reacting to noise; as Charlie says, why should it be easy to get rich? He applied the same signal-versus-noise test to Anheuser-Busch and shifting tastes toward hard seltzers. _[Anheuser-Busch, Charlie Munger]_ — [2023-03-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=miqfRmUDwFQ)
- **Sell a great business only when the valuation is a no-brainer egregious, when no rose-colored glasses could justify it; if you are confused, it is not yet time to sell.** Satyam Computers, bought in 1994 for about $10,000 (1% of his portfolio) when its Hyderabad real estate exceeded the business value and it was growing 70% a year, went from 40 rupees to 7,000 rupees, 150x in dollars, by early 2000; he sold within 10% of the peak for about $1.5 million and it dropped 85% nine months later. It was his first 100-bagger; he has had two so far and Reysas may be the third. _[Satyam Computers, Reysas]_ — [2023-03-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=miqfRmUDwFQ)
- **Selling is harder than buying; be extremely reluctant to sell and only sell when the valuation is egregious, not merely overpriced.** He has made more selling mistakes than buying mistakes. If a business earning $1 million bought for $8 million reaches $200 million, it should not have been sold at $30-50 million; past $100-150 million you can let it go. You can be sloppy and slow on selling — it's a great way to make your broker starve. Separate signal from noise: bad quarters are noise, but lost integrity, competitors eating their lunch, loss of low-cost position or secular decline are real signals. — [2023-04-11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ibsxgKdJNpA)
- **Circle the wagons: put your crown jewels in the center and protect them — the framework only works if you never touch the great compounders.** Named after 19th-century frontier settlers' defensive formation. Three recognitions: we will make many mistakes, this is a very forgiving business where you can be wrong 98% of the time, but only if you buy great economics at reasonable prices and hold forever — not selling when fully priced or overpriced, only possibly when egregiously overpriced. _[See's Candies, American Express, Coca-Cola, Berkshire Hathaway, Naspers]_ — [2023-04-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DtQVYvyO4Qg)
- **It's hard to beat the market without this framework because you'll be cutting the flowers and watering the weeds — watering weeds is fine, just don't cut the flowers.** The index outperforms most managers because it is too dumb to sell Amazon or Alphabet. Great businesses at small multiples are rare, which is why he hangs out in Istanbul — go fishing where the fish are. _[Amazon, Alphabet, Turkey]_ — [2023-04-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DtQVYvyO4Qg)
- **Berkshire put a quarter of book value into Coke in 1988 and never sold at the 1998 nosebleed valuation; even so, the full-period result is 12% versus 10.5% for the index, which leaves him genuinely unsure whether keeping Coke was right.** Coke returned 32% annualized from 1988-98 and only 4% a year since; Buffett has said in hindsight he should have sold in 1999-2000. _[Coca-Cola, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2023-05-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SP6kKi2nMz4)
- **Do not sell when things appear fully priced because great businesses surprise on the upside; selling may make sense only when egregiously overpriced, and he admits he can't tell where that line is.** Applying this a single great business could become 60-99% of a portfolio as with Naspers; Naspers and Buffett could tolerate it because Tencent and Berkshire are internally diversified. _[Naspers, Tencent, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2023-05-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SP6kKi2nMz4)
- **When you find yourself owning a fraction of a great business, pretty much never sell it unless the price is extreme, egregious and crazy.** His biggest recurring mistake has been selling very good businesses because they appeared overvalued. Ferrari, bought in 2012 via a company that owned it at an effective price under $15, is now over $300 (20x+ in 11 years); selling Ferrari and Maotai, both iconic one-of-a-kind companies, are among his biggest regrets despite making a lot of money on both. _[Ferrari, Kweichow Moutai]_ — [2023-06-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y0K1qVJdJxc)
- **The index does so well because it is too dumb to sell Microsoft, Google or Facebook, while mutual funds go in and out of stocks all the time.** The S&P only throws out a company when it is so long in the tooth that it's obvious; our views of what a business looks like in 5-15 years are usually wrong, so you must hold both the wrongs and the rights for a very long time to collect the fruits. _[Microsoft, Google, Facebook]_ — [2023-07-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HhA8WfnEw9I)
- **A simple '10 by 10' portfolio, about ten stocks at one-tenth of assets each held until they reach intrinsic value, works because investing is forgiving even if you are wrong half the time.** This was his personal approach from 1994 to 1999, investing only in public markets and waiting for positions to reach intrinsic value. — [2023-09-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MDuPszGThmE)
- **Owners of private businesses hold 90-95% of their net worth in one illiquid company and are perfectly comfortable, so in public markets going beyond roughly 5-10 stocks only hurts you.** You will not know the 11th business as well as your second-best business, so why buy the 11th instead of more of the second. He held more than 90-95% of his own net worth in his third startup for a long time, like the Chinese-restaurant couple or the barber. — [2023-09-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MDuPszGThmE)
- **Never selling winners is how the Davis family got rich: 98% of Grandfather Davis's insurance portfolio did nothing, but the 2% in AIG became 95% of the pie.** Davis bought a gazillion mostly mediocre insurance companies in the 1930s and never sold anything; AIG, bought when it was a tiny Shanghai insurer, grew north of a $100 billion market cap. Chris Davis, the third generation, now sits on Berkshire's board. _[AIG, Chris Davis]_ — [2023-09-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MDuPszGThmE)
- **Do not sell a great compounder when it is 20-30% overvalued; sell only when overvaluation is egregious, which becomes obvious when it happens.** Great compounders are rare and intrinsic value is error-prone: Amazon always looked optically overvalued because reinvestment depressed earnings and no one could see AWS before it surfaced. Microsoft's only clear sell point in 40 years was around 2000 at a $600 billion valuation. Amazon at $1.3 trillion would not bother him at $2-2.5 trillion. _[Amazon, AWS, Microsoft]_ — [2023-09-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kfgbTNWLMJE)
- **A Swiss Army Knife approach is best: buy cheap, stable anomalies when no obvious great business is available, but hold great businesses with long runways for dear life.** There are only so many great ideas one finds in a lifetime, so the rare great business must not be sold at a Graham-style intrinsic value target. — [2023-10-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w9oC1rPV5yQ)
- **Diversification benefits fall off fast: 4-5 positions in different industries is already diversified, 10 is significant, and going to 20-50 hurts you because you no longer know the businesses.** Staying narrow keeps you at the epicenter of your circle of competence; not knowing businesses well is itself a risk even in a diversified portfolio. — [2023-10-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w9oC1rPV5yQ)
- **Any number multiplied by zero is zero, so avoid ruin, but trimming a great, not-overpriced business just because it exceeds 25% of the portfolio is a big sin.** The Waltons have held Walmart at 90-95% of their assets for decades with no Walton running it; most wealthy founders are undiversified. Great opportunities are rare; anything you replace them with triggers a tax bill and is likely inferior. _[Walmart, Walton family]_ — [2023-10-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w9oC1rPV5yQ)
- **Selling Ferrari is one of his deepest regrets: when you find yourself owning a great business, don't sell it.** Fiat Chrysler had a market cap under $6 billion on $135 billion of revenue in 2012; Ferrari came out at about $16 a share and is now $310, nearly 20x. His roughly $20 million Ferrari stake would be about $400 million today against total fund assets of about $750 million. Guy Spier kept it. _[Ferrari, Fiat Chrysler, Guy Spier, John Elkann, Nestle]_ — [2023-10-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jZKOk-hlo8I)
- **Returns come from a roughly 4% hit rate: Buffett says only 12 of his 300-plus decisions in 58 years at Berkshire were spectacular, and his own 13x came from two 100-baggers.** A $100,000 position became $9-10 million and a $10,000 overseas bet became $1.5 million (150x); without those two, $1 million would have become only $2-3 million. The other 296 Berkshire decisions weren't losers, they just didn't move the needle. _[Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2023-10-17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EzMWPRx9-CY)
- **Of roughly 50,000 stocks worldwide, 99%-plus are either not understandable or too expensive, so the main job is saying no; finding one or two yeses a year is awesome.** Even one stock a year is just fine. — [2023-11-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IJwOjG5gwAw)
- **Munger's Peoria test: one-third each in the Ford dealership, the McDonald's franchise and the best apartment building in Peoria is an extremely well-diversified portfolio, and beyond about ten stocks diversification has diminishing returns.** The 11th business will be less well understood than the second, and going from 10 to 50 stocks gains little. He caps positions at 10% of cost but never trims winners. _[Charlie Munger]_ — [2023-11-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IJwOjG5gwAw)
- **Three Turkish bets make up 65-70% of one of his funds: Reysas, the dominant Coke bottler in Turkey that bottles in about 12 countries, and an airport operator running about 15 airports.** The $8 million Reysas stake grew to about $150 million and remains untrimmed because liquidation value implies $400-450 million for his share; a Coke or Pepsi bottler almost anywhere is a license to print money, and the airport operator is a monopoly-type business. He views these as his three Peoria businesses. _[Reysas, Coca-Cola Icecek, TAV Airports]_ — [2023-11-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IJwOjG5gwAw)
- **Stay as close to the center of your circle of competence as possible and don't over-concentrate: eight or ten stocks is fine, three may not be.** Because zeros will happen even with techniques to reduce them, the portfolio should be able to absorb a total loss in any one position. — [2023-11-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0qxxVBKd8CI)
- **Selling a great business because it doubled is a mistake; his friend Hayder sold Reysas at a $40M market cap despite an $800M liquidation value because he is a 'one-bagger guy'.** Pabrai sent him a bust of Charlie Munger to recite quotes before work each day; Hayder has since moved from selling at 2x to being willing to hold to 2.5x. _[Reysas, Charlie Munger]_ — [2023-12-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=A2vC2skCjCs)
- **Position sizing is simple: aim for a 10x10 portfolio with 10% bets, and never trim a position just because it has grown large.** Reysas could only be a ~1% bet ($8M of $700M) because of its $16M market cap, but it is now ~40% of one fund (~$100M of $270M); he reminds investors quarterly that he will not trim while it sits at roughly one-third of intrinsic value and could be worth $4-5B in 5-10 years. Efes and TAV were large enough for full 10% positions. _[Reysas, Anadolu Efes, TAV Airports]_ — [2023-12-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=A2vC2skCjCs)
- **Selling is much harder than buying, and if you own a great business with a big gain it is usually a mistake to sell on valuation alone; give it a lot of rope.** Many of his biggest mistakes were money left on the table by selling good businesses that looked optically expensive. Varun has tailwinds because Pepsi loves them and will hand them more geographies. _[Varun Beverages]_ — [2023-12-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=A2vC2skCjCs)

### Compounding & long-term holding (31)

- **You don't need to be right often; wait for the seven moons to line up and swing hard, as Rakesh Jhunjhunwala did with Titan.** Jhunjhunwala traded rapidly on four screens yet held Titan untouched for 25+ years; it grew from ~4% of his portfolio to a multi-billion-dollar position that would have been half his wealth even if the other 96% went to zero. He loved the Tatas' governance and just did nothing. _[Rakesh Jhunjhunwala, Titan, Tata]_ — [2023-01-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5P1c9bhhYPo)
- **Value investors have no information edge and rarely an analytic edge; the strongest edge is time horizon.** Bezos said Amazon gained an edge by looking out 5-10 years while competitors looked 1-3. The index is too dumb to know it owns Microsoft or Alphabet and too dumb to sell, holding them 20-30 years, which is why it does so well. _[Jeff Bezos, Amazon, Microsoft, Alphabet, S&P 500, General Electric]_ — [2023-01-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c7Oyv-Echa0)
- **The second route to a 100-bagger, identifying a great compounder and paying a reasonable or even expensive-looking price, is a harder game for him personally, though he is open to both.** With a crystal ball for 30-50 years a $1B market cap could become $200B; the cheap-asset game is a tad easier because auction markets and fear/greed oscillation deliver it. — [2023-01-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c7Oyv-Echa0)
- **Think of yourself as a minority owner of a great business and don't sell when it is fully priced or even overpriced, only when egregiously overpriced.** If Walmart went to 100x normalized earnings the family might sell, but at 20x, 30x or 40x do nothing. Fewer than 3-5% of listed companies qualify as great businesses; if you own a fraction of one, hang on for dear life. _[Walmart]_ — [2023-02-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ncYdcZEnH7E)
- **Investing is a very forgiving business: 96% of a portfolio can go to zero and you still do fine as long as you never touch the one crown jewel.** Rakesh Jhunjhunwala started with a couple hundred dollars, died at 62 with about $7 billion, and half of that was Titan Industries, a 4% position he put on 27-28 years earlier and never touched despite being a hyperactive trader elsewhere. _[Rakesh Jhunjhunwala, Titan Industries]_ — [2023-02-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UcJB1m3cXKw)
- **Investing is a very forgiving business: if you bought the Nifty 50 at its 1970s peak and 49 of 50 went to zero but you never touched Walmart, you still beat the S&P by about four points a year.** The Nifty 50 (McDonald's, P&G, Xerox, Kodak, IBM) was 'taken out back and shot' in 1973-74, but $2 of $100 left in Walmart for 50 years beats the index; the catch is nobody except the Walton family held Walmart the whole 50 years. Templeton said the best manager is wrong one in three times, probably half. _[Walmart, Nifty 50, Walton family, John Templeton, McDonald's, Procter & Gamble, Xerox, Kodak, IBM]_ — [2023-03-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=miqfRmUDwFQ)
- **When you own a fraction of a great business, just sit on your ass — selling Kotak and Blue Dart cost me 300-500x.** He sold his flat-for-five-years Kotak and Blue Dart positions in 2000 to recover $10,000; Kotak went up ~500x and Blue Dart 300-400x. One 'fake' Blue Dart certificate of 100 shares he kept for 15 years sold for 8-9 lakhs. _[Kotak Mahindra, Blue Dart, Sky Pack, Charlie Munger]_ — [2023-04-11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ibsxgKdJNpA)
- **Rakesh Jhunjhunwala only had to get one thing right — buying Titan in 2003 and, more importantly, holding it.** Jhunjhunwala started with $400 at 25 and died with $5.8 billion; his 4% position in Titan (about $3.4 million) grew to more than $2 billion with dividends. Investing is a very forgiving business. _[Rakesh Jhunjhunwala, Titan]_ — [2023-04-11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ibsxgKdJNpA)
- **Compounding is driven by three factors — starting capital, rate of return and runway — and a long runway alone makes a monthly SIP into an index fund astonishing.** You don't need to be a stock picker or find an advisor; just buy a midcap or small-cap index early, keep a savings rate and let the eighth wonder of the world work. — [2023-04-11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ibsxgKdJNpA)
- **If 49 of the Nifty 50 went to zero and you just held Walmart from its 1970 IPO, you would still have beaten the S&P — one held decision has outsized impact.** A 2% Walmart weight alone yields ~13.3% annualized versus 10.3% for the S&P over 52 years. Even buying the Nifty 50 without Walmart at the 1972 peak and holding through the 50% crash of 1973-74 returned 10.2% versus 10.3% — but everyone had exited by 1975. _[Nifty Fifty, Walmart, McDonald's, Coca-Cola, Procter & Gamble, Polaroid, Xerox, Kodak, Burroughs]_ — [2023-04-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DtQVYvyO4Qg)
- **Rakesh Jhunjhunwala's $3.4 million Titan bet in 2003 alone became $1.4 billion — a 400x return that would have carried him even if everything else went to zero.** He started with $400 at 25 and died at 62 with $5.8 billion, all passive investing; Titan was 4% of his $85 million portfolio, a little over 5% of the company, and his widow still holds it. Nick Sleep's record is similarly ordinary without Amazon and exceptional with it. _[Rakesh Jhunjhunwala, Titan, Nick Sleep, Amazon]_ — [2023-04-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DtQVYvyO4Qg)
- **The important thing was not buying the 12 winners but keeping all 300 decisions; investing is very forgiving if you don't cut the flowers and water the weeds.** With just those dozen decisions Berkshire produced almost 4,000,000% versus a small fraction of that for the S&P; Michael Goldberg, who hired Ajit, still gets $1 million a year from Berkshire decades later because it's still a great deal. _[Berkshire Hathaway, Michael Goldberg]_ — [2023-05-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SP6kKi2nMz4)
- **The Nifty 50 bought at peak 1972 valuations, with many zeros and no price discipline, still returned 10.2% annualized versus 10.3% for the S&P, and with Walmart at 2% and the other 98% at zero you'd have compounded 13%.** In 1972 Xerox was 49x, Avon 65x and Polaroid 91x trailing earnings and they fell 71%, 86% and 91% before eventually going to zero; the group halved in 1973-74 and by 1975 everyone had abandoned it. _[Nifty 50, Walmart, Xerox, Avon, Polaroid, McDonald's, Disney]_ — [2023-05-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SP6kKi2nMz4)
- **Three key lessons: the error rate will be huge, hold great businesses for dear life, and do not pay fancy prices for great businesses.** If Warren and Charlie have big errors, mere mortals will have bigger ones; focus on great businesses with great people and long runways, as with Titan, Coke, Amex, GEICO, Amazon, Tencent and Ajit Jain, whose ~$20 million bonus Buffett feels is missing a zero. _[Ajit Jain, Greg Abel]_ — [2023-05-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SP6kKi2nMz4)
- **Of the three compounding variables (starting capital, rate of return, runway), the runway is the one we control most, so prioritize longevity.** At 7% money doubles in 10 years, at 10% in seven; Buffett became a billionaire at 56 and ~99% of his wealth came in the last three decades, so his wish is to live as long as possible to keep compounding. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2023-05-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SP6kKi2nMz4)
- **Indexing is a wise choice for someone who can't pick wagons: it circles 500 great wagons that surely include the Walmarts and Costcos, and savings rate plus a long runway will take care of the rest.** Given to a questioner seeking an upper-middle-class retirement; he stressed savings rate and a healthy lifestyle over stock selection. _[Walmart, Costco]_ — [2023-05-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SP6kKi2nMz4)
- **The surest way to build a nest egg is to spend less than you earn and put the savings into mid-cap and small-cap index funds.** Control the savings rate, improve your skills and income, and you can reach $100,000 in 10-15 years or less without taking much risk. — [2023-05-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Qgtb7LnvP6Y)
- **Three things make even modest earners very wealthy: spend less than you earn, put savings in a low-cost index fund, and start as early as possible for the longest runway.** Munger says consistently spending 5% more than you earn gives a life of misery while spending 5-10% less gives a bountiful life; decades later you will have left your peers far behind. He wishes this were core high school curriculum. _[Charlie Munger]_ — [2023-06-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tYtG7ZvMSjM)
- **Chinese investors' high math skills lead to too much gambling and trading in the stock market; instead study businesses, find the great ones, buy them at reasonable prices and never ever sell them.** His closing advice to Chinese readers, echoing his Maotai and Ferrari regrets. — [2023-06-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y0K1qVJdJxc)
- **The most important thing to teach 9th or 10th graders is the logarithmic power of compounding and the rule of 72.** At 10% a year money doubles every seven years, so an 18-year-old with a 70-year runway gets close to 10 doubles (1024x): $1,000 saved at 18 becomes a million; spend less than you earn, put it in a compounding engine and don't mess with it. — [2023-07-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HhA8WfnEw9I)
- **Retirement savings should be opt-out, automatic into an index fund, with no loans or withdrawals, because it is too easy to shut off the engine.** People cash out 401ks when they leave jobs, pay the penalty and end up with $40-100K at 70 when it should be millions; nobody explains the logarithmic nature of compounding even when people enroll. — [2023-07-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HhA8WfnEw9I)
- **Even Warren Buffett made most of his money on about 4% of his bets, so investing is an art that tolerates a very high error rate only if you hold high-conviction winners for a very long time.** He realized this from Buffett's 2023 letter: one in 25 bets moved the needle; Shelby Davis's dynasty made 80-90% of its fortune from AIG, a sub-2% position he never sold among a zillion small insurance bets that mostly didn't work. _[Warren Buffett, Shelby Davis, AIG]_ — [2023-07-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HhA8WfnEw9I)
- **Think of yourself as a founder or partner in a private family business, not a stock trader; control is overrated.** The Waltons have held Walmart since 1970 with no control and no Walton running it; the IKEA founder had 99.99% of net worth in one company; entrepreneurs sleep fine with 99% in one business, so why should an investor use a different framework? _[Walmart, Walton family, IKEA, Google]_ — [2023-07-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HhA8WfnEw9I)
- **Giving a great business a lot of rope, holding it beyond the point where it seems to pass intrinsic value, is blasphemy to Graham but essential to true long-term wealth creation.** Intrinsic value is hard to estimate and being wrong is expensive, as Phil Fisher argued. Graham himself made most of his money holding GEICO for decades, which was half his net worth at death and beat the S&P by 7-8% a year, violating his own teachings. Pabrai's big mistake for many years was buying well below intrinsic value and selling right at it. _[Ben Graham, Phil Fisher, GEICO]_ — [2023-10-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w9oC1rPV5yQ)
- **The Native Americans were overpaid for Manhattan at $24; the screw-up was not investing it - at 7% it would be about $19-20 trillion today, more than the land is worth.** Rule of 72: 7% doubles every 10 years, ten doubles is 1,024x per century, so $24 in 1626 becomes $24 trillion by 2026. US total wealth is about $150 trillion and Manhattan's land at $1,000 a square foot is a fraction of that. _[Peter Minuit]_ — [2023-10-17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EzMWPRx9-CY)
- **Humans think linearly but compounding works on a log scale, which is why Einstein called it the eighth wonder - even Queen Isabella overpaid Columbus.** $30,000 to Columbus in 1491 at just 5% (doubling every 15 years, 35 doubles over 532 years, 2^35 = 32 billion) would be about a thousand trillion dollars today, double the entire wealth of the planet (about $500 trillion). _[Christopher Columbus, Queen Isabella]_ — [2023-10-17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EzMWPRx9-CY)
- **The janitor who left $4 million to his college should not be a surprise - given a modest lifestyle and a long runway, the number should have been much higher.** The average IRA balance at 65-70 is a pathetically small number, maybe $150,000, because people get in their own way. His daughter's $5,000 IRA at 18 doubling every five years reaches $5 million at 68, and every subsequent year's savings adds another $5 million. — [2023-10-17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EzMWPRx9-CY)
- **Compounding has three interchangeable variables - starting amount, runway and rate of return - and with a 60-80 year runway in the S&P you get roughly 150x on whatever you start with.** The S&P has done about 9% a year for a hundred years, doubling every eight years; a 60-year runway is 7.5 doubles (7 doubles = 128x, 8 = 256x). Steady savings over 30 years can dwarf a business exit at 50. Buffett, born 1930 and just turned 93, has run his engine for 82 years and would still be the richest person in the world had he not given money away. _[Warren Buffett, S&P 500]_ — [2023-10-17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EzMWPRx9-CY)
- **Never interrupt compounding unnecessarily - Munger's quote - so dollar-cost average into an index every month regardless of markets and never raid tax-deferred accounts for consumption.** Most humans are too smart for their own good and can't stay with the program like the janitor. He pulled $30,000 from his 401(k) at 25 to start his first business; it worked out, but taking tax-deferred assets into consumption plus penalties is a bad idea. _[Charlie Munger]_ — [2023-10-17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EzMWPRx9-CY)
- **The index works because it is too dumb to sell Apple or Microsoft and it captured NVIDIA's entire run from a $10-20 billion market cap - so for most people the answer is just to index.** The S&P 500's constituents are all very successful companies, the list is mostly static with a couple of changes a year, many members won't do well but they don't matter, and it is tax efficient. The leap from indexing to stock picking is huge. _[Apple, Microsoft, NVIDIA, S&P 500]_ — [2023-10-17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EzMWPRx9-CY)
- **Owning a great business at what looks like an overvalued price is not a problem; the one habit he still cannot fix is paying up for a great business in the first place.** Nick Sleep's Amazon bet made the rest of his portfolio's mistakes irrelevant; a 5% position that becomes a 100-bagger swamps being wrong on the other 95%. Buffett said 12 decisions in 60 years created most of Berkshire's value, roughly one every five years, and Munger could never convince Buffett to buy Costco. _[Nick Sleep, Amazon, Costco, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2023-12-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=A2vC2skCjCs)

### Moats & business quality (23)

- **Capitalism is creative destruction: almost every business created will eventually disappear, and any good mousetrap attracts competition that erodes its advantage.** Very few businesses from 100 years ago survive and almost none from 200-300 years ago; he cites a 700-year-old 40-room family hotel in northern Japan as the rare exception. Enduring brands like Coca-Cola, American Express, Pepsi and Visa are largely accidents of history. _[Coca-Cola, American Express, Pepsi, Visa]_ — [2023-01-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5P1c9bhhYPo)
- **Capitalism is brutal and businesses with moats are aberrations; a profitable business has a target on its back and most moats eventually get filled in.** The Thai-restaurant-in-a-small-English-town example: premium economics attract entrants until returns normalize. Coke's moat makes no objective sense, the formula is easily cloned and people preferred Pepsi blind in the 1980s Pepsi Challenge, yet the brand endures, though many switch if Pepsi is 20% cheaper. _[Coca-Cola, Pepsi, Visa, MasterCard, American Express]_ — [2023-01-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c7Oyv-Echa0)
- **Very few businesses survive 50, 100 or 200 years, so betting that Apple will be more valuable in 100 years is a bet he would take the other side of.** The oldest known business is a 30-room Japanese hotel run by one family for ~700 years and ~35 generations. Apple will likely exist in 10-20 years but may not be more valuable than in 2023. _[Apple, Wells Fargo, Coca-Cola]_ — [2023-01-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c7Oyv-Echa0)
- **Coke exploits the association tendency by advertising wherever people are happy, the Olympics, Super Bowl, movie theaters, and using celebrities, Pavlovian conditioning that makes you credit Coke for the happiness.** Buffett and Munger saw four or five mental models working in the same direction on Coke and knew they had a winner; cloning and reciprocity are also mental models. _[Coca-Cola, Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger]_ — [2023-01-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c7Oyv-Echa0)
- **The biggest risk in airports is animal spirits, when bidders overpay for new concessions; privately run airports are far better run than government ones.** Only 4-5% of the world's airports are privately run; LaGuardia today versus five years ago is incomparable and would not have happened under government ownership. _[TAV Airports, LaGuardia]_ — [2023-02-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ncYdcZEnH7E)
- **He would be more interested in Microsoft than Apple because the iPhone is a kludgy device that a future interface shift could displace, and Apple's 30% App Store take rate is not win-win.** Apple has enormous consumer trust and brand but animosity from developers; Amazon's enterprise customers hold no such negative view. Apple should do well for 10 years, but he wouldn't bet on 20. _[Microsoft, Apple, Amazon, Mark Zuckerberg]_ — [2023-02-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ncYdcZEnH7E)
- **Extrapolating a business 10-30 years out is very hard because creative destruction comes from left field, as Uber did to a seemingly bulletproof airport parking operator.** Wally Park at LAX had leather car dividers and high-frequency shuttles that no competitor cloned for decades; he once thought he'd buy it if it came up for sale, then Uber ended the need to park at airports. _[Wally Park, Uber]_ — [2023-02-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UcJB1m3cXKw)
- **Only about 300 of more than 10,000 airports worldwide are private, and that number will grow because privatization is a win-win, as LaGuardia's transformation shows.** Operating airports can be a good business if you don't overpay; most private airports run on build-operate-transfer concessions of 20-50 years that revert to governments. _[TAV Airports, LaGuardia Airport]_ — [2023-02-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UcJB1m3cXKw)
- **Identifying great businesses is trivial (200 of the S&P 500 qualify and they show up in the numbers); the hard part is which will do best for an investor from today, because when you are the 201st analyst the prospects are already priced in.** Great businesses show high returns on equity without leverage and long reinvestment runways: Coca-Cola, Visa, MasterCard, American Express, FlightSafety, GEICO. Munger at the 2023 Daily Journal meeting said the biggest human flaw is denial; a manager mandated to beat the S&P by five points with 20 large-cap names should not even try. _[Coca-Cola, Visa, MasterCard, American Express, FlightSafety, GEICO, Charlie Munger, Daily Journal]_ — [2023-03-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=miqfRmUDwFQ)
- **Durability is the hallmark of a great business, but capitalism puts a target on every high-return mousetrap and most invaders succeed, so talk about great businesses with humility.** Only GE survived from the Dow of 100 years ago and now it is gone too; IBM jumped curves many times but is a shadow of itself. The oldest business he knows is a 700-year-old hotel in Kyoto in its 36th generation; at 300-500 years you are left with liquor companies, and investing in vices does well. Apple, Alphabet, Amazon and Microsoft are solid for 10 years, maybe 20, but he would not bet any thrives in 40. _[GE, IBM, Apple, Alphabet, Amazon, Microsoft]_ — [2023-03-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=miqfRmUDwFQ)
- **Almost all businesses are very fragile — if a business loses revenue for a month, about 95% won't be around.** Bill Gates built Microsoft's cash reserve to survive two years with no revenue, which 99% of businesses cannot do; Berkshire keeps its cash in short-term treasuries rather than any bank for the same reason and has for 50 years. _[Microsoft, Bill Gates, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2023-04-11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ibsxgKdJNpA)

- **Chuck Akre's three-legged stool: highest-integrity managers with skin in the game, very high returns on invested capital with reinvestment ability, and a very long runway.** Pabrai visited Akre in one-traffic-light Middleburg, Virginia in November 2022; Akre's top holding is American Tower and when told 'I found the next American Tower' he replied 'son, the next American Tower is American Tower.' _[Chuck Akre, American Tower]_ — [2023-05-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SP6kKi2nMz4)
- **Ajit Jain is a very good bookie: Berkshire's willingness and trusted capacity to take huge payouts lets it charge roughly three times the actuarial risk.** Berkshire collected $800 million to insure two $1 billion Chinese satellites reaching orbit (Pabrai guessed $400M), and charged the California Earthquake Authority several billion, about four times the risk, for 8.0+ coverage because nobody else could write it. _[Ajit Jain, Berkshire Hathaway, California Earthquake Authority]_ — [2023-05-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SP6kKi2nMz4)

Car manufacturing is a terrible business; car dealerships are a great one. _[Tesla, Elon Musk, GM, Ford, Stellantis]_ — [2023-11-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IJwOjG5gwAw)

Pakistan volumes went from 40M to 400M cases in 15 years. _[Coca-Cola Icecek, Coca-Cola]_ — [2023-12-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=A2vC2skCjCs)
