### Management & capital allocation (21)

- **Do not reinvest in your business unless incremental capital earns at least 20-25%; if you invest 20 crores you should see 4-5 crores come out.** Cement companies are on a treadmill of building plants that project low teens returns and may deliver 9%; entrepreneurs are optimists and should discount their own projections. Needing lots of leverage to make the numbers work is a red flag, since great businesses earn high ROE without leverage. — [2023-01-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5P1c9bhhYPo)
- **If your business cannot compound capital well, treat it as a cash cow and put the cash into a low-cost mid-cap or small-cap index fund.** This gets double-digit returns with little work and rupee-cost averaging over time reduces risk. — [2023-01-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5P1c9bhhYPo)
- **Plant new seeds with tiny bets in adjacent businesses and treat the small invested capital as a tuition bill.** Because payoffs are asymmetric (max loss is 1x, upside can be 10-100x), serial small bets are worth pursuing; once a second engine works, shift the accelerator to whichever has better returns on capital. The Reysas father-son team does exactly this with $0.5-1 million bets. _[Reysas]_ — [2023-01-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5P1c9bhhYPo)
- **The Reysas founder's only test is how quickly a dollar invested comes back; if not within two to three years in dollars, he is not interested.** The father never went to college and does not know the term return on equity, yet reinvests at 25-35% returns; Pabrai will not sell at $1 billion and intends to leave them alone for 20 years, targeting $5 billion. _[Reysas]_ — [2023-01-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5P1c9bhhYPo)
- **Overlaying cheapness with goodness produces lollapalooza results: Reysas was interesting less as a three-cent dollar than because management will not invest capital below a 25-35% return.** A three-cent dollar gives 30x; if the dollar becomes a $20 bill through high-return reinvestment, three cents becomes $20. Buying a compounder at 100 cents still works, but at three or five cents it is off the charts. _[Reysas, Charlie Munger]_ — [2023-01-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c7Oyv-Echa0)
- **What attracted him to Reysas was not liquidation value but reinvestment: the father-son team demand payback in dollars within 2-3 years, implying 25-35% IRRs.** They enter new businesses by starting small to gain competence, then scale; he plans to let it ride 20 years and hopes to 'go to my grave with it', imagining $10-30 billion by 2040-2043. He has no desire to sit on the board; they can run circles around him and he hasn't seen them do anything dumb in 15 years. _[Reysas]_ — [2023-02-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ncYdcZEnH7E)
- **The most valuable piece of Reysas is the redeployment engine: a father and son who only invest if they get their money back in dollars or euros within two or three years, which forces them into great businesses.** The father never went to college and doesn't know ROE or IRR, yet built the largest private freight rail car fleet, largest truck fleet (about 2,000 trucks), lift rental and vehicle inspection businesses, redeploying cash flows at 25-35%. Only $50 million of capital ever went in (a $40 million IPO and $10 million rights issue) and no dividends were paid, producing over $1.5 billion of value in under 15 years. _[Reysas]_ — [2023-02-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UcJB1m3cXKw)
- **Judge management by track record only and completely ignore their projections; managers are optimists who see through rose-colored glasses rather than deceivers.** A long history under the same manager reveals whether they under-promise and over-deliver and whether they have skin in the game; he could not find a decision at Reysas in recent years he disagreed with. _[Reysas, Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger]_ — [2023-02-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UcJB1m3cXKw)
- **Judge management by the track record, not by what they say, because CEOs are optimists who believe their own Kool-Aid, and like Napoleon you want lucky generals.** Coca-Cola was run by idiot managers for 35-40 years who bought Paramount Pictures and shrimp farms in China, and the business still did well, so great past performance is usually the business, not the manager. What happened in the past is not subject to debate; forecasts and stories are hocus-pocus. _[Coca-Cola, Paramount Pictures, Warren Buffett]_ — [2023-03-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=miqfRmUDwFQ)
- **Founder-CEOs, even great operators, often don't understand buybacks because cash leaves the treasury with no immediate pop in the stock — it takes Henry Singleton-style faith.** He sent Shinoken a PowerPoint in Japanese on buybacks; they only nibbled, so he sold in frustration, and a year or two later the founder took the whole company private at a spectacular discount. Reysas has woken up to the mistake of not buying the whole company at a 50% premium and has been buying back shares. _[Shinoken, Reysas, Henry Singleton]_ — [2023-04-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DtQVYvyO4Qg)
- **Stock-based compensation is heads they win, tails they don't lose; the better model is Constellation Software's, where managers buy shares with after-tax bonuses.** Silicon Valley overdoses on giving equity to everyone because it's non-cash and boards don't understand its value, then hides it with adjusted EBITDA. Mark Leonard draws no salary or bonus; Berkshire managers bought stock with their own earnings; Bill Gates never granted himself options, whereas Larry Ellison's comp at Oracle was a tax on shareholders even though he'd have worked as hard anyway. _[Constellation Software, Mark Leonard, Berkshire Hathaway, Oracle, Larry Ellison, Bill Gates, Microsoft]_ — [2023-04-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DtQVYvyO4Qg)
- **You don't need to identify the Pony Ma or Sam Walton upfront; with a 98% error rate you're fine as long as one is among 30 yo-yos, and you only really get to know a business after owning it a few years or after it drops 40%.** After four years owning Reysas he finally met the founder and understood why it enters new businesses and becomes number one: he is an Energizer bunny doing 72 hours of work in 24, similar to what Buffett says of Greg Abel; screen on historic ROIC, then let the wheat separate from the chaff. _[Reysas, Pony Ma, Greg Abel]_ — [2023-05-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SP6kKi2nMz4)
- **Amazon's frugality — Bezos's door desk, a $170,000 salary cap and only 1-2% annual dilution — is a signal that value is hiding behind reported earnings.** Peers dilute 3-5% a year through stock comp; Bezos never awarded himself options, a bonus or even the maximum salary. The head of Amazon India also made his desk out of a door for the symbolism. _[Amazon, Jeff Bezos]_ — [2023-05-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Qgtb7LnvP6Y)
- **When judging people or companies, don't listen to what they say — look at the track record and don't try to project forward.** Munger gave Li Lu money because his record made it a no-brainer: a Tiananmen student leader smuggled to the US, three simultaneous Columbia degrees at the top of his class without knowing English, and $1 million made by investing the float on his scholarship money. Same for Motherson Sumi and Rain Industries — the history in black and white matters more than meeting Jagan Reddy. _[Li Lu, Charlie Munger, Motherson Sumi, Rain Industries, Jagan Reddy]_ — [2023-05-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Qgtb7LnvP6Y)
- **Munger did not buy BYD because Li Lu liked it; he studied Wang Chuanfu's early history and connected him to Edison, Ford and Gates before investing.** Li Lu's initial BYD investment was almost venture capital. Wang, one of the youngest of 7-8 siblings, was staked by his brother; BYD cut battery costs by making a small glove box clean instead of a whole Japanese-style clean room, and Wang lives in the workers' apartment blocks, creating a culture where people will do anything for him. _[BYD, Wang Chuanfu, Li Lu, Charlie Munger, Thomas Edison, Henry Ford, Bill Gates]_ — [2023-06-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y0K1qVJdJxc)
- **Outside the US, Canada, India and parts of Western Europe, he needs trusted ground cover, and people and governance matter more than macro.** The Turkish families he invested with (the Coke bottler family also holds the McDonald's franchises and an AB InBev JV) are among the highest quality, most ethical people he has met, higher quality than he would get in the US; without a Buffett-Munger-literate local he can't do much with a Mexican stock tip. _[Anadolu Group, Turkey]_ — [2023-07-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HhA8WfnEw9I)
- **He prefers the Amazon way of many small bets nurtured on traction over the Facebook way of one all-or-none bet on the Metaverse.** Bezos buries products like the Fire phone that don't get traction; Bill Gates, over a 2.5-hour dinner in Omaha 2023, said Apple doesn't do R&D and is top-down by Steve's design, and would go long Amazon, Microsoft and AMD. _[Amazon, Facebook, Apple, Microsoft, AMD, ASML, Bill Gates]_ — [2023-07-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HhA8WfnEw9I)
- **A business owner should reinvest only what the business can absorb at 20-40% low-risk returns and index the rest.** Most YPO businesses aren't capital intensive and can't absorb even another $1-10 million at the returns they already generate. — [2023-10-17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EzMWPRx9-CY)
- **Assess management by track record, not by what they tell you: compare what they said they would do with what transpired, and check whether they under-promise and over-deliver.** Exceptional management on a mediocre moat is not good enough; the ideal is an incredible moat with great management overlaid on top. — [2023-11-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0qxxVBKd8CI)
- **Management skin-in-the-game is a good mental model but can lead you astray: Chuck Akre passed on TransDigm because executives sold their stock as soon as it vested, yet the business kept compounding.** TransDigm's private-equity roots normalized the pattern of shareholders cashing out. Akre is right 99% of the time and there are no called strikes; Pabrai himself passed because it was nowhere near a P/E of one, one of many things he wrongly let go because they looked optically expensive, like Amazon. _[TransDigm, Chuck Akre, Amazon, Nick Sleep]_ — [2023-11-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0qxxVBKd8CI)
- **Investment committees do more harm than good; the correct model is Buffett giving Todd and Ted total autonomy, even to put all $15 billion each into one stock.** A committee would never reach consensus on Turkey and would end up owning the seven biggest S&P 500 stocks because nobody gets fired for buying IBM. Finding good investments is easier than finding good managers, who need both a track record and enough runway. _[Berkshire Hathaway, Todd Combs, Ted Weschler, IBM]_ — [2023-11-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0qxxVBKd8CI)

### Markets, cycles & macro (25)

- **He never has a view on markets or recessions; forecasting 500 businesses is a fool's errand when even one business's trajectory is hard to call.** Nobody foresaw the Ukraine invasion at the start of 2022 and COVID is still around three years on; macro noise is irrelevant to whether a specific company like Kapoor Watches engages its customers over the next 1-5 years. - **When one part of the market is frenzied, basic brick-and-mortar businesses get very cheap — do a complete 180 into Ben Graham deep value.** The day Nasdaq peaked on March 9, 2000 Berkshire hit a multi-year low; funeral homes, steel mills and tankers traded at single-digit multiples and he bought a funeral home at 2x earnings. - **Bitcoin investors will in the end be very sorry, and algorithmic trading is outside my circle of competence — none of the 10-20 richest people are algo traders.** Bubbles are common and can go on for a long time; 14 years of Bitcoin history does not mean the future is great. He holds neither a long nor a short position. _[Bitcoin]_ — [2023-05-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Qgtb7LnvP6Y)
- **The error rate in investing is high because humans project present circumstances to infinity, as with NVIDIA's euphoria at a $1 trillion market cap.** NVIDIA was up almost 200% in five or six months of 2023; a DCF of plausible 10-year cash flows would be hard to stretch to $1 trillion. ### Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US (36)

- **Turkey is a dream market because locals 'play the market', with the free float turning over every nine days, transferring wealth from the active to the inactive.** High inflation, a collapsing currency and departed foreign investors made it optically cheap when he began visiting in 2018-2019 with a local Buffett/Graham disciple friend; he quotes Buffett that the stock market transfers wealth from the active to the inactive. _[Reysas, Warren Buffett]_ — [2023-01-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5P1c9bhhYPo)
- **Indian wealth and asset management has such a long runway that he could pay 20x earnings and still do well, because household savings are shifting from mattresses, gold and real estate into financial assets.** The business needs no capital, has high ROE, and assets stick to the brand: when IIFL hired senior Kotak wealth managers they brought only 15% of their assets while 85% stayed with Kotak. He suggests a basket of the listed fund houses, letting Raamdeo Agrawal run it, and not touching it for 20-30 years. _[Kotak, IIFL, Motilal Oswal, Raamdeo Agrawal]_ — [2023-01-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5P1c9bhhYPo)
- **Indian families can now send money abroad and putting about a fourth of family wealth into a low-cost S&P 500 index fund is a good, low-effort choice.** At about 10 basis points a year you own Amazon, Microsoft, Salesforce and other businesses with long runways; averaging in over time makes a 5-10% market drop irrelevant. _[Amazon, Microsoft, Salesforce]_ — [2023-01-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5P1c9bhhYPo)

- **Turkey in 2018 was a no-brainer that smart investors refused to even look at because they couldn't get past the country to the company.** Market cap to GDP was a very small fraction versus over 100% in the US, and everyone had exited; after visiting 80-90 businesses over five years with a Graham-style local friend as unpaid analyst, he owns just three Turkish companies, none correlated with Turkish inflation. _[Turkey]_ — [2023-07-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HhA8WfnEw9I)
- **India is a good hunting ground because of secular tailwinds: China in the penalty box, a demographic dividend and a growing population.** Before Turkey he had invested in India and made trips to Korea, China and Japan; India remains his usual default outside the US. _[India, China]_ — [2023-07-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HhA8WfnEw9I)
- **Turkey was a poker game against blindfolded players: foreign investors had all left and local investors are gamblers whose float turns over completely every nine days.** Of 200-300 listed Turkish companies, excluding promoter stakes, the entire float changes hands roughly every nine days. He invokes Buffett's line that the stock market transfers wealth from the active to the inactive. He owns three Turkish businesses: a warehouse operator, a Coke bottler and an airport operator, all widely mispriced. _[Turkish warehouse operator, Turkish Coke bottler, Turkish airport operator]_ — [2023-09-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MDuPszGThmE)
- **He fully expected the Turkish lira to be decimated before investing in Reysas and it had no impact on the decision, because prime Istanbul warehouses with inflation-indexed leases have global value.** Warehouses leased to Amazon, Carrefour or IKEA, like cement and steel, carry global value. The lira went from 5 to over 28 per dollar (80%+ devaluation), yet Reysas is up 20-30x in dollars. _[Reysas, Amazon, Carrefour, IKEA]_ — [2023-10-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w9oC1rPV5yQ)
- **Markets stereotype with broad brush strokes, so when a country like Turkey is deemed uninvestible a few babies get thrown out with the bathwater; that irrational behavior is what he hunts for.** He met 60-70 listed Turkish businesses; most would genuinely face headwinds, but a few were irrationally cheap. TAV Airports has contractual euro revenues with lira costs, so devaluation is a tailwind; the Coke bottler gets ~70% of revenue outside Turkey. All three had off-the-charts owners, management and capital allocation, better than much of the developed world. The clouds over Turkey never lifted, yet Reysas rose 20x in dollars. _[Reysas, TAV Airports, Coca-Cola Icecek]_ — [2023-10-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w9oC1rPV5yQ)
- **Turkey's extremely short holding periods make mispricing likely, which is how he bought a third of Reysas at a $24 million market cap against a $600-800 million liquidation value.** Turkish companies cycle through their entire non-insider float in nine days. He paid about $8 million in 2019; the market cap is now about $600 million US, and in lira the return is effectively infinite despite the currency collapse. _[Reysas, Haider (Istanbul fund manager)]_ — [2023-10-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jZKOk-hlo8I)
- **Buffett was picking through Japan because a 33-year bear market since the 1990 bubble has taught generations of Japanese to avoid equities, making it a fertile hunting ground.** The Nikkei peaked near 40,000 in 1990 and is still below that. The five trading companies have global footprints and pay large dividends, so Japan's declining population and employee-first culture are irrelevant to them. Pabrai's new 2023 handbook copy already shows a stock at a P/E of 1.2. _[Japanese trading companies, Shimano, Japan Company Handbook]_ — [2023-10-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jZKOk-hlo8I)
- **In emerging markets like Turkey, buy the highest-quality businesses run by the highest-quality management, because the 'emerging market' discount is nonsense applied by people who haven't done the work.** He met 60-70 Turkish businesses over several years and made three investments. The Coke bottler has exclusive rights in Turkey and about 12 other countries including Pakistan, two-thirds of volume outside Turkey, Coca-Cola owns 20%, and its professional managers are better than any US bottler's. _[Coca-Cola Icecek, Coca-Cola, Reysas, Guy Spier]_ — [2023-10-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jZKOk-hlo8I)
- **Turkey is a market full of gamblers where the average company cycles through its entire market cap every nine days, versus one to two years on the NYSE, which paradoxically gave him the liquidity to build a large position.** He expected Reysas to trade by appointment but found ample volume from people who buy at 10 AM and sell at 3 PM. _[Reysas]_ — [2023-11-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IJwOjG5gwAw)
- **In Japan, look for businesses whose revenues are tied to exports and for management focused on shareholder value, because a declining population and employee-first culture are headwinds that must be handicapped.** Buffett's 2020 purchase of the five Japanese trading companies worked because their footprint is largely outside Japan. Many Japanese firms carry twice the employees they need and see cash as belonging to employees, hurting capital providers. Japan still screens cheap after decades of flat-lining. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2023-11-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0qxxVBKd8CI)
- **The same quality of bottling business can be bought at a P/E under 10 in Turkey versus a nosebleed multiple in India, so compare similar businesses across geographies.** Coca-Cola Icecek has ~$4B revenue, ~$400M net income, ~$3.7B market cap, ~1.6 billion cases (twice Varun's volume) and 6-9% growth, with possible upside from Bangladesh. India trades above 25x trailing earnings versus Turkey at ~7x. _[Coca-Cola Icecek, Varun Beverages, Anadolu Efes]_ — [2023-12-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=A2vC2skCjCs)
- **A declining population is a significant headwind, so in places like Japan or China favor businesses whose fortunes are tied to markets outside the country; India's rising population and per capita GDP are its trump card.** He finds China much harder, took it off his radar during COVID when he couldn't travel, and notes Buffett's five Japanese trading company bets work because their assets are largely outside Japan. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2023-12-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=A2vC2skCjCs)
- **In the US, losses come from your own mistakes rather than fraud, whereas in Turkey or China you must handicap governance, but judging people transcends borders.** Per Buffett, a few people are clearly exceptional and a few clearly not, while most you cannot judge; the Anadolu family's reputation let AB InBev sell 50% of the Russian beer JV with nothing down. _[Anadolu Efes, AB InBev, Warren Buffett]_ — [2023-12-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=A2vC2skCjCs)

### Psychology & temperament (32)

- **Reciprocation is hardwired but uncalibrated, so small favors create disproportionate goodwill; he exploits this by mailing prospective investors a package with a $50 pen and books.** The brain evolved reciprocation from sharing kills in small groups but cannot remember the size of a favor; only about 1 in 200 return the package, and the minimum investment to reciprocate is $3 million. You want large parts of the world to feel they owe you something. _[Charlie Munger]_ — [2023-01-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5P1c9bhhYPo)
- **The one-, two- or three-cent dollar bill exists today, tomorrow and in five years; the only question is how many pages you are willing to flip and rocks you are willing to turn.** Munger's answer to 'this is so much work' is 'why should it be easy to get rich?' One and done is better than zero and done, and he keeps hunting. _[Charlie Munger]_ — [2023-01-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c7Oyv-Echa0)
- **The number one skill set in investing is patience, because payoffs may come in 10, 20 or 30 years.** He challenged the UT student fund for planning to sell inherited positions that prior teams put heavy horsepower into, and noted their short tenure works against long-term investing. — [2023-02-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UcJB1m3cXKw)
- **Our brains were wired to survive the African savannah, not to invest, so the best we can do is be aware of biases and sidestep some pitfalls — nobody sidesteps them all.** He recommends rereading Munger's psychology of misjudgment essay and Cialdini's book; commitment and consistency bias is part and parcel of who we are. _[Charlie Munger, Robert Cialdini]_ — [2023-04-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DtQVYvyO4Qg)
- **You don't need to be high quality to attract high-quality people — just find people of higher quality than you, and kindness is the base trait.** Buffett's advice: identify the classmates you admire most, ask what qualities cause that admiration, and incorporate them. No kind person dies without friends. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2023-05-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Qgtb7LnvP6Y)
- **Surround yourself with givers and be a giver — eliminate takers and matchers.** From Adam Grant's Give and Take; Buffett and Munger are givers. Dakshana never asks scholars to donate, yet many give back many times the $2,500-3,000 spent on them — that voluntary giving is the signal for identifying givers. Dakshana itself should be a giver organization, not a matcher. _[Adam Grant, Dakshana Foundation]_ — [2023-05-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Qgtb7LnvP6Y)
- **Passive index investing gives a great result; crossing into active stock picking is a different game mastered mainly by taking arrows in your back.** Learn from your own and others' mistakes, and start with a framework, beginning with how many stocks your temperament lets you hold (5, 10, 20 or 30). — [2023-06-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tYtG7ZvMSjM)
- **Many aspects of investing cannot be taught; a hyperactive trader is hard to convert into someone who buys one stock a year and holds for decades.** Know your temperament, aptitude and style; read everything by Buffett and Munger and watch the hundreds of hours of Berkshire meetings at buffett.cnbc.com to form your framework. _[Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2023-06-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tYtG7ZvMSjM)
- **There are no called strikes in investing: not buying NVIDIA costs nothing even if it becomes a $10 trillion company.** What matters is what you actually invested in; FOMO and the euphoric flavor of the day are a major source of errors. _[NVIDIA]_ — [2023-06-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tYtG7ZvMSjM)
- **Predicting a business's future trajectory is inherently error-prone, so an investor must be a pessimist and an optimist at the same time.** Managers leave or arrive, regulations and import duties change, competitors act; saying a business will be worth three times as much in 5-10 years is by definition a high-error exercise. — [2023-06-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tYtG7ZvMSjM)
- **All investment manager misery stems from the inability to sit quietly in a room and do nothing.** A paraphrase of Pascal; combined with his father's rule that one good wife and one good friend are all you need, he argues less is more and quality beats quantity. _[Blaise Pascal]_ — [2023-06-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tYtG7ZvMSjM)
- **Be very rational in business and investing but less rational in relationships, which need emotion; Munger balances the two well.** At 99, physically declined and no longer playing golf or club bridge, Munger shows no cognitive decline; rationality is central to his success. He is easygoing, eats whatever is served, and the family rations his See's candy to 2-3 times a month, so he gorges at the Berkshire and Daily Journal meetings where no one can stop him. _[Charlie Munger, See's Candies]_ — [2023-06-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y0K1qVJdJxc)
- **You are not entitled to an opinion unless you can state the other side's argument as well as your own; humans become irrational the moment they hold an opinion or ideology.** He gives Munger's examples of Harvard affirmative action and the Russia-Ukraine war, where one should understand both sides. Holding both sides of an argument in the brain simultaneously is very difficult for most humans. _[Charlie Munger]_ — [2023-06-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y0K1qVJdJxc)
- **Shorting is a little bit dumb, and shorting someone like Elon is very dumb.** Said in response to Bill Gates's famous Tesla short. _[Tesla, Bill Gates]_ — [2023-07-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HhA8WfnEw9I)
- **He is fundamentally a game player who only plays games where he has an edge: bridge, blackjack, investing and philanthropy, and all of them must be fun.** Psychologists who profiled him concluded he likes games he thinks he can win. He has no blueprint for the next investment or where Dakshana will be in five years; if things are fun they get done well. — [2023-09-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MDuPszGThmE)
- **When there is purity of purpose the universe conspires to help you; be a giver and ruthlessly eliminate takers and matchers from your life.** Citing Adam Grant's 'Give and Take', givers end up receiving ten times more, as with the agenda-free Buffett lunch. Dakshana should have failed in India but worked because the team was purer of purpose than he was. He deliberately befriended Munger's Friday bridge circle because they were the highest quality people he had ever met and all givers; we become who we spend time with. _[Adam Grant, Charlie Munger]_ — [2023-09-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MDuPszGThmE)
- **Adopt a founder's mindset: a founder would not sell for 20-30% above his estimate of value but would happily sell at 500%.** Giving a business rope means you may sell a 30x or 50x winner 20-30% below its peak when it goes into decline, but 'there are far worse tragedies'; the downside of getting off a great runway is much worse. — [2023-09-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kfgbTNWLMJE)
- **The reciprocation tendency has no calibration engine, so a small unsolicited gift can create a disproportionate sense of obligation.** He sends prospective investors a physical package with a book and a Cross pen; only 1-2 in 100 return it, and for the rest 'the pen is equal to a few million dollars' minimum investment. Cialdini describes the same mechanism used by salespeople. _[Pabrai Investment Funds, Robert Cialdini]_ — [2023-09-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kfgbTNWLMJE)
- **Bridge and investing are both probabilistic games with no absolutes, which is why Buffett, Munger and many great investors play; taking up bridge makes you a better investor.** Every investment has 'hair on it', e.g. what if Andy Jassy leaves Amazon or the FTC handcuffs it. He plays 5-6 hours a week, learns fastest playing with far better partners, and is now attending all three US national tournaments; Bridge Base costs about $99 a year. _[Amazon, Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger]_ — [2023-09-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kfgbTNWLMJE)
- **Probabilistic thinking is essential to investing and bridge is the best way to build that muscle: 30 minutes to learn, a lifetime to master.** He played bridge for years before investing; Buffett and Munger gained a lot from it. Studying business histories always yields a range of outcomes, and games like bridge and blackjack train you for that. He was banned for life from a Vegas casino for a blackjack system that was not card counting. _[Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger]_ — [2023-10-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w9oC1rPV5yQ)
- **A rational investor should accurately weigh emerging-market and currency risks rather than be paranoid about them.** He is not concerned about overweighting emerging markets or currencies as long as the specific business risks are correctly assessed. — [2023-10-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w9oC1rPV5yQ)
- **Humans are hardcoded by genetics and early life experience, so at 82 Buffett was still doing the same treasure hunt in the Japan Company Handbook that he did as a teenager.** In 2012 Pabrai saw the Japan Company Handbook on Buffett's desk and dog-eared pages of companies he liked; Pabrai believes the five Japanese trading company positions filed on August 30, 2020 came out of that handbook. _[Warren Buffett, Japan Company Handbook, Mitsui, Mitsubishi]_ — [2023-10-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jZKOk-hlo8I)
- **Be like a salmon fisherman with a spear: long dry spells are normal, and when a juicy idea shows up it may take two days or four months of work.** Fiat Chrysler took about four months of reading including Harvard case studies on Marchionne; Reysas was so simple he was buying shares less than a week after meeting the company. _[Fiat Chrysler, Reysas]_ — [2023-10-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jZKOk-hlo8I)
- **Know your own owner's manual: industrial psychologists told him he plays single-player math games where the outcome depends on him, so running a 170-person company was a ridiculous mismatch and a one-man fund was perfect.** A YPO forum 360 review 24 years ago; one of the psychologists became an original fund investor. Since COVID he works from home, is more productive with no human interaction, and stopped going to his Austin office. _[Pabrai Investment Funds]_ — [2023-10-17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EzMWPRx9-CY)
- **He is not a risk taker - he looks for no-brainers in places with irrational hatred and irrational behavior, where the whole float turns over every nine days and he's buying from gamblers.** Turkish retail investors buy at 10am, sell at 3pm and aim for 10%; Buffett says the market transfers wealth from the active to the inactive, like playing bridge with someone who doesn't look at the cards. In the US float turns over maybe 1.5-2 times a year. _[Warren Buffett, Turkey]_ — [2023-10-17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EzMWPRx9-CY)
- **Investing has a high error rate, with even the best managers wrong at least one in three times per John Templeton and more likely half the time, so focusing only on anomalies is what makes the odds interesting.** 'Wrong' means the stock flatlines or drifts rather than doing what you expected. Keep your radar up for weird things that make no sense. _[John Templeton]_ — [2023-11-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IJwOjG5gwAw)
- **Expect to be wrong about half the time; the investing business is so forgiving that being right one in ten can work if that one is a massive home run.** Sir John Templeton said the best analyst is wrong one in three times. A zero in a 10-stock portfolio costs 10%, not the end of the world; Valeant hit 30% of Sequoia's portfolio through run-up rather than initial sizing. Buffett's 2023 letter said 12 decisions in 58 years made Berkshire, a hit rate under 4%. _[John Templeton, Valeant, Sequoia Fund, Warren Buffett]_ — [2023-11-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=0qxxVBKd8CI)
- **He has a very low emotional response to most events, a hard-coded trait that is an advantage in business and investing.** Who we are is fixed by genetics and the first five or six years of life; he became aware of this only when others held up a mirror, and it also has disadvantages in life. — [2023-12-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gghOEu8u6pE)
- **Ego and arrogance are the natural filter; judge people by how they treat those three or four levels below them, who their friends are, and how they spend their time.** People put up fronts that a short meeting cannot always penetrate, but to the extent you can see past them it is very helpful. Fairness gets in the way of being the best version of yourself. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2023-12-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gghOEu8u6pE)
- **In 2009 his worry was not his own wealth but that investors would exit at the bottom, because once they leave you can never make it back for them.** The funds were down ~65% from peak versus ~40% for the index; thankfully exits were limited. _[Pabrai Investment Funds]_ — [2023-12-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gghOEu8u6pE)
- **A spreadsheet of what each holding is worth versus its quoted price became his rope out of the well in 2009, just as an astrologer was his bankrupt father's rope.** When Pabrai was 10 or 11 in Bandra, his rational engineer father knowingly paid an orange-robed astrologer for rosy forecasts because he needed energy to start the next business. Spending more time on intrinsic values than market prices kept a sensible outlook. — [2023-12-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gghOEu8u6pE)
- **Use Buffett's inner scorecard: fawning and criticism both have little impact if you hold a realistic, holistic view of your own good, bad and ugly.** Buffett's test: would you rather be the greatest lover known as the worst, or the worst known as the greatest? People criticize Gandhi, Buffett, Munger, even Jesus; he is a lowlife by comparison, so he learns from critics where he can and otherwise ignores them. _[Warren Buffett, Mahatma Gandhi]_ — [2023-12-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gghOEu8u6pE)

### Buffett & Munger lessons (36)

- **Poor Charlie's Almanack is the best book in his library, better than a college education, and he rereads it every year.** Munger's Psychology of Human Misjudgement speech distills 50 years of experience into an hour of reading; understanding and overlaying the ~25 mental models gives a huge advantage in business, career and personal life. _[Charlie Munger]_ — [2023-01-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5P1c9bhhYPo)
- **The Berkshire asset most likely to survive 200 years is Burlington Northern, because it owns rights of way, land and port connections, whatever the freight technology becomes.** In a conversation a few weeks earlier Munger agreed and added the utilities; neither mentioned Coke, which Pabrai thinks has a decent shot but is uncertain over 200 years. _[Burlington Northern, Berkshire Hathaway, Charlie Munger, Coca-Cola]_ — [2023-01-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c7Oyv-Echa0)
- **Munger calls declining the second 1,500 shares of Belridge Oil in 1977 the greatest mistake of his life; he should have sold something else because nothing he owned was a 20-cent dollar.** Belridge traded at ~$120M market cap with a 15% yield, owned its Bakersfield land outright, and was bought by Shell two years later for $3.5B, ~30x. Rolled into Berkshire at ~$300 a share in 1979, Charlie's ~$30K became ~$1.5B; the declined shares would be worth ~$7.5B, more than his net worth. _[Belridge Oil, Charlie Munger, Shell, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2023-01-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c7Oyv-Echa0)
- **Munger's success comes not from his large brain or reading 400-500 books a year but from 30-50 etched mental models he can overlay on a situation instantly.** Observing how Charlie functions over dinners and Bridge taught more than his words. Get the models in, believe in them, and gain fluency to apply three to five at once; when several point the same way you get lollapalooza effects. He rereads The Psychology of Human Misjudgement in Poor Charlie's Almanack every year. _[Charlie Munger, Poor Charlie's Almanack]_ — [2023-01-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c7Oyv-Echa0)
- **Munger's Belridge Oil mistake shows that overrating a manager's flaw and underrating a business's basic economics is how great investments get passed up.** In 1977 Munger bought 300 shares at $115 (~$35,000) at 10-15% of liquidation value, then declined 1,200 more because the CEO was an alcoholic; Shell bought Belridge in 1979 for $3.6 billion (30x) and the proceeds went into Berkshire at ~$300/share, now ~$500,000, roughly 45,000x. 'The oilfield didn't drink.' _[Charlie Munger, Belridge Oil, Shell, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2023-02-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ncYdcZEnH7E)
- **Even Buffett says most of his capital allocation decisions in 58 years were no better than so-so, and Berkshire's results came from about a dozen truly good decisions, roughly one every five years.** Out of roughly 80 whole businesses and 125-150 stocks Berkshire has bought, Pabrai estimates at least half were outright mistakes; his guess at the dozen winners is Ajit Jain, Apple, Berkshire Hathaway Energy, BNSF, GEICO, See's, Washington Post, Cap Cities/ABC, Coke, AmEx, Bank of America and National Indemnity. Berkshire compounded about 20% a year, roughly 3.7 million percent versus about 24,000% for the S&P. _[Berkshire Hathaway, Warren Buffett, Ajit Jain, Apple, BNSF, GEICO, See's Candies, Coca-Cola, American Express, Bank of America, National Indemnity]_ — [2023-02-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UcJB1m3cXKw)
- **Buffett's Occidental and Chevron bets are coupon-clipping bets, 'US treasuries on steroids', because Permian fracking has 90%-plus drilling certainty and OXY pumps all cash into buybacks and dividends with no speculative exploration.** Munger once said he'd love an Exxon that committed to zero further capex and paid out all field cash flows; OXY behaves that way. Munger's failure to buy enough Belridge Oil in 1977 was one of his biggest mistakes. Berkshire's size forces spreading bets, as with buying all four airlines. _[Occidental Petroleum, Chevron, Exxon, Belridge Oil, Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger]_ — [2023-02-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UcJB1m3cXKw)
- **Buffett's 2022 letter admits most of his capital allocation decisions were so-so and about a dozen truly good decisions, one every five years, produced the results; the lesson is that the flowers were never cut and the weeds never watered.** Over 58 years Berkshire made roughly 200 decisions (about 80 acquisitions and 120 stocks); Pabrai guesses a good hundred were mediocre or poor. Buffett compounded 19.8% a year versus 9.9% for the S&P, a 3.8 million percent gain versus 24,700%, not even the same zip code. _[Berkshire Hathaway, Warren Buffett, Helzberg Diamonds, Jordan's Furniture]_ — [2023-03-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=miqfRmUDwFQ)
- **Munger read Barron's for 50 years, roughly 25,000 ideas, acted on exactly one (Tenneco in 2003), turned $10 million into $80 million, and handed it to Li Lu because his track record made it a no-brainer.** Tenneco's bonds were at 20 cents on the dollar when Munger bought. Li Lu, a Tiananmen student leader who did three simultaneous Columbia degrees with no English, turned the float on his scholarship money into $1 million by graduation; Munger's $80 million became $800 million and is now perhaps $1.2-1.4 billion. _[Charlie Munger, Tenneco, Li Lu]_ — [2023-03-03](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=miqfRmUDwFQ)
- **Even Warren Buffett's hit rate is about 4% — 12 decisions out of 300-plus made most of Berkshire's results in 58 years.** Buffett's 2023 letter says Berkshire has a few truly extraordinary businesses, many pretty good and a very large number of mediocre; he bought 80-plus companies, made 10 key hires and bought at least 210 stocks. Munger says removing the top 15 decisions would make their record useless. _[Berkshire Hathaway, Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger]_ — [2023-04-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DtQVYvyO4Qg)
- **Even Buffett's results came from about a dozen truly great decisions out of roughly 300, a 4% hit rate, and at least half of Berkshire's 80-plus acquisitions were probably outright mistakes.** From the 2023 letter: 80 acquisitions, at least 210 stocks and ~10 key hires over 58 years; his guess at the dozen is Ajit Jain, GEICO, Coke, Amex, See's, Apple, BNSF, MidAmerican, National Indemnity, Gillette, Washington Post and Cap Cities/ABC. _[Berkshire Hathaway, Ajit Jain, GEICO, Coca-Cola, American Express, See's Candies, Apple, BNSF, MidAmerican Energy, National Indemnity, Gillette, Washington Post, Capital Cities/ABC]_ — [2023-05-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SP6kKi2nMz4)
- **The biggest lesson from Munger and Buffett is that they never dwell on past accomplishments — they solve a problem, eliminate it from their minds and move to the next one.** Munger bought the Doheny Ranch (tens of thousands of acres, two miles of beachfront, worth $10-20 billion) for $75 million and donated it to UC Santa Barbara the next day, then never mentioned it again; Buffett does the same with GEICO and Burlington Northern. Be a Karma Yogi who does the job without expecting reward. _[Charlie Munger, Warren Buffett, Doheny Ranch, UC Santa Barbara, GEICO, Burlington Northern]_ — [2023-05-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Qgtb7LnvP6Y)
- **Finding great investments is like Buffett picking up discarded racetrack tickets or reading every page of Moody's Manual — determined, dogged anomaly hunting.** At 11-12 Buffett collected thousands of thrown-away tickets at Ak-Sar-Ben and had Aunt Alice cash the winners; in his twenties he went through 1,000-2,000 companies in Moody's Manual to find a $15 million market cap with $25 million of earnings. Per the Upanishads, your deepest desire is your destiny. _[Warren Buffett, Moody's Manual]_ — [2023-05-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Qgtb7LnvP6Y)
- **Selfless giving makes the universe conspire to help you — the 2008 Buffett lunch I bid on only to say thank you produced a friendship with Munger.** Buffett set no time limit and turned every question into a learning opportunity, unlike hurried 45-minute cafeteria lunches with tech CEOs; the introduction to Munger led to 30-50 Friday bridge sessions and dinners. Living in the time of Warren and Charlie is like meeting Gandhi, Einstein or Newton. _[Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger]_ — [2023-05-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Qgtb7LnvP6Y)
- **Zero-commission phone trading has hurt investors; Buffett's 20-punch-card rule or a five-year minimum holding rule would help them.** Low frictional costs increase the propensity to trade in and out; slowing activity and reducing the number of decisions is counterintuitively beneficial. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2023-06-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tYtG7ZvMSjM)
- **The most important lessons from Munger came not from what he said but from observing how he interacts with his eight kids, grandchildren, friends and fishing buddy, and how he spends his day.** Behind the blunt Berkshire-meeting exterior is a warm, loving, rational man who lives simply: Buffett has been in the same home since 1954 (67 years) and Munger in a home he designed since about 1964-65. Books like Poor Charlie's Almanack and Lowenstein's 'The Making of an American Capitalist' cover the rest. _[Charlie Munger, Warren Buffett, Poor Charlie's Almanack, Roger Lowenstein]_ — [2023-06-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y0K1qVJdJxc)
- **Buffett gifts about $17,000 a year, the tax-free limit, to roughly 30 family members at Christmas without judging them, while Munger gave half his Berkshire shares to his eight kids in the one year with no estate tax.** Munger's wife died in the single year the US had no inheritance tax; he split half his Berkshire stock eight ways, about $125M per child then, worth perhaps $500M each today. Many of the children, like Howard Buffett in Ukraine, run foundations, so most of that money will end up improving society. _[Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger, Berkshire Hathaway, Howard Buffett, Coca-Cola, Gates Foundation]_ — [2023-06-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y0K1qVJdJxc)
- **Berkshire should do nothing with Apple until there is a permanent secular decline, because you can never cash out at the top anyway.** He sees no concern for Apple for at least 5-10 years; Apple is only a fourth or fifth of Berkshire, which also has MidAmerican (a 50-bagger from $2B to nearly $100B), the railroad, $130-140B cash and $30B a year coming in, so focus on deploying the incoming money. _[Apple, Berkshire Hathaway, MidAmerican Energy, BNSF]_ — [2023-07-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HhA8WfnEw9I)
- **The complete Buffett education is free: about 150 hours of Berkshire annual meetings on buffett.cnbc.com plus the letters and transcripts, yet almost no one is interested.** He listened to every annual meeting from the past 25-plus years twice while showering and shaving each morning, taking six or seven months per pass, and is on his third pass, currently in the 2001 afternoon session, learning more each time. _[Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2023-09-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MDuPszGThmE)
- **Paying over $650,000 for the Buffett lunch was a cheap tuition bill; he was willing to bid $2 million, about 3% of the wealth he had made by cloning Buffett, and his only agenda was to say thank you.** In 2007 he was worth about $85 million, most of it from plagiarizing Buffett. Guy Spier joined capped at $250,000 for two seats. The agenda-free lunch led to a friendship with Munger, whom he enjoyed even more, and standing invitations to Buffett's Sunday brunch with directors and celebrities; the last lunch went for about $19 million. _[Warren Buffett, Guy Spier, Charlie Munger]_ — [2023-09-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MDuPszGThmE)
- **Buffett closed his partnership in 1969-70 because markets were extremely overheated and he could find nothing to buy, which left him with dry powder to 'kill it' after the 1973-74 crash.** Buffett was worth $25-30 million (over $200 million today) at around age 40 and rolled his stake into Berkshire. Munger kept his partnership and got clobbered in the 60-70% slow-motion crash of 1973-74, ending it in 1974. Buffett went from a 'sex-starved man on a deserted island' in 1969 to 'in a harem' in 1975; 1975-81 and the 1980s were incredible periods. Buffett says most of the interesting things in his life happened after age 47. _[Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2023-09-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MDuPszGThmE)
- **Charlie Munger asks the best questions and insists you have no business holding an opinion unless you can state the other side just as eloquently; rereading 'The Psychology of Human Misjudgment' each year gives a big edge.** Munger attributes his success to being rational, and answers Dakshana fork-in-the-road questions before Pabrai finishes articulating them despite never visiting India. Our brains are a mishmash of ancient and modern wiring, so understanding those quirks is a leg up; Poor Charlie's Almanack is the book to read. _[Charlie Munger]_ — [2023-09-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MDuPszGThmE)
- **Munger is the architect of Berkshire and Buffett the general contractor; Munger's willingness to be number two to Buffett shows the power of his mind, and he was right about paying up for Costco long before Buffett.** Munger asked 'why wouldn't I want to be number two to Warren Buffett?' Buffett's hijacker joke ends with Munger wanting to talk once more about Costco and Buffett saying 'shoot me first'; Buffett now regrets never taking a Costco stake. They have disagreed many times but never had a real argument. _[Costco, Charlie Munger, Warren Buffett]_ — [2023-09-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MDuPszGThmE)
- **Buffett's Japanese trading company bet is a model low-risk bet: he borrowed the entire $5 billion in yen at about 0.5% to buy stocks yielding about 8%, with no currency risk.** Announced on his birthday, August 30, 2020, stakes over 5% in Mitsui, Mitsubishi, Marubeni, Sumitomo and Itochu; ~$400 million of dividends against $25 million of interest. Three years later dividends doubled, stocks doubled to quadrupled, the $5 billion became $12-13 billion and income is ~$800 million a year. The stocks were at multi-year lows and Japan was still 30-40% below its 1990 high. _[Mitsui, Mitsubishi, Marubeni, Sumitomo, Itochu, Berkshire Hathaway, Warren Buffett]_ — [2023-09-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kfgbTNWLMJE)
- **Read Munger's 'Psychology of Human Misjudgment' every year; it distills 30-40 years of his stumbling into 30-plus models you can absorb in a day or two.** Association tendency explains why Coke wants to be anywhere humans are happy (Olympics, World Cup, NFL, movie theaters) and uses celebrities; understanding the quirks in human wiring gives you a leg up on other humans. _[Charlie Munger, Coca-Cola, Poor Charlie's Almanack]_ — [2023-09-29](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=kfgbTNWLMJE)
- **Berkshire's insurance edge rests on Nebraska's superior regulatory regime, massive overcapitalization ($500 of equity per $100 of premium) and an implicit parent guarantee earned in the 1980s.** Nebraska regulators let Berkshire invest float in equities and even treat Burlington Northern (bought for ~$40B, now worth $120-130B+) as a bond inside the insurer; Berkshire recently filed to move the railroad out. In the 1980s Berkshire voluntarily paid every claim of liquidated subsidiaries with 130-140% combined ratios, so regulators treat it like Fannie Mae/Freddie Mac with an implicit guarantee. _[Berkshire Hathaway, Burlington Northern, Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac]_ — [2023-10-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w9oC1rPV5yQ)
- **Insurance may become a small business at Berkshire in the distant future because the model only works with an Ajit Jain, just as Stone Trust only works with a Francis Chu.** He cites Munger saying this a few years back and says it would not surprise him if Berkshire runs off the business when Ajit is no longer running things, since he has not heard of a second Ajit. _[Berkshire Hathaway, Ajit Jain, Charlie Munger]_ — [2023-10-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w9oC1rPV5yQ)
- **Buffett's edge has always been a dogged, painstaking search for overlooked winning tickets, from discarded racetrack stubs to flipping 10,000 pages of Moody's Manuals.** As a teenager at Ak-Sar-Ben he collected discarded tickets and found winners; in his early twenties he flipped through every page of the Moody's Manuals twice, finding anomalies like Western Insurance with a $15 million market cap earning $25 million. Pabrai bought a 1953 Moody's Manual on eBay to see it. _[Warren Buffett, Western Insurance, Moody's Manual]_ — [2023-10-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jZKOk-hlo8I)
- **Like Munger, don't dwell on past success; keeping brain cells focused on the problems at hand is what keeps you going like the Energizer Bunny.** Past accomplishments take up less than one-tenth of 1% of Charlie's mind; what occupied him was solving Daily Journal's succession problem. Pabrai changed himself after observing this. _[Charlie Munger, Daily Journal]_ — [2023-10-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jZKOk-hlo8I)
- **Buffett's framework for investing is the same one entrepreneurs use to allocate excess capital - highest return, lowest risk - which is why a business owner with no investing experience could beat 90% of fund managers.** Reading the first Buffett biographies in 1994 at age 30 he saw mutual funds holding hundreds of stocks with 80% turnover, violating Graham and Buffett's rules 'like saying I don't believe in gravity'. He tested the theory with $1 million after tax; in five years it was $13 million, north of 70% a year. Buffett: 'I'm a better businessman because I'm an investor and a better investor because I'm a businessman.' _[Warren Buffett, Ben Graham]_ — [2023-10-17](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=EzMWPRx9-CY)
- **Buffett's PetroChina bet was a no-brainer anomaly: $12 billion of earnings against a $35 billion market cap, about 3x earnings with a roughly 15% dividend yield, and the stock quickly tripled.** Discussed at the 2005 Berkshire meeting; the $400 million investment was Buffett's first in China, with 90% government owned and the annual report stating 45% of cash flow would be paid out. He said he'd have preferred Exxon, BP or Chevron at that valuation but nothing else in the world was priced like that. _[PetroChina, Warren Buffett, Berkshire Hathaway, Exxon, BP, Chevron]_ — [2023-11-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IJwOjG5gwAw)
- **He bid for the 2007 Buffett lunch as a tuition payment: with a net worth of $84 million largely built on Buffett and Munger's intellectual property, $2 million (2.5%) seemed appropriate, and the auction capped out at $650,000.** Guy Spier capped himself at $250,000 and wired about $200,000; the money went to GLIDE in San Francisco. The three-hour lunch unexpectedly led to friendships, and Buffett, competitively calling Charlie 'utterly boring', arranged a Munger lunch that Pabrai enjoyed even more, followed by Friday bridge at LA Country Club. _[Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger, Guy Spier, GLIDE]_ — [2023-11-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=IJwOjG5gwAw)
- **Be a harsh, unfair grader of people: bring the 4 in 100 who impress you into your inner circle and discard the other 96, including the 92 you cannot form an opinion about.** Buffett told him at their lunch that he is not a great judge of people; in a cocktail party of 100 he could identify only 4 exceptional and 4 arrogant turnoffs. With near-infinite good people on Earth there is no penalty for excluding a good one but a big penalty for including a bad one. Since moving to Austin two years ago he met ~30 people one-on-one and only one became a good friend. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2023-12-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gghOEu8u6pE)
- **Charlie Munger never looked back at his achievements; all his energy went into the problem in front of him, and that forward focus is a better mental model than dwelling on past success.** Days after Munger died at 99.9, Pabrai recalls him moaning about Berkshire's excess cash and his search for a Daily Journal CEO successor rather than discussing his legacy over 14 years of bridge and dinners. His father's prayer-corner quote: 'Success is not a summit or a peak; anything you do can be done better.' _[Charlie Munger, Berkshire Hathaway, Daily Journal]_ — [2023-12-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gghOEu8u6pE)
- **Charlie Munger's greatest lesson was not what he said but how he lived: he never looked back, showed no self-pity through near-blindness and his wife's death, and just 'soldiered on' to the next problem.** Over a 14-year friendship from 2009 they met for dinner 4-5 times a year and monthly bridge at the LA Country Club. Munger once called him to say he was beating himself up too much over the Horsehead loss: learn from losses, but do not learn too much, and move on. Their last dinner was a month before Munger died. _[Charlie Munger, Horsehead Holdings, Daily Journal, Costco]_ — [2023-12-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=A2vC2skCjCs)
- **Leverage is how Rick Guerin, Buffett and Munger's third partner, got knocked out: margin calls in 1973-74 forced him to sell Berkshire to Buffett at $40 a share.** Buffett told him that a slightly above-average investor can get rich over a lifetime without leverage and can never get hurt, but Rick never got to play out his hand. Guerin brought See's Candies and Blue Chip Stamps to Buffett and Munger, and the three of them operated in a no-competition era similar to Turkey today. _[Rick Guerin, Berkshire Hathaway, See's Candies, Blue Chip Stamps]_ — [2023-12-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=A2vC2skCjCs)

### Mistakes & lessons learned (24)

- **He started 28 years ago buying great growing businesses, compounded $1M to ~$13M from 1995 to 2000, then switched to Graham deep value when the fund launched in 1999 to sidestep the dot-com bubble.** On March 9, 2000, the day Nasdaq peaked near 5,000, Berkshire hit a multi-year low; Nasdaq then fell ~75% to ~1,200 while his funeral homes and steel companies did extremely well. Buying growing intrinsic value usually beats buying discounted dollar bills. _[Pabrai Investment Funds, Berkshire Hathaway, Nasdaq]_ — [2023-01-18](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=c7Oyv-Echa0)
- **Selling Ferrari because it looked optically expensive was one of the dumbest things he did; he would have three times the money had he held.** Via Fiat Chrysler (bought in 2012 at $5 billion market cap on $140 billion sales, under 4% of revenue) Pabrai Funds owned north of 1% of Ferrari. Ferrari has 80% margins and demand rises with price: the $421,000 Purosangue sold out and trades for ~$1 million. 'Old too soon and wise too late.' _[Ferrari, Fiat Chrysler, Guy Spier]_ — [2023-02-09](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ncYdcZEnH7E)
- **After decades he learned that in a whole mispriced market you should go after the highest-quality businesses rather than the cheapest ones, which the 'old Mohnish' would have done.** Halkbank traded at a P/E of 0.1 because its chairman ignored Iran sanctions and the CFO was jailed at Rikers; he told his friend 'I can deal with hair, but not so much hair' and moved up to the 1x P/E names. _[Halkbank]_ — [2023-02-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UcJB1m3cXKw)
- **Selling Fiat Chrysler and Ferrari was one of his larger mistakes: a $60 million, 10%-of-fund bet in 2012 returned about $250 million but would be worth about $600 million had he held.** Fiat Chrysler had a $5 billion market cap on $140 billion revenue (4% of sales); RAM trucks earned $10,000 a truck behind an import ban, and trucks, Jeep and minivans generated about $10 billion cash flow, with 80% of Ferrari inside. His roughly 1% of Ferrari (about $20 million of cost) is now worth about $400 million, a 20x. 'Old too soon and wise too late': do not be quick to sell. _[Fiat Chrysler, Ferrari, Sergio Marchionne, RAM, Jeep]_ — [2023-02-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UcJB1m3cXKw)
- **Highly levered businesses have no staying power when the first headwinds come — my father went bankrupt every three or four years.** His father was brilliant at spotting offering gaps and starting businesses with zero money in 10 different industries, but took every rupee banks would lend and stepped on the gas, so businesses of 300-400 people blew up; the family had no money for rent or groceries in the busts. — [2023-04-11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ibsxgKdJNpA)
- **I should have switched back from the Graham playbook to growth investing around 2012 — I was about eight years late.** The best way to invest is usually to buy businesses that grow over time; the Graham playbook only made sense in extreme euphoria. Having run it comfortably for 13 years he didn't switch until around 2020, and even then carefully because 2022 valuations were crazy again. — [2023-04-11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ibsxgKdJNpA)
- **In 2007-09 the funds fell 65-67% versus 37% for the market; I was selling P/E of 3 to buy P/E of 2 and then made 140% in 2009.** He did not see the financial crisis coming even after Michael Burry walked him through credit default swaps in his San Jose office in October 2008 — God took the horse to water but the horse didn't drink. _[Michael Burry]_ — [2023-04-11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ibsxgKdJNpA)
- **Even the best investors are wrong half the time, so separate signal from noise and cut losses when the data says you were wrong — as with Alibaba.** In a 10-stock portfolio more than half are probably mistakes, compounding at 4% instead of 15%. Chinese government actions against Alibaba destroyed value and are impossible to handicap, so it went into the too-hard pile; he moved the money to Prosus, which he thinks is a better bet on Tencent. _[Alibaba, Prosus, Tencent, China]_ — [2023-04-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DtQVYvyO4Qg)
- **Silicon Valley Bank, his fund's first investment on July 1, 1999, shows the dilemma: selling after a 150% gain in 2000 missed 23 years of 25% compounding, yet holding would have ended at zero in 2023.** He bought it at slightly above book with an undisclosed basket of warrants as a no-downside way to play the bubble; his tentative answer is perhaps capping a position at 50%. _[Silicon Valley Bank]_ — [2023-05-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SP6kKi2nMz4)
- **Many of his buy decisions were exceptional and the sell decisions horrible, and he expects this to keep happening.** No investor has ever assembled Walmart, Amazon, Costco and Tencent together; accept errors, study what you own, and err on the side of patience because being trigger-happy is a bigger risk than failing to sell optimally. — [2023-05-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SP6kKi2nMz4)
- **Seritage was a liquidation-value bet where the 80/20 prime properties were supposed to carry the value, but with rising rates the old $30 price now looks too optimistic and there is no need to circle the wagons around it.** The stock went from the thirties to $6-7, which looked too low, but real estate distress has changed the picture; he is willing to let it go. _[Seritage Growth Properties]_ — [2023-05-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SP6kKi2nMz4)
- **I should have switched back from Graham bets to great businesses around 2012, not 2020 — those eight years were suboptimal.** He started in the mid-90s as a buy-and-hold tech investor, switched to Graham in 1999 as the bubble formed (fund up 70% in year one, ~30% annualized while Nasdaq lost 75%), but got too comfortable with Graham-type bets. Today he has almost come full circle to buy-and-hold, though tech now comes public later and richer so he hasn't fully returned to tech. _[Pabrai Investment Funds, TransTech]_ — [2023-05-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Qgtb7LnvP6Y)
- **Alibaba was a mistake that went sideways because of state actions from left field, yet he still favors focusing on the micro over the macro.** A 40-50% error rate is par for the course; even Buffett, the best of the best, has a 50% error rate on businesses he buys. _[Alibaba, Warren Buffett]_ — [2023-06-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tYtG7ZvMSjM)
- **Selling Maotai on Li Lu's advice, after Munger ('God') had told him he would still own it when he died, was one of his biggest regrets; it more than doubled after he sold.** Li Lu suggested Maotai a few years back; Pabrai made 5-6x, then Li Lu called citing distribution/corruption concerns and told him to sell. His daughter ignored the advice and kept her shares. He bought at a tenth of the current price and is now going to take another look. _[Kweichow Moutai, Li Lu, Charlie Munger]_ — [2023-06-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Y0K1qVJdJxc)
- **Buffett's ability to keep adding to Apple at five times his first purchase price shows he is not anchored, a great skill Pabrai admits he lacks as a cheapskate.** He was having a hard time finding things in the US in 2023 partly because he didn't fully grasp how strong the tech tailwinds and businesses like Amazon were; his 13Fs sometimes carry only two or three names. _[Apple, Amazon, Warren Buffett]_ — [2023-07-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HhA8WfnEw9I)
- **His biggest career mistake has been repeatedly selling great businesses too soon; concentration is the only way to build wealth, and once independently wealthy taking some chips off the table is forgivable but holding great businesses is better.** The Turkish warehouse operator is already more than 60% of one of his funds and he tells investors every quarter to leave if uncomfortable. He hopes to hold the Coke bottler (a dozen countries plus the number one beer brand in another dozen) and the airport operator for a very long time. Still, capitalism is brutal and no business survives forever; the oldest is a 700-year-old hotel in Kyoto, and he would not fault the Waltons for putting half into the S&P 500. _[Turkish warehouse operator, Turkish Coke bottler, Turkish airport operator, Walmart]_ — [2023-09-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MDuPszGThmE)
- **Buying Stone Trust Insurance was a mistake he reversed quickly because insurance is a commodity, price-taker business where the dumbest competitor sets the price.** Buffett says the average insurer is a terrible business; once a carrier is A-rated the lowest bid wins. At the first board meeting he knew he did not want to be there, sold for about what he paid, and returned most capital to investors. Buyer Francis Chu, a vastly superior operator, took premiums from ~$65M to ~$50M but runs a 62% combined ratio. _[Stone Trust Insurance, Francis Chu, Warren Buffett]_ — [2023-10-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w9oC1rPV5yQ)
- **Investing is a forgiving business where even the best investor is wrong about half the time; the key is recognizing mistakes and reversing them before they consume brain cells.** He calls it putting the toothpaste back in the tube, which is not designed to happen. Seeing insurance claims at the individual level taught him how the sausage is made. _[Stone Trust Insurance]_ — [2023-10-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w9oC1rPV5yQ)
- **Turning down Francis Chu's repeated offers to keep a 20-25% stake in Stone Trust was a case of being 'old too soon and wise too late'; a Chu-underwriting plus Pabrai-investing pairing would do very well.** Each earn-out payment came with another offer to roll into a stake and he kept saying no because he had underestimated Chu. Chu is a classic Graham investor and great operator; Pabrai says he would take the offer today and it might still happen. _[Francis Chu, Stone Trust Insurance]_ — [2023-10-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=w9oC1rPV5yQ)
- **Time tells you when you are wrong: if after three to five years you are down 30%, the odds are high something is off in your thesis.** A stock must reach intrinsic value at some point, the bedrock of Ben Graham. You understand a business far better after investing because data keeps arriving, and sometimes the error is clear within three months. _[Ben Graham]_ — [2023-10-12](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jZKOk-hlo8I)
- **Watching his father's under-capitalized, over-leveraged businesses collapse in the first storm taught him to build resilience and focus on the downside while going for the upside.** His father was excellent at identifying and scaling opportunities but too aggressive; Pabrai deliberately built more resilience into his own businesses. — [2023-12-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gghOEu8u6pE)
- **His net worth peaked at $84M in June 2007 and bottomed under $20M in the GFC, but with no leverage and a modest lifestyle it did not change his life.** He was selling stocks at a P/E of 4 to buy stocks at a P/E of 2. In 2009 the Pabrai funds rose 110-130%, nearly doubling his net worth from the bottom, followed by several strong years. _[Pabrai Investment Funds]_ — [2023-12-01](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=gghOEu8u6pE)
- **A 50% error rate on what you buy is par for the course because you are forecasting a future with too many variables, and mistakes you cannot see yet are always sitting in the portfolio.** His biggest recurring theme of losses is leverage: a subprime mortgage lender bought in early 2007 went to zero (a 10% bet) and a leveraged zinc producer transitioning plants went bankrupt (another 10% loss). Debt removes a business's anti-fragility, so he tries to avoid leveraged businesses. _[Horsehead Holdings]_ — [2023-12-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=A2vC2skCjCs)
- **His Fiat Chrysler investment was a home run, but not appreciating the Ferrari brand inside it and selling early cost him more than $400M of additional gains.** In 2013 Fiat Chrysler had a $5B market cap on $140B revenue and Sergio Marchionne guided to 2018 profits above the market cap; $70M grew to over $350M. The ~$16M Ferrari slice made $70-80M but would be worth over $500M today; Ferrari is like a factory that produces Picassos, with special editions selling out at 85-90% margins. _[Fiat Chrysler, Ferrari, Sergio Marchionne, John Elkann]_ — [2023-12-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=A2vC2skCjCs)

### Career, entrepreneurship & life (52)

- **Entrepreneurs are already wired to be great investors because the 3-4% of time they spend on strategy uses the same brain cells as picking businesses to buy.** He quotes Buffett: 'I'm a better investor because I'm a businessman, and a better businessman because I'm an investor.' Buffett took that 4% strategy slice and expanded it to 80% of his time by making passive investments instead of doing the heavy lifting. _[Warren Buffett, TransTech]_ — [2023-01-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5P1c9bhhYPo)
- **Control is overrated; the market, competitors, customers and employees control you anyway, and the best position is passive investor.** Buffett never controlled Coca-Cola yet gets 1-2 cents from every eighth can opened; Pabrai's job at Reysas is just to cheer them on, meet once a year, and not sit on the board. 'If you don't have any employees, you have no problems.' _[Warren Buffett, Coca-Cola, Reysas]_ — [2023-01-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5P1c9bhhYPo)
- **Part-time investing turned $1 million into $13 million from 1995 to 2000, outearning his 70-80 person IT company in some years, which pushed him into full-time investing.** He spent 10-20 hours a week studying businesses after reading about Buffett in 1994. His two rules: if you are not excited to go to work on Monday, don't go; and hit the reset button. His YPO forum suggested owning the business without running it, and the new CEO sold TransTech within months. _[TransTech, Warren Buffett]_ — [2023-01-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5P1c9bhhYPo)
- **Entrepreneurs do not take risk; they do everything to minimize it, and 'heads I win, tails I don't lose much' was how TransTech was started.** He worked on the startup for 9-10 months before quitting at 25, with clients and cash flow already exceeding his salary; the downside was $30,000 of 401k and $70,000 of credit card debt that US bankruptcy law would wipe, and his bosses promised him his job back with a raise. Both later became Pabrai Funds investors. _[TransTech]_ — [2023-01-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5P1c9bhhYPo)
- **The Patels are the classic Dhandho case: 0.1% of the US population now controls 70-75% of US motels, built from nothing by being the lowest-cost operator.** Refugees from Uganda moved into motels, replaced staff with family, cooked vegetarian meals at home, undercut $35 rooms at $32, and used non-recourse leverage to buy the next motel for a cousin. When the book came out ~15 years ago the figure was 40%; now they own Hiltons and Marriotts too. _[Patels]_ — [2023-01-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5P1c9bhhYPo)
- **Everyone should get an 'owner's manual' from industrial psychologists, as he did in 1999, to discover who they really are rather than following prescribed paths.** A 360 assessment through his YPO forum showed he is a solo game player who likes games with odds in his favor and had no business running a 200-person IT company; the psychologists endorsed the yet-to-launch Pabrai Funds and one invested $100,000. He rereads the report annually, recommends Jack Skeen, and says kids should do it at 18. _[Jack Skeen, Pabrai Investment Funds]_ — [2023-01-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5P1c9bhhYPo)
- **Buffett's insight that being a businessman makes you a better investor and vice versa drew him in: investing turns the 4% of an entrepreneur's time spent on strategy into 80-90%.** After a small partial sale of his IT business in 1994 left him about $1 million after tax, he grew it to about $13 million in five years using Buffett's approach, then left the company in 1999 and started Pabrai Investment Funds as a hobby for friends. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2023-02-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UcJB1m3cXKw)
- **The brain is culled and optimized between roughly ages 10 and 20, making that the only window to truly specialize, and his childhood of helping his father's failing businesses gave him 'several MBAs before 18'.** Bill Gates had 10,000 hours of coding by 18-19; Buffett read every finance book in the Omaha library by 14-15; Germany's early apprenticeships explain why China cannot uproot its manufacturing. His father went bust every three or four years from over-leverage, and at 11-12 Pabrai and his brother helped figure out how to survive one more day. _[Bill Gates, Warren Buffett]_ — [2023-02-28](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=UcJB1m3cXKw)
- **The window from age 11 to 20 is the only time in life when the brain is optimally set up to specialize, so start early.** Bill Gates started programming at 11 and had 10-15,000 hours before 20; Buffett bought his first stock at 11; Pabrai got his own accidental business MBA by sitting as his father's 'board of directors' at 12 and going on sales calls at 16. Education systems force a jack-of-all-trades approach that wastes this window. _[Bill Gates, Warren Buffett, Michelangelo, Leonardo da Vinci]_ — [2023-04-11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ibsxgKdJNpA)
- **You get good at a business when it is facing adversity, because that is when you turn over every rock.** Each night he and his brother tried to figure out how to keep his father's collapsing business alive for one more day; his father learned the jewelry business from a stranger on a flight and exploited a UAE duty arbitrage that paid for Pabrai's US college. — [2023-04-11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ibsxgKdJNpA)
- **A 100x trailing P/E on a software company is a signal of very high growth — better than buying the stock was starting a service practice around it.** In the 1990s he launched a PeopleSoft practice for a $1,000 ad, hired Paul Yates at $250,000, and had $3,000/day billing plus 12 developers at $2,000/day before Yates even started; he repeated this with Business Objects. Be an inch wide and a mile deep. _[PeopleSoft, Business Objects]_ — [2023-04-11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ibsxgKdJNpA)
- **Give children a meaningful sum at 18 with full control so they choose careers by passion, not pay, and tell them nothing more is coming.** Cloned from Bill Harlow, who put $6 million into Goldman accounts for his kids at 18; Pabrai funded UGMA accounts at $20-30,000 a year invested in 3-4 stocks, now seven figures each. Parents have 18 years to transfer values — without values the money is a problem, with values it is a huge positive. _[Bill Harlow]_ — [2023-04-11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ibsxgKdJNpA)
- **Reading must be fun; all knowledge is cumulative and business biographies are the best genre.** More than half the books in his library are unread; a book must draw him in within 10-20 pages. The Munjal/Hero Honda biography taught him bicycles are not low-tech and that Honda chose the Munjals over the Tatas for their family values. He will never retire — he could have stopped working at 33 but it would have been a useless life. _[Hero Honda, Munjal family, Honda]_ — [2023-04-11](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ibsxgKdJNpA)
- **Investing is like bridge — 15 minutes to learn, impossible to master in a lifetime — and after nearly 30 years my pattern recognition is faster and broader.** He is as excited about the game as in 1994; more competencies and refined mental models have accumulated, and lifelong learning serves you well. — [2023-04-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DtQVYvyO4Qg)
- **Commit to the truth and cut out even small white lies — the world runs on trust, not contracts, and the paybacks are enormous.** Inspired by David Hawkins' Power vs. Force; it feels uncomfortable at first but trust rises sharply, friends know you have their back, and you never have to remember your lies. The best contracts are the ones you never look at after signing. Candor about skipping weddings will be welcomed. _[David Hawkins]_ — [2023-04-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DtQVYvyO4Qg)
- **People everywhere hate talking about money, but asking about net worth, income and expenses in a confidential setting is the only way to give useful advice — and people feel relieved.** Guy Spier cringes when Pabrai asks these questions, yet friends share numbers they have never told anyone; a friend deciding between retirement and two jobs got concrete advice only after revealing his finances. _[Guy Spier]_ — [2023-04-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DtQVYvyO4Qg)
- **The human brain is set up to specialize between ages 11 and 20, but school makes you a jack of all trades, so parents must foster specialization outside school.** Buffett and Bill Gates specialized as teenagers outside the school system; parents should identify aptitudes at 10-12 and increase time on them. _[Warren Buffett, Bill Gates]_ — [2023-05-05](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=SP6kKi2nMz4)
- **The best way to learn is to teach — I do these student sessions to teach myself.** He says his ulterior motive is self-education, with the side effect that others learn too. — [2023-05-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Qgtb7LnvP6Y)
- **Be a harsh grader of friends: cut the bottom 80-95%, because there is no penalty for missing a great person but a real penalty for letting in a not-so-great one.** Every one of Munger's friends is exceptionally high quality though many are not wealthy, so Pabrai made all of Munger's friends his own and applied the same filter. In 15 months in Austin he invited 25-35 people for Assam tea and only one passed the filter — and that is fine, since there are infinite great humans and you need only half a dozen. _[Charlie Munger]_ — [2023-05-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Qgtb7LnvP6Y)
- **You need just one good wife and one good friend to live a happy life — less is more.** His father's saying; after one truly exceptional deep relationship, leave the rest to nature and osmosis while staying a harsh grader. — [2023-05-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Qgtb7LnvP6Y)
- **Investing in yourself early delivers the greatest returns, but pursue your passion rather than doing an MBA for pay or opportunities.** Only a couple of undergraduate courses, notably a public speaking elective chosen by coin toss, had lifelong impact; going to sleep a little wiser every day and reading for life compounds like a marathon. — [2023-06-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=tYtG7ZvMSjM)
