### Cloning & learning from great investors (13)

- **Nick Sleep's post-fund portfolio of one-third each in Amazon, Costco and Berkshire is beating everyone; his one mistake was halving Amazon at 60% of the pie to buy a terrible fourth business.** Sleep shut Nomad around 2012-14; he would have done better sticking with the original three, yet even with that mistake has done very well, showing how forgiving the business is. _[Nick Sleep, Amazon, Costco, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2025-01-31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JpGi2c7a1gw)
- **For me cloning is like breathing; humans think it is beneath them or cheating, but the small sliver who go all in on cloning become the best entrepreneurs.** If you can understand another smart investor's thesis and it is within your circle of competence, that beats figuring everything out yourself; even Berkshire's Apple position came from one of Buffett's two lieutenants and Warren put in 50x their capital. Dakshana itself succeeded only because it cloned a model beyond his pay grade. _[Berkshire Hathaway, Apple, Dakshana]_ — [2025-02-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Eww63NIxKew)
- **Sam Walton was the ultimate cloner, claiming no one had been inside more non-Walmart retail stores, and he learned from even terrible operators and from blunt truckers.** He lay on a Brazilian store floor to measure aisle spacing, praised a bad store's candle display, and brought donuts to truckers at 5 a.m. for unfiltered reports on Walmart problems. Bill Gates is another shameless cloner: Word from WordPerfect, Excel from Lotus, Windows from Apple, and Bing stands for 'But It's Not Google'. _[Sam Walton, Walmart, Bill Gates, Microsoft]_ — [2025-02-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Eww63NIxKew)
- **Value Investors Club is the modern Moody's Manual: read four or five write-ups a day as an input to ideas, then do all your own work within your circle of competence.** It is free with a 60-120 day delay, curated (members must post two rated ideas a year), around 500 write-ups a year; old write-ups still work, e.g. he recently invested in a company first written up in 2021. _[Value Investors Club, Moody's Manual]_ — [2025-03-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3xbhKOzNBW8)
- **Sam Walton built Walmart as a learning machine that cloned relentlessly from competitors, including Sam's Club copied from Sol Price's Price Club.** Walton spent more time in competitor stores than anyone, learned from losers ('did you see the candle display?'), and was found lying on a Brazilian store floor measuring aisle widths. Walmart did not innovate for its first 20-25 years; Sol Price influenced Walton, Sinegal and via them Amazon. _[Sam Walton, Walmart, Sol Price, Price Club, Costco, Amazon]_ — [2025-03-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3xbhKOzNBW8)
- **To distinguish skill from luck in a manager you need more than 10 years and preferably 20, and even then the index must be calibrated for over- or undervaluation.** Berkshire hired Ted Weschler in 2010 after he was down over 70% and 30 points behind the S&P in 2007-2009, based on his longer record. Ballmer took over Microsoft ridiculously overvalued and left it undervalued, while Satya Nadella started from a value stock. Anyone compared to the S&P over the last decade looks bad, but many yo-yos will beat the elevated S&P over the next 10 years. Selecting managers is one of the most difficult things to do. _[Ted Weschler, Berkshire Hathaway, Microsoft, Steve Ballmer, Satya Nadella, S&P 500]_ — [2025-04-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ePBZbS0cRAM)
- **Humans have an inexplicable aversion to cloning, so intense cloners like Sam Walton and Microsoft do extremely well.** The Walton family, 55 years after the IPO and 33 years after Sam's death, still owns 46% of Walmart and is America's richest family; Walton copied Sears, Kmart and every merchant he visited. Windows copied Apple, Word copied WordPerfect, Excel copied Lotus, Bing copied Google ('But It's Not Google', per Buffett), while Microsoft's billions in internal research produced nothing. _[Walmart, Sam Walton, Microsoft, Sears, Kmart, Apple, Google, Warren Buffett]_ — [2025-04-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YBinkgDRPHo)
- **He cloned Buffett's 1956-69 partnership fee structure (zero management fee, 6% hurdle, 25% of profits above) because in 30 years nobody else visibly had.** When he heard of Buffett in 1994-95 he could not find a single fund using the model, an 'offering gap'; it gave him a unique pitch that he only gets rich when investors get rich. Munger later said a few obscure people had copied it. _[Warren Buffett, Buffett Partnership, Charlie Munger, Pabrai Investment Funds]_ — [2025-04-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YBinkgDRPHo)
- **Nick Sleep returned all outside capital and put his own money one-third each in Berkshire, Costco and Amazon, then trounced everyone after 2014 while doing no work.** Nomad compounded at 18%+ from 2001 to 2013 with about $3 billion; had Nick done nothing his portfolio would be about $1.7 billion today, versus $1.4 billion after trimming Amazon into ASOS, and under $800 million had he gone into the S&P. _[Nick Sleep, Qais Zakaria, Nomad, Berkshire Hathaway, Costco, Amazon, ASOS]_ — [2025-05-02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NrTz1uiL3RU)
- **'Buffett and Munger Unscripted', which reorganizes the Berkshire annual meeting Q&A by subject, is even better than Cunningham's essays because the meetings are unscripted.** The annual meeting transcripts are on buffett.cnbc.com; Larry Cunningham did the same subject reorganization for the annual reports. _[Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger, Larry Cunningham]_ — [2025-06-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jW-L5NdvYkU)
- **The world will easily accept three to five of the same thing, so cloning an existing business puts you 90-95% ahead of humanity.** Bill Gates and Sam Walton were the greatest cloners: Word came from WordPerfect, Excel from Lotus, Bing from Google; Walmart cloned Sears and Kmart and Sam Walton claimed to have visited more retail stores than any human, learning even from a bad store's candle display. Howard Schultz cloned the Italian cafe for Starbucks. _[Microsoft, Walmart, Sam Walton, Bill Gates, Starbucks, Howard Schultz]_ — [2025-07-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vNBluvpgphs)
- **Cloning is one of the most powerful mental models precisely because most humans have an evolutionary aversion to it and think it is beneath them.** Herd-following aided survival in hunter-gatherer times, but people still resist copying proven ideas even when told to, so the edge endures. 'The world can accommodate three of the same thing'; almost everything that worked in his life was cloned. _[Charlie Munger]_ — [2025-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fW9j-mDNVt8)
- **He built Pabrai Funds in 1999 by cloning Buffett's 0-6-25 partnership fee structure, which nobody had copied in the 30 years since the partnership ended in 1969.** 0% management fee, 6% hurdle, 25% of the upside is a win-win; he told early investors to put all family money only with zero-fee managers, making him a monopoly. Munger later said a few obscure people had cloned it. In 2025, 56 years on, he is still waiting for the cloners. _[Warren Buffett, Pabrai Investment Funds, Charlie Munger]_ — [2025-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fW9j-mDNVt8)

### Circle of competence & checklists (17)

- **Avoid countries without basic respect for property rights and investor capital, such as Russia, Venezuela and Zimbabwe; you do not need a large circle of competence to do well.** John Arrillaga died a billionaire investing only within a mile of Stanford, knowing every building's history, rents and owners cold. _[John Arrillaga, Russia, Venezuela, Zimbabwe]_ — [2025-01-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MGqKFwtCWnU)
- **All intelligent investing is value investing; the Magnificent Seven fall in the 'too hard' pile because he cannot estimate their cash flows and they are not selling at three times earnings.** Nvidia could be a great value investment or ridiculously overvalued depending on what it produces in cash in 2030, a number he cannot figure out. He sees plenty of euphoria in large tech and thinks the next decade may not be a great place to invest in them, though he could be wrong. _[Nvidia, Magnificent Seven, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2025-01-31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JpGi2c7a1gw)
- **99% of stocks belong in Buffett's too-hard pile; NVIDIA, Palantir and Tesla go there because he cannot forecast their cash flows 5, 10 or 15 years out.** Buffett keeps a 'too hard' box on his desk. Tesla's valuation makes no sense on current cash flows, but Elon is constantly underestimated, which is exactly why it is too hard. _[NVIDIA, Palantir, Tesla, Elon Musk, Warren Buffett]_ — [2025-02-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HSq4QOCuuDA)
- **With 50,000+ stocks globally, being flexible and knowing nothing about 99.9% of them still leaves a few hundred where a no-risk, high-conviction bet is delivered on a platter.** He went to Turkey six years ago because it screened as the cheapest market in the world and a Ben Graham-style friend, now Turkey's second-largest fund manager, agreed to show him only companies he owned, starting with his highest-conviction stake. _[Turkey]_ — [2025-02-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HSq4QOCuuDA)
- **If you need Excel it is an automatic pass; the math on a great idea should be doable in your head and the thesis explainable to a 10-year-old in four or five sentences.** Buffett has never used Excel for investments. Example: an international stock exchange at a trailing PE of 30 growing 15-20% with 60% margins becomes under 10x earnings in two or three years, no spreadsheet needed. Conviction is hard if you must keep returning to a model. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2025-03-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3xbhKOzNBW8)
- **99% of investment ideas belong in Buffett's too-hard pile; of 50,000 stocks you will only ever understand a few hundred, and that small sliver is all you need.** The too-hard box physically sits on Buffett's desk; the key trait is the humility to know you cannot handicap most things. He puts 98-99% of what he sees in it, including Michael Burry's 2008 CDS pitch, which he still thinks was right to pass on. _[Warren Buffett, Michael Burry]_ — [2025-03-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3xbhKOzNBW8)
- **Be an inch wide and a mile deep like John Arrillaga, who became a billionaire investing only in real estate within two miles of Stanford, unlevered, buying distressed property in every downturn.** We do not need to know many things about many things, we need to know a lot about a little; if looking at Frontline, learn everything about tankers rather than moving on to airplanes next week. Nick Sleep: 'The best investors are entrepreneurs who never sold.' _[John Arrillaga, Nick Sleep, AerCap]_ — [2025-03-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3xbhKOzNBW8)
- **He ignores macro and AI because he cannot handicap them and brings nothing to that party; you can do extremely well without understanding the flavor of the day.** He knew the internet, electricity and the App Store were transformational but that is not where his edge is; Buffett's Apple was a one-and-done and is mostly sold. Play to your strengths. _[Apple, NVIDIA, Warren Buffett, John Arrillaga]_ — [2025-03-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3xbhKOzNBW8)
- **Approach circle of competence with humility: a question like how to handicap regulation usually means the business belongs in the too-hard pile, and 99% of businesses belong there.** Humans have difficulty giving up on a business they've spent time on. Even Buffett, a child prodigy, keeps a physical 'too hard' box on his desk (which was empty when Pabrai and Guy Spier toured his office in 2014) to remind himself most things he cannot understand. Be comfortable saying no very fast: understand 10 companies and have no clue about 10,000. _[Warren Buffett, Guy Spier, Long-Term Capital Management, Burlington Northern]_ — [2025-04-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ePBZbS0cRAM)
- **Cloning trims 50,000 stocks to 50-60 by taking 20 great investors' top holdings; then circle of competence cuts it to five or ten for a deep dive starting with why they bought.** Most of the time the correct answer to 'is this in my circle of competence?' is no, so about 45 of the 50-60 disappear. — [2025-04-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YBinkgDRPHo)
- **A tiny circle of competence is enough: John Arrillaga became a billionaire investing only in real estate within two miles of Stanford.** Better to be an inch wide and a mile deep than a mile wide and an inch deep; understand very few businesses extremely well and invest when it appears you cannot lose. _[John Arrillaga]_ — [2025-04-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YBinkgDRPHo)
- **The pre-investment checklist was built like the FAA's process: study failures of great investors and turn the obvious-in-advance reasons into questions.** Berkshire's Dexter Shoe failure from low-cost foreign manufacturing became a checklist question; when he categorized failures, the number one cause was leverage and the number two was misunderstanding the moat. _[Dexter Shoe, Berkshire Hathaway, FAA]_ — [2025-05-02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NrTz1uiL3RU)
- **If you have to ask whether something is within your circle of competence, you have already answered that it is not.** There is no penalty for a narrow circle; what matters is staying at its epicenter, and it expands naturally through reading and mistakes without any deliberate program. Buffett's 'too hard' box should get 99% of ideas. The most successful people are an inch wide and a mile deep; Charlie's friend John Arrillaga became a multibillionaire investing only in real estate within two miles of Stanford. _[Warren Buffett, John Arrillaga]_ — [2025-05-02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NrTz1uiL3RU)
- **If you cannot describe an investment thesis to a 10-year-old in about four sentences with very high conviction, pass.** Even a simple, impregnable thesis will have a high error rate, but the error rate is higher without one; most companies do not lend themselves to that clarity and you do not need to invest in most companies. — [2025-05-02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NrTz1uiL3RU)
- **Site visits and talking to workers build domain knowledge better than management access; for most of his career he did not speak to management teams at all.** He spent the last two years thousands of feet down in mines, at coal terminals, and on a trip to a large surface met coal mine in Mongolia. Coal executives take his calls because they are treated as pariahs, but access is not needed. _[Warrior Met Coal]_ — [2025-06-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jW-L5NdvYkU)
- **He looks bottom-up at hated, unloved and discarded businesses rather than bargain hunting by country, and other things equal prefers US governance.** Met coal and offshore drillers are US-governed global export powerhouses; it is hard to top what he found in Turkey, met coal and drillers, so he is not hunting in China. — [2025-06-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jW-L5NdvYkU)
- **If you cannot explain an investment thesis in three sentences to a 10-year-old, something is wrong with the investment.** He cites Einstein's four levels of intellect (smart, intelligent, genius, simple) with simplicity as the highest; boiling a cloned idea to its essence makes execution easy. — [2025-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fW9j-mDNVt8)

### Valuation & margin of safety (13)

- **A company with a $2 billion market cap that averages $1 billion a year of cash flow over 50 years before disappearing is an exceptionally great business, even if the yearly numbers are lumpy.** Met coal reserves run 50-plus years and new blast furnaces in Asia and India will run 30-50 years; that is what coal looked like in 2023. Whether the tail is 5, 10, 20 or 50 years, at that price you make money in every scenario. — [2025-01-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MGqKFwtCWnU)
- **Limit yourself to businesses where either the future cash flows are clearly visible or the discount is so extreme that cash flows do not matter; most of his investments are the latter.** Reysas had a $16 million market cap against $600-800 million of equity liquidation value (warehouses worth $800 million to $1 billion less $200 million debt), less than 3% of liquidation value, so no cash-flow model was needed. Reject all investments unless conventional metrics no longer make sense, and when a situation looks completely illogical but favorable, go all in because such opportunities are rare. _[Reysas]_ — [2025-01-31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JpGi2c7a1gw)
- **Public-market value investing is a game of singles where 100% losses are very expensive, unlike venture capital where winners return 100-10,000x and missing the winner is the real risk.** Templeton said the best analyst is wrong one in three times and most of us at least half the time. Bill Gurley's Benchmark passed on a sub-20-person Google (two PhDs both wanting to be CEO, crowded field with Yahoo and AltaVista) while Sequoia and John Doerr took the same pitch and made 10,000x; Sequoia's ability to do this decade after decade is 'magic DNA'. _[John Templeton, Bill Gurley, Benchmark Capital, Sequoia Capital, John Doerr, Google]_ — [2025-01-31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JpGi2c7a1gw)
- **Conviction in Reysas is easy because the reference point is liquidation value; intrinsic value only becomes the question once the stock reaches liquidation value.** The only thing he needs to understand about the business is what liquidation value is; holding below that is simple. _[Reysas]_ — [2025-01-31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JpGi2c7a1gw)
- **Great businesses can be severely overvalued for a decade and still reward patient holders, so overvaluation alone is a weak sell signal.** He wrote in 2000 that Infosys was ridiculously overvalued and returns were zero for 8-9 years, yet holding to today worked extremely well; Microsoft went from $600B to under $200B and was flat 2000-2012 but is still a 5-6x from 2000. _[Infosys, Microsoft, HDFC Bank, Asian Paints]_ — [2025-02-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HSq4QOCuuDA)
- **When the value gap is enormous you do not need to do much work before buying; the detailed study can come after.** On his Turkey trips he deliberately did no work before meeting companies and only studied Reysas over subsequent years; in Turkey he focused on businesses where currency and inflation are irrelevant. _[Reysas, Turkey]_ — [2025-02-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HSq4QOCuuDA)
- **NVIDIA at a $3 trillion market cap is not a trip to the pie counter because it would need to reach $100 trillion, more than the entire US market.** Auction-driven markets do not offer such outcomes at that starting size; the question for any buzzy stock is whether it is genuinely a pie-counter trip. _[NVIDIA]_ — [2025-02-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HSq4QOCuuDA)
- **Everything on the planet is on sale for a price: I quoted a Connecticut couple more than three times what I paid for my house, and being a value guy I would have moved for it.** Before sending pictures he required they disclose their identities and write a three-paragraph essay on why they would pay two to three times market; they did neither, offered 75% of his ask sight unseen, and he declined. — [2025-02-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Eww63NIxKew)
- **The best investments make no sense on the numbers; when something is 'too good to be true' and hits you in the head with a two-by-four, that is when you dive in.** Buffett found Western Insurance in the Moody's Manual trading at $15 with $25 of earnings per share and $80 book value; such positive anomalies are what to hunt for. _[Western Insurance, Warren Buffett]_ — [2025-03-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3xbhKOzNBW8)
- **Wall Street confuses risk with uncertainty, and low risk plus high uncertainty equals high returns.** Markets reward consistent cash flows like ADP's 50 years of growth with high multiples, while a high-uncertainty business like Frontline gets taken out back and shot; that is where opportunity lies. _[Frontline, ADP]_ — [2025-03-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3xbhKOzNBW8)
- **His four current positions share an unplanned commonality: all went through bankruptcy restructuring and emerged debt-free in capital-intensive industries, making them look like capital-light bets.** A debt-free miner is an oxymoron. Offshore drillers may trade at 10% of replacement cost; assets that would cost $10-20 billion were bought for $2 billion, so return on equity is spectacular. He made the met coal bet in 2023 and the offshore drillers bet in 2025. _[Warrior Met Coal, Valaris, Noble]_ — [2025-06-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jW-L5NdvYkU)
- **Dhandho means a way of doing business where the downside is non-existent: heads I win, tails I don't lose much.** Branson, Gates and Walton all built fortunes without taking risk. Everything in business is about risk reduction and free lunches, getting things done without capital. _[Richard Branson, Bill Gates, Sam Walton]_ — [2025-07-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vNBluvpgphs)
- **'Value investing' is a redundant term; all intelligent investing is value investing.** There is no such thing as anything else, so it should just be called investing. — [2025-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fW9j-mDNVt8)

### Portfolio concentration & selling (21)

- **He starts positions at 10% of a portfolio and never cuts winners for diversification's sake; investors who find the fund too large a share of net worth should cut their exposure instead.** His $400 million offshore fund owns 20% of Turkish REIT Reysas, whose market cap went from $16 million on his first 2019 visit to over $1 billion; Reysas is over 60% of that fund, which now holds only five stocks, and other funds reach 80-90% in the top four or five positions. Lowest-conviction ideas are the natural sale candidates when redemptions come. _[Reysas]_ — [2025-01-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MGqKFwtCWnU)
- **He cannot point to which of his current holdings will fail, but he knows some in the basket will not work, which is why a basket is needed.** It will become obvious in due course which ones do not work; that is the nature of investing. — [2025-01-31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JpGi2c7a1gw)
- **The fund has no fixed strategy: long-only equities, no leverage, options, derivatives or shorting, and purely opportunistic hunting where things are hated and unloved.** Munger: go fishing where the fish are and there are no fishermen, another reason not to spend time on the Magnificent Seven. He makes annual trips to Turkey, where extreme fear and hatred still make prices irrational. _[Charlie Munger, Magnificent Seven]_ — [2025-01-31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JpGi2c7a1gw)
- **He will not trim positions just because they become large: over two-thirds of his ~$400 million offshore fund is in two Turkish stocks and 90%+ in four names, and he told investors to manage concentration at their own level instead.** Reysas is more than half the fund and a second Turkish stock is 17-18%, with two coal bets at 15-20%. Investors with less than one-fifth of net worth in the fund should do nothing (no look-through position above 10% of net worth); those above should withdraw some into uncorrelated assets. It makes no sense to trim something at less than half of liquidation value when good ideas are so rare. _[Reysas]_ — [2025-01-31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JpGi2c7a1gw)
- **Have a heavy bias toward treating everything as noise; do not sell a high-quality business just because it became overpriced, but get off the bus in obvious secular decline.** Businesses with great moats and cultures have 50-75 year histories, and a stock picker should ride them as long as fundamentals are in place. — [2025-02-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HSq4QOCuuDA)
- **Trips to the pie counter are few, so load up in size: Turkey is now 60-65% of the portfolio in just two businesses and he told investors he will not sell.** Munger says load up on pie because you get few trips; Buffett says when it rains gold put out a bucket, not a thimble. Investors can sell fund units to cut concentration, but the fund will not sell. _[Turkey, Reysas, Charlie Munger, Warren Buffett]_ — [2025-02-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HSq4QOCuuDA)
- **You can't tell in advance which one of ten holdings is the Walmart, but if you own them all and don't mess with the ones with great economics and management, you will be fine.** Buffett made 400-500 investments over 70-75 years and said 12 moved the needle; one of the 12 was hiring Ajit Jain, whose sub-$100,000 search fee created a couple hundred billion dollars of value, which Munger called Berkshire's highest-return investment. _[Warren Buffett, Ajit Jain, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2025-02-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Eww63NIxKew)
- **Extreme concentration is the natural outcome of successful investing: keep your winners and the best will become 70-90% of the portfolio, as Berkshire did for Buffett and Munger.** Steve Ballmer, a hired gun whose CEO tenure returned ~4% a year, now has a net worth exceeding Bill Gates because his portfolio is essentially Microsoft plus some S&P and he never sold, and he put Satya Nadella in place. _[Steve Ballmer, Microsoft, Bill Gates, Satya Nadella, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2025-02-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Eww63NIxKew)
- **Plan B is to peel off 10-15% from Berkshire when a mother-lode anomaly appears, let it play out, then put the proceeds back into Berkshire, which gets you to 100x in half the time.** You have all the time in the world to research something for three months and let it go if it is not great, because Berkshire keeps compounding in the meantime. _[Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2025-03-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3xbhKOzNBW8)
- **It is almost always a mistake to sell a great business just because it looks fully priced; focus more on business quality than valuation and leave good businesses alone.** He calls this the mistake of most of his career: repeatedly selling good businesses that appeared expensive and being wrong every time about how expensive they were. Flowers are rare and weeds are plentiful, so do not cut the flowers. _[Warren Buffett, Dexter Shoes]_ — [2025-03-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3xbhKOzNBW8)
- **The mistress always looks better than the wife but may not be; only replace a holding when something in the portfolio is a 6.5 out of 10 and the newcomer is a 9.5, never in a 19-versus-20 game.** Following Munger's opportunity-cost framing, newness can make a new idea look better than it is. Buffett has permanent holdings like American Express, Coca-Cola and the wholly owned businesses, though Apple clearly was not one. Taxes and other frictions also weigh against switching. _[American Express, Coca-Cola, Apple, Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger]_ — [2025-04-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ePBZbS0cRAM)
- **He buys one or two things a year and would need no analysts; if the job is done right one never sells, and every sale means a mistake.** He kept two helpers from a failed business for deep dives but does not let them generate ideas; the hunt is for no-brainer anomalies that hit you over the head with a two-by-four or a cricket bat. — [2025-04-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YBinkgDRPHo)
- **It is dumb to sell a business purely because it looks overvalued, because you may not understand the business well enough to know whether it is actually overvalued.** Pabrai owned about 0.7% of Ferrari via Fiat Chrysler in 2014 and sold it as too expensive; the Fiat/Ferrari adventure turned $70 million into $260 million, but the Ferrari stake alone would be about $640 million now. Frontline was a 10% position sold for a double that then went up 350x. _[Ferrari, Fiat Chrysler, Frontline]_ — [2025-05-02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NrTz1uiL3RU)
- **Once you are rich, optimizing is likely to hurt more than help; keep a resilient anchor like Berkshire or the S&P 500 and let the rest ride.** Even when Nick Sleep's portfolio drifted to 80% Amazon and 10% each in Berkshire and Costco, the Berkshire slice alone was more money than he could spend in a lifetime, so it should not have mattered. Buffett's plan to put 90% of his wife's money in the S&P 500 is sound for the same reason: 500 dominant companies cannot sink at once. _[Nick Sleep, Berkshire Hathaway, Amazon, Costco, S&P 500]_ — [2025-05-02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NrTz1uiL3RU)
- **Separate businesses that are overvalued from businesses in secular decline; if the business is not in decline, leave it alone, but if there is secular decline, get off the bus as soon as possible.** Microsoft and Cisco in 2000 had intact moats but overvalued stocks. Reysas in Turkey is his easiest hold because it trades below liquidation value with no sign of decline; the decision only gets hard at egregious overvaluation, and he sets a high bar for 'egregious' because energizer-bunny managers like Elon Musk or Reysas's founder keep winning in businesses they had no prior competence in. He would pick Microsoft over Apple, whose lock on customers he considers weaker; Bill Gates told him at a Munger dinner that Apple is a peculiar company still running on Steve Jobs's vision and he would not go long. _[Microsoft, Cisco, Reysas, Elon Musk, Greg Abel, David Sokol, Apple, Bill Gates]_ — [2025-05-02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NrTz1uiL3RU)
- **You cannot know in advance which bets are the great ones, so make 10 or 15 bets and hang on to the one or two winners that become obvious; you only truly learn a business after you own it, especially when it drops 50%.** Buffett only knew Ajit Jain was great 20 years later; putting 95% into yesterday's winner is a bet that yesterday's winner is tomorrow's, which he could not get conviction for. Two bets, one of them resilient like Berkshire or the S&P, lets you totally relax and never 'go back to go'. _[Ajit Jain, Amazon, Berkshire Hathaway, S&P 500]_ — [2025-05-02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NrTz1uiL3RU)
- **Ideal bets are 10% each, but successful investing naturally ends with 40-80% in a single position, and that should be okay.** A Turkish stock bought at 2% of liquidation value grew to 40-50% of the portfolio and is being trimmed only because it is still undervalued. The Walton family owned about 46% of Walmart at the IPO 55 years ago and still owns 46% today, 33 years after Sam Walton died, never selling a share and building Bentonville from dividends. _[Walmart, Walton family, Reysas]_ — [2025-06-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jW-L5NdvYkU)
- **Buffett's 20-punch card and the fact that 4% of listed stocks generate 90% of returns mean you should make few, thoughtful bets or simply own the index.** Picking stocks gives about a one in 25 chance of landing one of the 4%; the index buys that 4% automatically. He declines to name specific stocks because it would hurt more than help. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2025-07-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vNBluvpgphs)
- **Circle the wagons around a multibagger: only about 12 of Buffett's hundreds of investments moved the needle, and the key was never selling them.** You cannot know before buying which stock will go 10x, 50x or 100x, but after owning it you may understand it well enough to know it is a great business that should not be sold. _[Warren Buffett, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2025-07-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vNBluvpgphs)
- **If the job is done right, your portfolio will end up 95% in one stock; a manager whose portfolio is not is not optimizing.** Truly great businesses run by great managers are rare but will find their way into most portfolios; the key is to shut off the brain, ignore intrinsic-value calculations, and let a 2-10% position grow to 90% as long as business and manager stay good. His problem was being 'too much of an idiot to keep them'. — [2025-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fW9j-mDNVt8)
- **Two businesses now make up close to 70% of one of his funds and he told investors he will not diversify or sell; those uncomfortable can redeem.** He advised anyone with under 20% of net worth in the fund to leave it alone; nobody called or redeemed, and he expects the same at 90%. — [2025-10-14](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=fW9j-mDNVt8)

### Compounding & long-term holding (20)

- **The Walton family's stake in Walmart has risen from about 36% at the 1970 IPO to the low 40s despite no family member running the company for 30+ years; that is the model for treating Reysas as a family business.** Sam Walton transferred shares to his kids before the IPO, avoiding estate taxes. Pabrai has watched Reysas for five or six years and sees exceptional capital allocators and good assets; all billionaires got there by being concentrated, and Munger said when you get a rare trip to the pie counter you must load up. He never expects to find another stock at 3% of liquidation value. _[Walmart, Sam Walton, Reysas, Charlie Munger]_ — [2025-01-31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JpGi2c7a1gw)
- **A second edition of The Dhandho Investor would make long-term buy-and-hold of exceptional businesses at reasonable prices the number one goal, with special situations as a Swiss Army knife side pursuit.** The anchor of the portfolio must be great businesses run by great capital allocators with great economics. You do not need to be a founder: riding the coattails of Bezos or Sam Walton with a hundred shares works, and the small investor's ability to go anywhere is a huge advantage since size is a big negative. _[Amazon, Walmart, Jeff Bezos, Sam Walton]_ — [2025-01-31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JpGi2c7a1gw)
- **If you are even slightly above average, spend less than you earn and use no leverage, you cannot help but get rich over a lifetime.** Rick Guerin, the third partner with Buffett and Munger, was in a hurry and used margin; in the 1973-74 drawdown he was forced to sell Berkshire to Buffett at $20 a share, now worth ~$700,000, a 35,000x. Buffett and Munger knew they would get rich but were not in a hurry. _[Rick Guerin, Berkshire Hathaway, Warren Buffett]_ — [2025-02-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HSq4QOCuuDA)
- **A know-nothing investor who cannot value a business should buy a low-cost broad index fund via SIP and ignore market swings.** The index is too dumb to know it owns Google and too dumb to sell it; it will hold Asian Paints, HDFC and Titan for 30-40 years while individuals dance in and out, and it removes the Xeroxes and Kodaks over time. _[Google, Asian Paints, HDFC Bank, Titan]_ — [2025-02-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HSq4QOCuuDA)
- **The single most important skill an investor needs is patience: if 49 of the US Nifty 50 went to zero and you only kept Walmart at 2%, you still beat the S&P.** The Walton family owned 36% at IPO and 44% today, 55 years later, with no Waltons in senior management. If you love watching paint dry you will do extremely well. _[Walmart, Nifty 50, Xerox, Polaroid, Kodak]_ — [2025-02-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HSq4QOCuuDA)
- **You only truly understand a business after you own it, and it can take years of ownership to recognize that you hold a compounder.** Some businesses like MasterCard or Google are obviously great beforehand, but most are learned from the inside; it took him five or six years to understand Reysas, which has no investor deck and little public data. _[MasterCard, Google, Reysas]_ — [2025-02-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Eww63NIxKew)
- **If a 1970s Nifty-Fifty portfolio had put 2% in Walmart at its IPO and the other 98% went to zero, it would still have beaten the S&P over 50 years: investing forgives a 98% error rate, and the key is letting great businesses stay in your portfolio.** The Nifty-Fifty (Coke, Kodak, Polaroid, Xerox, Colgate, McDonald's) was bought with no price discipline and got 'taken out back and shot' in 1973-74, with Coke down to ~6x earnings, yet the one Walmart would have carried everything. _[Walmart, Coca-Cola, Kodak, Polaroid, Xerox, Nifty-Fifty]_ — [2025-02-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Eww63NIxKew)
- **The Walton family went from 38% of Walmart at the 1970-71 IPO to 44% today by simply holding while the company bought back stock, paying no frictional costs or taxes.** Sam Walton gave the shares to his kids before the IPO (no estate tax), has been dead ~30 years, no Waltons run the company, and they ignored the 'helpers' urging diversification. _[Walmart, Walton family]_ — [2025-02-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Eww63NIxKew)
- **Life is all about doubles: at 10% a year Berkshire doubles every seven years, turning $10,000 into 128x in 49 years with no taxes and no activity.** Rule of 72: seven doubles over 49 years gives $1.33 million from $10,000 with no dividends or taxes; spend less than you earn and keep adding annual savings. _[Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2025-03-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3xbhKOzNBW8)
- **Start investing as early as possible because runway length dominates: a 22-year-old with a 90-year runway at 10% gets 13 doubles, turning each $10,000 into $8 million.** A small amount saved at 22 beats a larger amount at 32; Roth IRAs have no minimum age, only an earned-wage rule. Rakesh Jhunjhunwala compounded at 40% a year for decades starting with $10,000 borrowed, and Titan is still in its infancy. _[Rakesh Jhunjhunwala, Titan Industries, Indigo, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2025-03-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3xbhKOzNBW8)
- **If you had put $100,000 into the Nifty 50 in 1970 and 49 of the 50 went to zero but you held Walmart, you still compounded at almost 15% a year for 55 years and beat the S&P with a 98% error rate.** The 1973-74 crash was a slow-motion bloodbath and by 1975 nobody would admit owning the Nifty 50, which included losers like Xerox, Polaroid and Kodak alongside ADP, Coke, Amex and Disney. Most stock market returns come from a small sliver of companies, and even Buffett has a 3-4% hit rate, so most new ideas will disappoint. _[Walmart, Nifty 50, Xerox, Polaroid, Kodak, ADP, Coca-Cola, American Express, Disney]_ — [2025-04-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ePBZbS0cRAM)
- **The Walton family still owns 46% of Walmart 55 years after the IPO because they told every helper urging diversification to get lost, paying no taxes and no frictional costs.** Sam Walton transferred shares to his kids while Walmart was private and worth almost nothing, so almost no estate tax was paid; it has been 33 years since he died and the family has collected huge dividends. _[Walmart, Sam Walton]_ — [2025-04-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ePBZbS0cRAM)
- **Compounding has three variables (starting capital, rate of return, length of runway) and a long runway is the marvelous one, so he now plans on living until June 11, 2054.** Buffett bought his first stock at 11, considers the years before that wasted, and at 95 has an 84-year runway. Pabrai previously assumed he'd die in 2044 at 80 but 'God Google' gave him ten more years, leaving 29 years and three months as of the interview. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2025-04-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ePBZbS0cRAM)
- **Recognizing and hanging on to winners matters far more than avoiding value traps: a Nifty 50 portfolio with 98% going to zero but 2% in Walmart compounds at almost 15% for 55 years versus 10% for the S&P.** The 1960s-70s Nifty 50 (ADP, McDonald's, Coke, P&G, Xerox, Polaroid, Kodak, Avon) was decimated in the 1973-74 crash. Templeton said the best are wrong one in three times, and only 12 of Buffett's 400-plus decisions in 60 years moved the needle for Berkshire, a 3-4% hit rate. _[Walmart, Nifty 50, Xerox, Kodak, Polaroid, John Templeton, Warren Buffett, Berkshire Hathaway, S&P 500]_ — [2025-04-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YBinkgDRPHo)
- **Stock market returns follow power laws: a tiny sliver of businesses generates almost all of the return, so the key is to be in those businesses for the long term.** Assuming Walmart was 2% of the Nifty 50 and the other 49 stocks went to zero, the $2 in Walmart alone (roughly 64,000x over 55 years) still beat $100 in the S&P 500 (about 320x). The decision to hold, not the decision to buy, is what mattered. _[Walmart, Nifty 50, Xerox, Polaroid, Kodak, S&P 500]_ — [2025-05-02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NrTz1uiL3RU)
- **The Walton family kept 46% of Walmart for 55 years after the IPO, ignoring all the helpers pitching diversification, and became the richest family in America.** Sam Walton transferred ownership to his kids while Walmart was tiny and private, so no estate tax was owed; Pabrai notes their single-company approach is riskier than Nick Sleep's, which had a Berkshire anchor. _[Walmart, Walton family, Sam Walton]_ — [2025-05-02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NrTz1uiL3RU)
- **'We are all too wise, too late': truly great compounders are very few, so do not get cute selling when you think one is fully priced; sell only when it is crazily, egregiously overpriced.** He recalls selling positions at 3x and missing another 20x; even Bill Gates wishes he had kept his Microsoft stock. It took him a long time to learn that when you have something good, leave it alone. _[Microsoft, Bill Gates]_ — [2025-06-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jW-L5NdvYkU)
- **Investing outcomes depend on starting capital, length of runway and rate of return, and if the runway is long enough the other two barely matter.** The $23 paid for Manhattan in 1623 compounded at 7% (doubling every 10 years by the Rule of 72) would be $23 trillion by 2023, about one-sixth of total US household wealth of $150 trillion, more than the land is worth. Extend it back to 1523 and 2.3 cents does the same job. — [2025-07-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vNBluvpgphs)
- **Spend less than you earn, save the first dollar not the last, and start at 22 so that money can compound for 50 years in a broad index.** Put $5,000 of a $50,000 salary into savings first. $5,000 saved at 18 at 10% doubles seven times in 50 years, about 100x, to $500,000 at 68; add $5,000 every year and you end up with too much money without finding the next Nvidia. _[Nvidia]_ — [2025-07-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vNBluvpgphs)
- **Beginners should just buy the S&P 500 index or Berkshire Hathaway as a set-it-and-forget-it holding and focus their energy on their own work.** Open an account at Fidelity, Interactive Brokers or Robinhood; the S&P is somewhat overheated in mid-2025 and has long flat periods, but dollar-cost averaging over a long horizon is fine. BRK.B is like an index. _[S&P 500, Berkshire Hathaway, Nvidia, Microsoft, Apple]_ — [2025-07-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vNBluvpgphs)

### Moats & business quality (13)

- **Coal is a four-letter word: ESG pressure has made every factor of production treat coal companies like pariahs, which is irrational and creates opportunity.** CONSOL Energy, a 150-year-old low-cost thermal producer that never went bankrupt, was dropped by JP Morgan after decades despite borrowing nothing on $2-3 billion of revenue, and struggles to get workers' comp insurance even though it self-insures; CONSOL has since merged with Arch into Core Natural Resources. _[CONSOL Energy, Arch Resources, Core Natural Resources, JP Morgan]_ — [2025-01-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MGqKFwtCWnU)
- **'The Joys of Costco' shows the incredible moat of Costco, whose runway remains very long.** Munger read it and called it 'not exactly Shakespeare' but a very good effort; at least 30 minutes of every dinner with Charlie was about Costco, and the book drew more responses than any Christmas book he has sent. _[Costco, Charlie Munger]_ — [2025-01-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MGqKFwtCWnU)
- **Costco's moat comes from doing public service: a maximum 15% markup and sacred cows like the $1.50 hot dog build member trust and loyalty.** When Costco bought Levi's jeans at $9 that normally sell for $30-40, Jim Sinegal refused to price them above 15% over cost and sold them at $10. Costco pays entry-level staff about 50% more than Walmart ($20/hour minimum) without hurting profitability. Munger discussed Costco at nearly every meal. _[Costco, Jim Sinegal, Charlie Munger, Sol Price, Walmart]_ — [2025-03-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3xbhKOzNBW8)
- **You cannot know which businesses are the truly great ones until you have owned them for a while, but when you have one you will know it.** Humans are never able to appreciate in advance how great some good businesses can be; the framework change is to hold the exceptional fraction of a business rather than rotate into the next mistress. — [2025-04-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ePBZbS0cRAM)
- **Enduring moats are few and far between because capitalism competes everything away; approach businesses and their claimed moats with very jaundiced eyes.** The Walmart example and Buffett's 3-4% hit rate show how rare moats are. ASML and Nvidia have head-start moats that will last a while (ASML perhaps forever, like black magic), but Coca-Cola and American Express started moatless and stumbled into their models by accident; it is almost impossible to start a business intending to build a specific moat. _[ASML, Nvidia, Coca-Cola, American Express, Walmart]_ — [2025-04-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ePBZbS0cRAM)
- **A commodity producer at the low end of the global cost curve with long reserves and no debt has a wide, deep moat and a license to print money.** Saudi Aramco produced oil at $1-2 a barrel and would still profit at $20 when everyone else stopped; he owns a low-cost metallurgical coal producer close to port, with long-lived reserves and no debt, for which tariffs do not matter. _[Saudi Aramco]_ — [2025-04-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YBinkgDRPHo)
- **Industries with rapid change are the enemy of the investor, but value principles can be applied to a small sliver of tech businesses if you understand how the mousetrap works.** Nick Sleep and Qais Zakaria read hundreds of annual reports and saw that Amazon's losses were growth spending by a fanatical, efficient capital allocator making many small bets; AWS was an unplanned winner and Amazon converts cost line items into businesses, so he predicts it will enter parcel delivery and wreak havoc on UPS and FedEx. He thinks it likely that in 30 years 2025 will look like a bargain for Amazon. _[Amazon, Jeff Bezos, AWS, UPS, FedEx, Nick Sleep, Qais Zakaria]_ — [2025-05-02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NrTz1uiL3RU)
- **Coke is a flavored-water delivery pipe reaching billions of people that nobody can rebuild, which makes it more resilient than Microsoft; keep it and, like Harriet Green, live on the dividend and leave the principal.** Humans need about 64 ounces of fluid a day and some must be flavored; Coke can buy something like Gatorade and push it through the pipe. Buffett and Munger cracked Coke in the late 1980s, made money for 10-12 years, then little for a while, but you only need to get rich once. _[Coca-Cola, Gatorade, Microsoft, Harriet Green]_ — [2025-05-02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NrTz1uiL3RU)
- **Apple's innovation was singularly concentrated in Steve Jobs, so without him it may not reach the next paradigm; Bill Gates called it 'a very weird company'.** At a Munger Friday dinner three years ago Gates would not go long Apple despite Buffett's big bet. OpenAI with Jony Ive is trying to 'take the brick out of our hands', and if the brick is threatened Apple has a problem. Apple goes in the too-hard pile. _[Apple, Bill Gates, Steve Jobs, Tim Cook, OpenAI, Jony Ive]_ — [2025-06-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jW-L5NdvYkU)
- **Microsoft is as close to bulletproof as it gets because enterprises are aircraft carriers that cannot switch products on a dime, and recurring revenue is worth paying up for.** You can decide in five minutes to never use Google search again, but not to drop Microsoft products. He accepts its 30-35x multiple as high but justified; Satya Nadella is an exceptional leader. _[Microsoft, Satya Nadella, Google]_ — [2025-06-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jW-L5NdvYkU)
- **Every business starts without a moat; a moat is what makes it hard for competitors to take your customers, such as customers' habit of sticking with one barber.** Founders find offering gaps, and sometimes a moat gets built, as with Visa and American Express, which persevere and scale. _[Visa, American Express]_ — [2025-07-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vNBluvpgphs)
- **Apple is somewhat risky as an investment because everything emanated from Steve Jobs and nothing new has come out since he left.** The smartphone brick form factor will change at some point and the replacement is more likely to come from someone in a garage than from Apple. Disney had to buy Pixar because there was no Disney anymore. _[Apple, Disney, Pixar, Steve Jobs]_ — [2025-07-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vNBluvpgphs)
- **100% of businesses eventually go to zero, but IKEA's no-debt policy and rule that every new store must innovate show how to last far past the founder.** IKEA's founder made decisions with a 500-year view; every store was built from retained earnings. ### Management & capital allocation (10)

- **Knowing an industry is cyclical is not enough; you also need the right management team and capital structure to survive the murky entry period and fully capitalize on the boom.** He is open to copper miners and offshore drillers on the same thesis but says resilience to live to see the boom varies business by business. — [2025-01-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MGqKFwtCWnU)
- **He now talks to management and says avoiding it was a disservice to investors, though he still gets swayed by CEO salesmanship.** Meetings reveal how management thinks about capital allocation and culture over a 5-10 year horizon, not next quarter; for coal the 800-pound gorilla is the coal price, which no CEO can forecast, but meetings show which teams and cultures are best. _[Ben Graham]_ — [2025-01-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MGqKFwtCWnU)
- **Walmart embraced technology very early: Sam Walton flew a small plane to scout the first 50-70 sites between towns and invested heavily in IBM mainframes when Walmart was tiny.** Managers told him they couldn't run the place without automation, so he stepped up capex; he recommends Made in America. _[Walmart, Sam Walton, IBM]_ — [2025-02-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Eww63NIxKew)
- **Cannibals remain a tremendous mental model: a great business buying back shares at modest valuations turbocharges returns without dividend tax leakage, but buybacks at a bad business or high price incinerate wealth.** Walmart's buybacks raised the Walton stake even as they sold shares for charity; Eddie Lampert's Sears buybacks were a great way to destroy wealth. Both conditions, great business and non-overpaying price, must hold. _[Walmart, Sears, Eddie Lampert, Charlie Munger]_ — [2025-02-25](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Eww63NIxKew)
- **Buffett and Munger get results from managers by giving them freedom to build their own sandcastle and never second-guessing, so managers perform because they do not want to let them down.** Both have rough exteriors but warm hearts; Munger improved Costco quietly from the board with small suggestions rather than activism. _[Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger, Costco]_ — [2025-03-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3xbhKOzNBW8)
- **He treats Reysas as a family business with its founders and will not sell until they do, having discovered they are gifted capital allocators reinvesting at 20-35%-plus dollar returns.** He meets them once a year over bluefish on the Bosphorus and has not seen a single mistake in six years; his main job is to do nothing and play bridge. _[Reysas]_ — [2025-04-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YBinkgDRPHo)
- **Debt is the number one reason businesses fail, and Berkshire's Fort Knox no-leverage approach is a very good thing for shareholders.** Buffett and Munger said they could have earned higher returns with modest leverage but chose not to; insurance float gives them benign leverage. IKEA's founder was hell-bent on never having debt and thought about the company 500 to 1,000 years out. _[Berkshire Hathaway, IKEA]_ — [2025-05-02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NrTz1uiL3RU)
- **Greg Abel is more hands-on than Buffett, pursuing synergies and oversight across subsidiaries, and may be more aggressive than Buffett was in crises like 2008 and 2020.** Buffett delegated 'to the point of abdication' and never pursued synergies; Abel has CEOs interact and dives into businesses. Munger said Abel had qualities superior to Warren's. Berkshire Energy is well placed for the step-function grid investment AI data centers require, though wildfire liabilities blindsided them. _[Berkshire Hathaway, Greg Abel, Warren Buffett, Charlie Munger, Berkshire Hathaway Energy]_ — [2025-06-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jW-L5NdvYkU)
- **Costs are the one thing a business can always control, and disciplined cost-cutting like Walmart's and LVMH's is why their founders became the richest people.** Sam Walton chose the seven-letter name Walmart partly to save on signage. Bernard Arnault runs LVMH tight, negotiating mind-blowing real estate deals despite being in luxury, and became Europe's wealthiest person. _[Walmart, LVMH, Sam Walton]_ — [2025-07-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vNBluvpgphs)
- **Recruiting is a founder's number one job: A players want A players, and the first B player starts the journey downhill.** Elon Musk personally interviewed the first 3,000 SpaceX hires. The three non-negotiables are intelligence, integrity and willingness to work hard; hire slow, fire fast, and firing fast matters more. _[SpaceX, Elon Musk, Steve Jobs, Caliper]_ — [2025-07-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vNBluvpgphs)

### Markets, cycles & macro (16)

- **Industries with long gestation periods for new supply have violent boom-and-bust cycles, and understanding this mental model can be very lucrative if you go long at the right point in the cycle.** Warehouses take under a year to build so industrial real estate has mild cycles, while office towers take 3-5 years so a tightness in 2020 keeps towers starting through 2024 and delivers a five-year boom followed by a 5-10 year bust; he sees the same glut now in Austin luxury residential towers. He learned this from the First Industrial CEO, whose stock Buffett tipped in a charity wallet auction. _[First Industrial Realty, Warren Buffett]_ — [2025-01-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MGqKFwtCWnU)
- **Restarting a shut metallurgical coal mine is nearly impossible, making the coming supply response far weaker than in past cycles.** At PLV prices around $190-200/ton many Appalachian mines have shut, selling equipment, laying off miners and losing permits; a restart at $300 would need all-equity financing with no price visibility, miners who have left the industry, and equipment on 2-4 year backlogs at inflated prices. — [2025-01-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MGqKFwtCWnU)
- **Predicting markets is a fool's errand, but his current view is that the S&P 500 will return no more than 3-5% a year over the next 10-15 years.** He does not know whether that plays out as a big decline followed by robust returns or a flat line, and he makes no bets on it; he owns no tech and nothing related to AI, so his basic undervalued bets should be uncorrelated with the market. The DeepSeek correction did not change this. _[S&P 500]_ — [2025-01-31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JpGi2c7a1gw)
- **Asset classes can stagnate for 10, 20 or 30 years, so value investing cannot be judged on 5 or 10 years of underperformance as long as cash-flow streams remain intact.** Traditional non-tech value stocks may have delivered poor returns over the last decade, but that is part of the cycle. — [2025-01-31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JpGi2c7a1gw)
- **Markets go through long flat stretches and long booms; the Dow was 865 in both 1965 and 1982, then rose to ~12,000 by 1999, then was flat to 2012.** In 1982 Coke and P&G traded at 6-7x earnings. The Sensex since the 1991 reforms similarly shows zero stretches and 18-20% stretches but a tremendous average. _[Dow Jones, Coca-Cola, Procter & Gamble, Sensex]_ — [2025-02-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HSq4QOCuuDA)
- **The stock market is a theater where every seat must be occupied, so look for theaters with an illusion of smoke rather than real smoke.** When investors flee a market en masse the baby gets thrown out with the bathwater; that is why he went to Turkey. Most of the time the smoke is real and you do not need to go there. _[Turkey]_ — [2025-02-15](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=HSq4QOCuuDA)
- **In investing the small guy has the advantage because tiny anomalies that compound at very high rates cannot absorb large capital, so the space is continually vacated for the next generation.** Buffett says if he ran $1-10 million he would do 50% a year; below $100,000 the entire universe is available and the nooks and crevices offer very high returns on very small capital. _[Warren Buffett]_ — [2025-03-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3xbhKOzNBW8)
- **Circa 2025 the S&P 500 is overheated, so use Berkshire Hathaway class B shares as the index and dollar-cost average into them as Plan A.** The MAG7 and even the other 493 stocks trade well above historic multiples; in 2000 the only three $600B+ companies were Cisco, Microsoft and GE, and Cisco never regained that cap, Microsoft returned zero from 2000 to 2015, GE imploded. Berkshire holds a huge cash portion of its market cap. _[Berkshire Hathaway, Cisco, Microsoft, GE, MAG7]_ — [2025-03-27](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3xbhKOzNBW8)
- **Trump tariffs are mostly irrelevant; a business's future is driven by micro factors around it and its competitors, not global macro headlines.** Tariffs do not make DMart or IndiGo useless businesses; play the tariff out in the context of the specific business and it usually does not matter beyond some slowdown in global GDP. _[DMart, IndiGo]_ — [2025-04-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YBinkgDRPHo)
- **Turkey's gambler culture, where the float cycles every 21 days, let him buy a third of Reysas; the market transfers wealth from the active to the inactive.** Typical Turkish retail investors buy at 10 and sell at 3 for 10%; Buffett's quote could not be truer in Turkey. _[Reysas, Warren Buffett]_ — [2025-04-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YBinkgDRPHo)
- **Auction-driven markets overshoot and undershoot, which is the free lunch that lets investors buy assets well below what they are worth.** With about 50,000 stocks worldwide, many are mispriced at any time; negotiated transactions rarely offer this, so focus on the ones mispriced on the cheap side. Volatility is always the long-term investor's friend: when news moving Coke's price has weak correlation with its long-term cash flows, that is a sign of mispricing. _[Coca-Cola]_ — [2025-05-02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NrTz1uiL3RU)
- **For most investments the micro trumps the macro; pick bets where the thesis works across almost any macro environment so you can ignore macro entirely.** Saudi Aramco lifts oil at about $10 a barrel and makes money whether oil is 30 or 300; Ferrari sells $2-3 million cars at 85-90% margins to a list of collectors who will not flip them, so tariffs are irrelevant. _[Saudi Aramco, Ferrari]_ — [2025-05-02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NrTz1uiL3RU)

- **Warrior Met Coal is a debt-free, lowest-cost longwall producer of rare high-quality met coal with cheap barge and multi-railroad access to port, trading at about $2.5 billion against 40-50 years of reserves.** It will produce $1-2 billion of cash flow in some years (it has done so before), $500 million in others and $300 million in bad ones, and is extremely unlikely to have a losing year; 'where do I sign?' Coal logistics matter because transport cost per ton is high, and Buffett, Munger and Gates visited the Powder River Basin because Burlington Northern was the toll bridge for coal. _[Warrior Met Coal, Burlington Northern, Berkshire Hathaway]_ — [2025-06-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jW-L5NdvYkU)
- **Offshore drillers Valaris and Noble own fleets that would cost about 10 times their market cap to replace, and no new drillships have been built in about 10 years because day rates do not justify them.** A new $1 billion drillship needs ~$700-800k/day for a 12-14% return; current rates are in the $400s while old ships keep being scrapped, so the market is tightening. Offshore oil in Brazil costs $20-30 a barrel, about half of fracking. If rates reach $600-700 a day, Valaris and Noble would print almost their entire market cap in cash every year. _[Valaris, Noble]_ — [2025-06-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jW-L5NdvYkU)
- **The Patels came to control 80% of US motels from 0.1% of the population by running family-staffed motels that undercut competitors on price.** Expelled from Uganda by Idi Amin in the 1970s, they bought 10-20 room motels, lived in a couple of rooms, fired the staff, charged $19 against competitors' $25, ran higher occupancy, and bought the next motel for a nephew to run. _[Patels]_ — [2025-07-13](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=vNBluvpgphs)

### Geographies: India, China, Turkey, Japan, US (8)

- **Painting whole countries as uninvestible is a mistake; go fishing where the fish are, in distressed places with a mass investor exodus, but only in the highest-quality businesses for which the macro problem is irrelevant.** In Turkey from 2018 the currency was a basket case and inflation extreme, yet the exclusive Burger King franchisee kept growing like crazy; Argentina has few listed companies, Brazil more, and Hong Kong/China should not be dismissed wholesale. _[TFI TAB Gida, Burger King, Turkey, Argentina, Brazil, China]_ — [2025-01-21](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=MGqKFwtCWnU)

Warehouses are land, cement, concrete and steel, all inflation-indexed and globally valued, so the collapse of the lira did not matter in dollar terms; the stock is up 40-50x to a market cap over $1 billion and is still below a liquidation value north of $2 billion. _[Reysas]_ — [2025-01-31](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=JpGi2c7a1gw)

Farm-size restrictions are a shackle: the US feeds itself with under 2% in farming while a majority of Indians still farm when 5-10 million would suffice. — [2025-04-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YBinkgDRPHo)
- **Invest when things make no sense: Turkey in 2018-19 screened extremely cheap with everyone exiting, with one company at a P/E of 0.1.** He visited companies in the portfolio of an Istanbul value-investor friend ('too much Graham, too little Munger'), doing no prior work and focusing on businesses immune to currency and inflation. — [2025-04-22](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=YBinkgDRPHo)

Templeton sold him a 5% Reysas position for $1 million because someone in New York said exit Turkey. _[Reysas, TAV Airports, Templeton Funds]_ — [2025-05-02](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=NrTz1uiL3RU)
- **He remains 'long and strong' in Turkey: TAV Airports and the Reysas warehouse business, bought at compelling valuations, are on fire and need no action.** TAV has pure operating leverage: when passenger traffic rises 5-10% costs do not, so cash flows explode. 95-96% of world airports are government-run; privately operated LaGuardia and India's BOT airports show how much better private operators do. _[TAV Airports, Reysas, LaGuardia]_ — [2025-06-10](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=jW-L5NdvYkU)
